sections.title: NAME
sections.html: socketley - manage network runtimes (servers, clients, proxies, Redis-compatible caches, S3 object storage, DNS) in Docker-like style

sections.title: SYNOPSIS
sections.html:

socketley daemon [--cpus set] [--fast-lo [own|all]] [--fast-lo-limit P,G]

sections.title: DESCRIPTION
sections.html:
socketley is a high-performance Linux daemon and CLI that manages network runtimes (servers, clients, proxies, Redis-compatible caches, S3 object storage, authoritative DNS, MQTT brokers) in a Docker-like style — with clustering, WebSocket, Lua scripting, and io_uring async I/O.

TLS terminates on a server or cache listener, on both of a proxy's legs, and on a client's dial. A server runtime encrypts its own listening port with --tls --cert --key, and verifies client certificates with --ca. A proxy does the same on its own port, verifies client certificates with --client-ca, and reaches an https:// backend over TLS — verifying the chain and the endpoint's name, and presenting a client certificate with --client-cert --client-key. A client runtime dials its target over TLS with --tls, verifying the chain against --ca or the system trust store and matching the host from -t against the certificate; it presents its own certificate with --cert --key. There is no way to switch either check off — an unverified TLS client buys encryption against somebody recording the wire and nothing at all against somebody sitting on it. A cache terminates TLS on its own listener with the same three flags a server uses, and RESP runs on the decrypted stream, so a Redis client needs no change. The one thing it refuses is --tls together with --replicate: replication is not encrypted, so the pair would put the whole dataset on the wire in the clear. An mqtt broker terminates TLS on its MQTT and WebSocket ports with the same three flags, and with --ca takes the name of a verified client certificate as the client's user. A runtime carrying a configuration that cannot be honoured (for example one restored from a state file written by an older release) refuses to start rather than running in cleartext. See TLS under LIMITATIONS.

The io_uring event loop automatically takes advantage of advanced kernel features when available: multishot receive (one SQE services many reads) and registered file descriptors (skip per-op fget/fput overhead). Each feature is probed at startup and falls back transparently to standard ops on older kernels, so no configuration is needed.

sections.title: COMMANDS
sections.html:
daemon#

Start the socketley daemon. When installed system-wide (via .deb package or install.sh), the daemon is managed by systemd and starts automatically — you do not need to run this command manually. Use systemctl start socketley or systemctl enable socketley to control the service.

Details

When running from the build directory (development mode), start the daemon manually: ./bin/Release/socketley daemon &

Creates IPC socket at /run/socketley/socketley.sock (system install) or /tmp/socketley.sock (development mode). On startup, restores persisted runtime configurations. Runtimes that were running when the daemon last stopped are auto-started.

The daemon ignores SIGHUP, so a closed terminal or a stray kill -HUP leaves it running.

Takes --cpus set — the ring setting described under COMMON FLAGS, here shaping the ring this daemon is about to create rather than stating what a runtime requires of one. It is the command-line spelling of SOCKETLEY_CPUS, and the flag wins when both are given. It also takes --fast-lo (below) and the experimental Raft flags described under CLUSTER MODE. Any other argument is refused: this command used to ignore its command line entirely, so socketley daemon --cpus 0-1 started an unpinned daemon and exited 0.

It cannot be combined with --name or --cluster, which address a daemon that is already running — a ring's CPU set is fixed when the ring is created, so there would be nothing left for them to change.

Every runtime is its own process and every one of them inherits this set, so the set is also how many of them share a core. Measured with fifty idle servers beside one doing a ping-pong, the median round trip did not move — 30.2 against 29.4 microseconds — while the 99th percentile did: 156.5 microseconds on six cores against 51.7 on twelve. Idle runtimes are not free company, because each still wakes on its own stats interval; what they cost is paid by the tail of whichever one is working, and widening the set is the lever. The daemon itself stayed under one per cent of a core at fifty runtimes, and creating one took the same fourteen milliseconds at five as at fifty, so neither of those is the thing to watch.

daemon --fast-lo [own|all|trust]#

Put TCP pairs whose both ends are 127.0.0.1 or ::1 on a kernel shortcut. A BPF sockops program enters both sockets in a sockhash when the connection is established, and an sk_msg program places every send straight into the peer's receive queue, skipping TCP/IP, the loopback device and its softirq. Off unless given.

Details

all (the default when no mode is given) takes any local client connecting to a port one of this daemon's runtimes listens on, the runtimes among themselves, and every connection a runtime makes to a listener on 127.0.0.1 whoever owns it: a proxy with --backend 127.0.0.1:8080 in front of a local application, a client runtime or a Lua HTTP call to a local service. own takes only pairs whose both ends are this daemon's runtimes, such as a client runtime connected to a server runtime. trust is all without the receiver rule below: a send is redirected into a foreign receiver too, so a foreign client of a cache and a proxy's foreign backend are accelerated in both directions. It is for an operator who knows that every local process reading a socket of such a pair does so with recv, read or recvmsg.

Warning: a byte redirected into a socket waits in an ingress queue that only recvmsg drains. A local process that reads with splice(2), sendfile(2), TCP_ZEROCOPY_RECEIVE or a relay built on them (Go's io.Copy between two TCP connections, HAProxy with splicing) never sees those bytes: under trust it loses them, with no error on either side (measured: a backend reading with splice behind a proxy echoed 0 of 500 bytes). Such readers cannot be told apart from the outside, which is why all does not redirect into a foreign socket at all. Use all unless every local client and backend is known. socketley daemon stats reports which mode is running.

Under own and all a send is redirected only when the socket that will receive it is one of this daemon's workers' — a runtime that connects (its socket is marked when it does) or one that accepts on a runtime's listener. A send whose receiver is a foreign socket goes by ordinary TCP, and each direction of a pair is decided by its own receiver. This is because a socket that receives through the kernel's ingress queue can only be read with recvmsg: a foreign reader using splice(2), sendfile(2), Go's io.Copy between two TCP connections, or HAProxy's splicing would lose the redirected bytes, and those readers cannot be told apart from the outside. This bounds the shortcut to what it can accelerate safely: into a runtime always, out to a foreign peer never (unless trust is given).

What that means for the common shapes, measured on one box with alternating passes:

  • Runtime to runtime (a client runtime to a server runtime, both ends this daemon's) is accelerated in both directions under every mode: 64 B round trips 1.3–1.4x one connection and eight, 16 KB about 1.2–1.5x; a client runtime against a cache, off against all, 110–116K against 83–85K round trips a second with one in flight.

  • A foreign client of a cache is accelerated only on the request it sends in; the reply comes back by TCP. So a small request/large reply workload gains little under all: redis-benchmark (50 connections, 4 threads, six alternating passes, requests per second off / all / trust): GET -P1 240–279K / 222–250K / 387–667K, SET -P1 222–286K / 197–273K / 462–632K, GET -P16 2.3–4.0M / 2.7–3.4M / 5.3–6.9M, and a bulk reader of 64 KiB values 1377–1488 / 1276–1322 / 2464–3040 MB/s. A request that carries the payload does gain under all: 64 KiB SET pipelined 8 deep, 49.9K against 59.1K, 1.18x. Only trust takes the full gain of a foreign client.

  • A proxy in front of a foreign local backend accelerates, under all, the two legs that end in the proxy and leaves the two that end in a foreign socket on TCP, so a foreign backend that reads with splice keeps every byte. Under trust both are redirected: 64 B round trips through a proxy to a C echo backend, one connection, 44–48K off, 41–45K all, 86–88K trust.

Needs CAP_BPF and CAP_NET_ADMIN (root, or setcap cap_bpf,cap_net_admin+ep on the binary) and cgroup v2 at /sys/fs/cgroup. Without them the daemon logs fast-lo: unavailable, serving without it with the reason, and serves on the ordinary path. own attaches to the daemon's cgroup and all and trust to the root cgroup; the daemon's own processes are the workers its supervisor forked, whose pids it keeps in a map. Under all and trust the program fires for every process on the host, so it takes only sockets in the daemon's own network namespace — its netns cookie is baked in at load, and a container's identical 127.0.0.1 tuple is left alone. This needs SO_NETNS_COOKIE in the kernel; without it the shortcut refuses to attach rather than serve across namespaces. The programs and maps are anonymous and detached when the daemon exits.

What it costs:

  • The redirected backlog is bounded, by daemon --fast-lo-limit per-pair-MiB,global-MiB (default 4,64). A redirected send does not wait for the receiver, so the program counts each pair's sends and, each time the count passes a mark, asks a reconciler thread through a BPF ring buffer for the peer's true queue, which the thread reads with one exact sock_diag lookup and hands back within tens of microseconds. A reader that keeps up is snapped back and its pair stays on the shortcut however much it moves; a pair whose peer really holds the per-pair bound, or whose count reaches twice it unanswered, is tainted to TCP — which then gives the ordinary EAGAIN backpressure. A flag taints new sends once the sum across pairs reaches the global budget; a sweep once a second recomputes that sum and re-asks any check whose answer was lost, and an idle pair costs nothing. Without the bound a peer that stopped reading took 731 MiB before the kernel's global TCP memory (tcp_mem) ran out; with the default it stays near 4 MiB per pair.

  • The taint is permanent for the pair's life. This is what keeps bytes in order, since tcp_bpf_recvmsg drains the redirect queue before the TCP receive queue, so a byte sent by TCP after the taint is still read after the ones already redirected.

  • Two edges the bound does not catch tightly: a pair moving gigabytes a second whose answer is held up for more than about a millisecond (the reconciler starved of CPU) reaches the hard ceiling and is tainted, which costs speed and not bytes; and pairs stalling together are each checked at least every sixteenth of the global budget, so the sum they reach before the flag is raised is the budget plus a sixteenth per pair — eight pairs against 4,12 held 13.4 MiB, where checking only at the per-pair marks let them hold 23.5.

  • Shortcut bytes skip netfilter, conntrack and the loopback device: nftables rules on lo, tcpdump -i lo and the byte counters in ss do not see them; socketley daemon stats and the metrics endpoint say what the shortcut is carrying.

  • 127.0.0.1 and ::1, including 127.0.0.1 IPv4-mapped on a dual-stack socket; the rest of 127/8 stays on TCP. A runtime listens and a proxy or client runtime connects over IPv4, so a ::1 pair here is a Lua socketley.http() call to a local service on ::1, or to a name that resolves there first. With both ends entered a ::1 pair gains about what a 127.0.0.1 pair does (64 B round trips 1.3x against 1.4x, 16 KB 1.2x against 1.3x); a call that opens a connection per request gains nothing, since entering and leaving the sockhash costs about what the request saves (-3% at 64 B).

  • A pair enters only when both ends are in the map before its first byte, and a socket that sent a byte by TCP stays on TCP for its lifetime, so no byte overtakes another. A client sending TCP Fast Open data stays on TCP.

  • A --protocol tcp proxy's splice reads a queue a socket on the shortcut does not fill, so a proxied pair with a 127.0.0.1 leg stays on the copy path.

  • Under own and all a process that is not this daemon's is never redirected into — only its sends into one of our workers are, and our workers read with recvmsg. So a foreign relay copying between two TCP connections with Go's io.Copy or HAProxy with splicing on keeps every byte on the leg it receives, and needs no own to be safe. This is the receiver rule above; trust gives it up.

sudo socketley daemon --fast-lo &        # all
sudo socketley daemon --fast-lo own &
sudo socketley daemon --fast-lo trust &  # only if no local reader splices
daemon --name name [--cluster dir]#

Configure the running daemon for cluster mode. These flags are sent as IPC commands to the already-running daemon (auto-started if not running). --name sets the daemon's identity in the cluster. --cluster enables cluster discovery on the given shared directory (see CLUSTER MODE). The name can be changed at any time; if cluster mode is active, the cluster file is republished under the new name.

Details
socketley daemon --name node1 --cluster /shared/cluster
socketley daemon --name new-name   # rename while cluster is active
create type name [flags]#

Create a new runtime instance. type can be: server, client, proxy, cache, storage, dns, sync, idp, db, mqtt, mail, tunnel, metrics, mcp, or any registered type — see REGISTERED TYPES. name is a unique identifier for the runtime.

Details

With -s and a --lua script, on_start runs inside this command. A raise there does not take the runtime down — it is created and running, with whatever on_start established before it failed — but the command exits 1 and names the callback and the reason, so a start whose set-up did not run is not reported as a clean one. Fix the script and reload-lua to re-run it.

attach type name port [--owner name] [--pid pid]#

Register an external process as a runtime visible in ls/ps. The daemon does NOT bind the port or forward any I/O — the external process manages its own network connections. The runtime appears as running and can be inspected or removed like any other runtime.

Details
type#

Runtime type: server, client, proxy, or cache.

name#

Unique name for this external runtime.

port#

Port number the external process is listening on (informational only).

--owner name#

Optional owner runtime name.

--pid pid#

The process behind this runtime. Recorded so that socketley stop name sends it SIGTERM: without it the daemon has nothing to stop and the runtime only leaves the listing. An SDK-embedded process passes its own getpid().

Details

The pid must belong to the user issuing the command. The daemon signals it on the caller's behalf, and it will not do that for a process the caller could not signal themselves — on the packaged daemon, whose socket is shared with the socketley group, that would lend out the daemon user's privileges. A daemon running as root is unrestricted, since root can signal anything in any case.

add path [--name name] [-s]#

Register and manage an external binary (built with the C++ SDK). The daemon will fork+exec the binary and manage its full lifecycle: auto-restart on crash, re-launch on daemon boot, and normal start/stop/remove commands.

Details
path#

Path to the executable (must exist and be executable).

--name name, -n name#

Name for the runtime. If omitted, derived from the binary's filename (basename without extension).

-s#

Start immediately after adding.

The binary receives SOCKETLEY_MANAGED=1 and SOCKETLEY_NAME=name environment variables. When using daemon_attach(), these cause the binary to re-attach to the existing runtime entry and skip the atexit self-removal.

socketley add /usr/local/bin/myapp -s
socketley add /usr/local/bin/myapp --name chat
socketley stop chat
socketley start chat
socketley remove chat
start name|pattern... [-i]#

Start one or more runtimes. Accepts multiple names, glob patterns (*, ?, []), or a mix. With *, starts all non-running runtimes.

Details
-i#

Interactive mode. Starts the runtime and opens an interactive session. For server: stdin is broadcast to clients, received messages appear on stdout. For client: stdin is sent to server, received messages appear on stdout. For cache: stdin accepts cache commands, responses appear on stdout (like redis-cli). Refused for a proxy — it relays between a client and a backend and has no stream of its own for typed input to join. The refusal comes before the start, so the runtime is left exactly as it was; see LIMITATIONS. Press Ctrl+C to detach (runtime continues running). If the runtime is already running, attaches without restarting.

Details

A runtime lives in its own process, and the session reaches it: what is typed is delivered to the workers holding the connections, and their descriptor for the session is handed to each of them so what a client says arrives at the terminal with nothing of the daemon's between. Under --shards N that is every shard — a typed line reaches all of their clients, and any of them can be heard back.

A session survives a restart of the runtime it is attached to and is re-attached to the new workers. It does not end when the runtime is stopped: nothing tells it, and the operator has to press Ctrl+C.

For a runtime that lives in a worker process, start waits for the child to report before it returns — so the port is accepting by the time the command exits, and a refusal the child alone can judge is the command's own exit status rather than something ls shows two seconds later. Exit 1 names the runtime if the worker would not take its configuration, and carries the reason if the script's on_start raised. One budget of two seconds is spent for the whole command, not one per runtime: the children are forked together and come up concurrently, so a start of twenty costs about the same wait as a start of one. A child still starting after that, such as a storage runtime reading a large store's files after a crash, is waited for by the CLI rather than the daemon, which stays free: the CLI asks the daemon whether it serves yet five times a second, for as long as its workers keep using CPU, and answers 2 once they have used none for 15 seconds. create -s and restart wait the same way.

stop name|pattern...#

Stop one or more running runtimes. Accepts multiple names, glob patterns (*, ?, []), or a mix. With *, stops all running runtimes.

Details

A stopped runtime executes no script. Its on_stop runs, and then every set_timeout and set_interval timer and every socketley.subscribe registration it holds is severed, so nothing it armed can fire afterwards — and none of the three can be armed again until it is started, which is what stops a script that called socketley.stop on itself from putting one straight back.

remove name|pattern...#

Remove one or more runtimes from the registry. Cannot be undone. Accepts multiple names, glob patterns, or a mix. Running runtimes are stopped first. With *, stops and removes all.

runtime verb [args...]#

What belongs to one runtime is said with its name first, the verb read against its type; the global commands above and below are the ones no single runtime owns. socketley runtime help lists a runtime's verbs. Every runtime takes start, stop, restart, remove, show, stats, edit, reload, reload-lua and owner this way as well, and:

Details
cache#

get, set, del, exists, incr, decr, incrby, decrby, append, mget, mset, keys, size, expire, ttl, persist, lpush, rpush, lpop, rpop, llen, lrange, lindex, sadd, srem, sismember, scard, smembers, hset, hget, hdel, hlen, hgetall, publish, flush, load, memory, send — each as the RESP command of its name, its arguments after it

db#

query, backup, restore

mqtt#

pub, sub, sessions, kick, retained

idp#

user, login, logout, ssh-cert, ssh-ca

dns#

dnssec

tunnel#

invite, set, list, shares, revoke

mail#

send, queue, show, flush, drop, dns, trace, usage, suppressed, forgive, unsubscribed, resubscribe, learn, export, import, sieve

metrics#

query, query_range, series, targets, rules, alerts, logs, stats

server, client, proxy#

send

A type's verb comes before the lifecycle's of the same name: a metrics runtime's stats is its store's, and socketley stats name the runtime's. A runtime named as a global command, such as stop or mail, is reached by the older forms at the end of this section; for metrics, tunnel and mail, the command of the type's name takes the runtime of that name by its verbs, so socketley metrics query asks the runtime named metrics.

socketley shop query customers '{"where":{"country":"de"}}'
socketley broker pub --qos 1 sensors/temp 21.5
socketley auth user add jonas
socketley edge invite pi --http home=idp:auth
socketley metrics logs '{level="error"}' --since 1d
socketley mycache get session:42
socketley web stop
send name [message]#

Send a message to a running server or client runtime. For servers, the message is broadcast to all connected clients. For clients, the message is sent to the connected server. Respects the runtime's mode setting (fails if mode is receive-only).

mail send --to address [--cc|--bcc address] [--from address] [--reply-to address] [--subject text] [--text text] [--html file] [--attach file[:type]] [--inline image] [--header 'Name: value'] [--raw]#

A message written and queued by a mail runtime, which answers its queue id: its text from --text or stdin, an HTML part beside it from a file, attachments in base64, every flag but --to said as often as needed. A name or address may be Name <a@b>. Without --from a runtime with --no-reply sends from no-reply@ its first domain. --raw queues stdin as the whole message, its headers its own. A message past 4 MiB goes to the runtime by a file in its outbox under the state directory, so one up to --max-size is sent whole; a message to a server or a client that begins with - is given after --. A :type after an attachment is taken as its type only where it is one, type/subtype, and the file does not exist with it. --inline sends an image inside the message, which its HTML shows as cid:name by the image's file name, so a reader sees it without fetching anything. See MAIL FLAGS.

Details
socketley send m --to ops@example.com --subject "Backup done" --text ok
df -h | socketley send m --to "Ops <ops@example.com>" --subject "Disks" \
    --attach report.pdf:application/pdf
mail send --template file --to address|idp:idp[/group]|db:db/collection|json:file [--set name=value] [--lua file] [--ad] [--no-check] [--rate-limit n[/m|/h]] [--test] [--test-to address]#

A message for each recipient, of their own, from a template: an HTML file, or --text for plain text alone, and the subject, with placeholders. {{name}} is the recipient's value of that name, {{name|otherwise}} says what stands where they have none, and {{{name}}} puts a value into the HTML as it is, which escapes every other. The values are --set, given for every recipient, and what each recipient's source says of them: an address of --to has its email; idp:idp the idp's accounts that are not disabled, those of a group after a slash, each with its username, name, email and every field it keeps but its password; db:db/collection the collection's documents, each with its fields, an object's below its name (address.city); json:file a JSON array of objects, or one a line. Each needs an email, and a name is written into its To. With an HTML template the plain part beside it is the HTML's text, its links written out. The messages go at --rate-limit a second, or a minute or an hour after a slash (300/m; two a second unless it says), so a new sender's first thousand do not land in the spam folder for coming at once; what was skipped or failed is said by recipient, and a line says how many were sent.

Details

A template is Lua. {{ expr }} is the value of any Lua expression and {% code %} runs where it stands, a tag alone on its line taking the line with it:

{% if vip then %}<p>Your code: {{code}}</p>{% end %}
{% for _, p in ipairs(products) do %}
<li>{{p.title}}: {{ string.format("%.2f", p.price) }}</li>
{% end %}

A name with dots is a field below another, no value rather than an error where one on the way is missing, and a list of words is written joined by commas. html(s), url(s) and raw(s) escape, percent-encode, and keep a value unescaped; include("file") puts in another template, from beside this one, filled for the same recipient. A template reaches its recipient's values, what the script defines, string, table, math, os.date and os.time, and no file and no process. --lua file.lua runs once before the first recipient and reaches all of Lua; on_recipient(r) is called with each recipient's values before their message is written, to change them, or to leave the recipient out by returning false and why, and on_link(url, r) with each link of the HTML but the one to unsubscribe, its answer the link written and nil keeping it. An error in Lua is a message that cannot be written, said with its file and line.

A template is filled strictly: a recipient whose message has a name with no value and no default is skipped, and one whose message is the first stops them all before any is sent, as does a first the runtime refuses, since a template that fails its first recipient is wrong for all of them. --no-check lets a name with no value be empty, and sends on past a first refused. --test shows the first recipient's message and how many there are, and sends nothing; --test-to sends that message, its subject marked [test], to the address it names alone.

--ad marks an advertisement. Each goes to one recipient, never to one who unsubscribed, with a link to unsubscribe of their own where the template says {{unsubscribe}}, or below what it says, and List-Unsubscribe naming it and a mailto: (RFC 2369), with List-Unsubscribe-Post for a provider's one click (RFC 8058), and List-Id naming its list by its sender, such as <news.example.com> (RFC 2919). The link is https://webmail/unsubscribe where the runtime has --web and --domain, whose GET asks and whose POST unsubscribes, so a scanner opening every link unsubscribes no one; the mailto: is unsubscribe@domain with the token in its subject. A token is the address and an HMAC of it under the runtime's key, so it is kept nowhere and forged by no one. What is no advertisement still goes to an address that unsubscribed.

socketley send m --template autumn.html --inline logo.png --to db:shop/customers \
    --from news@example.com --subject "Hello {{name|there}}, your code {{code}}" \
    --ad --rate-limit 5
socketley send m --template autumn.html --to idp:auth/vip --set code=VIP30 --test
socketley send m --template order.html --lua shop.lua --to db:shop/orders --test-to me@example.com

If no message is given, reads from stdin:

echo "hello" | socketley send myserver
cat data.txt | socketley send myclient

The word send may be left out when something is piped in, so echo "hello" | socketley myserver is the same command. This form is only taken when standard input is not a terminal, which is also every script, pipeline and CI step — so a mistyped command reaches it too. When nothing arrives on standard input, socketley cannot tell a misspelled command from a runtime that was piped zero bytes, and says so, naming both readings and leading with the typo:

$ socketley gibtsnicht < /dev/null
unknown command: gibtsnicht
  If gibtsnicht is a runtime you meant to send to, nothing arrived on standard input:
    echo 'data' | socketley gibtsnicht
stats name|pattern...#

Display runtime statistics including total connections, messages processed, bytes in/out, and type-specific counters. Accepts multiple names, glob patterns, or a mix. With *, shows stats for all runtimes.

Details

One field describes how the runtime's I/O is running rather than what it has done, and it is read from the ring itself rather than from what was asked for — a cpuset can refuse the pinning, and a runtime whose real CPU set cannot be read back is one nobody can debug:

cpus#

The CPU set in force, in the same spelling --cpus accepts, with (not applied) appended when the pinning was attempted and refused.

dial_attempts#

Client only. The dials this client has made, beside total_connections which counts the ones the kernel found a peer for. A non-blocking connect answers EINPROGRESS for every target that is not already there, so a dial is an intention and the two figures come apart exactly when a target is flapping or gone — a client reconnecting all afternoon shows one climbing and the other standing still. Every other runtime counts total_connections at something that happened to it: the server and the cache at an accept(2), the proxy once on_auth has admitted the client.

upstreams#

Server only, and only when -u was given: how many of the configured upstreams the kernel says are connected, over how many were configured. The left number answers the same question dial_attempts separates for a client, and for the same reason — it used to be raised one line after the non-blocking connect(), so a server whose upstream host was not there at all reported upstreams:1/1 for twenty-five seconds out of thirty. It is a flapping upstream that makes the two numbers differ, and an unreachable one that makes the left stay at zero.

For a runtime running in its own process this describes that process's ring, not the daemon's.

daemon stop#

Stops the daemon this invocation would talk to, over its socket rather than by pid, taking every runtime it supervises with it. It answers before it goes, and exits 2 when nothing is serving that socket.

daemon stats#

The daemon's own figures as key:value lines, the shape stats gives a runtime. Today that is the loopback shortcut (daemon --fast-lo), whose bytes tcpdump -i lo and nftables never see: fast_lo is off, own, all, trust, or unavailable with fast_lo_reason saying why. When attached: fast_lo_sockets_shortcut and fast_lo_sockets_tcp count the entered sockets that send by the shortcut and those pinned to TCP for good (as of the last once-a-second sweep; a pair is two sockets, and each direction is its sender's); fast_lo_entered counts sockets entered since start; fast_lo_tainted_bound, _unanswered, _budget and _peer_off count taints by reason — the peer really held the per-pair bound, no answer came before twice the bound, the global budget was reached, the peer was not on the shortcut (it received by TCP before it could enter, or had closed); fast_lo_held_bytes is the unread redirected backlog summed across pairs, which the global budget (fast_lo_budget_bytes) is compared against, an upper bound for a pair below 64 KiB; fast_lo_over_budget is 1 while new sends are being tainted for it. The metrics endpoint carries the same as socketley_fast_lo_info{mode}, socketley_fast_lo_sockets{path}, socketley_fast_lo_entered_total, socketley_fast_lo_tainted_total{reason}, socketley_fast_lo_held_bytes, socketley_fast_lo_budget_bytes, socketley_fast_lo_pair_limit_bytes and socketley_fast_lo_over_budget. The counting is one atomic add per entered socket and per taint, never per send.

A new username ends the account's sessions and tokens, which carry the old one to every runtime that takes them. logout ends every session and refresh token the account holds; passwd does too. show prints the fields, the password as set and never its hash. totp on turns on a second step of signing in: it prints the key, and the otpauth:// link that gives it to an authenticator app, and from then on a web sign-in asks the six digits the app shows after the password, a code taken once at every shard and across a restart, the last step taken kept with the account (RFC 6238); off turns it off. app-password add makes a password of four groups of four letters for one mail app, printed once, which signs in over SMTP, IMAP, POP3 and JMAP and is taken back on its own by remove; with the second step on, mail apps sign in with these alone, since they have no code to give. Every daemon that has registered itself, with its pid, whether it still answers, and the executable serving it — which differs per socket once a daemon built on the SDK is running.

Details

An asterisk marks the one this invocation would talk to; SOCKETLEY_SOCKET selects another. The list is a set of files, one per daemon, written after the socket is served and removed on a clean exit; every entry is probed rather than trusted, so a daemon that was killed outright is reported dead rather than listed as running, and its file is removed once its pid is gone too.

restart name [edit flags] [-i]#

Stop and start a runtime in one step, with any edit flag given applied in between — which is how a setting that cannot change while a runtime runs is changed at all:

Details
socketley restart api -p 9001
socketley restart ns-proxy --shards 1

One command and not a stop followed by a start, because the runtime being restarted may be the one the command travels through: an entrance proxy carries the dashboard it was asked from, so the stop arrived and the start never did, and the entrance stayed down with its configuration unchanged. The daemon does all of it, so whatever becomes of the caller's connection the runtime ends up running. A flag the edit refuses leaves the runtime running and unchanged.

The flags are edit's, read by edit and never handed to start: handing them there had a flag's VALUE read as a runtime name and that runtime started, which is why they were refused for a while. -i is restart's own and attaches to the runtime once it is up. A runtime that was stopped is started, as it was before, flags or no flags: it is the lifecycle verb, and it means one thing. For a change that is to be stored WITHOUT starting anything, see edit --restart below.

A runtime's new worker is forked only once its previous worker has exited, since that process holds the ports, unix paths and files until then; the start, reload or create -s that brought it up answers after that fork, and the daemon serves everything else meanwhile. The previous worker is given five seconds before it is killed, or a cache writing its dump that dump's own bound, so a command can outlast the CLI's five-second wait for an answer while the runtime still comes up.

reload name|pattern...#

Restart one or more running runtimes (stop + start). Accepts multiple names, glob patterns, or a mix. Non-running runtimes are skipped. With *, restarts all running runtimes.

Details

A runtime that lives in a worker process has its child taken down and forked again, so the script on disk is re-read and a change to it takes effect. The command waits for the new child, exactly as create -s does, and answers for it: exit 1 naming the runtime if the worker refuses the configuration it was handed, and exit 1 with the reason if the reloaded script's on_start raises. Success stays silent.

reload-lua name|pattern...#

Hot-reload the Lua script attached to one or more runtimes. The Lua context is destroyed and re-created from the original script path. Accepts multiple names, glob patterns, or a mix. Runtimes without Lua scripts are skipped. With *, reloads Lua on all runtimes that have scripts loaded.

Details

on_start runs again, on the new script, and this is the whole difference between reloading a file and reloading a runtime. Everything a script establishes at run time lives in its Lua context — every socketley.subscribe registration and every set_timeout or set_interval timer — and destroying the context destroys all of it. Since the ordinary place to make those is on_start, a reload that did not re-run it left the runtime serving with no subscriptions and no timers, and said nothing. So: anything on_start does must be safe to do twice. socketley.create there is the case that costs something, and it refuses a name that already exists rather than duplicating it.

on_stop does not run for the outgoing script. The runtime is not stopping — it keeps its listener, its clients and its state right through the reload — and on_stop is where a script says goodbye to exactly those.

An on_start that raises is reported like a script that would not load: exit 1, with the reason on the terminal. The new script is in force in that case, with whatever its on_start managed before it failed; a script that would not compile leaves the previous one running instead. The message says which.

A runtime that runs in a worker is asked rather than reloaded here: its script lives in that process and only that process can re-run it. The command waits for the worker to report the declaration the new script makes — bounded the way create bounds its own wait — so that when it returns, a gateway in front of that runtime is already enforcing what the edited script says, including when the edit removed the routes table altogether. A worker that does not answer in time leaves the previous declaration in force and says so in the log; a script that does not compile leaves the previous one running, as it does in the daemon.

A reload that succeeds prints nothing and exits 0. A script that would not load is named on stdout with the reason — the parse error, or whichever filters or routes rule it broke — and the command exits 1. The runtimes that did reload are still reloaded, and the ones that did not go on running the script they had, so the message is the only sign that an edit is not live.

show name|pattern...#

Print runtime JSON configuration to stdout. Accepts multiple names, glob patterns, or a mix. With *, prints all runtimes.

edit name [flags] [--restart]#

Edit a runtime's configuration. When called with flags (e.g. -p 9001), applies the changes directly. --restart stops the runtime first and starts it again afterwards, which is what a setting refused "while running" needs — and import takes it the same way, before the document:

Details
socketley edit ns-proxy --shards 1 --restart
socketley show ns-proxy | socketley import ns-proxy --restart

The daemon does the stop, the change and the start as one command, so a caller whose connection the runtime carries cannot be cut off between them; see restart. A change the runtime refuses leaves it running and unchanged — it was stopped and started around the refusal, since whether a setting needs that is only answered by applying it, and an edit that is refused rolls back whole. A runtime that was already stopped stays stopped. The flags accepted here are a subset of the ones create takes: the common settings (-p, -b/-bp/-bt/-bpt, --log, -w, --max-connections, --rate-limit, --global-rate-limit, --idle-timeout, -g), the server and client flags, and the proxy mesh flags (--strategy, --health-*, --circuit-*, --backend-timeout, --retry, --retry-all), and a tunnel's own flags, such as an agent's --offer, which a running tunnel takes only with --restart. Anything else — including --lua, --drain, --reconnect, the proxy's --backend, --protocol and --sidecar, and every cache flag — is refused with unknown flag and exit status 1; change those through the editor or import, which reach the full field set.

Four flags reach a running runtime of any type at once: --max-connections, --rate-limit, --global-rate-limit and --idle-timeout. They are the limits a runtime reads at the moment it uses them — one per accept, one per message, one per idle sweep — so changing one changes the next decision and nothing already decided. The daemon sends the edited configuration to every shard.

On a proxy nine more do, for the same reason: they are routing and mesh policy, read when a backend is picked, a request is armed or a failure is counted, and nothing is built from them. --strategy, --health-interval, --health-path, --health-threshold, --circuit-threshold, --circuit-timeout, --backend-timeout, --retry and --retry-all. --health-interval re-times the sweep already armed, so at most one period of the old value elapses before the new one applies.

--health-check is not among them, and is the one proxy flag whose reason differs from the others': it arms a sweep timer when the runtime starts, so turning it on has no timer to arm. It is stored and applies at the next start like everything below.

Every other flag edit accepts on a running runtime is stored and takes effect at that runtime's next start. Not as policy: a -p is a bound socket, the TLS flags are a context the open handshakes already used, a proxy's backends are open connections, and a server's --http directory decides what a request in flight is being answered from. None of those can change under a connection that exists. So show reports the new value while the runtime holding the port keeps the old one, until ‘socketley restart name’. The flags that cannot even be stored while running say so and change nothing: -p, --listen and --shards.

The TLS flags are an exception only in what they refuse. Editing is the usual way to put encryption on something that already exists, so on every runtime type --tls, --cert, --key and --ca — and, on a proxy, --client-ca, --client-cert and --client-key — are accepted here. Certificates are read when a runtime starts, so a running one keeps the identity it handshook with until it is restarted. What it trusts is refused instead of stored while it runs, since a stored one would be shown while the old one went on deciding who gets in: --tls on a runtime without it, --ca naming another file, and on a proxy --client-ca, --client-cert and --client-key, and the same fields in import; --restart takes them. An edit that would leave the set incomplete — a certificate with no --tls, --tls with no key pair on a listener, half a client-certificate pair, or --tls on a cache that replicates — is refused and changes nothing, so a mistyped flag cannot leave a runtime half-configured. See LIMITATIONS. When called without flags (or with only -r/--reload), opens the runtime's JSON configuration in $VISUAL, $EDITOR, or vim. After saving, changes are validated and applied.

edit name -r#

Interactive editor mode with auto-reload. After saving changes, the runtime's Lua script is automatically hot-reloaded. Alias: --reload.

export dir#

This daemon's setup written as Lua into dir: config.lua with an include of a file for each runtime under runtimes/, a dns runtime's zones under zones/ and a handler script under lua/, in an order that makes a runtime before those that name it. A runtime another made, such as a dns runtime's entrance, is made again by that one and left out; the daemon's own settings are carried from its configuration file. What the runtimes read and the setup does not hold — a credentials file, a token file, a certificate outside the state directory — is named at the top of config.lua, to be put on the next machine as well. Their data is not in it. The setup is read back and each runtime planned from it before the command ends, so one that it would make otherwise is named and the exit code is 1; a directory that holds a config.lua already is refused. See A machine's setup under LUA CONFIGURATION.

export --full file [--compress fast|best|none] [--threads n]#

The setup and its data in one tar archive, gzip around it unless --compress none says otherwise (best looks longer for what repeats, as gzip -9 does; what does not get smaller, as photos and attachments, goes in as it is), compressed a MiB at a time on as many threads as the CPUs it may run on, or --threads n, into one stream any gzip reads: the state directory — every runtime's file, the mailboxes' index, the idp's accounts and keys, the Sieve scripts, the calendars' journals, the DKIM and DNSSEC keys, the certificates — the daemon's configuration directory, and what each runtime keeps elsewhere: a storage runtime's buckets, a cache's file and its journal, a zone, a script, a file of tokens. A db runtime that runs is written by its own backup, which holds what it holds at one moment, rather than copied while it writes; a cache gives what its file and its journal hold, what a crash would leave it, every write but the last --persistent-interval where it journals; the Lua setup export writes goes in beside them. Not in it: a log, what a runtime writes as its output, a backups directory, and the files a sync runtime carries, which are the user's own; each is named when the command ends. Run as root or as the daemon's user, while it runs or not, the archive written 0600 and only once it is whole.

Details
socketley export --full /var/backups/socketley-$(date +%F).tar.gz
restore file [--force]#

What export --full wrote put back where it was, owned by the users it was owned by where they are on this machine, each file written beside its place and moved there whole. The daemon is stopped first, and started again brings every runtime back from its state as it was, running where it ran. A state directory that holds runtimes already is refused unless --force; a path outside those the archive's manifest names refuses the archive. Besides this machine's state and configuration directories, a path the manifest names under /etc, /usr, /root, /boot, /run, /var/spool and the like, or among a home's hidden files, is left where it is and named, for tar to take out by hand; no file is restored setuid or setgid, and outside the state and configuration one the archive says root owns is owned by the daemon's user.

Details
systemctl stop socketley
socketley restore /var/backups/socketley-2026-10-25.tar.gz
systemctl start socketley
import name [--restart] json#

Update a runtime's configuration from a JSON string. With no json argument the document is read from standard input instead, so show pipes straight into import:

Details
socketley show name | socketley import name

That form has no command-line length limit, which the quoted one does. Whitespace outside string literals is stripped before the document is sent, so the pretty-printed output of show is accepted as-is. Accepts the same fields as the interactive editor (see below). Fields marked (read-only) are ignored. Fields marked (requires restart) cannot be changed while the runtime is running. Port, protocol, and UDP settings cannot be changed while running.

A field the document does not mention is left alone. Only what is named is applied, so a partial document changes only those fields. Clearing one is written out rather than implied — "tls": false, "cert_path": ""—becauseadocumentthatsimplyomittedafield used to CLEAR it, and a runtime configured for TLS could be handed {"name":"x"} and answer in cleartext afterwards with the command reporting success.

import is also the fuller of the two ways to reconfigure a runtime. edit takes a subset of the flags: it has no cache-specific ones at all, and no --backend or --lua. Anything it refuses with "unknown flag" can still be set by dumping the document with show, changing the field and importing it back.

A JSON document is held to the same rules the flags are: on every runtime type tls, cert_path, key_path and ca_path are accepted as a complete set and refused as an incomplete one. On a cache a document setting tls alongside replicate_target is rejected outright and nothing is applied, because replication is not encrypted (see LIMITATIONS). mesh_client_ca, mesh_client_cert and mesh_client_key belong to a proxy alone.

Clearing any of them is written out and never implied, the same rule the paragraph above states for every field: a document that simply omits a field leaves the runtime's own value in place. That is how a runtime restored from an older state file with certificate paths it can no longer read is made startable again — by naming them empty, not by deleting the lines:

socketley show name > cfg.json
# set the TLS and mesh paths to "" in an editor, do not delete the lines
socketley import name "$(cat cfg.json)"

Deleting them used to clear them, and that is what changed: a runtime configured for TLS could be handed {"name":"x"} and answer in cleartext afterwards, with the command reporting success.

A document that leaves out name and type is about the runtime the command names, with that runtime's type, so one field is changed with one key:

socketley import ui '{"domain":"storage"}'

Update a runtime's configuration from a JSON string. With no json argument the document is read from standard input instead, so show pipes straight into import:

sections.title: Edit: JSON Configuration Fields
sections.html:
The interactive editor opens a JSON file with the following fields. Fields marked (read-only) are ignored on import. Fields marked (requires restart) cannot be changed while the runtime is running — stop the runtime first.

Identity fields:

nameRuntime name (requires restart)
id6-char hex identifier (read-only, ignored on import)
typeRuntime type: server, client, proxy, cache, storage, dns, sync, idp, db, mqtt, mail, tunnel, metrics, mcp (read-only, ignored on import)
was_runningInternal daemon state (ignored on import)

Common fields (all types):

FieldTypeDescription
portnumberListener/connection port (requires restart)
listenstring"unix:/abs/path.sock" — an AF_UNIX listener instead of a port (server/proxy/cache; requires restart)
log_filestringState transition log file path
write_filestringMessage write file path
lua_scriptstringLua script path (absolute)
bash_outputboolOutput messages to stdout
bash_prefixboolPrefix messages with [name]
bash_timestampboolPrefix messages with [HH:MM:SS]
max_connectionsnumberMax concurrent connections (0 = unlimited)
rate_limitnumberMessages/sec per connection (0 = unlimited)
global_rate_limitnumberMessages/sec across all connections (0 = unlimited)
idle_timeoutnumberClose idle connections after N seconds (0 = disabled)
congestionstringTCP congestion control of accepted connections (--congestion)
drainboolGraceful shutdown (flush writes before close)
tlsboolTerminate TLS on the listener (server, proxy); dial TLS (client)
cert_pathstringPEM certificate (server, proxy; needs tls); on a client, the certificate it presents
key_pathstringPEM private key (server, proxy; needs tls); on a client, the key for cert_path
ca_pathstringClient CA for mutual TLS (server, needs tls); on a proxy, the trust store for TLS backends; on a client, the trust store for its target
targetstringClient target host:port (requires restart)
cache_namestringConnected cache runtime name
groupstringGroup tag for dynamic proxy discovery

Server fields:

FieldTypeDescription
modestring"inout", "in", "out", or "master"
udpboolUse UDP instead of TCP (requires restart)
master_pwstringStatic password for master mode
send_tostring"sender", "others", "master", comma separated
http_dirstringStatic file root, as --http
http_cacheboolHold those files in memory, as --http-cache
compressboolCompressed copies (--compress)
originsstringOther web origins that may open a WebSocket, as --origins
upstreamsarrayUpstream addresses, as --upstream

Client fields:

FieldTypeDescription
modestring"inout", "in", or "out"
udpboolUse UDP instead of TCP (requires restart)
reconnectnumberAuto-reconnect max attempts (-1=off, 0=infinite)

Proxy fields:

FieldTypeDescription
protocolstring"http" or "tcp" (requires restart)
strategystring"round-robin", "random", or "lua"
rootstringA FastCGI proxy's directory (--root)
fastcgi_rootstringIt as the application server sees it
indexstringThe index script (default "index.php")
compressboolCompressed copies (--compress)
backendsarrayList of backend addresses ["ip:port", "@group", ...]
health_checknumber0 disabled, 1 TCP connect, 2 HTTP GET — the number --health-check stored
health_intervalnumberHealth check interval in seconds (default 5)
health_pathstringHTTP health check path (default "/health")
health_thresholdnumberFailures to mark unhealthy (default 3)
circuit_thresholdnumberErrors to open circuit (default 5)
circuit_timeoutnumberSeconds before half-open (default 30)
backend_timeoutnumberSeconds for the first response byte (default 2, 0 = off)
retry_countnumberRetry count (0 = disabled)
retry_allboolAlso retry non-idempotent methods
mesh_client_castringCA for certificates clients present (needs tls)
mesh_client_certstringClient certificate presented to backends
mesh_client_keystringIts private key (both or neither)

These are the names in the document, which are not in every case the names of the flags or of the Lua configuration keys that set the same things: the document spells them retry_count, mesh_client_ca, mesh_client_cert and mesh_client_key, where --retry and --client-ca are the flags and retry and client_ca are the config-file keys. There is no sidecar field: it is a flag and a config key that sets several of the fields above, and nothing writes or reads it in a state document.

FieldTypeDescription

notify_targetsstringThe event notification webhooks file, as --notify-targets (requires restart)
replication_targetsstringThe replication endpoints file, as --replication-targets (requires restart)
fsyncstring"always", "interval" or "never", as --fsync (requires restart)
syncstring"never", "active" or "per-user", as --sync; absent is never (requires restart)
fsync_intervalnumberSeconds between the filesystem syncs of --fsync interval, as --fsync-interval (requires restart)

Example JSON (server):

{
    "name": "api",
    "id": "a1b2c3",
    "type": "server",
    "port": 9000,
    "was_running": true,
    "lua_script": "/home/user/handler.lua",
    "max_connections": 100,
    "rate_limit": 1000,
    "mode": "inout"
}
settings [-a|--all] [-j|--json]#

Every SOCKETLEY_* setting as the daemon and the processes it starts see it: its value, and whether that came from the daemon's environment, from the settings table of its configuration file (see Daemon Configuration), or is the default, with what it is for. The plain listing holds the knobs an operator may turn; --all adds the test suite's hooks, the variables a command reads from its own environment, and the ones the daemon sets for what it starts, each marked in a FOR column. --json prints the same rows as an array of objects with name, env, value, from, for and meaning. Every variable under ENVIRONMENT is one row.

dashboard#

Print the URL of the built-in web dashboard. Requires daemon.metrics_port to be set in the daemon configuration file (see Daemon Configuration). The dashboard provides a live-updating view of all runtimes, connections, and throughput. It listens on loopback and answers a Host other than this machine's 403, so a page whose name was rebound to 127.0.0.1 reads nothing; a request that carries Via, which no page can set, is a proxy's and is served whatever its Host, so a proxy with --domain and --auth can put it on the internet. Its pages are never framed, sniffed, cached or named in a Referer. Example output:

Details
Dashboard: http://localhost:9100/
ls [--json | -j | --format json] [--silent | -s] [columns]#

List all runtimes (all states). Docker-style output with columns: ID, NAME, TYPE, PORT, CONN (connections), OWNED BY, STATUS, CREATED, GROUP. With --json or --format json, outputs a JSON array of runtime objects. With --silent or -s, prints only runtime names (one per line).

Details

The STATUS column of a running runtime is its uptime, followed by two notes when they apply. (N restarts) means the daemon found the worker dead and forked a replacement that many times; the uptime is the replacement's, and a runtime holding state in memory — a cache above all — lost it at every one of them. The JSON form reports the same number in restarts.

NOT RESPONDING means the worker process is alive and has said nothing for fifteen seconds while spending at least half a core. A worker publishes on every completion, so one doing any work at all is heard from within a quarter second: silence means either idle, which costs no CPU, or stuck inside a callback, which costs a core. Only the second is reported, and it is only reported — nothing is killed, because a script deliberately computing for a long time looks the same from outside the process. A worker stuck without spending CPU, blocked rather than spinning, is indistinguishable from an idle one and is not reported.

The JSON form carries a listen field beside port: empty for an ordinary runtime, and unix:/path/to.sock for a server started with --listen. The PORT column shows - for one of those, since it has none.

When more than one daemon is running, a line under the table says how many and which one answered — including when the table is empty, because a listing from the wrong daemon looks exactly like an idle machine. It is printed only for the default table: --json, -s and the column selectors are what scripts read and carry nothing extra. ps does the same.

Column selectors — pass one or more to show only those columns: --id, --name, --type, --port, --status, --conn, --owner, --created, --group.

ps [-a | --all] [--json | -j | --format json] [--silent | -s] [columns]#

List only running runtimes. Same format as ls. With --json, outputs a JSON array (includes uptime field). With --silent or -s, prints only runtime names (one per line).

Details

A runtime that did not come up is in state failed, and ps does not list it — so a runtime that failed to start produces no row here, and if nothing else is running, no output at all. That is the state you go looking for when something did not start, so look for it with ps -a or ls.

-a, --all
List runtimes in every state, not only running. The STATUS column then carries the state (Created, Stopped, Failed) in place of an uptime, and --json reports it in the status field. Bare ps is unchanged, so anything parsing it keeps seeing running runtimes only.

Column selectors: --id, --name, --type, --port, --uptime, --conn, --owner, --created.

--status and --uptime are two names for one column, headed UPTIME. It holds an uptime for a running runtime and the state (Created, Stopped, Failed) for anything else, so under -a a row can read Failed beneath a header saying UPTIME. That is the same column ls heads STATUS; the header is left alone because scripts select on it.

owner name#

Show ownership info for a runtime: parent name, children list, and on_parent_stop policy (stop or remove).

cluster [subcommand]#

Inspect the cluster. Requires a running daemon with cluster mode enabled (via daemon --name + daemon --cluster). The cluster directory is read from the daemon automatically.

Details
ls#

List all daemons in the cluster with runtime counts and heartbeat status.

ps#

List all runtimes across the entire cluster.

group name#

Show all members of a specific group across the cluster.

show daemon-name#

Print a daemon's raw cluster JSON file.

stats#

Show cluster summary: daemon counts, runtime totals, group membership.

watch#

Continuously refresh the cluster view every 2 seconds (Ctrl+C to stop).

ping#

Ask the daemon to identify itself. Prints socketley-daemon version pid dev:ino path for the daemon serving the socket, where the last two fields name the executable it is running — its device and inode, and its /proc/self/exe link, which carries (deleted) once the file it was started from has been replaced. The path is last because a path may contain spaces. A daemon built before those fields existed answers with the version and pid alone, and is not treated as a different build for it.

Details

Every command runs this first, before it sends anything: a connect(2) that succeeds only proves something is listening on the path, not that the thing listening is a daemon, and a command written to a stranger is a command delivered to a stranger. A path held by something that does not answer this is refused, with nothing sent to it.

help | --help | -h#

Print help. What it prints depends on where it is printing to.

Details

On a terminal, it opens the interactive browser: a menu, not a page, reached by number and taking no topic argument — everything is behind the menu.

Anywhere else— a pipe, a redirect, a CI step — it prints a plain-text summary of the commands and exits 0. Neither standard input nor standard output being a terminal is what decides it; there is no flag, because socketley --help is what a person types either way and only the destination differs. A menu drawn into a pipe is a menu nobody can answer, and it used to arrive with a screen-clear escape at the front of the captured output and an exit status of 1 behind it — this project's code for bad input, reported to a caller whose only mistake was asking for help.

Does not require, and does not start, a daemon. The browser is man/socketley-help.sh under the source tree the binary was built in, and /usr/share/socketley/socketley-help.sh otherwise — nearest first, so a binary built in a tree prints that tree's help rather than an installed copy from another version. If neither is readable the command says so and exits 2, the installation's fault and not bad input. This page is the reference and that browser is the tour — they cover the same ground and are kept in step with each other.

version | --version | -v#

Print the socketley version number and exit. Does not require, and does not start, a daemon. Standard output is the version number in every case; anything about the daemon on the socket goes to standard error, so $(socketley version) is unaffected by all of it.

Details

Reported there: a daemon whose version differs, and — since the version is one compile-time literal that every build of a release carries — a daemon still executing a file that has since been replaced at the path it was started from. That second one is the ordinary case of rebuilding while a daemon holds its runtimes, and the reason a new flag can be rejected by a daemon reporting the same version as the binary that has it.

It is reported only when the daemon and this CLI name the same executable path. Running the CLI from a copy elsewhere on disk says nothing: a copy is not evidence about anybody's build, and comparing inodes across different paths would report one on every command.

--lua lua_file#

Load Lua orchestration configuration. Optionally configures daemon name and cluster mode, then creates multiple runtimes from a single config file.

Older forms#

The forms of before the runtime came first, kept so a script goes on working:

Details
db-backup db file#

is db backup file.

db-restore db file#

is db restore file.

db-query db collection#

is db query collection.

mqtt-pub mqtt#

is mqtt pub,as mqtt-sub, mqtt-sessions, mqtt-kick and mqtt-retained are its sub, sessions, kick and retained, and mqtt-passwd is mqtt passwd.

mqtt-sub mqttmqtt-sessions mqttmqtt-kick mqttmqtt-retained mqttmqtt-passwd file#

as above.

idp-user idp#

is idp user,and idp-ssh idp ca is idp ssh-ca.

idp-ssh idp#

as above.

dnssec dns#

is dns dnssec.

tunnel edge invite#

(set, list, shares, revoke) is edge invite.

metrics metrics verb#

is metrics verb.

mail [mail] verb#

is mail verb;withoutanameittakesthedaemon'sonemailruntime.

is mail send.

sections.title: DAEMON FLAGS
sections.html:
These flags configure the running daemon via IPC commands. The daemon is auto-started if not already running. One daemon serves a socket: it holds a lock on the socket's path with .lock appended for as long as it runs, and a second one started meanwhile — by hand, or by a command's auto-start — waits until the first answers and exits 0, or exits 1 after ten seconds of a holder that never does.

--name name | -n name#

Set this daemon's identity. Required before enabling cluster mode. Can be changed at any time; if cluster mode is active, the cluster file is republished under the new name (old name is removed).

--cluster dir#

Enable cluster mode on the given shared directory. Each daemon publishes its runtime state there every 2 seconds and scans for peer daemons. Proxy @group backends automatically discover runtimes on remote daemons. In Docker Compose, mount a shared volume at this path. The advertised host address is set automatically via gethostname(3). Requires --name to be set first.
