sections.title: COMMON FLAGS
sections.html:
These flags work with all runtime types:

-p port#

Set listener port (server, proxy, cache, storage, dns) or target port (client). -p address:port sets --bind as well.

--bind address#

The IPv4 address the listener port is bound on, alone, such as 127.0.0.1 for a runtime only a reverse proxy on the same host reaches; without it, or with 0.0.0.0, every address. Changed while stopped, by edit, or by import's bind field, and named in ls --json. An address that is not one is refused when it is given; one the host does not have fails the start.

-s#

Start immediately after creation.

--test#

Dry run: the type, the name and every flag are checked, and then nothing is kept. No runtime is left in ls, no state file is written and the name is free for the create that follows. It used to keep the runtime -- unstarted, unsaved, and holding the name until the daemon restarted -- which made the real create answer "runtime already exists", and made start on it bind a port no state file would ever bring back.

Details

It does not bind the port, and a --lua script is loaded — which is what validates it, and runs its top level — but on_start is not called, because nothing is started. What it answers is whether this command line is one create accepts.

--log file#

Append one line per state transition to file:

Details
2026-09-10 11:48:22 api created
2026-09-10 11:48:22 api running
2026-09-10 11:48:31 api stopped

Dated as well as clocked, because this file outlives a day, unlike the daemon's own log. Created with mode 0600 and opened for append, so a restart adds to the record rather than replacing it.

The first line is the state the runtime was in when the flag was given, which is how created appears at all: it is the state a runtime is constructed in, before any flag has been parsed. Giving --log by edit to a runtime that is already serving therefore opens the file with a running line, which is where the record starts rather than a transition anybody made.

What is recorded is the state ls reports, which is the daemon's. A runtime lives in its own process and that process keeps its own copy of the same value; both carry the path, and both writing would double every line. One consequence is visible and worth expecting: an out-of-process runtime whose worker refuses its configuration records created, running and then failed, because running is what the daemon had asked for and reported for the moment before the worker answered.

The path must be absolute. A relative one would be resolved against the daemon's working directory — wherever it was started, and / under systemd — so it is refused rather than written somewhere the operator would not think to look.

A path that cannot be opened or written is reported once, at ERROR, and then not again.

-w file#

Write every received message to file, one line each, in the bytes they arrived in — this is the file half of -b, and it is written at the same point in the runtime, where the message is counted.

Details

The file is created with mode 0600 on the first message and not at the start, so a runtime nothing is sent leaves nothing behind, and it is opened for append, so a restart adds to it rather than truncating it. Under --shards N the N workers share the one path: an append this size is atomic on a regular file, so the lines interleave without tearing.

Unlike -b, the bytes are not scrubbed of control characters. That scrubbing exists to stop a peer driving the operator's terminal with an escape sequence, and a file is not a terminal.

The path must be absolute, for --log's reason above.

-w takes effect on a runtime that is already serving, so edit name -w other.log moves the writing without a restart. A path that cannot be opened or written is reported once, at ERROR, and then not again — a runtime under load would otherwise put one line in the log per message through it.

The files written by -w and --log are held open once written, so a file renamed away keeps receiving the lines; rotate them with logrotate's copytruncate.

--lua script#

Attach Lua configuration script with callbacks. A script that does not load refuses the command with exit 1, and the reason is printed — the parse error, or whichever filters or routes rule it broke — rather than only the fact.

-b#

Output received messages to stdout (bash mode).

-bp#

Output messages with runtime name prefix: [name] message

-bt#

Output messages with timestamp: [HH:MM:SS] message

-bpt , -btp#

Output messages with both timestamp and prefix: [HH:MM:SS] [name] message. Both spellings are accepted and mean the same thing; only -bpt was documented, so -btp worked and could not be looked up.

--max-connections n#

Limit maximum concurrent connections. New connections beyond this limit are immediately closed. 0 means unlimited (default). Alias: --max-conn.

--read-buffer size#

How much may be accumulated FROM one connection before it is refused, with K/M/G suffixes. Default 1M. The inbound twin of --write-buffer, and like it, every runtime has one.

Details

The largest single value inside that buffer is half of it, which leaves room for the framing around it. So the default gives a cache a 512K ceiling on any one value — and those were already the two numbers this was compiled with, 1 MiB of accumulation and 512 KB of value, so the halving is named here rather than introduced. An unconfigured runtime accepts exactly what it accepted before.

Raise it for a cache holding documents rather than fields: Redis's own proto-max-bulk-len defaults to 512M, a thousand times this. Lower it for a runtime facing the open internet, where the buffer is memory a client controls. Values under 64K are raised to it rather than refused, because the derived value ceiling would otherwise be under what an ordinary form post or JSON document needs.

It is per connection, and nothing bounds the sum but --max-connections, which defaults to 0 — no limit. Measured on a cache with 200 connections: one that has sent nothing costs about 13 KB, and one holding an unfinished command costs the whole of what it has sent, up to this buffer. So the figure to size against is --read-buffer × --max-connections, and at both defaults that product is unbounded: the ceiling is the worker's descriptor limit, over a million here. An unfinished command is not a malformed one and nothing refuses it — only its size is bounded, and only per connection.

A value past the ceiling is answered -ERR value is larger than this cache accepts (limit N bytes) and the connection is closed, which is what Redis does for a bulk length it will not take — the body was never read, so there is no framed position to continue from. It is deliberately NOT -ERR protocol error: the command was framed correctly and only its value was too big, and a client library told its framing is broken reconnects and sends the same value again. A length that genuinely does not parse still gets the protocol error.

One caveat, measured: the refusal is written and then the connection closed, so a client still sending when that happens receives an RST and Linux discards the queued reply. Overshoots up to about two megabytes read the reason; one eight times the ceiling does not. Raising the bound is the answer for a deployment that needs the larger values.

Editable on a running runtime, and the change takes at once: the bound is compared on every read and the value ceiling is derived at each parse, so nothing holds the old number.

--write-buffer size#

How much may be owed to ONE connection before the runtime stops waiting for it, with K/M/G suffixes. Default 8M. Every runtime has a write queue, so this applies to all four types — a client's queue is the one that fills when its server stops reading.

Details

This is arithmetic rather than a preference. The queue is per connection, so the bound multiplies:

100 streams        800 MB
1,000 streams        8 GB     (a box with 11 GiB serves about this many)
10,000 streams      80 GB     not possible

8M is right for a few large transfers and wrong by about sixty for many concurrent streams; nginx serves ten thousand with 32-64 KB apiece. Nothing could previously say which shape a runtime was, because these were two compile-time constants. Measured, 400 sends of 64 KB into a peer that is not reading: a default runtime takes 129 of them and one at --write-buffer 256K takes 5.

It is a throughput knob as well, and which direction helps is the same question read from the other side. A 1 MiB chunked response, against a C floor that puts the same bytes on the wire with one write(2) per chunk, in microseconds over that floor per request:

                8 streams    64 streams    RSS
128K             +75.7        +139.0        45 MB
256K             +51.6        +128.1        52 MB
1M               +17.6        +218.1        74 MB
8M (default)     +27.3        +234.0       106 MB

So a deep queue wins with few streams and loses with many: at 64 streams, dropping the default to 256K is 28 per cent more throughput for 22 per cent less CPU per request, and at 8 streams the same move costs 24 per cent.

The reason is the cache and not the queue, and the two settings measured against each other are the proof: same code, same bytes, the same number of copies, one number changed. CPU per MiB served at 64 streams, with the profile taken from the same window as the rate so that a component divides inside one run:

                total   memmove   kernel copy   page clearing
8M (default)     315      103          87            29
256K             254       40          43            30

Both copies halve. Ours is one memmove per byte either way and the kernel's _copy_from_iter is one copy per byte either way, so neither does less work — the bytes are closer. L2 is 4 MiB per core here and L3 is 16 MiB shared; at 64 streams the default owes up to about 69 MB at once, out of both, while 256K owes about 8 MB and stays in. A C floor doing the same one copy per byte, into a buffer it reuses, spends 29 and 21 on those two components, so what is left once the working set is accounted for is small.

This was measured the wrong way first and the wrong way is worth naming: a share from one profile multiplied by a total from another run. Each share was sound — 32.7 and 27.6 per cent of a core — but the core was doing different amounts of work in the two runs, so the product was a figure with no referent.

The sweep also measured 64K and got a figure 0.6 to 0.9 per cent from 128K, which is right: a value under 128K is raised to it, so those two arms are one buffer measured twice, and that spread is the harness repeating itself rather than a difference.

One number and not two: the pacing watermark that on_writable fires on is derived from this and never set beside it. A pair could be set inconsistently, and a watermark above the bound is a runtime that paces only after it has already closed the connection. A script reads the derived value as self.watermark(), which is a call rather than a field because the answer moves.

It is half the bound while the runtime is keeping up, and when the runtime is holding more than 8 MiB in total it becomes that budget divided by the live connections instead — never above the configured half, never below 64 KB, and back to the half once the backlog has been gone for 50 milliseconds. What the operator sets is the bound, which is memory and decides when a connection is closed; how deep a producer is allowed to run before it pauses is a cache question, because these bytes are written here and then read again by the kernel copying them into a socket.

Measured on a 1 MiB chunked response, seven interleaved passes, responses byte-identical in every arm: 4,480 responses a second at 16 streams against 5,273, and 3,634 at 64 against 4,221 — and unchanged inside the spread at 8 and at 128. Dividing by the connection count without asking whether anything was actually backed up was tried first and cost 19 per cent at 8 streams, where the queues never fill and the only effect is stopping a producer four times as often.

This does not bound memory. The peak is still the bound times the connections that reach it, because a bound that shrank under a live connection would close it for a backlog it had been allowed to build. For many clients at once that is still this flag's own job: 60 MB at --write-buffer 256K against 146 at the default, on the same load.

Values under 128K are raised to it rather than refused: the watermark is half the bound and the largest single entry these queues build is 64 KB, so a smaller bound is a runtime that cannot send one message. Editable on a running runtime, and the change reaches the script at once — the bound is read on every send rather than cached anywhere.

--rate-limit n#

Limit messages per second per connection using a token bucket algorithm. Excess messages are silently dropped (server); a cache answers error: rate limited, since its protocol has a way to say so; on a proxy the connection is closed instead, because a request dropped in silence leaves its client waiting for a response that is never coming — a hang rather than a refusal. The bucket starts full, so a connection may spend a whole second's allowance at once and then waits for it to refill. 0 means unlimited (default).

Details

Not accepted on a client, together with --max-connections and --idle-timeout. All three describe inbound traffic, and a client opens one connection outward and accepts none, so there is nothing for any of them to act on. They were taken and reported before — show answered "rate_limit": 5 on a runtime with no rate-limiting code at all, which tells an operator a control is in force that does not exist. Refused at create, edit and import alike; import writes the field without passing the flag parser, so a guard in one place is not a guard.

Refused rather than implemented, because each could be given a meaning and each meaning is a decision. An outbound throttle has to say what becomes of a message that may not go yet — queue it and report success for something that leaves in ten seconds, fail the send, or drop it. An idle timeout has to say what happens after the close, since a client reconnects the moment its connection is dropped.

On a proxy a token is charged per read completion rather than per HTTP request, which is the same event --global-rate-limit is charged on and the same one total_messages counts; a client that pipelines four requests into one segment therefore pays one token.

A client refuses the flag: it limits what arrives, and a client has nothing arriving from connections of its own.

--global-rate-limit n#

Limit total messages per second across all connections using a shared token bucket. Excess messages are silently dropped (server) or responded with an error (cache). 0 means unlimited (default).

Details

Refused on a client for --rate-limit's reason: it caps the total across all inbound connections, and a client has one outbound connection.

--idle-timeout duration#

Close connections that have been idle (no data received) for longer than this. A sweep timer runs every 30 seconds to check for idle connections. 0 means disabled (default). A bare number is seconds; a suffix of s, m, h, d or w spells seconds, minutes, hours, days or weeks (300 and 5m both work).

Details

This closes connections that are quiet, which is not the same as closing ones that are dead, and it is not needed for the second. Every accepted TCP connection is given TCP keepalive at 60/10/3 — a minute of silence, then three probes ten seconds apart — so a peer that loses power, or vanishes behind a NAT that forgot it, is reaped without any timeout being set. A websocket that says nothing for an hour is quiet and alive, and keepalive leaves it alone; only --idle-timeout closes that one. A unix listener is not given keepalive, having no peer that can disappear silently.

--congestion name#

The TCP congestion control every connection a server, a proxy, a cache or a storage accepts runs, by the kernel's name for it — bbr, cubic, reno — set once on the listener, which each accepted socket inherits. Without it the host's default (net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control) stands. A loss-based control such as cubic halves its rate at every lost packet; bbr paces to the path's measured bandwidth and holds it. One 32 MB download over 100 Mbit and a 50 ms round trip, three interleaved runs:

Details
loss   cubic              bbr
0%     10.21 MB/s         10.13 MB/s
1%     0.38-0.49 MB/s    9.76-9.87 MB/s
2%     0.26-0.27 MB/s    9.59-9.63 MB/s

The kernel decides what may be chosen: a process without CAP_NET_ADMIN only what net.ipv4.tcp_allowed_congestion_control lists, and only a control already loaded (modprobe tcp_bbr). A name it refuses fails the start, and the log says why; it is never quietly the default instead.

--drain#

Enable graceful shutdown. When stopping, the runtime closes its listener but flushes all pending write queues before closing connections.

Details

Refused on a client, which has no listener and no inbound connections: what a client owes its peer on the way down is a separate question from this one, and the flag did nothing there.

--cpus set#

The CPUs this runtime's I/O may run on. Accepts max, a range such as 0-3, or a list such as 0,1,2,3 whose elements may themselves be ranges (0-1,3). Default max, which applies no pinning at all — not a mask of the CPUs that are online now, so a CPU that comes online later is still available to the loop.

Details

A CPU this machine does not have, a descending range, or a set that comes out empty is refused when the runtime is created. It is never quietly rounded up to max: a config written for a sixteen-core machine and deployed on a four-core one would otherwise run nowhere near where its author believes, and every measurement taken afterwards would be measuring something else.

A ring's CPU set is fixed by the kernel when the ring is created, and a ring belongs to a process, not to a runtime: every runtime inside one daemon shares that daemon's ring. So this flag states what a runtime requires, and create refuses a requirement the ring it would run on does not meet, naming the socketley daemon flag or the SOCKETLEY_CPUS setting that would satisfy it. It cannot be changed with edit. The value in force is reported by socketley stats.

It is persisted with the runtime, and the same refusal is made again when a persisted runtime is restored: a daemon restarted without the setting that satisfied a runtime's requirement leaves that runtime failed, with the reason in the daemon log, rather than starting it on a ring that does not meet it and reporting the ring it got. A runtime that asked for nothing records nothing and is never refused for it.

--tls--cert file--key file--ca file#

All runtime types. Encrypt this runtime's transport. What that means depends on whether the role listens or dials.

Details

On a server, proxy or cache, TLS terminates on the runtime's own listening port, and --tls requires both --cert file (a PEM certificate, chain allowed) and --key file (its PEM private key) — a listener has to have something to terminate TLS with.

A cache terminates TLS exactly as a server does, and everything above the record layer is unchanged: RESP is still auto-detected from the first byte of the decrypted stream, so a Redis client speaks the protocol it always did with TLS switched on, and the line protocol works on the same port. This is what allows a cache to be reached across a network it does not trust.

On a client, TLS is dialled rather than terminated, and --tls on its own is the complete configuration: there is no listening port to hold a certificate, and the peer is verified against the system trust store by default. --cert file and --key file are optional there and mean the certificate this client presents when the peer asks for one (mutual TLS); half a pair is refused, because it would present nothing while the flags said otherwise.

--ca file means one thing on each role, because only some of them verify a peer they dialled. On a server or cache it enables mutual TLS: a client must then present a certificate signed by that CA, and one that does not is rejected during the handshake. On a proxy it is the trust store used to verify the certificate a backend presents — the proxy's own listener asks for client certificates with --client-ca file instead. On a client it is the trust store for the peer named by -t; without it the system store is used. See mTLS Flags under PROXY FLAGS.

A dialled connection — a client's target, a proxy's backend — is verified on two counts, and neither can be turned off. The chain must be signed by something in the trust store, and the certificate must be valid for the host that was dialled: the name in -t for a client, matched against the certificate's DNS SAN, or against its IP SAN for an address literal. The name checked is always the one configured, never one read back out of the certificate that arrived. TLS 1.2 is the minimum version. There is deliberately no skip-verify option: a TLS client that does not verify buys encryption against an eavesdropper and nothing at all against somebody in the path, while reporting itself as encrypted either way.

A listener speaks TLS 1.2 and 1.3. Over 1.2 it offers only ECDHE key exchange with AEAD ciphers, Mozilla's intermediate list, and it resumes a session from its own cache rather than from a ticket, whose key lives as long as the process and would open every session it ever sealed to whoever learned it.

Trust stores are read when the runtime starts, and a listener's certificate and key are looked at again every two seconds: replaced on disk — by --acme, certbot or a copy — they are taken up for the handshakes from then on, without a restart and without dropping a connection, once both load and match. A pair that does not is kept out, said once in the log, and the old one goes on serving. The certificate file is sent with every certificate in it, so a CA's intermediates go with the leaf. A certificate that cannot be loaded, a key that does not match it, and any incomplete combination (--tls without a key pair on a listener, a key pair or a trust store without --tls, half a client-certificate pair) are refused: the runtime goes to the failed state and nothing binds the port or dials the target. There is no fallback to cleartext on any path. A client whose peer fails verification drops the socket and re-dials on its usual backoff; it never retries in the clear.

These flags are refused on a client or a server combined with --udp (that would need DTLS), and on a server combined with --upstream (the upstream leg would still dial in cleartext). On a cache they are refused together with --replicate host:port — replication is not encrypted, so the pair would stream the whole dataset in the clear off a port that reports itself as encrypted. See TLS under LIMITATIONS.

--acme name[,name...]--acme-email address#

server, proxy, cache, storage. A certificate for the names from an ACME CA, Let's Encrypt unless SOCKETLEY_ACME_DIRECTORY names another, issued and renewed by the runtime itself: --acme turns on --tls and keeps the certificate and its key in state-dir/.acme/name/, for the first name. Until the CA has issued one, a self-signed certificate valid for a week stands in, so the listener starts at once; the issued one replaces it within seconds, and is renewed when it has less than thirty days left, tried again after a minute, then twice as long each time up to six hours, with the CA's reason in the log. A name reserved for examples, tests or local use (example.com, example.net, example.org, and anything under .example, .test, .invalid, .localhost, .local, .internal, .home.arpa or .alt) is not asked of Let's Encrypt, which issues for none of them: it keeps a self-signed certificate valid for a year, and the log says so. With SOCKETLEY_ACME_DIRECTORY set they are asked for like any other, since a CA of one's own may issue them. --acme-email is the account's contact, where the CA writes before a certificate expires.

Details

A runtime on port 443 proves its names over TLS-ALPN-01, on its own listener: the CA's handshake asks for acme-tls/1 by the name, is shown a challenge certificate for it, and no other handshake is, so a proxy on 443 alone is enough. Any other runtime proves them over HTTP-01: the CA asks http://name/.well-known/acme-challenge/token on port 80, and every socketley server, proxy and storage of the daemon answers that path on any port, for a token the daemon is waiting on, before it routes, serves or runs a script, so a runtime on port 80 — the proxy that redirects to HTTPS, say — is all it takes. Any other token goes where the path would have gone, so a site's own files there, as certbot's webroot writes them, are served as before. A name is a DNS name with a dot; an address is refused.

A wildcard, *.example.com, is proven over DNS-01, the one challenge that can: the answer goes to the daemon's dns runtimes as the TXT record of _acme-challenge.name (see Names runtimes are reached by under DNS FLAGS), the CA is told to look SOCKETLEY_ACME_DNS_WAIT seconds later, and the record is gone once it has. It needs a dns runtime of the same daemon that is authoritative for the zone, and, if the zone has secondaries, the time for them to take the new serial. SOCKETLEY_ACME_CHALLENGE=dns-01 proves every name that way, for a host whose port 80 is closed.

socketley create proxy web -p 443 --acme example.com,www.example.com \
    --acme-email ops@example.com --backend 127.0.0.1:8080 -s
socketley create proxy plain -p 80 --backend 127.0.0.1:8080 -s
--domain [name[,name...]]#

The names the runtime is reached by; with no name after it, the runtime's own (create server chat --domain is reached as chat). They are names a dns runtime with --publish answers for with this machine's addresses: a name without a dot is taken under each zone it serves (chat is chat.example.com for example.com), one with a dot as written, and *.name covers every name beneath. A runtime removed takes its names with it. On a storage runtime the flag is its own and also names the virtual hosts of its buckets (see STORAGE FLAGS), which are published with the wildcard beneath it. The names of --acme are published too.

-g name--group name#

Assign the runtime to a named group. Groups enable dynamic proxy backend discovery: a proxy using @groupname as a backend will route to all running members of that group at connection time. New group members are discovered automatically without restarting the proxy.

Details

A member joins its group when it is actually listening, not when it is created. For a runtime that runs in its own process this is a few milliseconds after create returns, because the port is bound in that process and the daemon publishes the member once the worker reports it. Until then the member is absent from the group rather than present and refusing connections — being routed to an address that is not accepting yet would trip the routing proxy's circuit breaker against a member that is merely young.

--listen unix:/path/to.sock#

Listen on an AF_UNIX socket instead of a TCP port. Taken by every runtime that listens — server, proxy, cache and storage; a client dials out and listens on nothing, so on one the flag is refused with a pointer at -t unix:, the connect side of the same socket. The other half of --backend unix:/path/to.sock under PROXY FLAGS, so a proxy and the backend it fronts can talk on one host without a loopback TCP stack between them — or serve its own front door on one.

Details

What it is worth, measured on a cache serving the same client over both, on Linux 7.2.2: a round trip falls from 10.64 to 6.57 microseconds, and throughput at pipeline depth 1 rises 2.2x to 2.4x. Most of that belongs to the kernel and not to this daemon — Redis over its own unix socket gains 2.0x on the same box, so any server on one machine can have it. TCP exists to make an unreliable link reliable, and over loopback there is no link — but sequence numbers, windows, retransmit timers, an skb per direction through IP, and netfilter walking every packet all run regardless. On a host running Docker, netfilter alone is 0.9 microseconds of that round trip. An AF_UNIX socket has none of it.

The saving is per message and not per operation, so a pipelining client sees much less of it: at depth 100 it is 0.016 microseconds an operation. That is still 1.25x here, because at that depth the cache's own per-message work is only about 8 microseconds and the saving is a quarter of it; Redis, whose per-message work is nearer 32 microseconds, gains 1.02x and may as well not bother.

Without --shards a runtime on a unix socket is one core; with it, each shard binds a node of its own, see below. Reach for it for a local sidecar.

Every unix stream socket on the data path has a 1 MiB send buffer. That is each one accepted off a --listen unix: node or a companion node, the one a proxy dials to a --backend unix: or to a local runtime's node, and the one a client dials with -t unix:. On a unix stream socket the sender's buffer is the whole of the flow control, an accepted socket inherits nothing from its listener, and the kernel's default is 208 KB. socketley asks for 512 KiB, which the kernel doubles; the request is capped at net.core.wmem_max, which is 212992 on a stock kernel, so there the buffer is 416 KB. Measured on one connection of pipelined 64 KB GETs: a reader that pays for each read (a Python client reading 4 MiB at a time) went from 2.2 to 3.0 GB/s, with the cache spending 41% less CPU per byte; a TCP proxy in front of a local cache, reaching it over its node, 10% more; a reader that reads cheaply was already at about 10 GB/s, bound by the cache's core, and is unchanged, as are small requests. It is a ceiling and not an allocation: an idle connection holds nothing in it, and a connection whose reader has stopped holds at most 1 MiB in the kernel, where it held 208 KB.

Mutually exclusive with -p, with --udp (that would be a unix datagram socket, which is a different thing and is not this), with --tls (a unix socket is not on a network; the permissions on the node are what restrict it), and on a cache with --cluster (cluster members advertise ports out of a formula, and RESP has no way to write a filesystem path as a node address). Each combination is refused at start with the reason in the daemon log, rather than one of the two winning quietly.

--shards is not among them. A sharded runtime binds one node per shard, name#i.sock, which is the rule the daemon's companion nodes already follow. N processes binding one path would unlink each other's node, and only the last to bind would stay reachable; N paths are N listeners. See Sharding under SERVER FLAGS for which node a caller should pick, which is a real question on a cache and not one on a server.

The path must be absolute and shorter than 108 bytes, which is what the kernel's sun_path holds. Both are refused when the flag is read — the kernel truncates a long path silently, and a trimmed path names a different socket, very possibly a real one belonging to something else.

Under --shards the rule is applied to the longest node, not to the path as typed. name#15.sock is three bytes longer than name.sock, so a path that fits can still be a set that does not — and the shard that did not fit would fail at its bind with the earlier shards already serving. It is refused at configuration instead, naming the longest node rather than the one that was typed.

The socket node is created 0600. Connecting to a unix socket needs write permission on the node, so leaving that to the umask means a daemon running under umask 0 publishes a listener anybody on the machine can talk to. There is deliberately no flag to widen it: a peer running as another user cannot connect, and the way round that today is a parent directory the operator owns and controls.

The node is removed when the runtime stops. One left behind by a daemon that was killed, or by a machine that lost power, is taken over on the next start — but only after connecting to it to check that nobody is serving it. A path that something IS serving is refused, so a second runtime cannot take a live socket away from the first.

A server listening this way is reachable as a proxy backend both by its path and by its runtime name. It is deliberately NOT offered as an @group member: a group's members are resolved to network addresses per request, and an entry the group path cannot dial would take a turn of the round-robin and answer 503 with it.

socketley create server app --listen unix:/run/app.sock --http /srv/www -s
socketley create proxy  gw  -p 8080 --backend app -s
socketley create cache  kv  --listen unix:/run/kv.sock -s   # redis-cli -s works

sections.title: The node beside the port
sections.html:
A server or an unsharded cache that listens on a TCP port also listens on an AF_UNIX node, created by the daemon in a directory named after its own socket — <socket>.rt/— and named after the runtime. Named after the socket and not simply placed beside it, because the default socket is /tmp/socketley.sock and every user on the machine shares that directory. Nothing has to be configured for it, and nothing about the port changes: a runtime created with -p 9000 is reached on 9000 from anywhere, exactly as before. The node is additional, never a replacement — nothing outside this machine can reach one.

It exists for one caller: another runtime on this machine. A proxy whose backend is written as a runtime name takes it. So does one whose backend is written as an address — but only while a running runtime publishes exactly that host and port. A name asks for the runtime and may choose how to reach it; an address asks for the address, so the substitution holds only while the two are the same thing. Move the runtime to another port and the address means what it says again.

What it is worth, measured on this box on Linux 7.2.2 with the same proxy in front of the same server and only the backend leg differing: a request falls from 25.33 to 22.68 microseconds, and the whole process tree spends 4.0 microseconds less CPU on each one — 12 of 12 interleaved passes, median of the per-pass differences. The CPU saves more than the clock does, which is what a saving under load looks like: a serial round trip waits on wakeups, and the freed CPU has nowhere to go until there is a second request wanting it.

The node is 0600 in a directory the daemon creates 0700. Only the user the daemon runs as can reach it. Measured: another local user reaches the port and is refused on the node with EACCES, and cannot list the directory or create a node in it either. The port is not narrowed by any of this — it is exactly as open as it was — but the leg between two runtimes no longer travels over something every local user could also connect to.

The directory is checked and not merely created. A mkdir(2) answering EEXIST says a directory is there and nothing about whose it is, so the daemon stats it: anything that is not a directory it owns, with no group or other access, turns companion nodes off for the whole daemon and says so once in the log. Without that check a stranger could create the directory first and hold a live node at a path the daemon was about to publish — and a live node is one the bind refuses to take, which would leave the path published and served by them.

Two things it takes away, both worth knowing before relying on them:

  • A firewall rule on loopback does not apply. nftables and iptables see packets, and an AF_UNIX socket produces none. A rule that drops traffic to a runtime's port does not stop another runtime reaching it over the node.

  • tcpdump -i lo shows nothing. The proxy writes one line to the daemon log per backend at start, naming the path it will use; that line is the only evidence the node was taken.

A runtime gets no node when it is neither a server nor a cache, when it has no port — one already on --listen unix: has nothing to add — when it is --udp, or when its listener is TLS, since a cleartext node beside an encrypted port would undo what the port was configured to give. A proxy keeps its port alone, and so does a cache with --shards: a path is one node and N processes would unlink each other's, which is why --listen gives each shard a node of its own. One rule decides both what the daemon publishes and what a runtime binds, so a type that is not wired to a listener is never advertised as having one — a path published into thin air is a backend that is simply down. A proxy configured with backend TLS keeps TCP for the same reason, rather than quietly dropping the encryption it was asked for.

sections.title: Between runtimes on one machine
sections.html:
Everything one runtime asks of another — socketley.send, self.route, and a server's --cache name — used to travel through the daemon: up one control socket and down the other. The daemon still carries the first such crossing, and then introduces the two processes to each other with a socket pair neither had before; the ones after it go straight across.

There is nothing to configure and nothing to see from outside. The pair has no path in the filesystem, so it can be neither connected to nor squatted — only the two processes that were handed the ends can use it. The daemon logs one line naming the pair when it introduces them, and socketley stats name reports peer_links, peer_direct and peer_relayed so a crossing that went the long way can be told from one that went across.

What it is worth, measured with a server posting every cache command to a cache runtime, the two arms differing only in whether they were introduced: a round trip falls from 31.60 to 21.14 microseconds and the process tree spends 10.75 microseconds less CPU per command — 12 of 12 interleaved passes, median of the per-pass differences. A third of the round trip was the daemon.

A crossing falls back to the daemon whenever the link is not usable, so nothing depends on it: a link that never forms, or one whose peer has gone, costs the speed it would have saved and nothing else. Routed connections are pinned to whichever path they opened on and keep it for their whole life, because a message that changed route mid-stream could arrive ahead of one sent before it.

sections.title: Which port a runtime is on
sections.html:
ls, ps, stats and the metrics endpoint report the port a runtime binds — which is not always the one it was configured with. A runtime created without -p takes its type's default (8000 for a server, 8080 for a proxy, 9000 for a cache), and those surfaces used to print the configured zero: the PORT column read -, ps --json and stats read 0, and no command would tell an operator which port their runtime was actually answering on.

show is deliberately not in that list. Its output is the state document, and it goes back in through import, so writing the default into it would pin a runtime that had been left to take whichever default its type has.

A runtime that binds no port at all — a client, a --listen unix: listener, a process registered with attach, or a server reachable only through its owner — reports 0.

sections.title: One address, one runtime
sections.html:
A runtime is refused a start when another runtime on this daemon is already serving the address it would bind — a TCP port, a UDP port, or a --listen unix: path. The refusal names both runtimes and reaches the terminal, and on the boot restore it names both in the daemon log.

The kernel will not refuse it. Every listener is opened with SO_REUSEPORT, because that is the whole mechanism behind --shards: N worker processes of one runtime binding one port and letting the kernel hand each connection to one of them. A second runtime claiming the same number is indistinguishable from a second shard, so the bind succeeds and the connections split between the two at random. Measured before this was refused, on two servers created on one port: both started, both listened, nothing was logged, and twenty messages arrived nine and eleven.

What is still accepted, because it is not one address: --udp beside TCP, which are separate namespaces in the kernel — a datagram server and a stream server on the same number are two listeners that never meet; a restart, which passes through stopped and takes back its own port, since the rule reads state and not configuration; --shards, whose workers are one runtime; and a runtime that binds nothing at all — a client, a process registered with attach, or a server reachable only through its owner.

A clustered cache holds more than one: the configured port, and base+1..base+N for the shards, which is the formula CLUSTER SLOTS publishes. A runtime that had taken one of those would be sent keys it does not hold.

The refused runtime is left in the state it was in — created or stopped, not failed — because nothing was built and nothing broke. Stop the runtime named in the refusal, or give one of the two an address of its own.

sections.title: SERVER FLAGS
sections.html:
--mode mode#

Message flow direction: inout (bidirectional, default), in (receive only), out (send only), master (one client claims master, only master's messages are broadcast).

Details

A direction is not an answer. In inout with no script, every message is repeated to other connections and not to the one that sent it, so a single client talking to itself hears nothing and a second client hears everything. See --send-to.

Relayed messages are held for a connection until the server knows what protocol it speaks, and delivered once it does — through that protocol's framing, so a WebSocket client receives them as frames rather than as raw text. A connection is classified by its first message. This matters because the alternative is a corrupted handshake: a client whose opening move is an HTTP request or a WebSocket upgrade would otherwise be sent relay bytes in front of the response it is waiting for.

A client that connects and sends nothing is served anyway, after a delay of at most 250 ms, and is treated as a plain line-delimited TCP client from then on. Such a client has nothing outstanding for the relayed bytes to arrive in front of, so there is no handshake to protect. The delay is paid once per connection, not once per message: everything relayed after the first delivery goes out immediately. A client that has sent part of a request and not finished it is not covered by this and is held until its request completes, however long that takes — that one is waiting for an answer, and the answer must come first.

The hold is capped at 64 KB per connection. Past that the oldest held messages are dropped to make room, so a client that stays silent through more than 64 KB of relay traffic in under 250 ms receives the most recent messages and not the whole backlog. The cap is per connection and applies only before classification; once a connection is classified, relay traffic goes straight to its write queue and the ordinary --max-connections and write-queue limits govern instead.

A connection that speaks HTTP is not in the relay set and receives no relayed messages at all, from the request that identifies it as HTTP onward. HTTP has no framing for a message the server sends on its own: before a response such a message replaces the status line the client is parsing for, and between two keep-alive requests it is read as the status line of the next response. There is no point at which it would be well formed, so it is not sent rather than delayed. A WebSocket connection is unaffected — it arrives over the same HTTP, but once upgraded it has framing for server-initiated messages and receives everything. That is the supported way for a browser client to receive relay traffic.

A connection that speaks RESP is excluded on the same grounds and from the command that identifies it as RESP onward. RESP2 matches replies to commands by their order on the stream and by nothing else, so a relayed message is read as the reply to whatever that client asks next; and what the relay writes is the message text, not a RESP value, so a Redis client reads a plain letter where a type byte belongs and answers with a protocol error. Encoding it as a value would not help, because the only channel RESP2 has for a server-initiated value is pub/sub, which the client enters with SUBSCRIBE and which a server runtime does not implement. A RESP client on a relaying server still receives its own replies, anything a script addresses to it by client id, and the answers to cache <command> messages; what it no longer receives is other clients' traffic.

--send-to who[,who...]#

Who the built-in path answers when no script does, as a comma separated set of recipients: sender (the connection the message came from), others (every other connection, the master excepted), master (the master connection, which only --mode master ever has).

Details

The recipients are disjoint, so they compose: --send-to sender,others reaches everyone including the sender, and --send-to sender,master answers whoever spoke and sends the master a copy. There is no all for that reason — sender,others already says it, and one behaviour under two spellings is the mistake this flag was built so as not to repeat.

Unset keeps what the mode has always done: inout answers others, and master drops what a non-master says.

In --mode master the flag decides what happens to a NON-master's message; the master's own still reaches everyone else, which is what the mode is. --send-to master forwards prefixed — the sender's descriptor stays in front of the line so the master can tell two clients apart. --send-to others,master is a moderated room the master reads along with.

Refused rather than accepted and ignored, per recipient: in and out answer nobody at all, and master names a connection no other mode has.

In inout, and for the master's own message in master, a script's on_message takes precedence over every recipient: when it is defined, nothing is sent automatically and self.send or self.broadcast decides. What a non-master says in master mode has never reached on_message at all — only on_client_message, which does not suppress anything — so there the recipients apply whether or not a script is loaded.

Before this flag existed, UDP and TCP disagreed: a UDP sender received its own datagram back and a TCP sender did not. others is now what both do unset, and --send-to sender,others is the old UDP behaviour under a name.

--udp#

Use UDP instead of TCP. The server binds a single SOCK_DGRAM socket. Peers are auto-registered on first datagram. Each datagram is one message (no line-parsing). Broadcast sends to all known peers via sendto(). Not available for cache or proxy.

Details

An exposed UDP server can reflect traffic. With no Lua handler every datagram is relayed to every other peer that has sent one, and a peer is learned from a source address, which a sender can forge; keep such a server on a trusted network or give it a Lua handler that decides.

Refused with --mode master, which this page called incompatible for a long time while nothing enforced it. Master mode claims a connection as the master and a datagram is not a connection, so the pair is not merely useless: a datagram beginning master reached that code with no sender and took the worker down with it.

--master-pw password#

Static password for master mode authentication. A client sends "master <password>" to claim master role. Only one master at a time; master is released on disconnect. Alternatively, use the on_master_auth(client_id, password) Lua callback for dynamic authentication.

Details

Failed attempts are counted per source address. A connection is refused at accept, before a byte is read, once that address has failed ten attempts within sixty seconds; the count decays after sixty seconds of quiet. This is a property of master mode and not of this flag — it applies whichever of the two authenticators is in use.

Requires --mode master, and is refused without it. The master prefix is read in exactly one place, so in any other mode the password is not a credential: it is an ordinary message, and a client that sends it has its password relayed to every other connection verbatim.

--no-master-pw#

(edit only.) Remove the password from a server that has one, which is what makes leaving master mode possible — the pair above is refused as a set, so a mode change alone would be refused while the password remained. It has a flag of its own because passing an empty string to --master-pw cannot express it: the daemon receives one line and splits it on whitespace, so an empty argument does not survive the wire and arrives as the flag with nothing after it.

--origins list#

The web origins, besides the server's own, whose pages may open a WebSocket here, comma-separated, such as https://app.example.com; * admits any. A handshake whose Origin is neither listed nor the Host it was sent to (or the X-Forwarded-Host of a proxy in front) is answered 403 Forbidden and closed, so a page on another site cannot drive the server, or the cache linked to it, through the browser of someone who can reach it. A client that sends no Origin, which is any client but a browser, is not affected.

--http directory#

Serve static files from the given directory over HTTP. When a browser makes a plain HTTP GET request (without a WebSocket upgrade header), the server responds with the requested file. GET / serves index.html. HTML files (.html, .htm) automatically get a WebSocket connection script injected before </head>.

Details

Note that this modifies the file it serves. Every .html and .htm response is rewritten on its way out, so a directory holding documents this server did not author — uploads, a generated report, a third-party page — is delivered altered, with a script that opens a WebSocket back to this runtime. There is no flag to turn it off; if that is not wanted, serve those files from something else. Content-Type is detected from the file extension. Every file answer carries an ETag of the file's inode, modification time and size, and a request whose If-None-Match names it is answered 304 with no body; no Last-Modified is sent, so a browser asks again on every load rather than trusting a copy it guessed was fresh, and a changed or replaced file is always sent anew. WebSocket upgrades continue to work as before on the same port. Only GET requests are served; other HTTP methods fall through to raw TCP handling.

Range requests. Every whole-file answer carries Accept-Ranges: bytes, and a request with a Range field is answered 206 Partial Content with Content-Range stating the file's whole length and Content-Length stating the slice. That is what lets a media player seek, and what lets an interrupted download resume — without it a player scrubs by downloading from the beginning, and Safari will not play <video> at all. All three forms are served:

Range: bytes=0-499      the first 500 bytes
Range: bytes=500-       from 500 to the end
Range: bytes=-500       the last 500 bytes

An end past the file is clamped to the last byte. A range starting at or past the end is 416 Range Not Satisfiable, carrying Content-Range: bytes */<length> — which is how a client that was not told the length learns it.

Two requests are answered with the whole file instead, both deliberately. A multi-range request (bytes=0-9,20-29) needs a multipart/byteranges body, which this does not produce; RFC 9110 14.2 permits ignoring the field, and the whole file is more useful than a wrong slice. And a range on .html or .htm is ignored because the injected script above changes the body's length, so a byte offset into the file is not an offset into what is served — those responses do not claim Accept-Ranges either, rather than inviting a seek that cannot be honoured.

Concurrency of the zero-copy path. A file is sent with sendfile(2) from the event loop, on a socket made non-blocking for that call alone, so no pipe is held and nothing caps how many go at once; measured against the io_uring splice it replaced, a 2 MiB file costs 85 us of CPU instead of 158 and 64 slow readers hold no kernel threads instead of 64. A window not in the page cache is spliced through a pipe instead, so the loop never waits on the disk, and what follows is about that pipe. A file used to be sent with splice(2) through a pipe, which keeps the bytes out of user space entirely. That pipe used to be one per runtime, so exactly one connection at a time could take the path and everything else fell back to a read into memory followed by a write. Measured on 4 MiB files, seven interleaved passes of each build:

concurrent   before      after     factor
1            2.9 ms      2.9 ms     0.98
2           11.9 ms      4.2 ms     2.80
4           26.1 ms      5.3 ms     4.97
8           55.8 ms     10.5 ms     5.33

Each connection now makes its own pipe. How many exist at once is a budget in bytes and not a count — 64 MB of kernel pipe, divided by the pipe size, which follows --write-buffer capped at 1 MB. So the default allows 64, and a runtime configured small because it serves many streams gets MORE pipes out of the same budget rather than fewer. Past the count the read path serves the remainder exactly as it did before.

A file goes this way from 64 KiB on a plaintext connection, but only a window out of the page cache reaches for a pipe, so a server of warm images never sits against this budget; one that does gets the read path, as before.

That boundary is worth knowing, because the fallback is not merely slower. Worker throughput and RSS on 4 MiB files:

                     at/below the count      past it
default (64)         12.7-14.2 GB/s          1.20 GB/s
                     RSS 35 MB               RSS 234 MB
--write-buffer 512K  12.3-14.0 GB/s at 128 concurrent, RSS 36 MB

The read path allocates the WHOLE file per request, which is why memory there follows concurrency times file size while the pipes do not: the kernel fills a pipe's buffer as it is used. That is also why the count is 64 and not the 8 it was first set to — the pipes cost less than the fallback they avoid, and 8 put the boundary at about ten concurrent requests.

On a TLS listener there is no zero-copy path at all, and this is the bound to know before serving large files over one. Splicing would hand the peer plaintext in the middle of an encrypted stream, so every request takes the read path whatever the pipe budget says. Measured, worker RSS on a 256 MB file:

plaintext, one request        +2 MB          (splice)
TLS, one request            505 MB          about twice the file
TLS, three concurrent     1,250 MB

Twice, because the file is read into memory and the response is then assembled around it — the same doubling recorded for a 400 MiB .html, where it came to 1219 MiB. It is held for the duration of the request, and it is the client that decides how many such requests there are: ten concurrent 256 MB requests would be about 5 GB.

--http-cache bounds the multiplication but not the size. The file is held once and shared, so concurrency stops mattering, at the cost of holding it permanently from startup — measured at 154 MB for a 64 MB file, which is the file plus the two prebuilt responses. Otherwise keep the files a TLS listener serves small, or put a plaintext listener behind something else that terminates TLS.

The repair is a read path that works in bounded pieces, as the request side now does with on_http_body, rather than one allocation the size of whatever was asked for. That is a change to the most intricate function in this path and is not made here.

A slice is never stored in the revalidation map and never answered from it. The map is keyed by path and holds the whole file's response, so a stored 206 would answer every later request for that path with one reader's slice and that reader's Content-Range.

The client's Connection request header decides whether the connection is reused, with the HTTP version supplying only the default (keep-alive for 1.1, close for 1.0). A request carrying Connection: close is answered with Connection: close and the server then shuts down its own write side first, so the 60-second TIME-WAIT that follows is held on the server's fixed listening port instead of on one of the client's ephemeral ports. The header is parsed token-wise and case-insensitively, so Connection: close, TE counts as close.

Without --http-cache this is the development mode, and a file edited on disk is picked up by the next request. It reaches that without re-reading the file every time: the response is kept in memory and one statx(2) per request decides whether it is still the file's response. The check is on the device, the inode number, the size and the modification time together — the inode number is part of it because writing a new file and renaming it over the old one, which is what mv, cp, git checkout and most editors actually do, leaves the size and can be given back the old timestamp exactly.

The memory this uses is bounded, unlike --http-cache's, because it fills from whatever is requested rather than from a directory the operator can see the size of before starting: once the kept responses reach 64 MiB in total no further file is added, and the per-file cap depends on whether the connection asking has a faster path available at all.

plaintext, not .html    64 KiB   anything larger goes by sendfile instead
TLS, or an .html         1 MiB   neither has a sendfile arm

That split is measured rather than tidy. A kept response is sent by copying it into the socket; sendfile sends the page cache by reference and copies nothing, but costs a call and a descriptor of its own. One core, interleaved, in us of CPU a request, kept against sendfile: 4.7 against 7.9 at 8 KiB, 10.4 against 11.4 at 64 KiB, 15.6 against 14.3 at 128 KiB and 27.8 against 23.9 at 256 KiB — so past 64 KiB keeping a file makes serving it dearer, and costs the map twice its size besides.

A TLS connection cannot sendfile at all, since that would hand the peer plaintext in the middle of an encrypted stream, and an .html has a script injected into it — so for those two the larger cap stands, and there the map is what keeps a file from being read, and allocated, once per request.

A file that is not kept is not read either, outside those two cases: it goes from the page cache to the socket without passing through this process. See SOCKETLEY_HTTP_REVALIDATE to switch the whole mechanism off, which also puts every size back on the copying path.

--http-cache#

When used with --http, reads all files into memory at startup instead of consulting the filesystem on each request. Faster for production, and the difference from plain --http is one statx(2) per request. The cache is rebuilt on reload-lua, and only then: a file edited on disk is not picked up, which is the reason to use this flag and the reason not to.

--compress#

With --http, send a file's compressed copy beside it, made by the site's build — app.css.br or app.css.gz for app.css — to a client whose Accept-Encoding takes that coding, br before gzip, with Content-Encoding and the copy's own ETag; every file answer then says Vary: Accept-Encoding. Never a copy older than its file, one for a range, one beside a page (whose copy lacks the injected script), an image, a video, a woff font, a zip or a pdf. A copy asked for by its own name is sent as itself. With --http-cache the copies are kept at start beside the files, judged against them then. The same measurement as the proxy's: a page's 3.8 MB of scripts over 10 Mbit and 50 ms in 0.97 s rather than 3.51. Nothing is compressed or decompressed by the server. Each file is held twice, once with a Connection: keep-alive response header and once with Connection: close, so that a cache hit stays a refcount bump and still answers with the header the client asked for.

-u host:port--upstream host:port#

Add an outbound upstream connection. The server connects to the specified host:port on startup and auto-reconnects with exponential backoff (1s–16s) if the connection drops. Multiple -u flags may be specified, or multiple addresses separated by semicolons (e.g. -u "feed:9000;cache:6379"). Each upstream gets a stable 1-based conn_id for use in Lua callbacks.

Details

Upstream Lua callbacks:

on_upstream(conn_id, data)#

Called for each newline-delimited message received from an upstream.

on_upstream_connect(conn_id)#

Called when an upstream connects (including reconnects).

on_upstream_disconnect(conn_id)#

Called when an upstream disconnects.

Upstream Lua actions:

self.upstream_send(conn_id, msg)#

Send a message to a specific upstream.

self.upstream_broadcast(msg)#

Send a message to all connected upstreams.

self.upstreams()#

Returns a table of currently connected upstream conn_ids.

--cache name#

Link this server to an existing cache runtime. Clients can then send "cache <command>" messages (e.g. "cache set foo bar", "cache get foo") which are executed against the linked cache and the response returned to the sender only. Normal messages are still processed according to the server's mode.

Details

The link also archives: every ordinary message is written to that cache. A message that is not a cache command is stored under an auto-incrementing integer key — 1, 2, 3 and on — as well as being handled by the server's mode. So two clients saying hello and world to a linked server leave get 1 answering hello and get 2 answering world. The counter is per server and starts again when the server restarts, so a --persistent cache keeps growing across restarts while keys are overwritten from 1 upward. Link a cache to a server only when that archive is wanted; a server that merely wants its clients to be able to reach a cache pays for a write per message.

The command is not executed on the connection that asked for it. The server hands it to the daemon and answers when the reply comes back, one turn of the event loop later, so a cache command costs a round trip that the same command typed at the cache's own port does not. See Cache Access via Server below for what that guarantees and what it costs.

sections.title: Sharding
sections.html:
--shards N#

Serve this server from N worker processes instead of one, sharing the listening socket through SO_REUSEPORT. The kernel gives each incoming connection to one of them. 1 to 64; the default is 1, which is what every server was before this flag was offered here.

A runtime is one process and therefore one event loop on one core. This is the only way to give a single server more than that.

With or without --lua. A scripted server used to refuse this flag, because the three things a script can ask about its clients were answered per PROCESS: on four shards self.connections() reported a quarter of them, self.broadcast reached a quarter of them, and self.clients() listed a quarter of them — as descriptors, so an id from one shard named a different socket on another. None of it was reported.

Each of those now crosses a shard boundary. self.connections() sums every shard's own published figure out of a shared mapping, with no round trip. self.broadcast and socketley.send addressed to this runtime reach every shard's clients, once each. self.clients() lists the whole runtime — this shard's descriptors, plus a stable handle for each client a sibling holds — and self.send on one of those handles reaches the shard that owns it.

Per-connection state is per shard, and that is what sharding means. A connection belongs to exactly one shard, so every callback about it runs there and nowhere else. on_connect for a client a sibling accepted fired in that sibling, and on_message for it will too. A script therefore holds no state for the ids self.clients() hands it from another shard: it can name them, count them and send to them, and it has never seen them arrive. Design the script for that — keep cross-connection state in a cache runtime, which every shard reaches, rather than in a Lua table at file scope, which each shard has its own copy of.

self.route works from a shard. Routing hands a live client to another runtime, which answers it while this shard keeps the socket and relays the bytes; the target is reached across the process boundary as from any worker, so --shards changes nothing about it. A routed client belongs to the shard that accepted it, like every other connection. unroute, get_route and owner_send read this shard's own tables.

What it bought, measured. One server runtime in --http mode with --http-cache, driven by socketley_bench proxy http-keepalive over 64 keep-alive connections; seven interleaved passes, median of the per-pass ratios. The cores are the SERVER processes' own — daemon plus workers, from /proc/<pid>/stat — and not the box's, because a box-wide figure includes the benchmark client and at this concurrency the client is the larger half of it.

shardsthroughputcoresper core
1126,497 req/s0.99127,775 req/s
8451,097 req/s4.7894,372 req/s

3.57x at eight shards, with the per-pass ratios spread from 3.18x to 4.26x.

That figure is a server's, and does not transfer to a cache. A server's shards are interchangeable, so every one of them answers every request. A cache's are not: the shard a connection lands on relays every key it does not own, and behind one address that is (N-1)/N of them. Measured at four shards that is 1.75x rather than a server's 3.57x, and at two it is 1.05x for 1.91 cores. See CACHE FLAGS for the table.

One shard is exactly one core. 0.99 of one, at every concurrency tried, while the machine had fifteen more sitting idle. That is the whole case for this flag stated as a measurement: a server does not run out of machine, it runs out of the single event loop it is allowed.

Per-core efficiency falls by about a quarter, and that is the price. 127,775 req/s per core at one shard against 94,372 at eight. Sharding buys throughput with cores, not with efficiency; if the machine has cores that are otherwise idle that is a good trade, and if it does not, this flag makes things worse rather than better. Do not set more shards than the machine has cores to give them.

Measure with enough connections to feed the shards, or the flag looks worse than it is. The same eight shards driven by only 16 connections read 294,917 req/s and 2.54x — not because they were slower but because they were starved: the arm used 4.12 cores where the 64-connection run used 4.78, and SO_REUSEPORT hands out whole connections, so sixteen over eight shards is two apiece with an uneven tail and the slowest shard gates the pass. A shard count above the client's concurrency measures the client. The load is balanced per connection, not per request. SO_REUSEPORT picks a shard when the connection is accepted and never revisits it, so one heavy long-lived connection makes one shard hot while the others idle, and the spread over a small number of connections is uneven — eight connections over four shards were measured landing 3/2/2/1. Sharding helps a server carrying many comparable connections; it does nothing for a server carrying one big one.

The surface still answers about the runtime, not the shard. ls shows one entry, stats reports the connection count summed across the shards and labels each shard's detail text, stop and remove take all of them down, and the count is persisted so a daemon restart brings back the number that was asked for. The count may be changed with edit only while the runtime is stopped, for the same reason -p may.

--shards gives each shard a node of its own. SO_REUSEPORT is not what a unix socket does — N processes binding one path would unlink each other's node and only the last would be reachable — so the path is not shared. A base of /run/app.sock becomes /run/app#0.sock, /run/app#1.sock, and so on, one per shard, and a caller picks any of them. A base with no .sock on the end gets the index appended instead.

Refused only when the longest of those names would not fit: the kernel's limit is on the node, and a shard whose name is truncated is a shard nothing can reach. The refusal names that longest member.

See Sharding under PROXY FLAGS for the fuller treatment of the flag.

sections.title: Multi-Protocol Auto-Detection
sections.html:
Server connections automatically detect the protocol from the first bytes received. No flags are needed — all four protocols coexist on the same port:

TCP (newline-delimited text)#

Default. Lines terminated by \en are delivered as messages.

HTTP#

Detected when the first bytes are a valid HTTP method (GET, POST, etc.). Requests are handled by the on_http_request Lua callback if defined, or by the static file server if --http is set, or responded with 404 otherwise. HTTP/1.1 keep-alive is supported, and an explicit Connection request header overrides the version's default — see --http for what the server does with it.

WebSocket#

Detected when an HTTP request contains Upgrade: websocket. The server completes the RFC 6455 handshake and transparently frames/deframes messages. The on_websocket callback fires after the upgrade. A browser page from another origin is refused with 403 unless --origins lists it. A text message that is not valid UTF-8 fails its connection with close code 1007 and never reaches a script; a fragmented message is checked once it is whole. A message the server relays without a script — to other clients, back to its sender, or to the master — goes out as the kind of frame it arrived in, text or binary. A message a script sends goes out as text when it is valid UTF-8 and as binary otherwise, as does a line relayed from a TCP client.

RESP (Redis protocol)#

Detected when the first byte is *. Useful for cache-linked servers or custom RESP-based protocols. Like an HTTP connection and for the same reason, a RESP connection is not in the relay set: it is answered, but it is not sent other clients' messages. See --mode under SERVER FLAGS.

How much it waits for before deciding. The tests above read four bytes — every HTTP method is matched on four characters, the RESP markers on two — so a connection that has sent fewer than that is normally left to send more.

A completed line is the exception, and it has to be: a client that writes hi\en and waits to be answered will not send a fourth byte until it is, so waiting for one would be waiting for something that only arrives after the answer. A line that ended inside four bytes cannot be an HTTP method — each is four characters and none contains a newline — so the protocol is decided there and then, as RESP if the first two bytes say so and as TCP otherwise. Short lines are ordinary input on a line protocol and are delivered like any other.

This is about the first line only. Once a connection's protocol is known, lines of any length are delivered as they arrive.

Browser example, from a page the server serves itself or one --origins lists:

const ws = new WebSocket("ws://localhost:9000");
ws.onmessage = e => console.log(e.data);
ws.send("hello");
