sections.title: Request Framing
sections.html:
The server frames an HTTP request by exactly the rules the proxy uses, and they are the same rules because they are the same code. A request whose header block gives no answer, or two answers, to "how long is the body" is answered 400 Bad Request and its connection is closed. That happens when the block contains any of:

  • a bare LF or a bare CR — every line must end with CRLF

  • whitespace between a field name and its colon (Content-Length : 6)

  • a continuation (obs-fold) line, i.e. one starting with a space or tab

  • a field line with no colon, or with an empty field name

  • more than one Content-Length field, or a Content-Length together with a Transfer-Encoding

  • a Content-Length that is not a whole decimal number (Content-Length: 6x)

A tab is legal optional whitespace around a field value — a Content-Length separated from its colon by a tab rather than a space is an ordinary request and is served, as is a value with trailing whitespace. Values reach on_http_request with that whitespace removed from both ends.

Transfer-Encoding depends on what the script asked for, and on which coding it is.

  • chunked alone, with a script that defines on_http_body: decoded, and the body delivered in pieces like any other. There is no length to bound it by, which is what chunked is for.

  • chunked alone, without that callback: still 501 Not Implemented, because nothing is going to read the body incrementally and a body whose end this end cannot find is refused rather than treated as though it had none.

  • gzip, chunked: 501 even with the callback. Chunked is the final coding, so the chunk sizes do delimit it, and the bytes inside are still compressed — taking the framing off and handing them on as the body would hand on gzip and call it the body.

  • A coding that is not chunked at all, such as gzip by itself: 400 Bad Request, because nothing can say where the body ends.

So a chunked request through a socketley proxy to a socketley server is served when the server's script takes bodies and answered 501 when it does not; the proxy forwards the framing verbatim either way and relays whatever comes back. Content-Length remains the simpler form and is what a client that knows its own length should send.

Why a server bothers with any of this, when it is the last recipient and has nobody to disagree with: it usually is not. The moment anything sits in front of it — this proxy, or any other — there are two parsers reading one byte stream, and a header a strict parser ignores and a lenient one honours moves the boundary between one request and the next. Since the server serves pipelined requests without waiting for another read, a body it wrongly measured as empty is read as the next request: one message in, two answered, and the client chooses what the second one says. Compliant clients emit none of these shapes.

A request whose header block is still arriving is held until the terminating blank line, subject to a 16 KiB header limit (431 Request Header Fields Too Large) and a 10 second header deadline (408 Request Timeout). The deadline is answered rather than dropped in silence, the same status the proxy sends for the same case: a client that gets a bare close cannot tell a deadline from a crash, a firewall or the wrong port.

The deadline is the same one the proxy applies, and for the reason given there: it is fixed, is not configurable, and is deliberately independent of --idle-timeout, which defaults to 0 and so cannot end a half-sent request — a client that sends a request line and then stops sends no further bytes for the 16 KiB limit to count. It starts at the first read that left the block incomplete and later bytes do not renew it. Neither an idle keep-alive connection between requests nor a slow request body is measured against it.

The server notices it on the sweep that runs every 30 seconds, so a connection is closed between 10 and 40 seconds after it stops speaking; a proxy has a chain of its own and closes between 10 and 20. The deadline is the same in both.

sections.title: Cache Access via Server
sections.html:
When a server is linked to a cache with --cache, clients can send "cache <command>" messages to execute commands directly against the linked cache. The response is sent back to the sender only (never broadcast). Normal messages are still processed according to the server's mode.

socketley create cache store -p 9001 -s
socketley create server api -p 9000 --cache store -s
# Client sends: "cache set foo bar" -> receives "ok"
# Client sends: "cache get foo" -> receives "bar"
# Client sends: "hello"            -> handled by the server's mode, AND
#                                     stored in `store` under the key "1"

The last line is the part that surprises people. An ordinary message is archived into the linked cache under an auto-incrementing integer key as well as being handled normally; see --cache under SERVER FLAGS.

The request is asynchronous. The server does not run the cache's command interpreter itself — it posts the command and answers the client when the reply arrives, which is the next turn of the daemon's event loop. That is a round trip the synchronous version did not pay, on the order of tens of microseconds on loopback; it is what allows the cache to be a different process later without anything on the client's side changing. Nothing else waits on it: the server keeps serving every other connection while the reply is outstanding.

What holds:

  • Replies on one connection come back in request order, so a client may pipeline cache commands and match answers to questions positionally.

  • A command addressed to a cache that is not running is answered with an error: line rather than with silence.

  • A client that shuts down its write side after asking still receives its answer: the connection is held open until every reply it is owed has been written.

What does not: nothing is promised about the order of a cache reply against other traffic on the same connection. A broadcast goes to every client except the sender and a cache reply goes to the sender alone, so there is no interleaving to define.

A connection may have at most 4096 unanswered cache commands outstanding, and the daemon at most 32768 across all of them. A client that pipelines past its share is disconnected rather than refused in place: a refusal written now would arrive ahead of the answers already queued in front of it, and a client that cannot tell which answer belongs to which question has no protocol left.

Default port: 8000

sections.title: CLIENT FLAGS
sections.html:
-t host:port | unix:/path/to.sock#

Target server to connect to. Default: 127.0.0.1:8000.

Details

unix:/path/to.sock dials the socket node a runtime with --listen unix: serves — the connect side of the same address, judged by the same rules (absolute, under the kernel's sun_path limit). Refused with --udp and with --tls, for the listener's reasons under COMMON FLAGS.

--mode mode#

Message flow direction: inout (bidirectional, default), in (receive only), out (send only).

--udp#

Use UDP instead of TCP. Creates a connected SOCK_DGRAM socket. Each datagram is one message (no line-parsing). Not available for cache or proxy.

--reconnect [max-attempts]#

Enable automatic reconnection with exponential backoff when the connection is lost. Backoff starts at 1 second and doubles each attempt to a ceiling of 16 seconds, with up to half a second of jitter — the dials of a client whose target is gone fall at 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 16, 16 seconds. Set to 0 for infinite attempts (default when flag is given without a value). Set to a positive number to limit reconnection attempts. A negative count is refused: -1 is what the stored field holds for "off", so the flag whose only purpose is to turn reconnection on used to turn it off, silently and at exit 0. Reconnection is off until the flag is given, which is how it stays off.

Details

A client flag, and refused on a server, a proxy or a cache: it re-dials a connection this runtime made, and those three take connections rather than make them. It was accepted and reported by show on all four, and read by the client alone.

"When the connection is lost" includes a peer that never says so. A close sends a FIN or an RST and is acted on at once, but a machine that loses power, a link that partitions or a firewall that forgets an idle flow send nothing at all, and an idle client that never writes would never find out. Every client socket therefore carries TCP keepalive: 60 seconds idle, then three probes ten seconds apart, so a peer that has silently gone is noticed in about 90 seconds and the backoff above starts from there. There is no flag for it — the kernel's own default is two hours, which for this purpose is the same as never.

A client also takes the TLS flags — see --tls under COMMON FLAGS. --tls alone dials the target over TLS and verifies it against the system trust store; --ca file supplies a trust store instead, and --cert file with --key file present a certificate to a peer that asks for one. The host in -t is the name the certificate has to be valid for. A verification failure costs the socket and the client re-dials on the backoff above; it is never retried in cleartext, and there is no way to skip the check. --tls with --udp is refused — that would need DTLS.

sections.title: PROXY FLAGS
sections.html:
--listen unix:/path/to.sock#

Serve the proxy's front door on an AF_UNIX socket instead of -p. The full treatment is --listen under COMMON FLAGS. With --shards each shard binds a node of its own, base#N.sock, because SO_REUSEPORT is not a path.

--backend addr#

A hostname is resolved off the request path. A backend named by hostname is looked up when the proxy starts and, if that fails, again on the proxy's periodic sweep, on a thread of its own — never while a request is being served. A request that arrives before the name resolves is refused rather than waiting for it. That is deliberate: the daemon has one thread for every runtime it holds, so a resolver that hangs on the request path stops not only this proxy's clients but every server, cache and client in the same daemon. The cost is that a name which starts resolving is picked up within one sweep instead of immediately.

Details

IPv4 only. Every address this daemon resolves is AF_INET: a backend, an upstream, a client target and every listener. A hostname that has only a AAAA record resolves to nothing and the backend is reported unreachable, with no line anywhere saying why. This is a property of the whole daemon and not of this flag; it is written here because this is where an operator meets it first. The one address that is not an internet address at all is unix:/path/to.sock below, which resolves nothing because there is nothing to resolve.

Add backend server. Can be ip:port, unix:/path/to.sock, a runtime name, or @groupname to dynamically target all running members of that group. Repeatable or comma-separated. Group backends are resolved at connection time, so new group members are picked up automatically without restarting the proxy.

An address may carry a scheme: https://host:port is reached over TLS, http://host:port in cleartext, and a bare host:port follows whatever the backend-TLS options below say. The port may be omitted after a scheme, in which case it is 443 or 80. See mTLS Flags for what verifies such a connection.

unix:/path/to.sock reaches a backend over an AF_UNIX socket instead of loopback TCP. A sidecar proxy and the process it fronts are on one host, and loopback TCP charges that pair for a whole stack — sequence numbers, checksums, windows — on a connection that never sees a wire. Measured on a quiet machine, 64-byte round trips through this proxy: one connection unpinned, 41.4 us over TCP against 37.0 us over AF_UNIX; eight connections unpinned, 66,620 round trips a second against 85,217 — 16 to 28% depending on where the scheduler puts the three processes.

The throughput figure is the one to plan with, and why is worth stating. What the swap removes is CPU: 17.5 us of it per round trip across proxy and backend over TCP against 14.5 over AF_UNIX, which is to the tenth what a two-process ping-pong predicts for that leg. On one core with a single connection almost none of it shows up as latency — 21.5 us against 20.7 — because a serial round trip there is waiting on wakeups rather than on work, so freed CPU has nothing to do. A proxy under load is short of exactly that CPU, which is why the same change is worth under a microsecond in the first measurement and a fifth of the throughput in the second.

The path must be absolute, and shorter than 108 bytes, which is what the kernel's sun_path holds. Both are refused at create/start rather than at traffic time: the kernel truncates a long path silently, and a trimmed path names a different socket — quite possibly a real one belonging to something else. A relative path is refused because it would be resolved against the daemon's working directory, which is not something the operator writing the flag can see.

A unix backend is never reached over TLS. --ca, --client-cert and --client-key encrypt every backend leg at once, so a proxy given both them and a unix: backend is refused at start rather than quietly connecting in the clear. Filesystem permissions on the socket node are what restrict access to it.

A socket path that is not there, and a stale socket node left behind by a process that has gone, both answer the client 502 — the same answer an unreachable TCP backend gets, and for the same reason: that is the far end failing, not this one.

fastcgi://unix:/path/to.sock or fastcgi://host:port is an application server spoken to by FastCGI — php-fpm, or anything else that takes the responder role — instead of HTTP. Such a proxy needs --root, speaks --protocol http to its clients, and has no backend of any other kind; each of these is refused at create. Deadlines, retries, the circuit breaker and the TLS listener work on it as on any backend. A connection to the application server is not kept: one of php-fpm's workers serves a connection for as long as it lasts, so a kept one would hold that worker from every other request, and with more of them than workers the rest would wait in its backlog until their deadline.

A request goes, in this order: to the first path segment ending in .php that is a regular file beneath --root (what follows it is PATH_INFO); to a directory's --index; to an existing file that is no script, which the proxy serves itself; and otherwise to the index script at the top of --root, as a front controller is, with the path in REQUEST_URI. A script is found with openat2(2) and RESOLVE_BENEATH, so a link out of the root is never one; an absolute link is followed only when its target stays inside. Because a script must exist, /upload.jpg/x.php is never handed to the interpreter, whatever cgi.fix_pathinfo says.

Never served, as a script or a file: a path that walks up, a hidden segment but .well-known, and the names a site keeps but does not hand out — a name ending in ~, one holding .php., and the extensions, also with .gz or .br after them, bak, old, orig, save, swp, swo, tmp, dist, inc, sql, ini, log, phtml, phar, phps and php3–php8. They are 404.

A file is served with its type, an ETag and Last-Modified, answers If-None-Match, If-Modified-Since, If-Match and If-Unmodified-Since (RFC 9110 13.2.2), one range with If-Range, GET and HEAD alone (405 otherwise), under keep-alive. A file up to 16 KiB is kept in memory after its first GET, 64 MiB in all, and asked of the disk with one statx(2) a request, which a file replaced under its name answers; a larger one is sent with sendfile(2) on a plain connection, 4 MiB a turn at most, and read through the ring instead of waited on where it is not in the page cache, and over TLS read 256 KiB at a time.

A Proxy header is never passed on (httpoxy), nor any header whose name holds an underscore, which a server would read as the same variable as its dashed twin. HTTPS is on when this proxy ended TLS, or an entrance in front of it did and said so over the loopback. An upload that sends Expect: 100-continue is told to continue by the proxy, since an application server never says so. What a script writes to STDERR reaches the log, at most twenty lines a minute. An X-Accel-Redirect is nginx's internal redirect and is answered 502; a script hands a file out with readfile().

--root directory#

The directory a FastCGI proxy's scripts and files are in, absolute.

--compress#

Send a file's compressed copy beside it, made by the site's build — app.css.br or app.css.gz for app.css — to a client whose Accept-Encoding takes that coding, br before gzip, with Content-Encoding and its own ETag; every file answer then says Vary: Accept-Encoding. A copy older than its file is never sent, since that is a build that changed one and not the other, nor one for a range, which is of the file, nor a copy whose file is missing or kept from the public, nor one beside an image, a video, a woff font, a zip or a pdf, whose format is compressed already; a compressed copy of a name kept from the public is kept from it too, with or without the flag. Nothing is compressed or decompressed by the proxy, so no compression library is linked and nothing a client sends is decoded.

--fastcgi-root directory#

The same directory as the application server sees it, when that differs (a server in a container), named to it in SCRIPT_FILENAME and DOCUMENT_ROOT.

--index name#

The script a directory and an unmatched path go to (default index.php).

--strategy strategy#

Load balancing strategy: round-robin (default), random , lua (custom via on_route callback).

--protocol protocol#

http (default, path-based routing) or tcp (raw byte forwarding).

Details

In tcp mode a client that shuts its write side with shutdown(2) has that half-close passed on to the backend, and the return direction is held open until the backend itself closes. That is the only way a byte relay can tell a backend where a request ended — there is no framing to say so — and it is what makes nc -N, a one-shot redis-cli, and any shell pipeline into the proxy work: each of those sends, half-closes, and then reads the answer. The half-close is issued only once everything the client sent has actually reached the backend socket, so it cannot overtake the request it terminates.

What ends the hold is the backend's own close, a client that resets, or --idle-timeout where one is set. A half-closed client is held no longer than one that never half-closed: a TCP relay has no request and no response, so no deadline sweep applies to either.

Default port: 8080

HTTP mode: Requests to /<proxy-name>/* are forwarded with prefix stripped.

In http mode a request carrying an upgrade offer — an Upgrade header together with a Connection header listing the upgrade token — is forwarded with both of those headers intact, rather than having them stripped as hop-by-hop. If the backend answers 101 Switching Protocols, that response is relayed verbatim and the connection becomes a bidirectional byte relay until one end closes. This is what makes ws:// work through a proxy in http mode. See WebSocket and other protocol upgrades under LIMITATIONS for what the proxy does and does not do with such a connection.

--domain name[,name...]#

On a proxy, the names it is reached by through the entrance (see --proxy under DNS FLAGS). Reached by name, it serves under no /name/ prefix: the path and the Host go to the backend as they came, as a site behind it expects them. From a hop on this machine — the entrance in front of it — X-Forwarded-Proto and X-Forwarded-Host are kept rather than written over, so the backend is told the scheme the client used, not the cleartext hop between them.

Details
socketley create proxy hub -p 8089 --bind 127.0.0.1 \
    --backend 127.0.0.1:8088 --domain hub --backend-timeout 5m -s
--auth bearer:file|basic:file|idp:runtime|none#

Who may send a request through, asked before any of it reaches a backend. bearer: admits Authorization: Bearer token with a token that is a line of file (blank lines and lines starting with # aside). basic: admits HTTP Basic with an access key and its secret key from file, a credentials file as a storage runtime's --credentials reads it, of a user who is an admin there; a key outside any [user] is the default owner's, an admin. A request without them is answered 401 with the WWW-Authenticate to answer in, and the backend is never sent the Authorization field. The file is read again when it changes, at most once a second; one that is gone or does not parse refuses everybody, and says so in the log. An address that fails five times within fifteen minutes is refused even the right answer, 429 with Retry-After, until fifteen minutes after its first failure, an IPv6 address by its /64; behind the entrance, a hop on this machine, the address is the last in X-Forwarded-For, the one the entrance heard from. Each failure is logged with that address. A connection let in is asked again every second while its exchange lasts, an upgrade's tunnel included, and closed once what let it in would not: a token gone from the file, a sign-in ended or an account disabled. Set at create; edit changes it on a stopped proxy.

Details
socketley create proxy stats -p 9191 --bind 127.0.0.1 \
    --backend 127.0.0.1:9190 --domain metrics \
    --auth basic:/etc/socketley/storage-ui.creds -s

idp:runtime puts a sign-in in front of every route: the sign-in cookie of the idp runtime of that name in this daemon, verified here against the key it publishes beside its state, each session once and then remembered until it expires. A browser without one, a GET or HEAD that accepts HTML, is sent with 302 to sign in and back to the address it asked for; anything else is answered 401. The backend is told the account's fixed id in X-Forwarded-User, its username in X-Forwarded-Preferred-Username and its address in X-Forwarded-Email, which a client's own of those names never reaches; the provider's own cookies are taken out of the Cookie field it is sent, every other cookie kept. The cookie reaches a proxy on another name only when the provider's --cookie-domain covers both.

socketley create proxy wiki -p 8100 --backend 127.0.0.1:3000 \
    --domain wiki.example.com --auth idp:auth -s
--redirect-https [port|none]#

Answer every request with 308 to the name it asked for and its path, over HTTPS on port (443 when not given, and then not written into the URL). An ACME HTTP-01 challenge this daemon holds is still answered first. A dns runtime whose entrance is on 443 makes one on port 80 as its child.

sections.title: Sharding
sections.html:
--shards N#

Serve this proxy from N worker processes instead of one, sharing the listening socket through SO_REUSEPORT. The kernel gives each incoming connection to one of them. 1 to 64; the default is 1, which is what every proxy was before this flag existed.

A runtime is one process and therefore one event loop on one core. This is the only way to give a single runtime more than that. It is worth reaching for only when a proxy is saturated — below saturation a single connection is bound by the cost of a cross-core wakeup, and another process cannot help with that.

A shard is an implementation detail of a runtime, not a runtime. ls shows one entry, stats reports the connection count summed across the shards and labels each shard's detail text, stop and remove take all of them down, and the count is persisted so a restart brings back the number that was asked for.

It is a declaration, and not every type may make it. Sharding is correct exactly when nothing is shared between connections, and nothing can detect that — not the flags, and not the script, because a table at file scope is indistinguishable from one that happens never to be read twice. So the operator declares it, and the flag is offered only where they are in a position to. A cache shards by key ownership: each shard owns the slice of the keyspace that hashes to it, and a command naming a key some other shard owns is forwarded to that shard, executed there, and answered back through the connection that asked. A SET on one connection and a later GET on another therefore agree, whichever shards they happened to land on — see Sharding under CACHE FLAGS for what that costs. A client refuses it because it has no listening socket to share. A server may shard with or without --lua; each shard loads the script into its own interpreter, so per-shard state is per-shard and is not shared between them — see Sharding under SERVER FLAGS for what that means for a script.

One combination is refused on every type. --shards with --listen unix: is refused because SO_REUSEPORT is not what a unix socket does — N processes would unlink each other's socket node and only the last to bind would be reachable.

What it bought, measured. An http proxy in front of four --http backends, driven by wrk:

shardsthroughputCPU per shard
140,285 req/s1.00 cores
294,401 req/s0.99 cores
4150,175 req/s0.91 cores
8142,775 req/s0.47 cores

3.73x at four shards, and close to linear: each shard stays at a full core until the machine runs out of them. Eight shards on a ten-core box is past that point and buys nothing — the per-shard figure halving is what running out looks like. Do not set more shards than the machine has cores to give them.

The backend tier saturates first. That is the first thing anyone will hit, and it is not a property of this flag. The same proxy in front of a single backend stops at 2.14x however many shards it is given, with the backend pinned at exactly 1.00 cores — the shards were idle and waiting on it. A sharded proxy needs something behind it that is not one process, whether that is several backends, a --strategy across a group, or a backend that is itself sharded. Measure what saturated before reading a number as this flag's ceiling.

It does nothing for --protocol tcp, for a different reason. A tcp proxy moves bytes with IORING_OP_SPLICE, which io_uring preps REQ_F_FORCE_ASYNC — so that data path never runs on the shard's event loop at all. It runs on io-wq kernel threads, and it was therefore never bounded by the number of processes: at one shard, a tcp proxy under 100 connections was measured holding 11 threads, 10 of them iou-*, and burning 1.85 cores. Sharding such a proxy adds processes to a path that is already parallel, and throughput does not move. If you shard a tcp proxy and see no change, this is why. The ceiling --shards exists to lift is the http one above, where the runtime really is one event loop on one core.

The load is balanced per connection, not per request. SO_REUSEPORT picks a shard when the connection is accepted and never revisits it, so one heavy long-lived connection makes one shard hot while the others idle, and the spread over a small number of connections is uneven — eight connections over four shards were measured landing 3/2/2/1. Sharding helps a proxy carrying many comparable connections; it does nothing for a proxy carrying one big one.

The shard count may be changed with edit only while the runtime is stopped, for the same reason -p may: applying it to a running proxy would mean retiring workers out from under live connections.

entries.summary: Serve this proxy from N worker processes instead of one, sharing the listening socket through SO_REUSEPORT. The kernel gives each incoming connection to one of them. 1 to 64; the default is 1, which is what every proxy was before this flag existed.

sections.title: Health Check Flags
sections.html:
--health-check [tcp|http]#

Enable active health checks for backends. In tcp mode, the proxy opens a TCP connection to each backend at the configured interval — success means the port is listening. In http mode, the proxy sends an HTTP GET to --health-path and considers the backend healthy on a 2xx response. Unhealthy backends are removed from the load balancer pool until they recover.

--health-interval duration#

Interval between health checks. Default: 5 seconds. A bare number is seconds; the suffixes s, m, h, d and w are accepted (30 and 5m both work).

--health-path path#

HTTP health check path. Default: /health. Only used when --health-check is set to http.

--health-threshold n#

Number of consecutive health check failures before a backend is marked unhealthy. Default: 3. A single successful check restores the backend.

entries.summary: Enable active health checks for backends. In tcp mode, the proxy opens a TCP connection to each backend at the configured interval — success means the port is listening. In http mode, the proxy sends an HTTP GET to --health-path and considers the backend healthy on a 2xx response. Unhealthy backends are removed from the load balancer pool until they recover.
Interval between health checks. Default: 5 seconds. A bare number is seconds; the suffixes s, m, h, d and w are accepted (30 and 5m both work).
HTTP health check path. Default: /health. Only used when --health-check is set to http.
Number of consecutive health check failures before a backend is marked unhealthy. Default: 3. A single successful check restores the backend.

sections.title: Circuit Breaker Flags
sections.html:
--circuit-threshold n#

Number of consecutive backend errors (connection refused, timeout, 5xx) that trips the circuit breaker to the open state. While open, all requests to that backend fail immediately without attempting a connection. Default: 5.

--circuit-timeout duration#

How long an open circuit stays open before transitioning to half-open. In half-open state, a single probe request is allowed through — if it succeeds, the circuit closes (fully healthy); if it fails, the circuit re-opens. Default: 30 seconds. A bare number is seconds; the suffixes s, m, h, d and w are accepted (30 and 5m both work).

--backend-timeout duration#

How long a backend may take to produce the first byte of a response before the request is given up on. The request is then retried on another backend if --retry allows it, and answered 504 Gateway Timeout otherwise; either way the backend is charged with an error, so the circuit breaker above opens and takes it out of rotation. While the request body still arrives the wait runs from its latest bytes, and a client that stops sending a body the backend has taken all of is answered 408 Request Timeout instead, with no retry and no error charged. Default: 2 seconds. Set to 0 to wait indefinitely. A bare number is seconds; the suffixes s, m, h, d and w are accepted (30 and 5m both work).

Details

This is the only thing that notices a backend which accepts connections and then stops answering. Such a backend passes a TCP health check, and a request that never completes is recorded as neither success nor failure, so without a deadline it keeps its full share of the rotation and every request routed to it is held until the client gives up. HTTP mode only — TCP mode has no request/response framing to measure. Only the wait for the first byte is bounded, so a slow or streaming response body is never cut short once the backend has begun answering — unless the client has closed its side. Such a client cannot end the answer itself, so from then on the backend may go this long without sending a byte before both connections are closed, with no error charged; a backend that keeps sending is never cut short.

The 2-second default applies whether or not the flag is given. If any endpoint behind this proxy normally needs longer than that to begin answering — a report that is computed on demand, a cold cache, a long query — raise --backend-timeout to cover it or set it to 0 to disable the deadline. Left at the default, such an endpoint has its requests cut off at 2 seconds and is charged an error each time, which opens the circuit breaker on a backend that is working correctly.

sections.title: Retry Flags
sections.html:
--retry n#

Retry failed requests up to n times on the next backend in the pool (0 = disabled, default). Only idempotent HTTP methods (GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS) are retried unless --retry-all is set. For TCP mode, any failed connection attempt is retried.

--retry-all#

Also retry non-idempotent methods (POST, PATCH). Use with caution — the request body is replayed to the next backend, which may cause duplicate side effects.

entries.summary: Retry failed requests up to n times on the next backend in the pool (0 = disabled, default). Only idempotent HTTP methods (GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS) are retried unless --retry-all is set. For TCP mode, any failed connection attempt is retried.
Also retry non-idempotent methods (POST, PATCH). Use with caution — the request body is replayed to the next backend, which may cause duplicate side effects.

sections.title: What a Request That Never Reaches a Backend Is Answered
sections.html:
In --protocol http a client that has sent a whole request always gets a status line back, and which status it is names the end that failed. A retry, where --retry allows one, is tried first in every case below; these are what is sent when no retry is available or every retry also failed.

502 Bad Gateway#

The backend's answer. It refused the connection, was unreachable, could not be resolved, closed before a byte of the response arrived, or rejected the TLS handshake. The backend is charged to its circuit breaker. A client that retries a 502 immediately is asking a backend that has just said no.

503 Service Unavailable#

This proxy's own shortage, reached before the backend was asked anything: the local ephemeral port range exhausted (EADDRNOTAVAIL), descriptors exhausted (EMFILE, ENFILE), memory or buffers exhausted (ENOMEM, ENOBUFS), or a submission that did not reach the io_uring ring. Nothing is charged to any circuit breaker — the backend is healthy and the same request will very likely succeed on the next attempt. 503 is also the answer when there is no backend to send to at all: every member of an @group is out, or the single backend's breaker is open.

504 Gateway Timeout#

The backend accepted (or never finished accepting) and produced no first byte inside --backend-timeout. Charged to the breaker.

Two cases deliberately get no status line. --protocol tcp has no request and no response, so a byte pipe whose backend never came up is closed and nothing is invented for it. And a request whose backend has already put bytes on the client's wire is past the point where a status line could be written: it would land at an offset that is not a message boundary, and the client would read it as the middle of the response it is already receiving. Such a connection is closed, and the backend that produced an unfinished response is charged to its breaker so the next client is routed elsewhere.

A script runs when its runtime starts, not when it is created. create compiles the file — so one that does not parse is refused on the spot, by the command that asked — and the worker runs it. Without -s there is no worker yet and nothing has run: no top level, no socketley.subscribe, and no check of a global like tick_ms. Those happen at the start that forks the worker, and a refusal there is reported by that command.

It used to be otherwise for a runtime kept in the daemon, where create --lua loaded and ran the file at once. There is no such runtime now.

sections.title: Process Isolation
sections.html:
Every runtime runs in its own supervised worker process. There is no flag for this and nothing to configure: it is where a server, a client, a proxy and a cache each run.

A configuration file with daemon_process in it is refused rather than ignored, for either value, and the refusal names the line to delete.

What used to argue for keeping a runtime inside the daemon was the Lua API: thirteen calls were refused in a worker, and the count is now zero.

Reads of the map#

socketley.send, .list, .get and all four of socketley.cluster. The daemon pushes the worker a replica of the map and a snapshot of the cluster view, and these are answered out of them.

Changes to the map#

socketley.create, .start, .stop, .remove. Not out of the replica — being told what the map holds is not permission to alter it. They are asked of the daemon over a socket of the worker's own and they wait for the answer, so if socketley.create(...) then branches on what happened rather than on what was accepted. Measured: 9.95, 10.20 and 10.52 microseconds over three runs of 20000, on a path a script reaches deliberately and never per message.

Moving a connection#

socketley.pipe across two runtimes, and self.route(). Despite the name, neither hands a descriptor over: the origin keeps the socket and relays the bytes, and the target answers as though the connection were its own. Names travel; the connection does not.

One refusal survives, for one case: a worker forked by a daemon that could not give it the control plane these need — an older build, or one that could not create the socket. It says so, and says to restart the daemon.

A cross-runtime request costs about 50 microseconds more than the same call in one address space, measured, which a server doing --cache pays on every command.

A script's routes declaration is not given up. It is produced by running the script, which happens in the worker, and travels back to the daemon on the control socket the worker already holds; the placeholder publishes it to the proxies in front of the runtime. See Declared Routes.

The daemon forks and execs itself, hands the worker its configuration and its routing table over a control socket, and keeps a placeholder for it in the runtime map. What the CLI shows is unchanged: ps, ls, show, stats and the Prometheus endpoint report the same figures they would for an in-process runtime, because the worker publishes them and the daemon stores them where an in-process runtime would have written them.

The port is bound in the worker; no descriptor is passed across the boundary. If the worker dies the daemon restarts it and the runtime stays running; if it dies more than five times in ten seconds the runtime is left failed rather than being forked in a loop. Either way every other runtime is told to let go of connections routed to or from it, because a killed worker runs no teardown of its own.

Lua callbacks run inside the worker, against the worker's own state, and a cache's PUBLISH reaches the worker's subscribe callbacks. The figures the daemon reports were read by the worker when they were printed. See Out-of-process runtimes under LIMITATIONS.

sections.title: mTLS Flags
sections.html:
A proxy has two legs and each has its own half of mutual TLS. The names say which: client here always means "a TLS client", and the proxy is one of those towards its backends while its own callers are ones towards it.

--client-ca path#

The CA that a certificate presented by a client must be signed by. This is mutual TLS on the proxy's own listening port, so it requires --tls --cert --key; without them it is refused, because on a cleartext port it would authenticate nobody while show reported mutual TLS.

--client-cert path--client-key path#

The certificate and key this proxy presents to a backend that asks for one. Both or neither: half a pair loads nothing, so it is refused rather than leaving a leg that presents no certificate after the flag said it would.

Any of --ca, --client-cert and --client-key also turns the backend leg itself to TLS, for every backend — none of the three means anything against a cleartext peer, and honouring them without encrypting would be the fail-open reading of all three. Use an https:// backend address instead to encrypt one backend and leave its neighbours alone.

A TLS backend connection is verified, always: the chain against --ca file when one is given and against the system CA store otherwise, and the certificate against the endpoint the request was routed to — a host name matched against the certificate's DNS names with partial wildcards refused, an address literal against its IP SAN. TLS 1.2 is the minimum version. There is no option to disable any of that; a backend presenting a private-CA or self-signed certificate needs that CA in --ca file or in the store OpenSSL reads. A backend whose certificate fails either check is answered 502 (or retried, where --retry is set) and is charged to its circuit breaker — the request is never sent in the clear as a fallback.

Connections to a TLS backend are pooled and reused, like cleartext ones — a run of forty requests to one https:// backend costs one handshake rather than forty. The session is pooled with the descriptor, so the reused connection is the same record layer part way through the same stream, not a new one over an old socket. A pooled socket goes back only to the endpoint it was opened to, which is also the name its certificate was verified against and the name sent as SNI, and never survives a restart: the trust store and client certificate the leg verifies against are rebuilt when the runtime starts, and the pool is emptied when it stops. Before a socket is reused, whatever is waiting on it is decrypted and inspected — a session ticket or a key update is consumed and the connection kept, application data is a response nobody asked for and the connection is dropped rather than handed to the next client. --health-check http works alongside it and probes over TLS, verifying the backend's certificate to the same standard the data path does — a backend it cannot verify is marked unhealthy rather than reported healthy.
