sections.title: Sidecar Mode
sections.html:
--sidecar#

Convenience shorthand that enables a service-mesh-ready configuration in a single flag. Equivalent to:

Details
--health-check tcp --circuit-threshold 5 --circuit-timeout 30 --retry 2 --drain

Individual flags can still be specified alongside --sidecar to override the defaults (e.g. --sidecar --health-check http --health-path /ready).

--sidecar does not set --backend-timeout, but it runs into it: the deadline is 2 seconds by default, and the circuit breaker --sidecar turns on is what the expiry is charged to. Five slow requests in a row open the circuit for 30 seconds. Add --backend-timeout seconds alongside --sidecar whenever the application behind it can take longer than 2 seconds to send its first response byte, or --backend-timeout 0 to switch the deadline off.

Example:

socketley create proxy myapp --sidecar --backend 127.0.0.1:3000 \
    -p 8080 --health-check tcp -s

socketley create proxy slowapp --sidecar --backend 127.0.0.1:3000 \
    -p 8080 --backend-timeout 30 -s

entries.summary: Convenience shorthand that enables a service-mesh-ready configuration in a single flag. Equivalent to:

sections.title: CACHE FLAGS
sections.html:
--listen unix:/path/to.sock#

Serve the cache on an AF_UNIX socket instead of -p — redis-cli -s connects to it, and both the plaintext and RESP protocols are detected as on a port. The full treatment is --listen under COMMON FLAGS; refused with --cluster, because members advertise ports out of a formula and RESP has no way to write a filesystem path as a node address.

Details

It is worth measuring before it is worth arguing about. On this box, one cache and one redis-server both loaded with the same keys, eight client processes, GET:

socketley over TCP      2,969,848/s        redis over TCP    1,411,960/s
socketley over AF_UNIX  4,517,387/s        redis over AF_UNIX 2,319,573/s

Both sides gain about half again, which is the TCP and netfilter path coming out of the measurement rather than anything either program does differently. On a box with conntrack loaded and nftables rules on the OUTPUT hook — any box running Docker — that path is not free, and a peer on the same machine does not need it.

--listen with --shards binds one node per shard.#

Shard i gets name#i.sock, inserted before the suffix, by the rule the daemon's own companion nodes already follow. The pair used to be refused, and the refusal's reason was sound for a design nobody was proposing: N processes binding one path unlink each other's node and only the last stays reachable. N paths are N listeners.

Details

The formula is the interface. On a server every shard answers every request, so a caller takes any node. On a cache they are not interchangeable, and that is where choosing pays: a caller that hashes the key the way CLUSTER KEYSLOT does and connects to that shard's node crosses nothing, which is the same saving --cluster buys between ports. A caller that picks a node at random still gets correct answers — the shard crosses to the owner — at the crossing's cost.

What that crossing costs, measured. One daemon pinned to four cores, eight redis-benchmark processes of twenty-four connections each on the other twelve, GET at depth 1; six interleaved passes with the order rotated, the first discarded, a clock probe on both ends of the run. Client CPU is recorded beside every row because a capped client inverts the sign of a comparison before it changes its size; it never passed 5.8 of its twelve cores.

arrangementGET/sx1coresus/op
1 shard240,6711.001.004.16
2 shards, one address251,9591.051.917.60
4 shards, one address421,0931.753.959.38
4 shards, slot-routed673,0172.803.655.43

Behind one address the shards buy far less than the cores they take. Two of them take 1.91 cores and return 1.05x; four take 3.95 and return 1.75x. Half the keys, then three quarters, belong to a sibling, and the per-operation cost of serving them roughly doubles — 4.16 us at one shard against 7.60 at two and 9.38 at four. Point a client that picks the owner at the same four shards and they return 2.80x at 5.43 us, which is most of what the crossings were costing.

How well the crossings batch decides the size of this, and the CLIENT decides that. The mesh queues a crossing and flushes once per loop turn, so requests that arrive together cross together. At the same 192 connections, twelve client processes of sixteen connections give the two-shard arm 0.90x where eight of twenty-four give it 1.05x — while the one-shard arm reads 235,421 and 240,671, unmoved. Measured on a floor of two processes and two rings, one crossing at a time costs 8.13 us where thirty-two in a batch cost 282 ns apiece. So a figure for this flag is a figure for an arrival pattern, and the one above is the friendlier of the two shapes tried.

The ceiling above that is the machine, not this flag. Four shards routed by key reach 2.80x. Four independent redis-server processes on the same four cores, driven the same way, reach 2.88x — and socketley is ahead of them in absolute throughput at every count tried, 1.12x at one and 1.09x at four. Neither scales linearly on loopback here, so a cache that must scale wants --cluster and a client that routes — and the 3.57x quoted for a server under SERVER FLAGS does not carry over.

Measured against the same cache on TCP with --cluster, both clients routing by key, four shards: at least 1.22x in AF_UNIX's favour. Two later passes read higher and are not quoted, because the TCP arm fell across them for a reason that was not the port pool (TIME-WAIT peaked at 1,235 of 28,231) and is not understood.

A remote client gets none of this. AF_UNIX is local, so the benefit lands on hops between processes on one machine. The hop that cannot take it today is a proxy in front of a sharded cache: a proxy does not read keys, so it would land on the wrong shard (N-1)/N of the time. Teaching it cache_shard_of would close that, and is not done.

--persistent file#

Persistent storage file. Cache is saved on stop and loaded on start.

Details

Written 0600. The dump holds whatever was cached, and because it is loaded on start it is not a record of what the cache held but what the cache will hold. Earlier versions wrote it 0644, readable by every account on the machine; a dump left by one of those is narrowed when the cache next loads it, with a line in the daemon log.

The mode is all this can control. Replacing a file needs write permission on the directory rather than on the file, so put file somewhere only this daemon's user can write — not a world-writable directory shared with other accounts.

With --shards each shard writes its own slice, and the set survives a changed shard count. One shard writes file itself; above one they are file.shard0, file.shard1 and so on. Each records the shard count it was written under and a fingerprint of the function that decides which shard owns a key, so a cache dumped at four shards and started at eight is redistributed rather than loaded into the wrong slices. Every key survives; measured across 1->4, 4->1, 4->8, 8->4 and 4->4.

A set that cannot be trusted refuses the start rather than serving part of itself: a missing slice is named, and files that disagree about the shard count — two runs' dumps in one place — are refused together. Slices left by a run with more shards are removed by the dump that supersedes them.

--persistent-interval duration#

Journal every accepted write beside the dump, flushed on this cadence: an acknowledged write reaches the kernel at most duration after it was accepted, so a killed or OOM-killed worker loses at most the last interval of writes instead of everything since the last stop or FLUSH. Requires --persistent; refused without it. Durations read as everywhere — 30s, 5m, 1h — and a bare number is seconds.

Details

The journal lives at file.journal (per shard, file.shardN.journal), written 0600. A clean stop and the admin FLUSH command write the dump and cut the journal behind it; an unclean stop leaves a tail, which the next start replays on top of the dump before serving. A tail torn mid-record by the crash is dropped at the last complete record, with the dropped byte count in the daemon log. TTLs are journaled as absolute deadlines, so a key that had five seconds left when it was written has whatever remains of those five seconds after a replay — possibly nothing.

The flush is a write into the kernel's page cache and deliberately not an fsync: the promise covers a dead process, not a dead machine. A power cut can additionally lose what the kernel had not yet written back.

A journal with records written under a different shard count (or a different ownership function) refuses the start rather than guessing at an order for one key's history across two files: recover under the split that wrote it and stop cleanly, or delete the .journal files to discard the tail.

--mode mode#

Access control mode: readonly (GET, SIZE only), readwrite (GET, SET, DEL, SIZE - default), admin (all commands including FLUSH, LOAD).

Details

readonly applies to this cache's own Lua script as well, and there it is quieter than on the wire. A client that sends a write is told "denied: readonly mode"; the twelve mutating self.* calls refuse by answering exactly what they answer when there was nothing to do — false for nine of them and an empty string for self.lpop and self.rpop. self.cache_mode() is how a script tells the two apart, and the return values are listed with the calls under LUA API.

--maxmemory size#

Maximum memory for cache data. Supports K, M, G suffixes (e.g., 100M, 1G). When exceeded, behavior depends on eviction policy. 0 means unlimited (default).

Details

Suffixes are K, M and G and nothing else: a value the parser cannot read whole is refused rather than half-read. That matters because the obvious near-misses used to be accepted silently — 100MB was taken as a hundred BYTES, and a value so large that the multiplication wrapped came out as 0, which is the spelling for "unlimited". Both are errors now.

--eviction policy#

Eviction policy when maxmemory is reached: noeviction (reject writes, default), allkeys-lru (evict least recently used), allkeys-random (evict random keys).

--resp#

Force RESP2 protocol mode for all connections (Redis wire protocol). By default, the cache auto-detects RESP mode when a connection's first byte is '*'. With this flag, all connections use RESP regardless.

--replicate host:port#

Connect as a follower to the specified leader cache. The follower receives a full data dump on connect, then receives ongoing write command replication. The follower operates in read-only mode.

Details

A value containing a newline replicates whole. The link carries one command per line, and a cache value is arbitrary bytes, so such a value used to end at its first line break on the follower and the remainder was interpreted as a command of its own — on the initial dump and on live writes alike, with both sides reporting success. A command that cannot be written as a line is now length-framed instead; one that can is sent unchanged, so a leader and a follower of different versions agree on every dataset that previously worked. A follower too old to understand a frame stores nothing for that command rather than storing a truncated value.

Replication is not encrypted, in either direction, so it cannot be combined with --tls: that pair is refused at create, by edit and import, and again at every start. A --tls cache also refuses the replicate command, so it never becomes a leader either. See TLS under LIMITATIONS.

A sharded cache cannot be a replication leader, and says so. A follower arrives as one connection and SO_REUSEPORT gives it to one shard; that shard must be the only writer its socket ever has, and the other shards have no socket to it at all. Promoting it anyway would send the follower one shard's writes and report success, so replicate is refused on a cache with more than one shard, naming the reason. The follower protocol has no per-shard sequence and no end-of-dump marker, which is what fanning the stream out would need first.

A sharded cache may be a follower. Every shard dials the leader and keeps the part of the stream its slice owns, so it holds the leader's keys once rather than once per shard — at the cost of each shard reading the whole stream.

--tls--cert file--key file--ca file#

Terminate TLS on this cache's listening port, exactly as a server runtime does on its own. --tls requires --cert file and --key file; --ca file additionally demands a certificate from every connecting client (mutual TLS). RESP and the line protocol both run on the decrypted stream, so an existing Redis client needs no change beyond speaking TLS. Described in full under COMMON FLAGS.

Details

Default port: 9000

--shards N#

Run the cache as N worker processes over one keyspace. Which shard owns a key is decided by CRC16 of the key modulo 16384 — Redis's own hash slot function, hash tags included — and each shard owns a contiguous range of those slots.

Details

The N shards share one port under SO_REUSEPORT: a client connects, the kernel gives it to whichever shard the four-tuple hashes to, and a key another shard owns is fetched from that shard over the mesh. The cache is one store as far as any client can tell.

That crossing costs CPU, and with N shards a random key is foreign (N-1)/N of the time. Measured on this build, 8 client processes × 50 connections, three interleaved passes per arm, medians, requests per second per server core:

four shards, clients on the shared port     63,849   15.66 us/req
the same runtime with --cluster, clients
  routed to the per-shard ports             87,401   11.44 us/req
four independent single-shard caches        87,663   11.40 us/req

Absolute levels are not comparable between machines or between sessions; the ratio within one interleaved sweep is what is claimed. The same pair measured again hours later on the same binary read 84,828 and 116,894 — every level a third higher, the ratio 1.387 against 1.369.

--lua under --shards: the script runs in every shard, and each one keeps its own slice. The keyspace calls of the self.* table — self.set, self.get, self.del and the seventeen beside them — act on the keys this shard owns and answer a key it does not exactly as they answer a refusal: false for the mutating ones, an empty string for self.get and the two pops, nil for self.sadd. A crossing is not available to them: the value has to be returned on the same turn and the mesh answers on a later one.

For a callback that runs in all N processes — on_start, a timer — that is exactly right: the shards partition the work between them and the keyspace is written once. For one driven by a connection — on_miss, on_write, on_delete — the key the callback was handed is always its own, and any other key it touches is somebody else's. self.owns(key) is how a script asks before it acts, and it is true for every key when the cache is one process.

self.publish is the exception that is not refused. The message goes to every shard, over the same mesh the wire's PUBLISH uses, because a subscriber is not a key and no shard owns it. What is this shard's alone is the count: the siblings report back on a later turn and this call answers on the turn it was made.

--public#

Serve peers on other machines. A cache has no password and answers every client with everything it holds, so by default it serves only this machine: a TCP peer whose address is not loopback is answered -DENIED and closed before a byte of its is read. This is Redis's protected mode, for the reason Redis has it. --public lifts it, and so does mutual TLS (--tls --ca), where the client certificate is the credential. A follower on another host needs its leader to be public for the same reason. Set at create; a running cache takes it through import.

--cluster#

Publish a routable slot map, so that a cluster-aware client sends each key straight to the shard that owns it and no crossing happens at all. Off by default.

Details

Read this before you type it: a cache with --cluster cannot sit behind a proxy used for access control. Client-side routing means the client connects to every shard directly. This cache tells it where they are, and the address it gives is the one the asking connection arrived on. Put the cache behind a proxy and the asking connection is the proxy's, so the map names the address the proxy reaches the cache on. Either the client can reach that address too — and the proxy's rules have just been bypassed by a map the cache handed out — or it cannot, and the client spends its retry budget on a connection refused. Neither outcome produces a log line.

This is not a limitation of this implementation. It is what client-side routing is, and Redis Cluster has exactly the same property. There is no setting that makes a routing client and a proxy enforcement point work together; the choice is which of the two you want. Without --cluster the cache is reached only through its one port, which is what a proxy in front of it depends on.

Each shard binds its own port. Shard i binds port+1+i, in addition to the shared port, which keeps working exactly as it does without the flag. A client that connects to a per-shard port has chosen that shard on purpose, and a key it does not own is answered with -MOVED slot host:port rather than fetched. That is what lets redis-cli -c, redis-benchmark --cluster, redis-py, go-redis, lettuce and node-redis route for themselves.

A cache with --cluster therefore needs port+1 .. port+N free, and refuses to start otherwise. The address a client is sent to is a formula, computed by whichever shard answers CLUSTER SLOTS, which has no way to learn whether its siblings bound their ports. A shard that ran without one would be advertised anyway and every client would spend its retries on a connection refused, so the start fails instead, naming the port and naming this flag. Without --cluster nothing but the shared port is bound and two four-shard caches one port apart work as they always did.

--cluster is legal at any shard count. At --shards 1 it publishes a cluster of one node on the base port and binds nothing extra, so a client can be written once and deployed at any N.

CLUSTER SLOTS, SHARDS, NODES, INFO, MYID, KEYSLOT and COUNTKEYSINSLOT are answered on every port and at every shard count, with or without this flag — a client that asks deserves a straight answer. CLUSTER INFO reports cluster_enabled:1 only when --cluster was given; without it the reply is cluster_enabled:0, and CLUSTER SLOTS publishes a single node holding every slot on the shared port, which is both true and safe. There is no cluster bus, no failover, no slot migration and no ASK: the map is a formula and there is one owner per slot for the life of the run.

On a per-shard port, a command that asks about the keyspace answers for that shard. DBSIZE, KEYS, SCAN, FLUSH and LOAD report or act on the slice that shard holds, which is what a cluster client means when it asks a node, and what redis-cli --cluster call adds up itself. On the shared port they still fan out across every shard and merge, as they always have. PUBLISH fans out on both, because a subscriber on another shard is a subscriber.

A multi-key command on a per-shard port whose keys are all owned by one other shard is answered with -MOVED; one whose keys span shards is answered with -CROSSSLOT. The second is not pedantry: redirecting it would send the client to a shard that would redirect it back.

entries.summary: Serve the cache on an AF_UNIX socket instead of -p — redis-cli -s connects to it, and both the plaintext and RESP protocols are detected as on a port. The full treatment is --listen under COMMON FLAGS; refused with --cluster, because members advertise ports out of a formula and RESP has no way to write a filesystem path as a node address.

entries.term: --listen with --shards binds one node per shard.
entries.summary: Shard i gets name#i.sock, inserted before the suffix, by the rule the daemon's own companion nodes already follow. The pair used to be refused, and the refusal's reason was sound for a design nobody was proposing: N processes binding one path unlink each other's node and only the last stays reachable. N paths are N listeners.
Persistent storage file. Cache is saved on stop and loaded on start.

Journal every accepted write beside the dump, flushed on this cadence: an acknowledged write reaches the kernel at most duration after it was accepted, so a killed or OOM-killed worker loses at most the last interval of writes instead of everything since the last stop or FLUSH. Requires --persistent; refused without it. Durations read as everywhere — 30s, 5m, 1h — and a bare number is seconds.
Access control mode: readonly (GET, SIZE only), readwrite (GET, SET, DEL, SIZE - default), admin (all commands including FLUSH, LOAD).
Maximum memory for cache data. Supports K, M, G suffixes (e.g., 100M, 1G). When exceeded, behavior depends on eviction policy. 0 means unlimited (default).
Eviction policy when maxmemory is reached: noeviction (reject writes, default), allkeys-lru (evict least recently used), allkeys-random (evict random keys).

Force RESP2 protocol mode for all connections (Redis wire protocol). By default, the cache auto-detects RESP mode when a connection's first byte is '*'. With this flag, all connections use RESP regardless.
Connect as a follower to the specified leader cache. The follower receives a full data dump on connect, then receives ongoing write command replication. The follower operates in read-only mode.

Terminate TLS on this cache's listening port, exactly as a server runtime does on its own. --tls requires --cert file and --key file; --ca file additionally demands a certificate from every connecting client (mutual TLS). RESP and the line protocol both run on the decrypted stream, so an existing Redis client needs no change beyond speaking TLS. Described in full under COMMON FLAGS.

Run the cache as N worker processes over one keyspace. Which shard owns a key is decided by CRC16 of the key modulo 16384 — Redis's own hash slot function, hash tags included — and each shard owns a contiguous range of those slots.

Serve peers on other machines.  A cache has no password and answers every client with everything it holds, so by default it serves only this machine: a TCP peer whose address is not loopback is answered -DENIED and closed before a byte of its is read.  This is Redis's protected mode, for the reason Redis has it. --public lifts it, and so does mutual TLS (--tls --ca), where the client certificate i
Publish a routable slot map, so that a cluster-aware client sends each key straight to the shard that owns it and no crossing happens at all. Off by default.

sections.title: Cache Protocol
sections.html:
A pipelined batch is answered in full or the connection is closed, and either way what it costs is bounded. One connection may owe 8 MiB; a batch's replies are built before the loop returns to the ring, so nothing drains while it runs and a batch has to fit inside that bound. Past it the client is closed, with a line saying which one and how much it was owed.

So the depth worth using is the one whose replies fit: sixteen 256 KiB values is 4 MiB and is answered whole, sixty-four is 16 MiB and is cut. For small values the bound is nowhere near — a 64 byte value at depth 16 is a kilobyte.

That bound used to be a number the runtime failed to keep. The batch loop did not stop when the connection had been marked closing, and flush_responses() answers true for a closing connection — a skip its callers read as success — so the 1 MiB cap on the reply buffer called a flush that did nothing and cleared nothing, and the rest of the batch was still parsed and still answered into it. Measured, one connection asking for a 256 KiB value and reading none of it:

                        before        after
    64 pipelined GET    +17 MB        +11 MB
   512 pipelined GET   +141 MB        +10 MB
  4,096 pipelined GET  +1,063 MB      +11 MB
 16,384 pipelined GET    +941 MB      +11 MB

A GET is about thirty bytes against a 256 KiB answer, so that was roughly 8,700 to one, bounded by nothing but how many commands fit in one read. It is flat now.

A cache serving large values spends most of its time copying them, and that is a property of the design rather than a defect to tune around. Profiled at 256 KiB values, 16 clients, one command in flight, sampling the worker process:

              userspace memcpy   kernel copy   page clearing
  GET               28%             18%            13%
  SET               42%             28%             —

A GET copies the stored value once, into the reply buffer, and the kernel copies it again into the socket. A SET copies twice: once out of the receive ring into the connection's parse buffer, and once out of that into the store. Removing the GET copy means writing straight out of the store while a send is in flight, which needs the store to promise that a value outlives it — a promise every mutating path would have to keep, including the LRU eviction and TTL expiry that an unrelated key's write can trigger. Removing a SET copy means accumulating a bulk body outside the parse buffer, which the replication, sharding and cluster paths would all have to carry. Neither is a local change and neither is made here.

Sharding is not the answer to it, which is worth knowing before reaching for --shards. Measured at 256 KiB values, 32 clients, against one shard:

                                   SET       GET    cpu/op
  1 shard                       14,903    14,503     66 us
  4 shards, client not routing  23,175     8,306    151 us
  4 shards, --cluster, routed   19,920    19,960    158 us

A sharded cache without --cluster relays a command that arrived on the wrong shard rather than answering -MOVED, which is what lets an ordinary client work against one at all — and relaying a 256 KiB value puts it through a second process, so GET comes out at 0.57 of the single shard. With --cluster and a client that routes, four shards buy 1.38x on GET and 1.34x on SET, against the 3.2–3.6x at eight shards that small messages see. Either way the arm burns about 2.4 times the CPU per operation.

So what is left for an operator is the value size itself. In one run at sixteen clients: 64 bytes costs 4.4 us of CPU per operation, 4 KiB costs 4.8, 64 KiB costs 11.4 and 256 KiB costs 40.8. No setting closes that gap.

The receive ring is sixty-four buffers of 64 KiB, and its footprint is what counts. A provided-buffer ring is touched in rotation, so what it costs is count times size against the core's cache rather than the size of one buffer. The ring was 512 buffers of 4 KiB, and raising only the size — to a 32 MiB ring — cost 4.5% at 64 byte values and 24.5% at 256 KiB. Holding the footprint near the core's cache instead, measured on one binary with only the two variables differing, seven interleaved passes, 4 KiB x 512 against 64 KiB x 64:

  SET, 16 deep, 1 KiB values, 50 clients     +22.4%
  SET, 16 deep, 1 KiB values, 1000 clients   +24.5%
  SET, 16 deep, 4 KiB values                  +9.8%
  small values, 64 KiB and 256 KiB values     within 1.5%

The same size in 128 buffers, an 8 MiB ring, lost 12% at 256 KiB values, and 32 of them ran dry under 1000 pipelining clients. The knob exists to be measured, and it has been.

A read of a key held as another type answers -WRONGTYPE over RESP. get on a list, llen on a string, hgetall on a sorted set: all of them used to answer as though the key were absent — nil, 0, an empty array — which is worse than an error because a caller believes it and goes to its database for something the cache already holds. The probe runs only where a read has already missed its own container, so a hit costs nothing and a store holding one type costs four empty() tests. mget is the exception, and Redis's: it answers nil per wrong-typed key.

The text protocol keeps its own answers — "nil", "end", 0 — because they are its documented contract and a text client is not a Redis client. Connect via TCP and send commands (newline-terminated, all lowercase).

Nine of the commands listed below are RESP only, and the line protocol answers "failed: unknown command" to them: client, config, eval, evalsha, hello, psubscribe, punsubscribe, script and smismember.

Six of those are protocol and administration. The other three have one reason between them: the line protocol has no spelling for a list of arguments, since everything after the key is the value so that a value may contain spaces. That leaves no way to write smismember's members, or the keys and arguments eval and evalsha take after their script.

Strings:

set key value#

Store a key-value pair. Returns "ok", "error: type conflict", or "error: out of memory".

get key#

Retrieve value. Returns value or "nil".

del key#

Delete key (any type). Returns "ok" or "nil".

exists key#

Check if key exists. Returns "1" or "0".

incr key#

Increment integer value by 1. Returns new integer.

decr key#

Decrement integer value by 1. Returns new integer.

incrby key delta#

Increment integer value by delta. Returns new integer.

decrby key delta#

Decrement integer value by delta. Returns new integer.

append key value#

Append to string value. Returns new length.

strlen key#

Return string length. Returns 0 if missing.

getrange key start endsubstr key start end#

Return the substring between two inclusive offsets, negative counting from the end, empty rather than an error when the range is inverted or the key absent.

setrange key offset value#

Overwrite from offset onward, zero-padding a shorter value up to it, and return the new length.

incrbyfloat key delta#

Add a floating-point delta and return the new value. Replicated as its result rather than as itself, because two builds may round the same addition differently and a follower would then drift from its leader.

getdel key#

Return the value and remove the key in one step.

getset key newvalue#

Set new value and return old value. Returns old value or "nil".

mget key [key ...]#

Get multiple keys. Returns one value per line (nil if missing), then "end".

mset key value [key value ...]#

Set multiple key-value pairs atomically. Returns "ok".

type key#

Return type of key: "string", "list", "set", "hash", or "none".

keys pattern#

List all matching keys (glob patterns, "*" for all). Returns keys then "end".

setnx key value#

Set key only if it does not exist. Returns "1" (set) or "0" (not set).

setex key seconds value#

Set key with expiry. Equivalent to SET + EXPIRE. Returns "ok".

set key value [nx|xx] [ex sec |px ms ] [keepttl] [get]#

Over RESP, set takes Redis's options. nx writes only if the key is absent and xx only if it is there; ex and px set a deadline in seconds or milliseconds. Either must be positive: zero or less is refused and NOTHING is written, because a key stored with a deadline that came out at zero and no deadline on it is immortal and its owner has been told the write worked. An argument that is not a number is refused as one, rather than as a syntax error about the word after it.

Details

keepttl leaves the deadline alone, which a plain set clears — it is what a session refresh needs, where the value changes and the hour it has left does not. Asking for keepttl together with ex or px is a contradiction and is refused rather than resolved in one of the two directions.

get answers the value that was replaced instead of "ok", nil when there was none — and answers it even when nx refused the write, which is what makes it a read-and-write in one round trip. A key holding something other than a string answers -WRONGTYPE rather than nil, because a caller asking for the old value wants to hear that.

psetex key milliseconds value#

Set key with millisecond-precision expiry. Returns "ok".

scan cursor [match pattern] [count n] [valuematch glob] [withvalues] [type t] [field f]... [valuerange min max]#

Cursor-based key iteration. Returns next cursor (0 = done), then matching keys, then "end". Use cursor=0 to start; repeat with returned cursor until 0 is returned.

Details

A numeric range, which a glob cannot express. valuerange takes the bounds a zset range already speaks -- -inf, +inf, and a leading ( for an exclusive one -- and keeps the values that fall between them. With field it is that field that has to be in range.

A value that is not a number matches NO range, not even -inf +inf. The whole of the value has to be the number: "30kg" is not thirty, and a reader that stopped at the digits would be answering a question nobody asked.

More than one condition at once. field may be given more than once, up to four times, and the rule is one sentence: a field applies to the value predicates that follow it, until the next field. So

scan 0 field city valuematch berlin field age valuerange 25 40

returns the hashes that satisfy BOTH -- a conjunction, not a choice, and a hash missing either field satisfies neither. The order does not change the answer.

Asking the same thing with two scans and an intersection in the client costs two walks and the transfer of both result sets: measured over 50,000 records where each condition keeps about a quarter and the pair keeps a fifteenth, 96.5 ms and 25,841 keys against 37.8 ms and 3,335. It is also the only way to get an answer that was true at one moment, because two scans are two walks of a keyspace that need not have held still between them.

A value predicate given before any field asks about the key's own value, as it always has -- and mixing the two in one scan matches nothing, because no key is both a string and a hash.

Asking what a FIELD of a hash holds. field walks the hashes and matches valuematch against what the named field of each one holds, rather than against the key's own value -- which is the question a database is asked, for the layout records are usually kept in. A hash WITHOUT the field does not match, not even a predicate that matches everything: that is a different answer from a hash whose field is empty, and asking for the empty one is valuematch "". With withvalues it is the field's value that comes back beside the key. From outside this is an hget per hash key: measured at 15.8 ms against 1.5 ms over 5,000 hashes, and that against a client already pipelining and already using type.

Returning the value beside the key. withvalues returns key and value interleaved, the way hscan returns field and value, so a client that wanted the records does not send a second mget for them: the walk had the value in hand when it matched the key. It restricts to strings for the same reason valuematch does. Measured as one page used as a query it is worth about a sixth of the operation, two round trips becoming one; over a whole keyspace it is worth less, because the bytes move either way and only the second lookup and the extra commands go. Note that the reply is then sized by VALUES rather than by keys, which is why count keeps its small default here and only a value predicate raises it.

Restricting to one type. type takes one of string, list, set, hash or zset in any case, and returns only keys of that type. It is close to free: the type of a key is the map it is stored in, and the walk visits the five maps in a fixed order anyway, so a restriction is a walk of one map instead of five. A name no type has matches nothing rather than everything.

Keep the options constant across an iteration. match, count, valuematch and type are properties of the whole walk, not of one call: the cursor names the map the walk has reached, so handing a cursor from a restricted walk back without the restriction resumes partway through the keyspace and never returns what came before it. The reverse direction is caught -- a value or type walk given a cursor from elsewhere starts its map again rather than trusting a bucket index belonging to a different table.

Filtering on the value. valuematch returns only the keys whose VALUE matches the glob, which a client would otherwise do by fetching the whole keyspace and discarding nearly all of it. Only a string key holds a single value, so a list, set, hash or zset never matches one, not even when it contains the pattern as a member. With valuematch present, count bounds the keys EXAMINED rather than the keys returned and defaults to 1000: the predicate is selective, so a page bounded by results would walk the whole keyspace in a single call. This is a scan and not an index. It costs about 8 per cent over a plain scan per key examined, and nothing is maintained on the write path.

What an iteration guarantees. A key that is present for the whole iteration is returned at least once, provided the store did not grow enough to rehash its table during it. A key may be returned more than once, and a key added or removed while the iteration is running may or may not appear — so a caller that is counting should count distinct keys rather than replies.

The exception is worth being precise about, because it is the one Redis does not have. A rehash moves keys between buckets, and a key moved into a bucket this iteration has already passed will not be returned by it. Redis avoids that with reverse-binary iteration, which needs a power-of-two bucket count; the tables here use prime counts and cannot offer one. The cursor carries the bucket count so a rehash is at least noticed: the map being walked restarts, which trades duplicates — allowed above — for the skip, which is not.

count is a hint, as it is in Redis. Whole buckets are returned, so a reply may carry somewhat more or fewer keys than asked for.

size [type t]#

Return the number of stored keys. Without type that is every type together, which is what DBSIZE answers over RESP; with it, the count of that one type and nothing else.

Details

Both are O(1): the count of a type is the size of the map it is stored in, so this is a lookup and not a walk. Counting the same thing with scan ... type is the whole map walked and every key name sent back -- measured at 50.6 ms against 0.107 ms over 50,000 hashes, and the gap widens with the keyspace because only one side of it grows. A name no type has counts nothing rather than everything.

Lists (ordered, deque-backed):

lpush key value#

Insert at front. Returns "ok" or "error: type conflict".

rpush key value#

Insert at back.

lpop key#

Remove and return front element. Returns value or "nil".

rpop key#

Remove and return back element.

llen key#

Return list length.

lindex key index#

Return element at index (negative = from end).

lrange key start stop#

Return range of elements (multi-line, "end" terminator). Negative indices supported.

lset key index value#

Replace the element at index. Answers "nil" when the key is absent and refuses an index past the end.

lrem key count value#

Remove up to count occurrences from the head, from the tail when negative, all of them when zero, and return how many went.

ltrim key start stop#

Keep only the inclusive range and drop the rest; a range that selects nothing removes the key, because an empty list is not a key here.

linsert key before|after pivot value#

Insert beside the first occurrence of pivot, returning the new length, 0 when the key is absent and -1 when the pivot is.

blpop key [key ...] timeoutbrpop key [key ...] timeout#

lpop and rpop that wait. The keys are tried in the order given and the first with anything in it answers at once; when none has, the caller waits until something is pushed or timeout seconds pass. 0 waits for ever. The reply names the key as well as the element, because with several keys the caller cannot otherwise tell which one it came from.

Details

The longest-waiting client is served first. A worker pool that served its newest member would starve the one that has been idle longest, which is the member most likely to be healthy.

Everything pipelined behind a blocking pop waits for it. This is the only command here that answers on a later turn than the one it arrived on, so the rest of that connection's input stays unparsed until the wait ends — otherwise the second reply would overtake the first.

Not available on a sharded cache, and refused by name. Every shard is a process of its own: the client waits in one and the key it waits on can be owned by another, and the crossing protocol carries answers to questions rather than a push arriving somewhere nobody asked. Refused the way replicate is, rather than blocking on a key this process will never see written.

What replicates is the pop and not the wait — a follower running blpop would be waiting for its own push and would never see the leader's.

rpoplpush source destinationlmove source destination left|right left|right#

Move one element from one end of source to one end of destination, returning it. rpoplpush is lmove src dst right left under its older name. The two keys may be the same, which rotates the list.

Details

Every refusal happens before the element is taken. This is the reliable-queue move: a job leaves the pending list and arrives in the processing one, and a worker that dies between the two is why the pattern exists. A wrong-typed destination, a memory limit or a destination on another shard are therefore all decided first — the element is never in neither list.

On a sharded cache the pair must hash to one shard. -CROSSSLOT otherwise, which is Redis's answer and not a crossing: moving it would be a write in one process that a refusal in another cannot undo.

Sets (unique unordered members):

sadd key member#

Add member. Returns "ok", "exists", or "error: type conflict".

srem key member#

Remove member. Returns "ok" or "nil".

sismember key member#

Check membership. Returns "1" or "0".

scard key#

Return set cardinality.

spop key#

Remove and return one member. The member is the one this process's iteration order reaches first, so it replicates as the srem it turned out to be rather than as itself — a follower running spop would pick a different one.

srandmember key#

The same member, left in place.

smismember key member [member ...]#

One 1 or 0 per member, in the order asked.

smembers key#

Return all members (multi-line, "end" terminator).

Details

Hashes (nested key-value maps):

hset key field value#

Set hash field. Returns "ok", "error: type conflict", or "error: out of memory".

hget key field#

Get hash field value. Returns value or "nil".

hdel key field#

Delete hash field. Returns "ok" or "nil".

hlen key#

Return number of hash fields.

hgetall key#

Return all fields and values (multi-line "field value\n", "end" terminator).

hkeys keyhvals key#

The fields alone, or the values alone.

hmget key field [field ...]#

One value per field, "nil" for a field that is not there.

hmset key field value [field value ...]#

Several fields at once.

hexists key field#

1 or 0.

hstrlen key field#

The length of a field's value, 0 when it is not there.

hincrby key field delta#

Add to a field read as an integer, creating it at delta if it is absent, and return the new value.

hsetnx key field value#

Set the field only if it does not exist. Returns 1 or 0.

hscan key cursor [match pattern] [count n] [valuematch glob]sscan key cursor [match pattern] [count n]zscan key cursor [match pattern] [count n]#

scan over one key's collection instead of over the keyspace: start at 0, pass back the cursor each call, and 0 again means the walk is done. valuematch is hscan\'s alone among the three: it asks what a field HOLDS, where match asks what it is called. A set's members and a zset's scores are not values in that sense, and both answer a syntax error rather than pretending -- one option meaning three things is worse than one option fewer. count is a hint and defaults to 10, as it does on Redis; a collection smaller than one bucket-load comes back whole with cursor 0.

Details

The cursor carries the collection's bucket count as well as its position, so a resume can tell whether the table it is going back into is the one it left. A rehash between two calls restarts the walk rather than silently skipping the elements that moved.

The order of fields is not the order they were set in. A hash is backed by an unordered map here, so hgetall, hkeys and hvals return the fields in an order this process decides. Redis keeps insertion order for a small hash because a small hash is a listpack there, and stops keeping it once the hash grows into a hashtable — so a client that depends on the order is depending on Redis's encoding, not on its contract.

Sorted sets:

A score per member, read back in score order. The type is exclusive like the other four: a key that is a string refuses zadd.

zadd key score member#

Add or re-score a member. Returns "1" when the member is new and "0" when it was already there and only its score moved. A score may be fractional and is parsed whole — 1x is refused, not read as 1.

zrem key member#

Remove a member. Returns "ok" or "nil". The key goes when its last member does.

zscore key member#

Return the score, or "nil".

zcard key#

Return the number of members.

zrank key member#

Rank counting from the lowest score, zero-based, or "nil".

zrevrank key member#

The same counting from the highest.

zrange key start stop [withscores]#

Members by rank, ends inclusive, negative counting from the last — the rules lrange has. With withscores each line is "member score". Terminated by "end".

zrevrange key start stop [withscores]#

The same walked from the highest score.

zincrby key delta member#

Add to a member's score, creating it at delta if it is not there, and return the new score.

zrangebyscore key min max [withscores]zrevrangebyscore key max min [withscores]#

Members whose score falls in the range, which is what a sorted set is kept for. Both ends are inclusive; a leading ( makes one exclusive, and -inf and +inf are the open ends. The reverse spelling takes its bounds the other way round, as Redis does.

zcount key min max#

How many fall in that range, with the same bound spelling.

zpopmin keyzpopmax key#

Remove and return the lowest-scoring member, or the highest, with its score. Replicated as the zrem it turned out to be, for the reason spop gives above.

zremrangebyrank key start stopzremrangebyscore key min max#

Remove a range by position or by score and return how many went. Emptying the set removes the key.

Details

Streams:

The stream commands are Redis 7.0's, with its arguments, its answers and its errors; the line protocol splits their words on spaces, so a field or value there cannot hold one, and answers an array one element a line followed by "end". An empty stream is still a key, as in Redis.

xadd key [nomkstream] [maxlen|minid [=|~] n [limit n]] *|id field value ...#

Append an entry and return its id. * takes the clock in milliseconds, or the last id's with its sequence counted up when the clock has not moved past it; ms-* asks for the next sequence in that millisecond. An id at or below the last one is refused. A replica and the journal receive the id it got, never *. maxlen ~ removes whole blocks of up to a hundred entries only, as Redis removes whole nodes, so it can leave more than asked for.

xlen key#

The number of entries.

xrange key start end [count n]xrevrange key end start [count n]#

Entries in id order, or the reverse, one a line as "id field value ...". - and + are the ends, a lone millisecond takes every sequence in it, and a leading ( makes a bound exclusive.

xdel key id [id ...]#

Remove entries and return how many there were.

xtrim key maxlen|minid [=|~] n [limit n]#

Remove from the oldest end and return how many went.

xread [count n] [block ms] streams key [key ...] id [id ...]#

Entries past each id, one a line as "key id field value ...". $ is the last id when the read was asked. block waits for the next xadd to any of the keys when there is nothing yet, 0 waiting for ever; a wait inside multi answers "nil" at once, and a script may not wait at all. On a sharded cache every key must belong to one shard, and a blocking read is served only by the shard that owns its streams — through that shard's --cluster port.

xgroup create key group id|$ [mkstream] [entriesread n]xgroup setid|destroy|createconsumer|delconsumer key group ...#

Make, move or remove a consumer group, or one of its consumers.

xreadgroup group g consumer [count n] [block ms] [noack] streams key ... id ...#

> delivers what the group has not delivered and records it as pending on the consumer, unless noack; any other id re-reads that consumer's own pending entries.

xack key group id [id ...]#

Take entries off the pending list and return how many were on it.

xpending key group [[idle ms] start end count [consumer]]#

The pending list: a summary, or entries with their consumer, idle time and delivery count.

xclaim key group consumer min-idle id ... [idle ms] [time ms] [retrycount n] [force] [justid] [lastid id]xautoclaim key group consumer min-idle start [count n] [justid]#

Take over entries another consumer left pending, the second walking the list from start and also answering the ids that xdel removed from under the group.

xinfo stream key [full [count n]] | groups key | consumers key group#

What a stream, its groups or a group's consumers hold.

xsetid key id [entriesadded n] [maxdeletedid id]#

Set the stream's last id and counters, which is how a replica is told them.

Details

Pattern subscriptions:

psubscribe pattern [pattern ...]punsubscribe pattern [pattern ...]#

Receive from every channel a glob pattern matches — *, ? and character classes, the same matching keys uses. The delivery is pmessage and carries the pattern as well as the channel, because a client subscribed to two patterns cannot otherwise tell which one matched.

Details

Every subscribe verb confirms with a count. subscribe, unsubscribe, psubscribe and punsubscribe each answer a three-element reply naming the verb, the channel or pattern, and how many subscriptions the connection now holds. A client library counts down from that number to know its own batch is complete — these used to answer "+OK", which gives it nothing to count.

A pattern costs a sharded cache its publish filter, and only then. A publish normally wakes just the shards whose filter says they may hold a subscriber of that channel. A pattern matches channels that do not exist yet, so it has no bit to set; a shard holding one is woken by every publish instead. Nothing changes for a cache that has no pattern subscriber.

Transactions with a check:

watch key [key ...]unwatch#

exec does nothing if a watched key was written between the watch and it — over RESP the reply is a nil array, whose type is how a client tells "did not run" from "ran and returned nothing", and over the text protocol the word aborted. Either way the watch ends, so a retry starts from a fresh one.

Details

Without this, multi is a batch: the commands run together and nothing checks that the world still looks the way the client read it. With it, the compare-and-set loop that a distributed lock or a counter needs becomes possible.

A write to a different key does not abort. The mark is set in one place, before the switch that runs the command, and it is driven by a list of read-only commands rather than a list of writes: a write missing from a list of writes would be a transaction committing over a change it never saw, silently, while a read missing from the read list is one retry too many. Commands that can touch anything — mset, del over several keys, flush, eval — mark every watcher rather than a list.

watch inside multi is refused, as it is on Redis: a watch taken after the queue started could not be checked against the reads that decided what to queue.

Scripting:

Lua, over RESP, with the script coming from the client.

eval script numkeys key... arg...evalsha sha1 numkeys key... arg...#

Run script, with the declared keys in KEYS and the rest in ARGV, both 1-based. redis.call runs a command and raises what it answers if that is an error; redis.pcall hands the error back as a table with err. redis.status_reply, redis.error_reply and redis.sha1hex are there; redis.log is accepted and writes nothing.

Details

A command that would outlive the script on the caller's connection is refused with -ERR This Redis command is not allowed from script, as Redis refuses it: eval, evalsha, script, multi, exec, discard, watch, unwatch, the four subscribe commands, quit, reset, hello, auth and client. A blocking pop answers at once, as its non-blocking twin would.

The return value is converted as Redis converts it: a number becomes an integer truncated towards zero, a string a bulk, a table an array up to its first hole — Lua's own rule for where an array ends — false a nil and true the integer 1. A table carrying err or ok is an error or a status rather than a list.

The interpreter is not the one --lua uses, and that is the point. COMMON FLAGS says of that one that it is not a sandbox: it has io, os, package and the whole of base open, which is the right trade for a script the operator wrote and the wrong one for a script that arrived over the network. This state is opened the other way round — base, string, table and math, with every loader removed by name. Under LuaJIT the one that decides it is ffi: require("ffi") is arbitrary memory access, which is a shell on the machine, so require is not there to reach it with. A client's script also cannot see the operator's globals, because the two states never meet.

A script holds the event loop of its shard while it runs. So it runs under the same count hook a Lua callback does, and a runaway one is stopped with a script exceeded the 10000ms deadline rather than holding every other client on that shard for ever. The bound is callback_timeout_ms or SOCKETLEY_LUA_TIMEOUT_MS, as it is for callbacks.

On a sharded cache a script is routed by the keys it declares. Not a convention here but the routing itself: the shard that owns KEYS[1] runs it, keys belonging to two shards answer -CROSSSLOT, and a script declaring no keys runs wherever it was asked. A script that reaches a key it did not declare is reaching into whatever store the shard it landed on happens to have.

script load scriptscript exists sha1 [sha1 ...]script flush#

The script cache. eval loads as well as runs, so a client may try evalsha first and fall back to eval on -NOSCRIPT, which is the usual shape.

Details

The cache is per shard, as it is per node on Redis Cluster. A sharded cache's shared port hands each connection to whichever shard the kernel picks, so a script load sticks to one of them. eval is what makes this self-healing; a client that wants evalsha to work everywhere sends script load to each per-shard port, which is what a cluster client does with each master.

Connection and introspection:

The set a client library sends before it sends anything of its own. Answering them is what lets a connection finish being made; refusing them by name is what lets a client fall back rather than fail.

hello [protover]#

The handshake. RESP2 only: hello with no argument or with 2 answers a map naming the server, the version, the protocol, this connection's id, whether the cache is clustered and whether it is a replica. hello 3 is refused with -NOPROTO, which is what a Redis before 6 answers and what every client falls back from — an unknown-command error is not a protocol negotiation failure and need not be handled as one.

info#

The fields a monitor reads back: version, connected clients, memory, commands processed, role, whether clustering is on, and the key count. On a sharded cache the key count is this shard's slice, for the reason dbsize answers that way on a per-shard port.

Details

The replication section is the one that differs by role, because half of its fields have no meaning on the other side. role answers master or slave. A follower adds master_host, master_port, master_link_status and master_sync_in_progress; a leader adds connected_slaves — the number of followers whose connection is live, not the number that ever attached.

master_link_status reads up once a full sync has finished and not when the socket opens, and master_sync_in_progress separates the two reasons it can read down: no leader was reached at all, or a dump is still arriving. A follower whose target was never usable leaves master_host empty and master_port at zero, which is the honest answer to "where".

config get parameter#

maxmemory answers with the configured limit; save and appendonly answer empty, which is true here; anything else answers an empty array rather than an invented value.

command#

An empty array. A client asks command for a table of arity and flags, this cache keeps no such table, and saying so is more useful than a table that is wrong.

echo messageselect index#

select 0 succeeds because there is one keyspace here; any other index is refused rather than ignored, so a client addressing database 3 learns it rather than quietly sharing database 0 with everybody else.

client id|getname|setname|setinfo#

setname and setinfo are what redis-py and node-redis send on connect and are accepted; id answers this connection's descriptor.

auth#

Refused by name. There is no password on a cache, and a silent success would tell a client it had authenticated.

Details

Transactions:

Grouping, not rollback. Between multi and exec a command is queued and answered "queued"; nothing has run, and a second connection reading the same key still sees the old value. EXEC then runs the queue back to back on an event loop that is single-threaded, so no other connection's command lands in the middle of it. A command that fails inside exec fails alone — the ones before it stay.

multi#

Begin queueing. Nested multi is refused.

exec#

Run the queue in order, then "end". Refused without a multi.

discard#

Throw the queue away.

Details

TTL / Expiry:

expire key seconds#

Set time-to-live. Returns "ok" or "nil" (key not found). A seconds of zero or less is a deletion, not an error: the key goes and the answer is "ok", which is what Redis does and what a caller whose own arithmetic came out at zero means.

ttl key#

Return remaining seconds, -1 (no ttl), or -2 (not found).

persist key#

Remove expiry. Returns "ok" or "nil".

pexpire key milliseconds#

Set millisecond-precision TTL. Returns "1" (set) or "0" (key not found). Zero or less deletes, as with expire.

pttl key#

Return remaining TTL in milliseconds, -1 (no ttl), or -2 (not found).

expireat key unix_seconds#

Set expiry to an absolute Unix timestamp (seconds). Returns "1", or "0" if there is no such key. A timestamp already past deletes the key and answers "1".

pexpireat key unix_ms#

Set expiry to an absolute Unix timestamp in milliseconds. Same answers as expireat.

Details

All four saturate rather than refusing: a deadline past the range of the clock means "never", and one past its other end means "already gone". Redis refuses these with an error instead, which is the one place this family answers differently on purpose — the number a client sent is honoured as far as the clock goes rather than rejected.

Pub/Sub:

subscribe channel#

Subscribe to a channel. Returns "ok". Messages are delivered as "message <channel> <payload>\n".

unsubscribe channel#

Unsubscribe from a channel. Returns "ok".

publish channel message#

Publish a message to all subscribers. Returns number of subscribers reached.

Details

Memory Management:

maxmemory #

Query current maxmemory setting. Returns bytes or "0" (unlimited).

memory #

Query current memory usage in bytes.

Details

Admin (requires --mode admin):

flush [path]#

Save cache to file (uses --persistent path if omitted).

load [path]#

Load cache from file.

Type enforcement: a key can only hold one data type. Writing to a key of a different type returns "error: type conflict". Under --maxmemory a write that does not fit is refused with "error: out of memory" (RESP: "OOM command not allowed when used memory > 'maxmemory'"), and the key it would have written is left exactly as it was. That includes a write over a key that already exists: overwriting a value, appending to it or replacing a hash field is checked against the limit like any other write. Multi-line responses (lrange, smembers, hgetall) terminate with "end\n".
