sections.title: RESP Protocol (Redis Compatibility)
sections.html:
The cache supports the RESP2 wire protocol for compatibility with Redis clients (redis-cli, Redis client libraries). RESP mode is auto-detected when a connection's first byte is '*', or can be forced with --resp.

Supported Redis commands, case-insensitive. A command not listed here is answered with an error naming it, never silently ignored.

Strings

SET (EX, PX, NX, XX, KEEPTTL, GET), GET, GETSET, GETDEL, GETRANGE, SUBSTR, SETRANGE, SETNX, SETEX, PSETEX, MGET, MSET, APPEND, STRLEN, INCR, DECR, INCRBY, DECRBY, INCRBYFLOAT

Keys

DEL, UNLINK, EXISTS, TOUCH, TYPE, KEYS, SCAN, DBSIZE, RANDOMKEY, RENAME, RENAMENX, COPY, FLUSHALL, FLUSHDB, EXPIRE, PEXPIRE, EXPIREAT, PEXPIREAT, TTL, PTTL, EXPIRETIME, PEXPIRETIME, PERSIST

RENAME carries the key's expiry with it, and so does COPY — renaming or copying is not a way to make an expiring key permanent. RENAME and COPY name two keys, so on a sharded cache both must belong to one shard and keys that do not are refused with -CROSSSLOT; a key cannot be half-moved. FLUSHALL and FLUSHDB are the same command here, because this cache has one keyspace and no SELECT-able databases to leave behind.

Lists

LPUSH, RPUSH, LPOP, RPOP, LLEN, LRANGE, LINDEX, LSET, LREM, LTRIM, LINSERT, LMOVE, RPOPLPUSH, BLPOP, BRPOP

Sets

SADD, SREM, SISMEMBER, SMISMEMBER, SCARD, SMEMBERS, SPOP, SRANDMEMBER, SSCAN, SINTER, SUNION, SDIFF, SINTERSTORE, SUNIONSTORE, SDIFFSTORE, SMOVE

Set algebra reads whole sets and answers one thing, so on a sharded cache it cannot be split across shards the way MGET or DEL can — an intersection computed on two shards separately is not an intersection. Every key must therefore belong to one shard, and keys that do not are refused with -CROSSSLOT, which is what Redis Cluster answers and for the same reason. Use a hash tag ({user}:seen) to place them together.

Hashes

HSET, HSETNX, HGET, HMSET, HMGET, HDEL, HLEN, HEXISTS, HKEYS, HVALS, HGETALL, HSTRLEN, HINCRBY, HSCAN

Sorted sets

ZADD, ZREM, ZSCORE, ZCARD, ZCOUNT, ZINCRBY, ZRANK, ZREVRANK, ZRANGE, ZREVRANGE, ZRANGEBYSCORE, ZREVRANGEBYSCORE, ZPOPMIN, ZPOPMAX, ZREMRANGEBYRANK, ZREMRANGEBYSCORE, ZSCAN

Streams

XADD, XLEN, XRANGE, XREVRANGE, XREAD (BLOCK), XDEL, XTRIM, XSETID, XGROUP (CREATE, SETID, DESTROY, CREATECONSUMER, DELCONSUMER), XREADGROUP (BLOCK, NOACK), XACK, XPENDING, XCLAIM, XAUTOCLAIM, XINFO (STREAM [FULL], GROUPS, CONSUMERS)

Replies and errors are Redis 7.0's, compared against a redis-server by test_cache_streams_vs_redis.sh; XINFO STREAM's radix-tree-nodes counts no tree, since the entries sit in blocks indexed by a sorted array. XADD, XGROUP CREATE and CREATECONSUMER are refused with OOM at the memory limit, as Redis refuses its denyoom commands; XREADGROUP and XCLAIM are not, which is also Redis's rule. An XREAD naming streams of several shards is answered -CROSSSLOT.

Pub/Sub

SUBSCRIBE, UNSUBSCRIBE, PSUBSCRIBE, PUNSUBSCRIBE, PUBLISH

Transactions

MULTI, EXEC, DISCARD, WATCH, UNWATCH

Scripting

EVAL, EVALSHA, SCRIPT LOAD, SCRIPT EXISTS, SCRIPT FLUSH

Connection and server

PING, ECHO, AUTH, HELLO, SELECT, QUIT, RESET, CLIENT (GETNAME, SETNAME, ID, REPLY, SETINFO), CONFIG GET/SET, COMMAND, INFO, CLUSTER

Where the answers differ from Redis on purpose

The RESP array limit is 1024 arguments, not 1024*1024: args[] is a stack array and a million views would be sixteen megabytes of it. A command over the limit is refused with an error that names the limit, and the connection is closed -- the stream is framed, but the arguments were never stored, so it cannot continue from a message it did not take.

Lua scripts share one interpreter state, so its globals are sealed: writing a global raises an error naming the variable, and the globals table itself is unnamed, so rawset and table.insert cannot reach it either. Use local for everything, including functions — local function f() end rather than function f() end, which is what Redis requires too.

One difference from Redis remains, deliberately: reading an undefined global returns nil here, as ordinary Lua does, where Redis raises. Blocking the WRITE is what closes the channel between two clients; erroring on the read only catches typos, and it would break a script that tests a global to see whether it is there.

Example with redis-cli:

redis-cli -p 9000 SET mykey myval
redis-cli -p 9000 GET mykey
redis-cli -p 9000 EVAL "return redis.call('GET', KEYS[1])" 1 mykey
redis-cli -p 9000 SUBSCRIBE news

sections.title: Database Backend
sections.html:
Cache runtimes support four Lua callbacks for DB-backed operation. Attach a Lua script with --lua and implement whichever callbacks you need using any Lua DB library (luasql-mysql, luasql-postgres, lsqlite3, etc.).

Callback|Signature|When called
on_miss(key)|-> value [, ttl_seconds]|GET returns nil — fetch from DB
on_write(key, value, ttl)|-> nothing|T{
After successful SET/SETEX/SETNX/MSET
T}
on_delete(key)|-> nothing|After DEL — delete from DB
on_expire(key)|-> nothing|After TTL sweep removes key

on_miss may return two values (Lua multi-return): the fetched string and an optional TTL in seconds. If the value is nil or empty, the GET returns nil to the client normally. If a value is returned, it is inserted into the cache and returned to the client transparently (read-through / lazy population).

on_write is called synchronously on the event loop thread. For write-heavy loads, use the write-behind pattern: buffer writes in Lua inside on_write and flush to the DB in on_tick every few seconds. This decouples SET latency from DB latency entirely.

Example (SQLite write-behind):

tick_ms = 2000
local db, pending = nil, {}

function on_start()
    local sq = require("lsqlite3")
    db = sq.open("/tmp/cache.db")
    db:exec("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS cache_kv (key TEXT PRIMARY KEY, value TEXT)")
end

function on_miss(key)
    for row in db:nrows("SELECT value FROM cache_kv WHERE key=" .. db:quote(key)) do
        return row.value, 300  -- value + 300 s TTL
    end
end

function on_write(key, value, ttl)
    pending[key] = value  -- buffer
end

function on_tick(dt)
    for k, v in pairs(pending) do
        db:exec("INSERT OR REPLACE INTO cache_kv(key,value) VALUES("..db:quote(k)..","..db:quote(v)..")")
    end
    pending = {}
end

function on_delete(key)
    db:exec("DELETE FROM cache_kv WHERE key="..db:quote(key))
end

See examples/cache/db-backend.lua for a full example with MySQL, Postgres, and SQLite backends.

sections.title: Replication
sections.html:
Cache runtimes support leader-follower replication.

The follower connects to the leader and receives a full data dump, then ongoing write commands are forwarded in real-time. Followers are read-only.

# Start leader cache
socketley create cache leader -p 9000 -s

# Start follower
socketley create cache follower -p 9001 --replicate 127.0.0.1:9000 -s

# Writes on leader are replicated to follower
echo "set key val" | nc localhost 9000
echo "get key" | nc localhost 9001    # Returns "val"

Example with netcat:

echo "set user:1 alice" | nc localhost 9000
echo "get user:1" | nc localhost 9000
echo "lpush queue task1" | nc localhost 9000
echo "hset user:1 name alice" | nc localhost 9000
echo "expire user:1 300" | nc localhost 9000
echo "subscribe news" | nc localhost 9000

sections.title: STORAGE FLAGS
sections.html:
A storage runtime serves the S3 API over one directory, so that unmodified S3 clients (boto3, the AWS CLI, rclone, SDKs) can put, get, list and delete objects on this machine's disk:

socketley create storage media -p 9000 --dir /srv/objects \
    --access-key AKIAEXAMPLE --secret-key wJalrXUtnFEMI -s

It runs in a worker process of its own like every other runtime, speaks HTTP/1.1 with path-style addressing (/bucket/key) and, given --domain, virtual-hosted style (bucket.domain/key) as well, answers errors as S3 XML (<Error><Code>...) and stamps every reply with an x-amz-request-id. The flags below are the runtime's own; -p, --listen, --tls, --cert, --key, --ca, --cpus, --max-connections, --idle-timeout and the common flags apply as documented under COMMON FLAGS.

--dir path#

Where the buckets live. Required, created if it does not exist, and made absolute against the caller's directory. A runtime is one process on one directory, or with --shards several that share it: two runtimes on one path would append to each other's journals.

--access-key key--secret-key secret#

The one pair of credentials requests are signed with (AWS Signature Version 4). They go together: one without the other is refused. The pair is kept in the state file and printed by show; prefer --credentials where that matters.

--credentials file#

A file of several pairs, one access:secret per line. Blank lines and lines starting with # are skipped, and the secret is everything after the first colon, so it may hold one. A line [id] begins a user, whose settings and keys follow it until the next; a file without one is a single owner, as described under Users. The path is made absolute against the caller's directory. The file is read at start, refused at create and start if it does not parse or holds nothing, and read again when it changes (checked at most once a second, on the next request): a key added to it works at once, a key taken out stops, and a file that has gone, is empty or no longer parses leaves the keys in force until it is repaired, with a warning in the log, so a half-written edit locks nobody out. A user's policy file is watched the same way. Connections are not dropped by a reload. A key given with --access-key is one of the set too.

--sse-key-file file#

The master key every object's data key is wrapped with under server-side encryption with S3-managed keys (SSE-S3): a file of exactly 32 bytes, or of 64 hex digits and an optional newline, that only its owner may read. A file the group or others may read, or of any other length, is refused at create and start, so the key is never on a command line or in the state file — only its path, made absolute against the caller's directory. It is read at every start. Without it a request for AES256 and a bucket default that would need one are refused with 501 NotImplemented; SSE-C needs no master key. Keep the file: an object sealed under one key is not opened by another, and is answered 500 InternalError saying so. See Server-side encryption.

--domain name[,name...]#

The domains the endpoint is reached under, such as s3.example.com: a request whose Host is bucket.domain (with or without a port) addresses that bucket, and its whole path is the key. A Host equal to one of the domains, an address, or any other name is path style as without the flag, so both styles are served at once. Names are DNS names, compared without regard to case; anything else is refused at create. See Virtual-hosted-style addressing.

--website-domain name[,name...]#

The domains buckets' websites are reached under, such as web.example.com: a request whose Host is bucket.domain is a browser's request to that bucket's website rather than to the S3 API, and is answered from the bucket's WebsiteConfiguration. Names are checked as for --domain, and a Host under both is the website's. See Website hosting.

--fsync always|interval|never#

When a write a client was answered for is on the disk. always (the default) syncs the object's file and its directory before the answer, so an answered write survives a crash of the machine. interval answers without those syncs and syncs the whole filesystem every --fsync-interval; never leaves it to the kernel's own writeback. Either way a crash of the process loses nothing, and a stop syncs everything before it says it was clean. See Durability.

--sync never|active|per-user#

Which sync runtimes the storage makes to pull its users' git repositories: never makes none (the default), active one for the whole storage, per-user one for each user. Each sync runtime is a process of its own, which is why none is made unless asked for. Applied by import; a change takes the runtimes a previous setting made away at the storage's next start. See Git repositories under the storage runtime.

--fsync-interval duration#

How often --fsync interval syncs the filesystem, 1 second to an hour; default 1s.

--notify-targets file#

The webhooks a bucket's event notifications may be sent to, one name url per line, with an optional third field ca=file naming the CA an https webhook's certificate is checked against (the system's when absent); blank lines are skipped, and so is a field that begins with # and the rest of its line:

Details
# name   url
audit    http://10.0.0.5:8080/s3-events
thumbs   https://thumbs.internal/hook ca=/etc/ssl/internal-ca.pem
feed     cache://events/stream/s3
live     cache://events/channel/s3
panel    server://dashboard
bus      mqtt://broker/storage/events
oncall   mail://m/ops@example.com,dev@example.com

A url may also name another runtime of the daemon: cache://runtime/stream/key appends each event to that cache's stream as an entry of one field event, cache://runtime/channel/channel publishes it on that channel, and server://runtime broadcasts it to the server's clients, and mqtt://runtime/topic publishes it on that broker's topic at QoS 1, answered once the broker holds it, and mail://runtime/address[,address...] mails it to those addresses through that mail runtime, its subject what the event is, answered once the message is in the spool; such a line takes no ca=. An event a cache refuses or a runtime that is not running is retried like a webhook that does not answer. A configuration names one as arn:socketley:webhook:::name. The file is refused at create and start if a line does not parse and is read at every start; its host names are resolved off the loop and again when a connection is refused (a host that does not resolve is logged and its events wait until it does). Without it every destination is refused. See Event notifications.

--replication-targets file#

The S3 endpoints a bucket's replication may write to, one name url region access_key secret per line, with an optional sixth field ca=file for an https endpoint, comments and blank lines as in --notify-targets:

Details
# name   url                          region     access key            secret
backup   https://s3.backup.internal   eu-west-1  AKIAREPLICATOR000001  wJal.../replicator

A configuration's Role names one by its last path segment, as arn:aws:iam::account:role/name; every copy to that endpoint is signed with the line's key and secret for the line's region. The file is refused at create and start if a line does not parse and is read at every start; show and the state file keep its path, and its secrets are never logged. Without it every replication configuration is refused. See Replication.

--acls#

Buckets given no ownership controls take ACLs, as S3 did before it disabled them by default and as RGW does; without it they are BucketOwnerEnforced. See the ACLs under Supported S3 operations.

--tls-offloaded addresses#

The proxies that terminate TLS in front of the runtime, as addresses or blocks (10.0.0.5, 10.0.0.0/24, IPv6 alike), comma-separated: a connection from one of them counts as one made over TLS, so it may carry SSE-C headers, aws:SecureTransport is true for it, and the URLs the runtime answers with are https. Its request's client is the address it put last in X-Forwarded-For, for aws:SourceIp, the access log and the count of failed sign-ins, which would otherwise hold every client behind the proxy as one. Refused at create when an entry is no address. A proxy that speaks HTTP/2 to clients holds an upload to its flow-control window per round trip, 64 KiB unless raised: behind Apache, H2WindowSize 524288 in the virtual host took a browser's upload from 1.2 to 5 MB/s over a line that carries 6. Far more costs the player: the browser sends its requests on the one connection behind as much of the upload as the window lets it queue, and at 16 MiB a request waited 0.5 to 1.1 s where it waits 0.05 to 0.1 s at 512 KiB.

--federation file#

The OIDC provider and the LDAP directory whose identities STS gives temporary credentials to, and the users they sign as, read at every start. See Federated identities.

--tiers file#

The S3 endpoints a bucket's lifecycle may move versions to, each a storage class named by its first field, in the format of --replication-targets; the URL's path is the bucket there and an optional prefix in it:

Details
# name   url                                region     access key            secret
COLD     https://s3.archive.internal/cold/a  eu-west-1  AKIATIER000000000001  wJal.../tier

The file is refused at create and start if a line does not parse and is read at every start. A tier's path is this runtime's own: what lies under it that no version here is is removed. See Tiers.

--nodes file#

Makes the runtime a node of a cluster, whose nodes each keep every bucket and take writes. The file names this node, every node by the S3 endpoint the others reach it at (this one included, with an optional ca=file for an https endpoint), and the key the nodes sign for each other with, the same in every node's file; comments and blank lines are as in --notify-targets:

Details
self  a
node  a  https://s3-a.internal:9000
node  b  https://s3-b.internal:9000
node  c  https://s3-c.internal:9000  ca=/etc/socketley/cluster-ca.pem
key   AKIACLUSTERNODES0001  wJal.../nodes
sync  1  5000

sync n [ms] is optional: a write is then answered only once n other nodes have it, or once ms milliseconds (5000) have passed whatever they say, after which its copies go on as they would without it; without it a write is answered once it is in this node's outbox. A file whose sync names more nodes than there are is refused.

The file is refused at create and start if a line does not parse, if self is none of its nodes, or if it names no key, and is read at every start, so a node added to the file is taken by each node once it starts again; show and the state file keep its path, and the key is never logged. The cluster's key is accepted beside the runtime's own credentials and is not one of them: a request signed with it writes what another node made, is judged by no bucket policy, and cannot be given to a user. See Cluster.

--anonymous#

Accept requests that carry no credentials at all. Required unless credentials are given: a runtime made with neither is refused, so an endpoint is never open by omission. With credentials as well, both kinds are served, and a request that does carry a signature is always verified — a wrong one is refused and never taken for an anonymous request. An anonymous request may send a body in unsigned aws-chunked framing (STREAMING-UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD-TRAILER), which is decoded and its trailing checksum checked; one signed in chunks (STREAMING-AWS4-HMAC-SHA256-PAYLOAD) is refused with NotImplemented because nobody is there to verify the signatures. Without --anonymous a request with no credentials is 403 AccessDenied unless its bucket's policy allows it, as described under Bucket policy.

--idp runtime#

The web interface and WebDAV in a browser take the sign-in of the idp runtime of that name in this daemon: an account signed in there is the user of the same name here, with the rights that user has here and no others, and an account that is no user here is answered 403. The page offers the provider's sign-in beside its own form, and signing out there signs out at the provider. The cookie reaches the storage only when the provider's --cookie-domain covers its name. Accounts of the storage's own users can be taken over by the provider with socketley idp-user idp import storage.

--mpu-expire duration#

Abort a multipart upload that has been open this long (24h, 7d; a bare number is seconds, as for every duration flag). Without it an upload is kept until it is completed or aborted, however old. Expiry is looked for while the runtime runs and once at every start, so an upload that outlived the setting while the runtime was stopped is gone when it comes back.

--scrub duration#

Read every object and version back once in this long (30d, 7d) and check its bytes against the MD5 its header names, so a file the disk changed is found before a client reads it. See Scrub. Without it nothing is read in the background.

--compress duration#

Compress each version once it has gone unwritten this long (1h, 7d), where it lies, so it takes less of the disk and reads back as it was. See Compression. Without it every body is stored as it was sent.

--max-bytes size#

A quota on the bytes the runtime holds, with the K/M/G suffixes of --maxmemory. A put that would pass it is answered 507 StorageFull and stores nothing, and the quota can be changed on a serving runtime with import. 0, the default, is no quota.

edit does not change these; import does, as it does for a cache, and refuses to move dir, anonymous, domain, fsync, fsync_interval or the access key, secret key, credentials file, SSE key file or notification targets file while the runtime is running (the contents of a credentials file are re-read by themselves). The quota and the expiry move under a serving runtime. --shards splits the runtime over several processes on one directory, as described under Sharding.

sections.title: What it shares with the other runtimes
sections.html:
TLS#

--tls --cert --key terminate TLS on the listener and --ca asks every client for a certificate that CA signed, as for a server or a cache. The certificates are read when the runtime starts, so reload installs a replaced one. Every accepted connection is given a session before its first byte is read, so a plaintext client meets the handshake and is refused, never served in the clear, and a peer that sits in the handshake for thirty seconds is dropped. A download over TLS is read from the file and encrypted; only plain TCP is sent by sendfile, so zero_copy_bytes stays 0 for it. TLS and --listen unix: cannot be combined.

The node beside the port#

A runtime with a port also listens on <daemon\socket>.rt/name.sock for callers on this machine, and a proxy given --backend name or a group the runtime belongs to dials that node and not the port. A proxy in front carries GETs and PUTs of any size: with --protocol tcp the request reaches the runtime exactly as signed, which is the form to use once requests are signed, and with the default http mode the client's path carries the proxy's own /name/ prefix, which is stripped before it is forwarded.

Limits and timeouts#

--max-connections closes a connection past the limit and --idle-timeout closes a keep-alive connection that has sat idle between requests, counted in timeouts.

--cpus#

is checked against the daemon's ring and shown by stats as it is for every type.

Persistence#

The configuration is saved with the runtime, and a daemon restart starts a runtime that was running with its objects, TLS settings and limits.

daemon --fast-lo#

A storage runtime reads every body with a receive and only splices from a file to a socket, never from a socket, so the loopback shortcut needs no exception for it: clients on the shortcut, directly or through a proxy, put and get byte for byte.

sections.title: Supported S3 operations
sections.html:
OperationRequestNotes
ListBucketsGET /The buckets the caller owns, or every bucket for an admin (see Users), sorted by name, with creation dates; max-buckets (1 to 10000), continuation-token and prefix page it as S3 does.
CreateBucketPUT /bucketBucketAlreadyOwnedByYou (409) if the caller owns it, BucketAlreadyExists (409) if another user does; InvalidBucketName (400) for a name S3 would refuse. x-amz-bucket-object-lock-enabled: true makes it versioned and locked for good; see Object lock below.
DeleteBucketDELETE /bucketBucketNotEmpty (409) while it holds objects, noncurrent versions or delete markers; open multipart uploads are aborted with it.
HeadBucketHEAD /bucket200, or 404 with no body.
GetBucketLocationGET /bucket?locationAn empty LocationConstraint.
PutBucketVersioningPUT /bucket?versioningStatus Enabled or Suspended; MfaDelete Enabled, or an x-amz-mfa header, is 501 NotImplemented. See Versioning below.
GetBucketVersioningGET /bucket?versioningAn empty VersioningConfiguration for a bucket never versioned.
PutObjectLockConfigurationPUT /bucket?object-lockObjectLockEnabled Enabled and an optional default retention; only while versioning is Enabled; Content-MD5 or a checksum required. See Object lock below.
GetObjectLockConfigurationGET /bucket?object-lockObjectLockConfigurationNotFoundError (404) for a bucket without object lock.
PutObjectRetentionPUT /bucket/key?retentionMode and RetainUntilDate, or an empty Retention to remove one; versionId; x-amz-bypass-governance-retention; Content-MD5 or a checksum required.
GetObjectRetentionGET /bucket/key?retentionNoSuchObjectLockConfiguration (404) for a version without one.
PutObjectLegalHoldPUT /bucket/key?legal-holdStatus ON or OFF; versionId; Content-MD5 or a checksum required.
GetObjectLegalHoldGET /bucket/key?legal-holdNoSuchObjectLockConfiguration (404) for a version whose hold was never set.
PutBucketEncryptionPUT /bucket?encryptionA ServerSideEncryptionConfiguration whose one rule is AES256, or aws:kms with an optional KMSMasterKeyID; aws:kms:dsse is 501 NotImplemented, and so is any rule on a runtime without --sse-key-file. See Server-side encryption below.
GetBucketEncryptionGET /bucket?encryptionThe rule; ServerSideEncryptionConfigurationNotFoundError (404) for a bucket without one.
DeleteBucketEncryptionDELETE /bucket?encryption204; the objects keep the encryption they were written with.
ListObjectVersionsGET /bucket?versionsprefix, delimiter, key-marker, version-id-marker, max-keys (at most 1000), encoding-type=url; Version and DeleteMarker entries by key, each key's newest first.
PutBucketCorsPUT /bucket?corsA CORSConfiguration of at most 100 rules and 64 KiB, replacing the one before; Content-MD5 checked. See CORS below.
GetBucketCorsGET /bucket?corsThe rules as they are kept; NoSuchCORSConfiguration (404) when there are none.
DeleteBucketCorsDELETE /bucket?cors204 whether or not there were rules.
(preflight)OPTIONS /bucket[/key]Answered from the bucket's CORS rules, with no signature.
ListObjectsV2GET /bucket?list-type=2prefix, delimiter, continuation-token, max-keys (at most 1000), start-after, encoding-type=url, fetch-owner; CommonPrefixes count against max-keys.
ListObjects (V1)GET /bucketmarker and NextMarker.
PutObjectPUT /bucket/keyStreamed; Content-MD5 checked; Content-Type, Cache-Control, Content-Disposition, Content-Encoding, Content-Language, Expires and x-amz-meta-* stored and returned; x-amz-tagging sets the object's tags; Expect: 100-continue and chunked request bodies accepted; If-Match (an ETag or *) writes only over that object, NoSuchKey (404) when the key holds none, and If-None-Match (* or an ETag) only when the key holds no such object, decided when the object is committed so two racing writers cannot both win; PreconditionFailed (412) otherwise; x-amz-server-side-encryption: AES256 or the SSE-C headers encrypt it.
GetObjectGET /bucket/keyRange (one range), If-Match, If-None-Match, If-Modified-Since, If-Unmodified-Since, response-* header overrides on a signed request (InvalidRequest, 400, on an anonymous one); every answer outside a website endpoint carries X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff and, but for a PDF, Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; sandbox, and is sent as Content-Disposition: attachment unless its type is an image, audio, video, font, text/plain, text/csv, PDF, JSON, ZIP or octet-stream, so nothing it holds runs on the web interface's origin; x-amz-tagging-count when the object has tags (on HEAD too); ?versionId= reads that version, and x-amz-version-id names it; an object stored under a client's key needs the SSE-C headers, on HEAD too.
HeadObjectHEAD /bucket/keyThe headers of a GET, from memory, or from the object's header when another shard owns the key; ?versionId= as for GET.
SelectObjectContentPOST /bucket/key?select&select-type=2A SQL expression over a CSV or JSON object, answered as an event stream. See S3 Select below.
GetObjectAttributesGET /bucket/key?attributesx-amz-object-attributes of ETag, Checksum, ObjectParts, StorageClass and ObjectSize; the parts of a multipart object paged by x-amz-max-parts and x-amz-part-number-marker, with their numbers, sizes and, when the upload had a checksum algorithm, each part's own checksum; ?versionId= and the SSE-C headers as for HeadObject.
GetObject, HeadObject by partGET|HEAD /bucket/key?partNumber=NPart N of a multipart object as a 206 with its Content-Range and x-amz-mp-parts-count; see Reading by part number below.
DeleteObjectDELETE /bucket/key204 whether or not the key existed; in a versioned bucket a delete marker, and with ?versionId= that version removed for good. If-Match (an ETag list or *), x-amz-if-match-last-modified-time and x-amz-if-match-size are asked of that version, or of the latest the marker would cover (a delete marker included, which only * passes): PreconditionFailed (412) when it does not match, and 204 with nothing removed when there is none, decided by the shard that owns the key as the delete is.
PostObjectPOST /bucket (multipart/form-data)A browser's upload by HTML form; see Uploads by form below.
DeleteObjectsPOST /bucket?deleteUp to 1000 keys, each with or without a VersionId and with the conditions DeleteObject takes as an ETag, a LastModifiedTime (an HTTP date or ISO 8601) and a Size, a key whose condition does not match answered PreconditionFailed among the errors; Quiet, Content-MD5 checked.
CopyObjectPUT /bucket/key + x-amz-copy-sourceWithin or across buckets; x-amz-metadata-directive COPY or REPLACE; x-amz-tagging-directive COPY (the default, the source's tags) or REPLACE (those x-amz-tagging names, or none); x-amz-copy-source-if-match and -if-none-match; onto itself only with REPLACE, from an older version or naming an encryption or a checksum algorithm; a source of key?versionId=ID copies that version. The copy is a single-part object whose ETag is the md5 of its bytes, encrypted as its own request or its bucket asks whatever its source's was; x-amz-copy-source-server-side-encryption-customer-* open an SSE-C source. Its checksum is FULL_OBJECT, of its own bytes, in the algorithm x-amz-checksum-algorithm names or else its source's (see Checksums below).
PutObjectTaggingPUT /bucket/key?taggingA Tagging document replacing the object's tags; Content-MD5 checked. See Object tags below. The tagging operations take ?versionId= too.
GetObjectTaggingGET /bucket/key?taggingThe tags in the order they were set; an empty TagSet for none.
DeleteObjectTaggingDELETE /bucket/key?tagging204 whether or not the object had tags.
CreateMultipartUploadPOST /bucket/key?uploadsContent-Type, the stored headers, x-amz-meta-* and x-amz-tagging are kept for the object; x-amz-checksum-algorithm names the checksum every part takes; x-amz-server-side-encryption or the SSE-C headers encrypt every part and the object.
UploadPartPUT /bucket/key?partNumber=N&uploadId=IDStreamed like a put, Content-MD5 and the checksums checked; a part sent again replaces the old one. N is 1 to 10000. A part of an SSE-C upload carries the upload's key.
UploadPartCopyPUT /bucket/key?partNumber=N&uploadId=ID + x-amz-copy-sourceThe whole source or x-amz-copy-source-range=bytes=first-last, a range past the source's end being 416 InvalidRange; a source of key?versionId=ID reads that version.
CompleteMultipartUploadPOST /bucket/key?uploadId=IDInvalidPart, InvalidPartOrder, EntityTooSmall (a part but the last under 5 MiB), NoSuchUpload, MalformedXML; If-Match and If-None-Match as for PutObject. A completion sent again after it succeeded is answered as the first was, for as long as the key holds the object it made.
AbortMultipartUploadDELETE /bucket/key?uploadId=ID204; NoSuchUpload afterwards.
ListPartsGET /bucket/key?uploadId=IDmax-parts, part-number-marker.
ListMultipartUploadsGET /bucket?uploadsprefix, delimiter, key-marker, upload-id-marker, max-uploads, encoding-type=url.
PutBucketLifecycleConfigurationPUT /bucket?lifecycleReplaces the bucket's rules; see Bucket lifecycle. Content-MD5 checked.
GetBucketLifecycleConfigurationGET /bucket?lifecycleNoSuchLifecycleConfiguration (404) for a bucket without rules.
DeleteBucketLifecycleDELETE /bucket?lifecycle204 whether or not the bucket had rules.
PutBucketPolicyPUT /bucket?policyA JSON policy of at most 20 KiB, replacing the one before; 204; MalformedPolicy (400) for one this runtime cannot honour exactly. See Bucket policy below.
GetBucketPolicyGET /bucket?policyThe document as it was given; NoSuchBucketPolicy (404) when there is none.
DeleteBucketPolicyDELETE /bucket?policy204 whether or not there was one.
GetBucketPolicyStatusGET /bucket?policyStatusIsPublic: whether an Allow lets everyone in from any address; NoSuchBucketPolicy (404) when there is none.
PutBucketLoggingPUT /bucket?loggingA BucketLoggingStatus naming a TargetBucket of the same owner, a TargetPrefix and SimplePrefix or PartitionedPrefix keys; an empty one turns logging off; TargetGrants is AccessControlListNotSupported (400). See Server access logging below.
GetBucketLoggingGET /bucket?loggingThe status as it is kept, an empty one for a bucket that is not logged.
PutPublicAccessBlockPUT /bucket?publicAccessBlockA PublicAccessBlockConfiguration, every setting false when left out. See Public access block below.
GetPublicAccessBlockGET /bucket?publicAccessBlockThe four settings; NoSuchPublicAccessBlockConfiguration (404) when there is none.
DeletePublicAccessBlockDELETE /bucket?publicAccessBlock204 whether or not there was one; answers to s3:PutBucketPublicAccessBlock, as on S3.
PutBucketNotificationConfigurationPUT /bucket?notificationA NotificationConfiguration whose destinations are webhooks of --notify-targets, replacing the one before; an empty one removes it. See Event notifications below.
GetBucketNotificationConfigurationGET /bucket?notificationThe configuration as it is kept, an Id given to a rule that had none; an empty one for a bucket without.
PutBucketReplicationPUT /bucket?replicationA ReplicationConfiguration whose Role names a target of --replication-targets, on a bucket whose versioning is Enabled, replacing the one before. See Replication below.
GetBucketReplicationGET /bucket?replicationThe configuration as it is kept, an ID given to a rule that had none; ReplicationConfigurationNotFoundError (404) when there is none.
DeleteBucketReplicationDELETE /bucket?replication204 whether or not there was one; versions already queued are still copied.
PutBucketQuotaPUT /bucket?quotasocketley's own: a BucketQuota of MaxBytes and MaxObjects, admins only. See Quotas below.
GetBucketQuotaGET /bucket?quotaThe quota as it is kept; NoSuchBucketQuota (404) when there is none. Admins only.
DeleteBucketQuotaDELETE /bucket?quota204 whether or not there was one. Admins only.
PutBucketWebsitePUT /bucket?websiteA WebsiteConfiguration: an IndexDocument, an ErrorDocument and up to 50 RoutingRules, or a RedirectAllRequestsTo alone. See Website hosting below.
GetBucketWebsiteGET /bucket?websiteThe configuration as it is kept; NoSuchWebsiteConfiguration (404) when there is none.
DeleteBucketWebsiteDELETE /bucket?website204 whether or not there was one.
GetSessionTokenPOST / Action=GetSessionTokenSTS's: temporary credentials for the signing user, DurationSeconds 900 to 129600 (43200). See Temporary credentials below.
AssumeRolePOST / Action=AssumeRoleSTS's: the same, DurationSeconds 900 to 43200 (3600), the RoleArn of a role the IAM API made, and a Policy that bounds the session.
AssumeRoleWithWebIdentityPOST / Action=AssumeRoleWithWebIdentitySTS's, unsigned: temporary credentials for an OIDC provider's token, as --federation maps it. See Federated identities below.
AssumeRoleWithLDAPIdentityPOST / Action=AssumeRoleWithLDAPIdentityUnsigned: temporary credentials for a user the LDAP directory binds, as --federation maps it.

A bucket's ownership controls (PutBucketOwnershipControls, GetBucketOwnershipControls, DeleteBucketOwnershipControls, or x-amz-object-ownership on CreateBucket) decide whether it takes ACLs. BucketOwnerEnforced, every bucket's default as S3 makes it now, disables them: every bucket and object has one grant, FULL_CONTROL to the bucket's owner, which GetBucketAcl and GetObjectAcl answer, and a write may ask only for that ACL (bucket-owner-full-control, or x-amz-acl: private from the bucket's owner, as rclone and s3fs send by default); any other canned ACL or grant is 400 AccessControlListNotSupported (InvalidBucketAclWithObjectOwnership on CreateBucket) and stores nothing. ObjectWriter and BucketOwnerPreferred take them, and with --acls so does every bucket given no ownership controls (GetBucketOwnershipControls is then 404 OwnershipControlsNotFoundError for it, as for an RGW bucket). There the canned ACLs (private, public-read, public-read-write, authenticated-read, bucket-owner-read, bucket-owner-full-control, log-delivery-write), the x-amz-grant-* headers (id=, uri= of AllUsers, AuthenticatedUsers or LogDelivery, emailAddress= of a user's email setting) and an AccessControlPolicy document set a bucket's ACL, kept as its document beside its policy, and an object's, kept in its header with its owner: the writer under ObjectWriter, the bucket's owner under BucketOwnerPreferred when the write gave that owner full control. A bucket's grants admit listing (READ), writes and deletes (WRITE) and its ACL (READ_ACP, WRITE_ACP); an object's admit its reads (READ) and its ACL, and are read when the object is, after the bucket's said nothing. An explicit Deny of a policy still refuses, the bucket's owner and an admin are admitted whatever the grants say, a public grant is 403 AccessDenied where the public access block blocks public ACLs and counts for nothing where it ignores them, a grantee that is no user is 400 InvalidArgument (UnresolvableGrantByEmailAddress for an email), and BucketOwnerEnforced is refused on a bucket whose ACL grants anything more than its owner's full control. A bucket's own tags (PutBucketTagging, GetBucketTagging, DeleteBucketTagging) are at most 50 under the rules of an object's, NoSuchTagSet (404) when there are none, and are kept and carried between shards like its CORS rules, in dir/bucket/tagging. Every storage class S3 has is taken, and the bytes are kept here as STANDARD's are. A class whose objects S3 reads at once (REDUCED_REDUNDANCY, STANDARD_IA, ONEZONE_IA, INTELLIGENT_TIERING, GLACIER_IR, EXPRESS_ONEZONE) is kept and named by HEAD, GET, the listings, GetObjectAttributes and an upload's ListParts and ListMultipartUploads; an archive class is named STANDARD, since its name would tell a client to restore what it can read now; a copy takes the class it names, STANDARD when it names none, and may name one to change an object's class in place; a version a lifecycle moved to a tier is listed and read with the tier's name as its class. A class S3 does not have is 400 InvalidStorageClass; x-amz-website-redirect-location is kept and returned like the other stored headers. Anything else — analytics, inventory — is answered 501 NotImplemented and never mistaken for the plain operation. A single put is at most 5 GiB and a key at most 1024 bytes.

sections.title: Uploads by form
sections.html:
A POST to a bucket whose body is multipart/form-data is S3's POST Object, the upload a web page makes with an HTML form (posted to a key instead, as to any key without a subresource, it is 405 MethodNotAllowed) and the fields generate_presigned_post and the SDKs' presigned POST write. The fields in front of the file (at most 20 KiB of them, else MaxPostPreDataLengthExceeded) say what the upload is: key (with ${filename} given the file's name), the headers a PutObject would carry (Content-Type, Cache-Control, Content-Disposition, Content-Encoding, Expires, x-amz-meta-*, x-amz-checksum-*, x-amz-server-side-encryption*), acl and tagging (a Tagging document), and success_action_status (200, 201 with a PostResponse document, or 204, the default) or success_action_redirect, a 303 to that address with the bucket, key and ETag in its query. The file is streamed into the object like a put's body, and fields after it are ignored, as S3 does.

A form with a policy is signed in its fields: as SigV4 (x-amz-algorithm, x-amz-credential, x-amz-date and x-amz-signature, an HMAC-SHA256 of the policy) or in the older form boto3 still writes by default (AWSAccessKeyId and signature, a base64 HMAC-SHA1 of the policy), the one place a signature other than SigV4 is taken, since it covers nothing but the policy. The policy is a base64 JSON document with an expiration (an expired one is AccessDenied) and conditions: {"field": "value"}, ["eq", "$field", "value"], ["starts-with", "$field", "prefix"] and ["content-length-range", min, max], field names compared without case, "$bucket" being the bucket posted to and a field the form leaves out being the empty string. A condition a field does not meet, or a field no condition names (but the signature and its key, the policy, the file and x-ignore-*), is 403 AccessDenied ("Invalid according to Policy: ..."), and a file outside the range is EntityTooLarge or EntityTooSmall, with nothing stored. A form without a policy is an anonymous PutObject: taken by a runtime with --anonymous, or where the bucket policy lets anyone put the key. Either way the bucket policy and a script's on_request see it as PutObject.

sections.title: Virtual-hosted-style addressing
sections.html:
S3 clients address a bucket by host name by default against AWS (https://bucket.s3.amazonaws.com/key), and most can be told to against a custom endpoint. Given --domain s3.example.com, a request with Host: photos.s3.example.com and path /2024/a.jpg is the object 2024/a.jpg in bucket photos, exactly as /photos/2024/a.jpg is with Host: s3.example.com or with any Host that is not a subdomain of a domain given, an address included. Everything before the domain is the bucket, dots and all; with several domains the longest that fits decides, and a Host equal to one is that endpoint, so --domain example.com,s3.example.com reads s3.example.com as the endpoint and not as bucket s3.

The signature needs nothing of its own: SigV4 signs the path as sent and the Host header, so a virtual-hosted request is verified over /key and its own host, and a presigned URL in either style verifies as it was written. What the runtime writes back follows the style of the request: the Location of CreateBucket (/bucket path style, the bucket's URL virtual-hosted), of a form upload and in CompleteMultipartUploadResult. x-amz-copy-source names bucket/key in both styles, as in S3. Clients need the bucket names to resolve to the runtime: a wildcard DNS record (*.s3.example.com), or on one machine --domain localhost since glibc resolves every name.localhost to the loopback. The usual settings are boto3's addressing_style: virtual (in the AWS CLI's config, s3 = addressing_style = virtual), rclone's force_path_style = false and an mc alias set with path lookup off.

A bucket whose name is not a single DNS label — one with dots — is still served path style, and the clients fall back to it for such names over TLS. Over --tls the certificate must cover every bucket's host name, which takes a wildcard certificate for *.domain next to the domain itself; a wildcard matches one label only, so a bucket with dots in its name fails verification virtual-hosted and is reached path style.

sections.title: Authentication
sections.html:
Requests are verified as AWS Signature Version 4, in both forms: the Authorization header and a presigned URL (X-Amz-Algorithm and the rest in the query, for GET, HEAD, PUT and DELETE). Signature Version 2, which awscli 1.x presigns with and older tools sign with, is verified as well, in both forms: Authorization: AWS key:signature, dated by Date or x-amz-date within fifteen minutes, and a URL's AWSAccessKeyId, Expires and Signature, good until Expires, which may lie at most a week (604800 seconds) ahead; its resource is the bucket and key as sent with the subresources S3 signs, and nothing of the body is signed. Whatever region the credential scope names, none included, is accepted. Every x-amz-* header a request carries must be among the signed ones, as S3 requires, but for an x-amz-content-sha256 header beside a presigned URL; one that is not is 403 AccessDenied and the request is refused. Every x-amz-content-sha256 mode a client sends is honoured: a hex hash is checked against the body as it streams (a body that is not the one signed is XAmzContentSHA256Mismatch and is not stored, and a presigned URL, which signs no payload, has its body checked against a hash its sender states in the header all the same, one that is no hash being 400 InvalidArgument), UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD has nothing to check, and aws-chunked bodies — STREAMING-AWS4-HMAC-SHA256-PAYLOAD, its -TRAILER variant and STREAMING-UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD-TRAILER — are decoded, with every chunk signature and a signed trailer verified, even when the aws-chunked body is itself carried in Transfer-Encoding: chunked. Nothing is held whole for any of them: the body goes through the same two staging buffers as an unsigned put.

The answers are S3's: SignatureDoesNotMatch (403) for a wrong secret or a request changed after signing, InvalidAccessKeyId (403), RequestTimeTooSkewed (403) for a request dated more than fifteen minutes from the runtime's clock, AccessDenied (403) for an expired presigned URL, for none at all where no bucket policy allows the request, and for a request a bucket policy denies, and AuthorizationHeaderMalformed (400). A denied request is answered before its body is read and the connection is closed.

sections.title: Users
sections.html:
A credentials file may name users. Each has an id, a display name, its own keys, optionally an identity policy, and optionally the admin flag:

# a key outside any user is the default owner, socketley, an admin
AKIAOPS000000000001:ops-secret

[alice]
name = Alice Example
AKIAALICE0000000001:alice-secret-1
AKIAALICE0000000002:alice-secret-2

[bob]
policy = bob.json
AKIABOB000000000001:bob-secret

[root]
admin = true
AKIAROOT00000000001:root-secret

[id] begins a user: 1 to 128 printable characters without spaces or any of /:*?,=[]"<>&. The lines after it, up to the next, are its keys (access:secret) and its settings (name = value): name is the display name (the id when it is not given), admin is true or false, policy is the user's identity policy, the JSON itself on that one line when it begins with {, and otherwise a file, relative to the credentials file's directory, and max_bytes is the most the buckets the user owns may hold together, a size such as 10G (see Quotas).Asettinghasits = before any colon, which an access key cannot hold. A key outside any user, and the pair given with --access-key, belong to the default owner, socketley, an admin. A file without users is that one owner, exactly as before users existed: every key may do everything to every bucket that no bucket policy denies. A user declared twice, a key given to two users, an unknown setting, or a policy that does not compile is refused at create and start naming the line, and on a reload leaves the users in force.

An identity policy is a bucket policy's grammar (see Bucket policy), with the same actions and conditions, without Principal (it is the user's own), and with resources in any bucket: *, or arn:aws:s3:::pattern matched as IAM matches an ARN, against the bucket name for a bucket action and bucket/key for an object action, where * spans /: arn:aws:s3:::logs-* names those buckets and every object in them, and arn:aws:s3:::logs-*/* the objects alone.

A bucket is owned by the user that made it, recorded on the second line of its dir/bucket/created (none for the default owner, as for every bucket made before users) and taken by every shard, at its making and at every start. ListBuckets shows a user the buckets it owns and an admin every bucket, unless one of the user's policies denies it s3:ListAllMyBuckets (on * or arn:aws:s3:::*), which makes it 403; every Owner element — ListBuckets, ListObjects, ListObjectVersions, the uploads and parts listings, GetBucketAcl and GetObjectAcl — is the bucket's owner with its display name, since an object of a bucket with ACLs disabled is its bucket owner's.

A signed request is decided in this order:

  • An applying Deny in the user's identity policy or in the bucket's policy refuses it with 403 AccessDenied.

  • An admin, the bucket's owner, and anybody on a bucket that is not there (which the operation answers NoSuchBucket) are let in.

  • An applying Allow in the identity policy or in the bucket's policy (naming the user by id, one of its keys, or *) lets it in.

  • Anything else is 403 AccessDenied.

A request without credentials to a bucket that is not there is answered 404 NoSuchBucket, as a signed one is. A request whose x-amz-expected-bucket-owner names another user than the bucket's owner, or whose x-amz-source-expected-bucket-owner does so for a copy's source bucket, is 403 AccessDenied before anything is done. A copy is also judged as a GetObject of its source in the source bucket. CreateBucket is a credentials-file user's whose identity policy does not deny s3:CreateBucket on the name, and a role's or a user's the IAM API made only where one of its policies allows it, as S3 judges them. The bucket policy's own operations stay open to the owner and admins whatever the policy says, and so do what no action names (ownership controls and the operations answered NotImplemented); another user needs an Allow for the former and is refused the latter.

sections.title: Temporary credentials
sections.html:
A user may ask the endpoint itself for temporary credentials, as of STS, with any STS client pointed at the runtime's URL:

POST / HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

Action=AssumeRole&Version=2011-06-15&DurationSeconds=3600
    &RoleArn=arn:aws:iam::000000000000:role/reader&RoleSessionName=ci
    &Policy=<an identity policy, URL-encoded>

The answer is an access key starting ASIA, a secret and a session token, which sign as the user whose key asked for them, with the token in x-amz-security-token or a presigned URL's X-Amz-Security-Token. The token carries the user's key, the expiry and the session policy, sealed with that key's secret, from which the session's secret is derived too: nothing is kept, so every shard and every restart takes it, and it ends at its expiry (400 ExpiredToken), or as soon as the key is gone from the credentials file (400 InvalidToken). The request is a form posted to /, signed for the service sts or s3; temporary credentials cannot ask for more, and a runtime without keys gives none. AssumeRole of a role the IAM API made (see IAM) is refused unless the role's trust policy names the caller, for longer than the role's MaxSessionDuration, and its session holds the role's policies and not the caller's. Any other RoleArn is 404 NoSuchEntity and gives the caller nothing. The session is bounded by its Policy (an identity policy's grammar, at most 2048 bytes), which only narrows it: what the policy does not allow is refused even to an admin or a bucket's owner, the bucket policy's operations included. GetCallerIdentity names the user or the assumed role that signed, a user the IAM API made by the UserId and the path it was given. A browser's form upload is not signed with temporary credentials.

sections.title: Federated identities
sections.html:
With --federation file the endpoint gives temporary credentials, unsigned, to an identity an OIDC provider or an LDAP directory vouches for. The file holds one setting a line, comments and blank lines as in --notify-targets, relative paths under its own directory:

oidc issuer https://id.example.org/realms/main
oidc client storage-console
oidc jwks   jwks.json
oidc claim  policy
role arn:aws:iam:::role/ci   builder
ldap url    ldaps://ldap.example.org ca=/etc/ssl/ldap-ca.pem
ldap dn     uid=%s,ou=People,dc=example,dc=org
ldap user   alice  =
ldap user   *      reader

AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity takes a JWT signed RS256, RS384, RS512, PS256, ES256 or ES384 by a key of the JWK Set file (RSA of 2048 bits and up, EC P-256 and P-384), read again whenever it changes and kept while a new one does not parse; its iss must be the issuer, its aud name a client, and exp, nbf and iat hold within a minute, else 400 InvalidIdentityToken (ExpiredTokenException once it ran out). A role line for the RoleArn names the user the session signs as; without one the token's claim (by default policy) must name exactly one user. AssumeRoleWithLDAPIdentity binds LDAPUsername with LDAPPassword as the dn template makes it (the name escaped as a DN value), over ldap:// or ldaps:// checked against ca= or the system's CAs, within five seconds on a thread of its own (503 ServiceUnavailable when the directory does not answer, 403 AccessDenied when it refuses); the user's own ldap user line, else the * one, names the user the session signs as (= for the same name). An empty password is refused before anything is sent.

Either session is the mapped user's, signed under its first key, with its rights, narrowed by a Policy as AssumeRole's is; a RoleArn naming a role the IAM API made is assumed when its trust policy names the mapped user, as AssumeRole's would be. A mapping to a user that is not there, or has no key, is 403 AccessDenied. The file is refused at create and start when a line does not parse, and read at every start.

sections.title: IAM
sections.html:
The endpoint answers IAM's API too, to an admin, to a user whose own policies allow the action, and never to a session: CreateUser, GetUser, ListUsers, UpdateUser and DeleteUser; CreateAccessKey (at most two per user), ListAccessKeys, UpdateAccessKey and DeleteAccessKey; CreateGroup, GetGroup, ListGroups, DeleteGroup, AddUserToGroup, RemoveUserFromGroup and ListGroupsForUser; CreateRole, GetRole, ListRoles, UpdateRole and DeleteRole; CreateLoginProfile, GetLoginProfile, UpdateLoginProfile, DeleteLoginProfile and ChangePassword; TagUser, UntagUser and ListUserTags; and for users, groups and roles alike Put, Get, List and Delete of an inline policy and Attach, Detach and ListAttached of the AWS managed policies AmazonS3FullAccess, AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess and AdministratorAccess. A request is a form posted to /, as aws iam and the SDKs send it, signed for iam with or without a region.

What it makes is kept in dir/.iam.json, written under a lock and renamed over, and read by every shard beside the credentials file: a change is in force on the shard that made it at once and on the others within 50 milliseconds, and a restart keeps it. A user's identity policy is the statements of its inline and attached policies and its groups' together; a user with none owns and reaches the buckets it makes, as a credentials-file user without a policy does. A user of the credentials file cannot be made again, and policies put on one stand beside the file's own: either's Deny refuses and either's Allow admits; such a user is not listed. A user is deleted once it has no keys, policies or groups or login profile left, a group once it has no members or policies, and a role once it has no policies. Policies are checked as identity policies are; a trust policy's statements with a condition let nobody in. ARNs name no account, arn:aws:iam:::user/name, as RGW writes them. OIDC providers, customer managed policies and permission boundaries are not served.

A login profile is a user's password for the web interface (and a WebDAV client's Basic credentials): at least 8 characters, kept as scrypt (N=2^14, r=8, p=1) and never as itself, for a user of the API or of the credentials file alike. A password that matched is not hashed again for five minutes, so a drive sending it with every request costs one hash and not one each. PasswordResetRequired makes the page ask for a new one before anything else; ChangePassword takes the old one and changes the caller's own. A password's sessions are sealed under a secret drawn with the profile, and a session made before the password was last set is no longer let in.

Four tags of a user the runtime reads itself: socketley:display-name (the name shown), socketley:email , socketley:max-bytes (the quota on the bytes of the buckets it owns, as the credentials file's max_bytes) and socketley:disabled (true: neither its password nor its keys sign in, while its buckets keep their owner and a share can still name it); other keys of that prefix are refused. A member of the group admins is an admin, as the credentials file's admin = true makes one. An IAM user makes a bucket only where a policy allows it, as S3 judges; the web interface gives the users it makes the inline policy socketley-libraries ( Bs3:CreateBucket R on B* R), and a user owns what it makes.

A user who is no admin may call an IAM action its identity policies allow, as iam:Action with * and ? (iam:List*, iam:*; "*" names S3's actions alone, so a policy written before IAM could be delegated gives none of it, and AdministratorAccess names iam:* beside it), on resources arn:aws:iam::account:user/path name, group/... or role/... in any account, where ${aws:username} is the caller's user id; ListUsers, ListGroups and ListRoles act on no resource, so only Resource : * covers them. A Deny wins and no Allow is AccessDenied. A key named by its id alone is judged as its owner's, a rename or a move needs both ARNs, and GetUser, CreateAccessKey, ListAccessKeys, GetLoginProfile, ListUserTags and ListGroupsForUser without a UserName act on the caller. Without any policy a user may do to itself what IAM's console lets every user: read itself, its keys, tags and groups, make, change and delete its own keys, set a first password, and change its password. An admin keeps every right whatever its policies say, and only an admin changes an admin or gives an identity IAM rights: a policy put or attached whose Allow names an iam: action, AdministratorAccess included, a group that has one, the group admins, and the socketley: tags are refused to anybody else. IAM actions this runtime does not answer are accepted in a policy and match nothing.

sections.title: CORS
sections.html:
A bucket's CORS rules let a page served from another origin use it from a browser: read objects, and upload with a presigned URL. They are set with PutBucketCors as S3's CORSConfiguration document, up to 100 CORSRule elements each holding one or more AllowedOrigin (with at most one * standing for any run of characters, and * alone for every origin) and AllowedMethod (GET, PUT, HEAD, POST or DELETE), and any number of AllowedHeader (at most one * each, compared without case), ExposeHeader, an optional MaxAgeSeconds and an optional ID of up to 255 characters. A document that is not one is 400 MalformedXML; an unknown method, a second wildcard or a 101st rule is 400 InvalidRequest, and a refused document leaves the rules that were there.

The rules are kept in dir/bucket/cors, written beside it, synced and renamed over it, so they survive a restart and a crash leaves the old rules or the new ones; they go with the bucket when it is deleted, and a bucket made again under the name has none. With --shards shard 0 writes them, whichever shard took the request, as described for the policy under Bucket policy: the request is answered once no shard can go on with the old rules, and a shard that was not running reads them from the file when it starts.

A preflight, OPTIONS on the bucket or on a key with Origin and Access-Control-Request-Method (and Access-Control-Request-Headers when the request will send others), is answered without authentication from the first rule whose origin, method and every requested header match: 200 with Access-Control-Allow-Origin (the origin, or * when the rule allows every origin), Access-Control-Allow-Methods, Access-Control-Allow-Headers (the headers asked for), Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true for a named origin, Access-Control-Expose-Headers and Access-Control-Max-Age when the rule has them, and Vary. A bucket without rules is 403 AccessForbidden ("CORSResponse: CORS is not enabled for this bucket."), a request no rule allows is the same with "This CORS request is not allowed", and a preflight without Origin or with a method S3 does not have is 400 BadRequest.

Every other request that carries an Origin some rule allows for its method gets the same headers but Access-Control-Allow-Headers, and one that also carries Access-Control-Request-Method is judged by that method and the headers it asks for and answered as that preflight, as S3 answers it, on every answer: errors and authentication refusals included, so a page can read why it was refused. A request from an origin no rule allows is served as before, with no CORS headers. A runtime none of whose buckets has rules looks nothing up for a request.

sections.title: Checksums
sections.html:
x-amz-checksum-crc32, -crc32c, -crc64nvme, -sha1 and -sha256 are taken over the body of a PutObject or an UploadPart when the request names one — in that header, in a trailer of an aws-chunked body (x-amz-trailer), or by x-amz-sdk-checksum-algorithm — and compared with the value the client gave: a mismatch is 400 BadDigest and nothing is stored. The checksum is kept in the object, echoed in the answer, and returned by GetObject and HeadObject when the request has x-amz-checksum-mode: ENABLED (except on a ranged read, which is not of the whole object), with x-amz-checksum-type saying what it is of. A multipart object has the checksum of its parts' checksums, and -N after it for the number of parts (COMPOSITE), as S3 does; a part with no checksum of its own gets the upload's algorithm anyway. An upload created with x-amz-checksum-type: FULL_OBJECT and a CRC (and every CRC64NVME upload, as in S3) has instead the CRC of its whole bytes, combined from its parts' CRCs and lengths without reading them again; FULL_OBJECT with SHA-1 or SHA-256, or COMPOSITE with CRC64NVME, is 400 InvalidRequest. A checksum a CompleteMultipartUpload carries is compared with the one the parts make, and a mismatch is 400 BadDigest with nothing stored. Each part's own checksum is kept with the completed object, beside its size (see Reading by part number), so a GetObject or HeadObject by part number with x-amz-checksum-mode: ENABLED answers the part's checksum, with the object's x-amz-checksum-type, and GetObjectAttributes lists it beside each part. A single-part object answers part 1 with its own checksum, and a copy, which keeps none of its source's part checksums, answers part 1 with its own whole one. An object completed before part checksums were kept answers its parts without one.

An object that arrives with no checksum is given S3's default, the CRC64NVME of its whole bytes, FULL_OBJECT: a PutObject, a POST form upload and an object a script puts take it on the pass that takes the ETag's MD5, and answer it as they would one the client named. An upload created with no algorithm keeps a CRC64NVME of each part beside it, shown to no client (UploadPart, ListParts and GetObjectAttributes answer none, and its parts by number are read without one), and its CompleteMultipartUpload combines them into the object's default without reading the parts again. An object stored before this, and an upload whose parts were written before it, has none, and is not given one until it is copied.

A CopyObject's checksum is of the copy's own bytes, FULL_OBJECT, as S3 makes it: in the algorithm x-amz-checksum-algorithm names (one the runtime does not take is 400 InvalidRequest), or else in its source's, under either metadata directive. A source whose checksum is already of its whole bytes gives the copy that value; a COMPOSITE one, or one in another algorithm, has the copy's taken from the bytes on the copy's one pass through them, as is every copy that is sealed or opened on its way. The CopyObjectResult carries it with its ChecksumType. A source with no checksum gives a copy the default, CRC64NVME, unless the request names another. A copy onto itself that names x-amz-checksum-algorithm is allowed under either directive, as S3 documents it for adding or changing an object's checksum; one that names nothing new is still 400 InvalidRequest. A copy made before this answers with its source's COMPOSITE value as it was stored. UploadPartCopy takes the upload's algorithm over the bytes it copies, whatever its source's checksum, and answers it in its CopyPartResult.

sections.title: Object tags
sections.html:
An object has at most 10 tags, set with PutObjectTagging or with x-amz-tagging (a URL-encoded query string, k1=v1&k2=v2) on a PutObject, a CreateMultipartUpload (they land on the completed object) or a CopyObject under x-amz-tagging-directive: REPLACE. A key is 1 to 128 characters and a value at most 256, counted as characters and not bytes, of letters, digits, spaces and + - = . _ : / @ (outside ASCII every character but a control, a format or private-use character is taken, which is wider than S3's letters, digits and spaces of every script); keys are unique and none begins aws:. Eleven tags are 400 BadRequest, any other breach 400 InvalidTag, a Tagging document that is not one MalformedXML, and a repeated key or a broken escape in x-amz-tagging InvalidArgument; a refused put stores nothing and a refused PutObjectTagging leaves the tags there were. GetObject and HeadObject say how many tags an object has in x-amz-tagging-count.

Tags live in the object's own header, beside its other metadata, and the journal record mirrors them like the rest, so they survive a stop, a crash and a lost journal. A tag change keeps the object's bytes, ETag and Last-Modified, as S3 does, by not rewriting the object: the padding of the header's first 4 KiB holds two tag slots of whole 512-byte sectors, and a change is written into the one the last change did not use, with a sequence number and a CRC32C, then synced (one write and one fdatasync(2)). A crash in the middle leaves a slot whose checksum fails, so the tags are those before the change, never a torn header, and the key's file is the truth a start after a crash reads them from. A set too big for the slots that are left (above about 1.5 KiB of tags with little other metadata, or any change to a header that fills its first 4 KiB) is written instead as a new file with the tags in its header and the bytes copied behind it, renamed into place like a put. On ext4 a change in place took 2.4 to 2.7 ms whatever the object's size, and a rewrite 12.6 ms for 4 KiB, 102 ms for 64 MiB and 1.07 s for 1 GiB. stats counts the two as tag_writes and tag_rewrites. A change goes to the shard that owns the key, waits behind its other writes in the key's lane, and is answered once the file says it and every shard has dropped what it holds of the key, so a GET or a GetObjectTagging on any shard sees it at once.

sections.title: Multipart uploads
sections.html:
An upload is a directory dir/bucket/mpu/id holding a meta file (the object it will become, in an object header) and one file per part, each an object header and its bytes, so the runtime finds them again after a stop or a crash. A part is written like a put — streamed, hashed, synced — and renamed to its number, so it is whole or not there; an upload is created, and its directory synced, before its id is given out. A part still arriving when the worker is killed leaves nothing behind. The upload id is 32 hex digits.

Most clients cut an object into parts of one size, and a part whose place in the object is known when it starts is written there: the upload also holds a data file with room for the object's header at the front, the first part of at least 5 MiB fixes the part size, and part n of that size (or a smaller last part) goes into data at its offset, its numbered file then holding only a header that names the place. The shard that owns the upload hands each place out once, so a part sent again, a part of another size and a part sent by UploadPartCopy get files of their own as above.

CompleteMultipartUpload checks the list against what was uploaded. When the parts listed are exactly 1 to N, all in place and of the fixed size but the last, it writes the object's header in front of them, syncs data and commits it as the object itself, so the bytes are written to the disk once. Otherwise it writes the header and copies the parts into a temporary file a megabyte at a time on the ring, the placed ones read from data, syncs it and commits it; an upload that was open across a restart, or whose copy-free completion failed, always copies. Either way the commit is a put's (rename, directory sync; the journal record behind the answer), so a crash during completion leaves the upload intact and no object; only then are the parts removed. The ETag is the md5 of the parts' md5s with -N, as S3's. A copy passes the bytes through the process because io_uring has no copy between two files; the loop never blocks on the disk, and the worker holds two one-megabyte buffers for it whatever the object's size. warp, the AWS CLI and boto3 upload anything above 8 to 16 MiB this way, so this is the path of every large upload: on a 4-vCPU VM, 64 MiB puts at four connections went from 3.2 to 6.5 per second when the copy went, and 256 MiB puts at two from 0.90 to 1.81. An upload is kept until it is completed or aborted unless --mpu-expire is set; its parts count against --max-bytes while they are held, and deleting a bucket that holds nothing but open uploads aborts them with it, as S3 does. A part sent again needs room for both copies until the new one lands.

sections.title: Reading by part number
sections.html:
GET /bucket/key?partNumber=N (and HEAD) answers part N of the object as S3 does, which is how the AWS CRT, the Java transfer manager and several Go clients download a multipart object in parallel: a 206 of the part's bytes, with Content-Range: bytes first-last/size, the part's Content-Length, the whole object's ETag and x-amz-mp-parts-count. Parts are numbered 1 to the part count in the order the completion listed them. A single-part object (a put, or any copy) is its own part 1, answered the same way without the parts count; an empty one is a 200 of nothing. A number past the part count is 416 InvalidPartNumber, one outside 1 to 10000 400 InvalidArgument, and a Range header beside it 400 InvalidRequest. The conditional headers apply as on a plain GET, before the part is looked at.

The part sizes are recorded in the object's header at CompleteMultipartUpload (as x-socketley-part-sizes, never sent to a client): one size when every part but the last has it, which is every in-place completion, and otherwise the list, up to 4 KiB of it. An upload with a checksum algorithm adds its parts' checksums, in base64, up to 4 KiB of them (x-socketley-part-checksums). The journal carries them as it carries the rest of the header. A longer list, which any upload S3 takes may need, follows the object's body in the file instead, 20 bytes and 12 more per part (24, and 12 and the checksum's width per part, when it holds checksums), with the header naming where it begins and its SHA-256 (x-socketley-part-layout); a part number of such an object reads the list from the file first, and a list that does not match its digest is 500 InternalError. An in-place completion whose checksums do not fit the room its header was given writes them after the last part in the same way, and still copies nothing. A multipart object completed before part sizes were recorded answers any part number within its count with 501 NotImplemented rather than a guess; a plain GET or a Range reads it as before.

CopyObject makes a single-part object, as S3 does: a multipart source's bytes are hashed on the way through and the copy's ETag is their md5, with no -N, and its checksum, when it needs one taken, is taken on that same pass.

sections.title: Versioning
sections.html:
PutBucketVersioning with Enabled makes every PUT, CopyObject and CompleteMultipartUpload of the bucket a new version of its key with an id of its own (32 hex digits), answered in x-amz-version-id; the versions before it stay, and GET, HEAD, DeleteObject and the tagging operations take ?versionId=ID to name one. A GET without one is the latest. A DELETE without one puts a delete marker in front of the key (204 with x-amz-delete-marker: true and the marker's id), after which a GET or HEAD of the key is 404 NoSuchKey with x-amz-delete-marker: true and a GET of the marker by its id 405 MethodNotAllowed; a listing leaves the key out. A DELETE with a version id removes that version for good: the marker, which undeletes the key, or the latest, after which the version behind it is the latest. An object written before versioning was enabled is the null version, which a GET, HEAD or GetObjectTagging of it names with x-amz-version-id: null. Suspended keeps the versions there are and writes the null version, which the next write or delete marker replaces. A bucket is never unversioned again, as in S3, and GetBucketVersioning of one never versioned is an empty configuration. MFA delete is refused with 501 NotImplemented. A version id that could not be one is 400 InvalidArgument, and one the key has no version of 404 NoSuchVersion.

The latest version of a key is its file at the usual path, so a read without a version id, on any shard, is the read of an unversioned bucket; a version that a new latest replaces is linked to dir/bucket/versions/ab/sha256(key).id and that directory synced before the new file is renamed over it, and the 256 directories of versions/ are made with the configuration, which shard 0 changes like the CORS and lifecycle documents (see Bucket policy); the owner of a key writes nothing to it while unsure of the configuration, and a write through another shard is then answered 503. Each version's header carries its id and its order among the key's versions. The shard a body lands on writes them into its header before the body is synced, and the key's owner keeps them unless a newer version of the key or a change of the bucket's versioning came first — including one it learns of only by reading the configuration again before the write — when it writes the header again with its own. A versioned put takes a file of the pool as an unversioned one does: it is answered at its rename, once the link of the version it replaces and that link's directory are synced, and the syncs of its own directory and of pool/ follow the answer. A crash that takes the rename leaves the put whole in pool/, and the next start links the version it would have replaced before moving it into place — also when the bucket was versioned only after the put was answered. A versioned put therefore waits for one sync more than an unversioned one when it replaces a version, and for none more when its key is new. A version removed for good is unlinked, or for the latest the version behind it is renamed over it.

The journal records each key's other versions and delete markers beside its latest object, so a start after a clean stop reads a versioned bucket from its journal as it does any other; a journal written before it did is read from the files once and written again. Any other start reads versions/ in the same parallel walk as data/: the headers give each key's versions in order and its delete markers, a version left under both its names by a crash between the link and the rename is kept once (as the latest), and a key whose latest file is gone is given its newest version back. 100,000 keys of three versions each start in 0.19 s after a clean stop (1.3 s when every start read the files) and in 0.86 s after a kill (1.3 s), with a warm cache on four CPUs. With --shards, all versions of a key are its owner's; a shard that does not own the key reads a version by its id from the file where it is, looking at the other place once if a rename moved it meanwhile, and a held copy of a latest is dropped on every shard before a new version, a marker or a removal that changes the latest is answered. ListObjectVersions asks every shard and merges their pages.

sections.title: Object lock
sections.html:
A bucket made with x-amz-bucket-object-lock-enabled: true is versioned and locked from the start, and PutObjectLockConfiguration locks a bucket whose versioning is Enabled, as S3 now allows (409 InvalidBucketState otherwise). A locked bucket's versioning cannot be suspended (409 InvalidBucketState) and its lock cannot be removed; a configuration without a Rule only drops the default retention. The default, GOVERNANCE or COMPLIANCE for a number of Days or calendar Years, is given to every new version that names no retention itself, counted from the moment it is written.

A version's retention is set by x-amz-object-lock-mode and x-amz-object-lock-retain-until-date on PutObject, CopyObject and CreateMultipartUpload (whose completed object has it), or by PutObjectRetention; its legal hold by x-amz-object-lock-legal-hold or PutObjectLegalHold. GET and HEAD return all three headers. A copy never takes its source's lock, only what its own request or bucket gives it. A lock asked of a bucket without object lock is 400 InvalidRequest, a date that is not in the future 400 InvalidArgument. PutObjectLockConfiguration, PutObjectRetention, PutObjectLegalHold, and a PutObject that names a retention or a legal hold, need Content-MD5 or an x-amz-checksum-* of the body (checked), as S3 requires, or a SigV4 signature over the body's SHA-256 (an x-amz-content-sha256 that is a hash, checked as well), which is all an SDK from before checksums sends; a PutObject that only receives the default does not.

A version under a legal hold that is ON, or under a retention whose date the server's clock (UTC) has not reached, cannot be removed: a DELETE or DeleteObjects entry that names it is 403 AccessDenied, and a DELETE without a version id still puts a delete marker in front of it. COMPLIANCE yields to nobody and is only lengthened. GOVERNANCE is lengthened by anyone and shortened, removed, made COMPLIANCE or deleted through only by a request with x-amz-bypass-governance-retention: true whose caller has s3:BypassGovernanceRetention — every key the runtime has, unless the bucket's policy denies it, and an anonymous caller only by an Allow of it. A legal hold yields to no bypass. A lifecycle rule never expires a locked version (a current one's expiry puts a delete marker, as it may), and DeleteBucket refuses a bucket that still holds versions.

The retention and the hold are entries of the version's header, so the journal and the index carry them too. A change is made by the key's owner under its lane and written in place into the header's tag slots, crash-safe as a tag change is: once a version has a lock its slot holds its tags, retention and hold together, so a torn write leaves the previous slot, and a header with no room is written again whole. A version that never had a lock keeps the slot an older binary reads. With --shards, a change or a removal through a shard that does not own the key is decided by its owner, the bypass travelling with it, and the bucket's configuration, like versioning, is decided by shard 0 in the order of the bucket's changes.

sections.title: Event notifications
sections.html:
A bucket's NotificationConfiguration (PutBucketNotificationConfiguration, GetBucketNotificationConfiguration) sends S3's event records to webhooks.
