Its QueueConfiguration, TopicConfiguration and CloudFunctionConfiguration entries are taken alike: an Id, a destination arn:socketley:webhook:::name that names a line of --notify-targets, one or more Event and an optional Filter of an S3Key prefix rule and suffix rule. The events emitted are s3:ObjectCreated:Put, :Post (a form upload), :Copy and :CompleteMultipartUpload; s3:ObjectRemoved:Delete (a key deleted, or a version removed by its id) and :DeleteMarkerCreated (a delete in a versioned bucket); s3:LifecycleExpiration:Delete and :DeleteMarkerCreated (a lifecycle rule's expiry, which sends no ObjectRemoved); and s3:ObjectTagging:Put and :Delete, each of them by its name or by *. The other names S3 has (ObjectRestore, Replication, ...) are taken and send nothing. A destination that is not a webhook's ARN, or names one the targets file does not give, is 400 InvalidArgument ("Unable to validate the following destination configurations", the ARN as ArgumentName) unless the request sends x-amz-skip-destination-validation: true; so are an unknown event, a filter rule other than one prefix and one suffix, two configurations with one Id, two that share an event on overlapping keys, and EventBridgeConfiguration, which this endpoint cannot reach; a document that is not a configuration is 400 MalformedXML. An empty NotificationConfiguration removes it. It is kept in dir/bucket/notification and changed by shard 0 like a bucket's other configuration documents.

Each event is POSTed to its webhook as S3's message, one record in a Records array, with Content-Type: application/json, Connection: keep-alive and X-Socketley-Event-Id, a number a receiver can deduplicate by:

{"Records":[{"eventVersion":"2.1","eventSource":"aws:s3",
  "awsRegion":"us-east-1","eventTime":"2026-10-02T12:00:00.123Z",
  "eventName":"ObjectCreated:Put",
  "userIdentity":{"principalId":"socketley"}, ...,
  "s3":{"s3SchemaVersion":"1.0","configurationId":"thumbs",
    "bucket":{"name":"photos","ownerIdentity":{...},
              "arn":"arn:aws:s3:::photos"},
    "object":{"key":"2026/a+b.jpg","size":5821,
      "eTag":"9b2cf535f27731c974343645a3985328",
      "versionId":"...","sequencer":"00063F7A2B1C0D9E"}}}]}

The key is form-encoded as S3 encodes it (a space as +, / kept, other bytes as %XX), a removal's record has no size or eTag, versionId is given in a versioned bucket, and the sequencer is sixteen hex digits that grow with every event of the shard that owns the key, so a key's events sort by it. userIdentity.principalId is the requester: the id of the user a signed request's key belongs to (socketley for a key outside any user), or anonymous for a request without credentials, let in by --anonymous or by a bucket policy; requestParameters.sourceIPAddress is the client's address (an IPv4 client on a dual-stack socket by its IPv4 address, a client on a unix socket by none). A lifecycle expiry names s3.amazonaws.com and no address, and a change a script makes through socketley.storage names neither. With --shards both travel to the shard that owns the key with the change.

A webhook named by a host name is resolved on a thread of its own, whose answer the loop reads from an eventfd through its ring, so no delivery and no request waits on the resolver: once at start, again after every address the host had refused a connection (at most once a second), and every minute while it is delivered to. A host with several addresses is tried address by address before it is resolved again. A stop waits for a resolve in progress, which the system resolver's own timeout bounds. SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_NOTIFY_HOSTS names a file of name address lines consulted before the system resolver, a test aid.

The shard that owns a key emits its events, whichever shard took the request, so a change is one event. Its record is appended to dir/.notify/outbox.shard when the change starts and synced beside the change's own syncs, together with every other record waiting at that moment, and the change is answered once both are durable, so an answered change's event survives a crash at no second sync on the request's path. The event is sent only once the change is durable, after a record saying it was made, which is synced before the next change of the key may start. A start keeps an event whose change has no such record only when the object files show the change (its ETag, size, time and version, or the key or version gone for a removal), so a crash never sends an event for a change that was not made. A webhook is sent up to four events at once, each on a connection of its own, and the events of one object one at a time and in the order they happened, so a removal never overtakes the write before it; an event about no object waits for the one before it of the same kind. A 2xx answer delivers it, and anything else, a refused or failed connection, or no answer in 10 seconds, is a failure tried again after 0.25 s, doubling to 8 s. A delivered event's record is followed by one saying so, written at once and synced with the next event's record rather than on its own, and a start sends again every event without one, so an event is delivered at least once, and more than once only when a crash or a 2xx lost on the way leaves its delivery unrecorded. The outbox is written again with only the undelivered events at every start, and empty once it has passed a megabyte with nothing left to send. At most 10000 events wait per shard: past that a new one is dropped, counted in notify_dropped, and its change answered all the same. stats shows notify_sent, notify_failed (attempts), notify_queued (waiting now), notify_dropped, notify_resolves (host names resolved), notify_connects and notify_reuses (deliveries that went on a connection kept from the delivery before), per shard.

A webhook's connection is kept for its next event, as a proxy keeps its backends', when the answer is HTTP/1.1, says nothing of Connection: close, and ends where its framing says; it is closed after 4 seconds with nothing on it, after a minute, so a moved host name is followed, and whenever the webhook has closed it, which is looked at before it is used. Over https this spares a handshake per event: 3,000 events to a local https webhook took 4.5 seconds on a connection each and 0.6 on one kept.

sections.title: Replication
sections.html:
A bucket's ReplicationConfiguration (PutBucketReplication, GetBucketReplication, DeleteBucketReplication) copies its new versions, and the delete markers its clients make, to buckets of another S3 endpoint — another storage runtime, or any S3. It is S3's document: a Role and one or more Rules, each with an ID, a Priority, a Status of Enabled or Disabled, the keys it names (a rule-level Prefix in the first schema, or a Filter of a Prefix, a Tag or an And of both, in the second), a Destination with the Bucket as arn:aws:s3:::bucket and optionally an Account, a StorageClass (sent as the replica's x-amz-storage-class) and an AccessControlTranslation to Destination, and DeleteMarkerReplication. The Role's last path segment names a target of --replication-targets, whose endpoint and credentials every rule of the configuration writes with:

<ReplicationConfiguration>
  <Role>arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/backup</Role>
  <Rule><ID>docs</ID><Priority>1</Priority><Status>Enabled</Status>
    <Filter><Prefix>docs/</Prefix></Filter>
    <Destination><Bucket>arn:aws:s3:::docs-copy</Bucket></Destination>
    <DeleteMarkerReplication><Status>Enabled</Status></DeleteMarkerReplication>
  </Rule>
</ReplicationConfiguration>

As in S3, a bucket whose versioning is not Enabled is refused one (400 InvalidRequest), and versioning cannot be suspended while it has one (409 InvalidBucketState); so are a second-schema rule without DeleteMarkerReplication, delete marker replication with a tag filter, rules of both schemas, two rules with one ID or one priority, and overlapping first-schema prefixes (all 400 InvalidRequest or InvalidArgument); a Role that names no target is 400 InvalidArgument, and a document that is not one 400 MalformedXML. ExistingObjectReplication Enabled, ReplicaModifications Enabled, a ReplicaKmsKeyID and replication time control or metrics are 501 NotImplemented rather than taken and not honoured; the destination bucket is not checked when the configuration is put. The document is kept in dir/bucket/replication and changed by shard 0 like a bucket's other configuration documents.

For every destination bucket the matching enabled rule of the highest priority decides; a version is copied when one does, and a delete marker when that rule replicates delete markers (a rule with a tag filter never names a marker; the first schema always replicates them). A version is written with x-amz-replication-status: PENDING in its header, which GET and HEAD answer, and becomes COMPLETED once every destination has it, or FAILED once one refused it, which stays FAILED; the status is written in place into the header's slot, which then carries it with the tags, the retention and the hold. What a version is copied by is decided when its metadata is made: a PutObject or POST, a CopyObject (whose source's status is never copied), a CreateMultipartUpload for the object its completion makes, and a script's put. A later tag change or tag removal of a version that is COMPLETED or PENDING is copied too, to the same version id there, as in S3; it has no status of its own, and one the destination refuses is logged and given up. Not copied, as in S3: a version removed by its id, a delete marker a lifecycle rule made, a version written before the configuration, and an SSE-C version, which has no status.

A version is copied by a signed PutObject streamed from its file — with its Content-Type, Cache-Control, Content-Disposition, Content-Encoding, Content-Language, Expires, website redirect, user metadata and tags, its MD5 as Content-MD5 and its full-object checksum, which the destination checks the bytes against — and a multipart version by a multipart upload in the same parts and part numbers, so the replica has the same ETag and composite checksum. An SSE-S3 version is read in the clear, over the target's https when its URL is one, and written with x-amz-server-side-encryption: AES256, which a destination without a master key refuses; a delete marker is a signed DeleteObject of the key, and a tag change a signed PutObjectTagging or DeleteObjectTagging of the version. Every request carries x-amz-replication-status: REPLICA. A storage runtime that is the destination judges such a write as s3:ReplicateObject, such a delete as s3:ReplicateDelete and such a tag change as s3:ReplicateTags (see Bucket policy), for a user the policies allow that and do not deny the write it stands for, and takes the header from nobody else, whose request is the plain write it is; it marks the version REPLICA, and never copies a replica or a replica's delete marker on, so two buckets that replicate to each other copy each change once. The request also names the source's version id in x-socketley-replica-version-id, which a storage runtime that is the destination gives the replica or its delete marker, as S3 does, as long as that id is still newer than every version the key has there and dated no more than fifteen minutes past the destination's clock; otherwise the replica gets an id of its own. Another S3 stores the replication header as it does and ignores the other, so there a replica's version id is its own. A replica's time and owner are the destination's own.

The shard that owns a key queues its copies, one entry per destination bucket, in dir/.replicate/outbox.shard, synced beside the change itself and before it is answered, as its events are (see Event notifications), so a crash never copies a change that was not made. Each target has up to 16 copies in flight, each on a connection of its own, a key's copies one at a time and in the order they were made; a body of 64 KiB or more that is not encrypted goes to an http target straight from its file by splice, without passing through the runtime. A refused connection, a stall of 10 seconds, no answer within 120 seconds of the whole request, and an answer of 408, 409, 429 or a 5xx other than 501 are tried again after 0.25 s, doubling to 8 s, and logged at the first of a run; any other answer, or a version whose bytes cannot be read, is FAILED and logged with the destination's error code. An entry is retired after the version's status is written, so a crash between the two copies the version again, which is harmless. A start queues the outbox again, and every version its index still calls PENDING with no entry, so an answered version is copied even if its entry was lost. A target's host name is resolved off the loop as a webhook's is; SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_REPLICATION_HOSTS is the test aid that points one elsewhere. stats shows replication_pending (entries waiting now), replication_completed and replication_failed (versions and delete markers), replication_retries, replication_bytes (body bytes a destination took), replication_connects and replication_reuses (requests that went on a connection kept from the request before, as a webhook's is), per shard.

sections.title: Cluster
sections.html:
The nodes of a cluster (--nodes) each keep every bucket, and every node takes reads and writes, so a client or a load balancer may use any of them. Each change a node makes is sent to every other node, from its replication outbox in the way a bucket's replication sends a version (see Replication), and is in that outbox, synced, before the client hears it was made: a version or an object (as a PutObject, or as a multipart upload in the same parts, so its ETag is the same everywhere), a delete marker, a tag change, a removal, a version removed by its id, a version's retention or legal hold, a bucket made with its owner, removed, or given or relieved of a configuration document (versioning, object lock, policy, lifecycle, CORS, encryption, tags, website, logging, quota, public access block, notification, replication), the IAM API's users, groups and roles, and share links with their downloads. What a node was sent it does not send on. A lifecycle rule's expiries are each node's own, since every node runs the bucket's rules; so are a bucket's event notifications, which only the node a change was made on sends, and its replication to another endpoint, which only that node copies.

Every node ends with the same state whatever order the changes reach it in. A version keeps the id, the time and the lock its node gave it, and one older than a key's latest goes behind it rather than in front; a node that has not yet heard of its bucket's versioning answers it 503 SlowDown until it has. An object of a bucket that keeps no versions is the write made last, by the time it was written on its node and then by the larger ETag; a removal is stamped with its time as well, and a node keeps a record of what it removed for 24 hours, across a restart, in dir/.removed.shard, so that an older write that crosses the removal on its way is not made. A removal is sent even by a node that did not have the key yet. The IAM document is the one changed last on any node, so two admins who change IAM on two nodes in the same moment keep only the later change. A share link's downloads are counted by each node and added up, so its limit holds across the nodes once their counts have met. A node answers a write it already has, or one older than what it has, 412 PreconditionFailed to the node that sent it, which takes that as delivered.

A node that was stopped is sent what it missed once it is back, as a replication target is; a change for a bucket another lane is still making or emptying waits for it up to 15 minutes, and is then given up and logged. A node more than 100000 changes behind a shard has that shard's queue for it let go, which bounds the memory a long absence takes, and is sent everything instead, as below, once it answers again. A node whose data is new to another — one that joined the cluster, or began again with an empty --dir — is sent everything that node holds: every node keeps a random id of its data in dir/.cluster-id, asks every other node for its id at start and every 30 seconds, and when an id is new sends the IAM document, the share links, every bucket with its documents, and every version, delete marker and object it holds, 500 keys at a time and asking first whether the node already has each, and last what it removed in the last 24 hours, noting how far it got in dir/.replicate/seed.shard.node so a restart goes on from there.

The nodes need the same credentials and the same --sse-key-file (an SSE-S3 object is sent in the clear over the node's endpoint and encrypted again there; use https between nodes that are not on one host), and their clocks within a second of one another, since the time a write was made decides between two writes of one key. An SSE-C object is not sent, as its key is its client's. stats shows, per shard, cluster_pending (changes waiting for another node), cluster_sent and cluster_failed (changes the other nodes took, and gave up), cluster_in (bucket, IAM and share records another node sent here), cluster_seeds (nodes this shard began to send everything to), cluster_seeded (versions and objects it queued for them) and cluster_seeding (nodes it has not yet queued everything for, or not yet asked) and cluster_overflows (queues let go), cluster_synced and cluster_sync_timeouts (writes answered once the nodes sync names had them, and once its wait was over).

Three nodes on one host, 4 KiB PutObject from 16 clients for 15 seconds: the two other nodes keep up as the writes come (4 changes waiting when the clients stop, none 0.4 seconds later). On a 4-vCPU VPS with the two other nodes on tmpfs, a node takes 1800 PutObject a second against 2660 alone, its own work per write growing from 450 to 557 microseconds of CPU, which is the write read back and sent twice; 1 MiB PutObject from 8 clients, 200 a second against 415 alone, at 5.7 against 4.4 milliseconds of CPU each, the two other nodes taking every megabyte on the same four CPUs.

sections.title: Scrub
sections.html:
With --scrub, every shard reads each version it holds back from its file, a key at a time in order, at a pace that makes one pass of the shard's bytes take the period, at least a megabyte a second; a pass begins a period after the last one began, and where a pass got to is noted in dir/.scrub.shard every 30 seconds, so a restart goes on from there. The bytes are checked against the MD5 the object's header names: a whole object's against its MD5, a multipart object's part by part against the ETag its parts make, and an SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS object's in its plaintext, which a chunk whose tag fails makes corrupt as well. An SSE-C object, whose key only its client has, and an object whose parts are not recorded, are passed over and counted as skipped.

A copy whose bytes differ is logged once as an error, however many passes find it. On a runtime that is no node of a cluster it stays as it is, to be restored from a copy. On a node of one (--nodes), a version named by its id, or an object of a bucket that keeps no versions, is asked for of the other nodes in turn by a HEAD that must answer its ETag; the first that holds it whole is asked to send it again, and the corrupt copy is taken away first, with no event, no copy sent to the other nodes and no record of a removal, and only while it is still the copy the scrub read. The node's copy comes back under its own id, behind the latest when it was behind it. Until it is back, a read of it on this node finds nothing.

stats shows, per shard, scrub_objects and scrub_bytes (read), scrub_corrupt (found, each once), scrub_skipped, scrub_passes and scrub_last_pass_ms (how long the last whole pass took), scrub_heals (corrupt copies another node was asked to send again) and scrub_unhealed (those no other node held whole).

sections.title: Compression
sections.html:
With --compress, every shard looks, a key at a time, at the versions written since its last pass that have now gone unwritten for the duration, and compresses each that is stored in the clear, is of one part and holds at least 4 KiB: its bytes are cut into chunks of 64 KiB, each compressed as an LZ4 block, or kept as it is when that is no shorter, and written beside the version with a table of where each chunk lies, then put in its place under its key's lane while it is still the version it was. A version whose first megabyte, or whole body, does not get an eighth shorter is left as it was. A pass begins once a quarter of the duration, and at least a second, has passed since the last one's window; what it took is noted in dir/.compact.shard, so each version is looked at once. The reads go at most 64 MiB a second.

Nothing a client sees changes: the ETag, the checksums, the size and the time are the version's, a range opens only the chunks it touches, a copy is made of the bytes and not of the chunks, and replication, the scrub, media and WebDAV read it as they read any other. A version under SSE, a multipart object and an object of under 4 KiB are never compressed.

stats shows, per shard, compressed_objects (versions compressed), compressed_skipped (read and left, as no shorter or changed meanwhile), compressed_failed, compressed_bytes_in and compressed_bytes_out (their bytes, and what they take on disk now), compressed_passes and compressed_gets (GETs whose chunks were opened from the file rather than from memory).

sections.title: S3 Select
sections.html: SelectObjectContent runs one SQL expression over an object stored as CSV (FileHeaderInfo USE, IGNORE or NONE, any field and record delimiter, quotes, comments) or as JSON (DOCUMENT or LINES), with an optional ScanRange, and answers in AWS's event stream, sent as HTTP chunks while the object is read: Records events as they come, a Progress event when asked for, then Stats (the bytes scanned, processed and returned) and End, or an error event when the object cannot be read past the 200. The expression is SELECT * or a list of expressions with AS, FROM S3Object with an alias and a JSON path (S3Object[*].items[*]), WHERE, LIMIT; columns by position (_1), by header name or by JSON path (s.a.b[0]); the comparisons, AND, OR, NOT, LIKE, BETWEEN, IN, IS NULL, arithmetic and ||; CAST, LOWER, UPPER, TRIM, CHAR_LENGTH, SUBSTRING, COALESCE and NULLIF; and the aggregates COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX. A record over 1 MiB is OverMaxRecordSize, and GZIP, BZIP2 and Parquet input are 501 NotImplemented. The object is read as a GET reads it, sealed, compressed or at a tier, and the request needs what a GetObject of it needs, SSE-C headers included. stats counts selects and select_scanned (the bytes their scans read).

sections.title: Tiers
sections.html:
A lifecycle rule's Transition or NoncurrentVersionTransition names a tier of --tiers as its StorageClass. When a version comes due, the shard that owns its key reads it and writes it to the tier with one signed PUT (its Content-MD5 the version's own when it is of one part), under prefixbucket/mtime-md5-version/key in the tier's bucket, so the same version of every node of a cluster is one object there; once the tier has it, the version's file here becomes its header alone, put in place under its key's lane while it is still the version that was read. A version under SSE, one larger than 5 GiB and a multipart object whose part list follows its bytes stay here.

A moved version is listed, and answered on GET and HEAD, with the tier's name as its x-amz-storage-class; a GET, a range or a part of it is read from the tier half a megabyte at a time, two windows ahead, with the size, ETag, time and checksums it always had. CopyObject and UploadPartCopy from it are 403 InvalidObjectState, as S3 answers for an archived object; the scrub, replication and a cluster's seeding pass it over. A quarter day after the last, each shard walks every tier's listing and removes there what no version of a key it owns is any more, an hour after the tier took it at the earliest, so a version deleted, expired or written over here is gone from the tier within six hours.

stats shows tier_moved and tier_moved_bytes (versions moved and their bytes), tier_failed, tier_moving (waiting and in flight), tier_reads and tier_read_failures (windows read back), tier_swept (objects removed at a tier) and tier_gets (GETs read from a tier).

sections.title: Server-side encryption
sections.html:
x-amz-server-side-encryption: AES256 on PutObject, CreateMultipartUpload or CopyObject (SSE-S3) stores the object encrypted under a key of its own, which is wrapped by the runtime's master key (--sse-key-file), and every answer about it — the PUT, the upload's steps, GET, HEAD, the copy — says so with the same header. A GET needs nothing: the plaintext comes back, its ETag is the MD5 of the plaintext as for any object, and ranges, partNumber and conditions work as they do in the clear. aws:kms (SSE-KMS) is the same, with the object's key wrapped by a key derived from the master key and the KMS key id the request names in x-amz-server-side-encryption-aws-kms-key-id, or the bucket default's, or arn:aws:kms:us-east-1:000000000000:alias/aws/s3 when neither names one: any key id is taken, no key is kept but the master key, and every answer names the id as the write gave it. An encryption context is taken and not kept. aws:kms:dsse is 501 NotImplemented, another value 400 InvalidArgument, a KMS key or context without aws:kms 400 InvalidArgument, and the header on a GET or HEAD, which only what writes an object chooses, 400 InvalidArgument.

PutBucketEncryption with an AES256 rule makes every new object of the bucket SSE-S3 when its request asks nothing else, and an aws:kms rule SSE-KMS under its KMSMasterKeyID: puts, copies into it, uploads begun in it and a script's socketley.storage.put. A bucket's rule is a document like its CORS rules, changed by shard 0 with every shard told first (see Bucket policy), kept in dir/bucket/encryption and read at every start; one that no longer parses still encrypts, with an error in the log. DeleteBucketEncryption stops it for new objects and leaves the ones it encrypted as they are.

SSE-C is the client's own key, sent with every request that touches the object as x-amz-server-side-encryption-customer-algorithm: AES256, -customer-key (the 32 bytes in base64) and -customer-key-MD5, as boto3 and the AWS CLI send them. It is taken over TLS only, the runtime's own or a proxy's that --tls-offloaded names: the headers over plain HTTP from anywhere else or a unix node are 400 InvalidRequest, and nothing is written. The key is never stored: the object's data key is wrapped under it, which only that key opens, so a GET or HEAD without the headers is 400 InvalidRequest, with another key 403 AccessDenied, and with a key-MD5 that is not the key's 400 InvalidArgument. CopyObject and UploadPartCopy open an SSE-C source with x-amz-copy-source-server-side-encryption-customer-*, and the parts of an SSE-C upload carry its key. As in S3, the ETag of an SSE-C object or part is not the MD5 of its bytes (it is derived from that MD5 under the data key), nothing of such an object is kept in memory between requests, and a script's socketley.storage.get of one is refused, since it has no key to give.

An SSE-C upload's part list is bound to its key when it completes, so a header rewritten to drop trailing parts does not read. S3 does not ask CompleteMultipartUpload for the customer key, but boto3 and the AWS CLI can send the three headers with it: then the key must be the upload's (403 AccessDenied otherwise) and the data key is wrapped again with the digest of the part list, as SSE-S3 does. A completion without them is bound instead by an HMAC-SHA256 of the object's encryption record and its part list, under a key derived from the --sse-key-file master key (HKDF), recorded in the header as x-socketley-sse-parts and checked before every read, which then needs that master key too. With neither, the completion is 400 InvalidRequest naming both ways out and the upload stays open to be completed again. An upload begun before this binding existed completes only with the headers, since its object could not be told from an older one with its HMAC removed; without them it is 400 InvalidRequest saying so. An object of an upload begun since is never read with its list unbound, a missing or wrong HMAC being 500 InternalError; one completed without the key before this binding existed is read as it was, unless it carries an HMAC that does not hold.

On disk an encrypted object is its header, which records the scheme (x-socketley-sse: format, SSE-S3 or SSE-C, the chunk size, whether the body is one stream or one per part, the master key's id and the wrapped data key), and then its plaintext in chunks of 64 KiB, each sealed with AES-256-GCM on its own as a random 12-byte nonce, the ciphertext and a 16-byte tag: 28 bytes per 64 KiB. In format 2, which every new object and upload is written in, a chunk is sealed with the part number its stream was uploaded as (0 for an object that is one stream), its index there and whether it ends the stream, and every stream ends in a chunk shorter than 64 KiB, empty when its length is whole chunks; a completed upload's data key is wrapped again with the digest of its part list, sizes and numbers. So a header cut back to a chunk boundary, chunks moved to another place or swapped between two parts of one upload, and a header that names fewer parts or other ones all fail to open rather than read as a shorter or mixed object. A range or a part reads and opens only the chunks it touches, and the empty chunk that ends a stream when the range reaches that end; a chunk that does not open ends the response there with a line in the log, and an object small enough to be read whole with its header, or whose data key does not unwrap, is answered 500 InternalError before anything else. Objects written in format 1, which bound a chunk to its index alone, are read as they were, and so are parts of an upload begun under it. The parts of a multipart upload are each a stream of their own, written where the object needs them as unencrypted ones are, and found again by the part sizes and numbers the object records (see Reading by part number). A copy of an encrypted object, or into an encrypted one, is opened and sealed again on its way through, under a key of its own; a tag change, a new version and the assembly of an upload move the sealed bytes as they are. The chunks are sealed and opened on the hashing threads (SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_HASH_THREADS) for bodies and windows of more than 64 KiB, and in line below. A GET of an encrypted object cannot be spliced from the file, so it is read a megabyte at a time, opened and written from memory, with the next megabyte read while one is sent; an SSE-S3 object of up to 60000 bytes is kept opened in memory like any other.

Not supported: SSE-KMS and bucket keys, and changing the master key — an object opens only under the key that wrapped its data key.

sections.title: Bucket lifecycle
sections.html:
A bucket's lifecycle configuration is S3's LifecycleConfiguration document, of at most 1000 rules, each with an ID (at most 255 bytes, unique, generated when left out), Status (Enabled or Disabled), the objects it covers as a Filter — empty for the whole bucket, or one of a Prefix, a Tag (a Key and a Value the object's tags must have), ObjectSizeGreaterThan and ObjectSizeLessThan (each in bytes and exclusive), or an And of a prefix, any number of tags and the two sizes, all of which must hold (or the older form, a Prefix of the rule's own) — and at least one action: Expiration by Days or by Date (midnight UTC), and AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload by DaysAfterInitiation. ExpiredObjectDeleteMarker (true, in an Expiration of its own), and NoncurrentVersionExpiration by NoncurrentDays, and with NewerNoncurrentVersions (1 to 100) only a version that many noncurrent versions of its key are newer than. Transition by Days (zero included) or by Date, and NoncurrentVersionTransition by NoncurrentDays, each to a StorageClass that names a tier of --tiers (any other is 400 InvalidStorageClass; see Tiers). NoncurrentVersionTransition takes NewerNoncurrentVersions as well. A second transition of either kind in one rule is refused with 501 NotImplemented and the configuration that was there stays; a document that is not one is MalformedXML, a value S3 would not take (Days of zero, a Date that is not midnight, a repeated ID, 1001 rules, an ObjectSizeLessThan of 0, a NewerNoncurrentVersions of 0 or over 100) is InvalidArgument, a tag key or value an object could not have is InvalidTag, and what S3 refuses as InvalidRequest is: one tag key twice in an And, sizes with nothing between them, and a tag or size filter on a rule that aborts uploads (an upload has neither yet) or one with ExpiredObjectDeleteMarker. The rules are synced into dir/bucket/lifecycle before the answer, so they survive a stop or a crash, and go with the bucket when it is deleted. With --shards a change is answered once no shard can go on with the old rules, and a shard unsure of them expires nothing in the bucket until it has read them (see Bucket policy).

The rules are carried out by a sweep in each shard over the keys and uploads it owns. An object expires Days days after its last write, rounded up to the next midnight UTC as S3 does (one written on the 1st at 10:30 with Days 1 goes at the midnight that begins the 3rd); with a Date every object under the rule goes from that midnight on, those written later too. It is removed exactly as a DeleteObject removes it — the unlink synced, then the journal record — and a script's on_delete is told. An object written again or given other tags after the sweep found it is judged as it is then, and a configuration changed or removed meanwhile is obeyed. The tags and size a filter asks about are the index's, in memory, so a filter on them costs the walk no reads. An upload is aborted DaysAfterInitiation days after it began, rounded the same way. In a versioned bucket an expiring latest version is covered by a delete marker, as S3 does, rather than removed; a noncurrent version is removed for good NoncurrentDays days after the version that replaced it was written, rounded the same way and filtered by the version's own tags and size; and with ExpiredObjectDeleteMarker a delete marker that is its key's only version left is removed. A pass runs at each start, within a second of a change to the rules and then hourly; it walks the index a page at a time with at most eight removals in flight and a pause between steps, so a bucket with a great many expiring keys is worked through without holding up other requests. stats counts what it did in lifecycle_expired and lifecycle_aborted, and each pass that removed anything says so in the log.

A PutObject's answer, and a GetObject's or HeadObject's of the latest version, carry x-amz-expiration (expiry-date="date", rule-id="id") when a rule will expire the object, naming the rule that does so first, as S3 does.

SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_LIFECYCLE_DAY_SECS is a test aid: read by the sweep alone, it makes a lifecycle day that many seconds (at most 86400) so a rule can be watched taking effect, with passes as often as every second. It is never meant for a runtime holding data anyone wants.

sections.title: Bucket policy
sections.html:
A bucket's policy is S3's JSON document, which can make a bucket or a part of it readable by anyone — static assets, downloads — while every other request to the runtime still has to be signed, and can refuse a signed key what it would otherwise be let do. For example, anyone may read the objects under public/:

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Sid": "PublicRead",
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Principal": "*",
    "Action": "s3:GetObject",
    "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::media/public/*"
  }]
}

What it takes is the part of S3's grammar this runtime can honour exactly, and a document asking for anything else is refused as 400 MalformedPolicy naming what it could not take, never accepted to do less than it says:

Version#

2012-10-17 or 2008-10-17, or none; Id any string.

Statement#

one statement or a list of them, each with an optional Sid (unique), Effect (Allow or Deny), Principal, Action, Resource and an optional Condition. NotPrincipal, NotAction and NotResource are refused.

Principal#

* or {"AWS": * } for everyone, signed or not; or {"AWS": [...]} naming this runtime's users and access keys, each as the key itself, as arn:aws:iam::account:user/name (the name is a user's id or an access key), or as arn:aws:iam::account:root for every key. A {"Service": ...} principal is taken and names no requester here, so a statement naming services alone matches nothing whatever its conditions, which are not checked: the policy S3 documents for a log target, letting logging.s3.amazonaws.com write, is taken as it is written. Federated and canonical-user principals and roles are refused.

Action#

one or a list of s3:Name with * and ? wildcards, compared without case, or * alone. A name must be one of S3's, and those this runtime does not implement (s3:RestoreObject, s3:GetBucketAnalyticsConfiguration, ...) are taken and match nothing. GetObject covers GetObject and HeadObject, by part too; PutObject covers PutObject, CopyObject, CreateMultipartUpload, UploadPart, UploadPartCopy and CompleteMultipartUpload; DeleteObject covers DeleteObject and DeleteObjects; ListBucket covers ListObjects, ListObjectsV2 and HeadBucket; PutBucketCORS and PutLifecycleConfiguration and PutEncryptionConfiguration cover the deletes of those configurations, and GetEncryptionConfiguration covers GetBucketEncryption; the rest are named as S3 names them (GetObjectTagging, AbortMultipartUpload, ListMultipartUploadParts, ListBucketMultipartUploads, GetBucketLocation, CreateBucket, DeleteBucket, GetBucketVersioning, PutBucketVersioning, ...). A request that names a version with ?versionId= is the version's action, as in S3: GetObjectVersion for GET and HEAD (and for a copy's source named key?versionId=), DeleteObjectVersion for DELETE and for each DeleteObjects entry with a VersionId (judged per entry, a refused one answered AccessDenied in the result), and GetObjectVersionTagging, PutObjectVersionTagging and DeleteObjectVersionTagging; ListBucketVersions covers ListObjectVersions. Object lock has GetBucketObjectLockConfiguration and PutBucketObjectLockConfiguration, GetObjectRetention and PutObjectRetention (also a write that names a retention), GetObjectLegalHold and PutObjectLegalHold (also a write that names a hold), and BypassGovernanceRetention, asked beside the action of a request that sends the bypass header. GetBucketNotification and PutBucketNotification cover the two notification configuration operations, and GetReplicationConfiguration and PutReplicationConfiguration the three replication ones. A write that sends x-amz-replication-status: REPLICA (PutObject and the steps of a multipart upload) is ReplicateObject instead of PutObject, such a DeleteObject is ReplicateDelete, and such a PutObjectTagging or DeleteObjectTagging is ReplicateTags: a user allowed those three and nothing else can be the destination's replication user. The header counts only for a user allowed the replication action, and a Deny of the write it stands for still refuses it; anyone else's request is the plain write, its header ignored.

Resource#

one or a list of arn:aws:s3:::bucket for the bucket itself and arn:aws:s3:::bucket/pattern for its objects, with * for any run of characters and ? for one; the bucket must be this one, or a pattern that covers it, as arn:aws:s3:::* does (that one, ending in *, covering the bucket's objects too, since IAM's * spans a slash), and a statement must have an action that applies to one of its resources (an object action to a key pattern, a bucket action to the bucket). Policy variables are refused.

Condition#

IpAddress and NotIpAddress on aws:SourceIp (addresses and CIDR ranges, IPv4 and IPv6, an IPv4 address mapped into IPv6 being the IPv4 address), and Bool on aws:SecureTransport (whether the connection is TLS), and StringEquals, StringNotEquals and Null on s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption (the request's x-amz-server-side-encryption header, compared as given: a request that does not send it equals no value, so StringNotEquals holds for it, and Null "true" holds for it alone). PutObject, CopyObject and CreateMultipartUpload carry the header; UploadPart, UploadPartCopy and CompleteMultipartUpload take the encryption their upload's creation chose and was judged on, so no statement with a condition on it applies to them, Allow or Deny. A bucket's default encryption is not the header, so S3's two statements that deny a PutObject without AES256 refuse a put that leaves it to the default. Every condition of a statement must hold. A client on a unix socket has no address, so it is in no range: an IpAddress never holds for it and a NotIpAddress always does.

Details

Beyond those, IAM's operator families on the keys a request here carries: String(Not)Equals(IgnoreCase), String(Not)Like with * and ?, Arn(Not)Equals and Arn(Not)Like as their string forms, Numeric... and Date... (an epoch second or an ISO 8601 time), Bool, Null and the IP pair, each with IfExists and the ForAnyValue: and ForAllValues: qualifiers. The keys: aws:Referer, aws:UserAgent, aws:SourceIp, aws:SecureTransport, aws:CurrentTime, aws:EpochTime, aws:username and aws:userid (the user's id, absent for a request without credentials), aws:PrincipalType, s3:prefix, s3:delimiter and s3:max-keys (a listing's query), s3:versionid and the s3:x-amz-... and s3:object-lock-... keys (the request's headers of those names), s3:RequestObjectTag/key and s3:RequestObjectTagKeys (the request's x-amz-tagging header), s3:signatureversion, s3:authType and s3:TlsVersion. A key the request does not carry fails its condition, except under IfExists, a negated operator or ForAllValues, as IAM has it. s3:ExistingObjectTag/key is refused, since the object's tags are not read before the request is judged, and so is any other key or operator.

A request to a bucket with a policy is authenticated as it always is, and then judged: a statement applies when its action, principal and resource match the request and its conditions hold, an applying Deny refuses the request with 403 AccessDenied whatever else applies, and an applying Allow lets in a request that carries no credentials, on a runtime without --anonymous, and a signed request of a user that does not own the bucket (see Users). A request whose signature is wrong is refused as before and never taken for an anonymous request; a presigned URL is a signed request. On a runtime with --anonymous every request without credentials is already let in, and a Deny for * still refuses it. A copy is also judged as a GetObject of its source, by the source bucket's policy, so an anonymous copy needs both. DeleteObjects names its keys in the body, so it is judged over every key of the bucket: a Deny over any key refuses it, and only an Allow over arn:aws:s3:::bucket/* lets an anonymous one in. A request a policy refuses is answered before its body is read. The policy's own four operations answer to ownership alone for the bucket's owner and an admin, so a policy can neither let an anonymous request read or change it nor lock the owner out of removing it. A request let in by a policy is still the Lua on_request hook's to refuse (see Lua), which never sees one the policy refused.

The document is compiled when it is set, and again when a shard starts, so a request is judged against compiled statements: a runtime none of whose buckets has a policy looks nothing up, a signed request to a bucket whose policy has no Deny looks up the bucket and nothing more, and only a statement that compares aws:SourceIp asks the kernel for the client's address, once per connection; the other keys are read from the request only when a statement that names them applies.

As in S3, a request a policy lets in is told a key is not there only if it may list the bucket the key would be in: a GET, HEAD or other object request for a missing key is 404 NoSuchKey when s3:ListBucket on the bucket applies to the requester (an Allow for an anonymous request, no Deny for a signed one or on a runtime with --anonymous), and 403 AccessDenied when it does not. For a copy the bucket is the source's.

The policy is kept in dir/bucket/policy, written beside it, synced and renamed over it, so it survives a restart and a crash leaves the old one or the new; it goes with the bucket. A stored policy that does not compile when a shard starts, because the file was edited or this version refuses what an older one took, is not skipped: the bucket refuses every request with 403 AccessDenied naming why, except Put, Get and Delete BucketPolicy and GetBucketPolicyStatus by the runtime's keys, so it can be read back and replaced or removed, and the log has an error saying so.

With --shards shard 0 makes every change of a bucket's policy and CORS, lifecycle and versioning configuration, one at a time per bucket, whichever shard took the request, and answers it only once no running shard can go on with the old document. It writes the new one beside the file as kind.new (empty for a removal), asks every other shard to stop serving the bucket until it learns how the change ended, and only when all of them have promised renames it over the file (or removes the file), tells them the new document and answers; a shard it cannot reach, because it is stopped, starting, wedged or cut off, fails the change with 503 ServiceUnavailable and nothing changes anywhere, since the file is removed and the shards that promised are released. A shard that promised and is never told the outcome serves nothing of that bucket (503 ServiceUnavailable, which clients retry) until it reads the outcome from the files: while kind.new exists the change is undecided, and once it is gone the file is the document. A shard re-reads them at its next request to the bucket and at its periodic sweep, so a lost message delays a shard and never leaves it with the old document; a request on another shard during the moment between a shard's promise and the rename can be answered 503 the same way. A shard that starts while a change is undecided, or takes a bucket up later than the others, reads the bucket's documents the same way before serving it. This costs a runtime with no change in flight one counter load per request.

entries.summary: 2012-10-17 or 2008-10-17, or none; Id any string.

one statement or a list of them, each with an optional Sid (unique), Effect (Allow or Deny), Principal, Action, Resource and an optional Condition. NotPrincipal, NotAction and NotResource are refused.

* or {"AWS": * } for everyone, signed or not; or {"AWS": [...]} naming this runtime's users and access keys, each as the key itself, as arn:aws:iam::account:user/name (the name is a user's id or an access key), or as arn:aws:iam::account:root for every key. A {"Service": ...} principal is taken and names no requester here, so a statement naming services alone matches nothing whatever its condition

one or a list of s3:Name with * and ? wildcards, compared without case, or * alone. A name must be one of S3's, and those this runtime does not implement (s3:RestoreObject, s3:GetBucketAnalyticsConfiguration, ...) are taken and match nothing. GetObject covers GetObject and HeadObject, by part too; PutObject covers PutObject, CopyObject, CreateMultipartUpload, UploadPart, UploadPartCopy and Complet

one or a list of arn:aws:s3:::bucket for the bucket itself and arn:aws:s3:::bucket/pattern for its objects, with * for any run of characters and ? for one; the bucket must be this one, or a pattern that covers it, as arn:aws:s3:::* does (that one, ending in *, covering the bucket's objects too, since IAM's * spans a slash), and a statement must have an action that applies to one of its resources (

IpAddress and NotIpAddress on aws:SourceIp (addresses and CIDR ranges, IPv4 and IPv6, an IPv4 address mapped into IPv6 being the IPv4 address), and Bool on aws:SecureTransport (whether the connection is TLS), and StringEquals, StringNotEquals and Null on s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption (the request's x-amz-server-side-encryption header, compared as given: a request that does not send it equals no

sections.title: Server access logging
sections.html:
A logged bucket's every answer is a line of S3's server access log format in objects delivered to its target bucket:

PUT /photos?logging
<BucketLoggingStatus>
  <LoggingEnabled>
    <TargetBucket>logs</TargetBucket>
    <TargetPrefix>photos/</TargetPrefix>
  </LoggingEnabled>
</BucketLoggingStatus>

A line names the bucket's owner and the bucket, the time, the client's address, the requester's access key (- for none), the request id, the operation (REST.GET.OBJECT, REST.PUT.PART, REST.PUT.VERSIONING, WEBSITE.GET.OBJECT and so on; a DeleteObjects is a REST.POST.MULTI_OBJECT_DELETE line and a BATCH.DELETE.OBJECT line for each key), the key, the request line, the status, the error code, the bytes of body sent, a put's size, the milliseconds from the request's start to its answer, the referer and user agent, the signature version and how it was given, the TLS cipher, the Host header and the TLS version; a field this runtime does not know is -, as S3 writes one it has nothing for. A line is written when the answer starts, so a download that is cut off is logged as sent.

Each shard holds its lines for each target and delivers them as one object once a minute's worth or 1 MiB are held, named prefixYYYY-MM-DD-hh-mm-ss-unique, or with a PartitionedPrefix prefixowner/us-east-1/bucket/YYYY/MM/DD/YYYY-MM-DD-hh-mm-ss-unique by the delivery's date. The object is put as a client's would be, encrypted when the target encrypts and replicated and notified when it is; one that cannot be put, the target having been deleted or gone past its quota, is dropped with a warning in the log. Lines still held when the runtime stops are lost, as at most a minute of them. The target must be a bucket with the same owner as the logged one; it may be the logged bucket itself, and the deliveries are not logged. The configuration is kept in dir/bucket/logging and changed by shard 0 like the bucket's other documents.

sections.title: Public access block
sections.html:
A bucket's public access block keeps it from being opened to everyone by mistake:

PUT /photos?publicAccessBlock
<PublicAccessBlockConfiguration>
  <BlockPublicPolicy>true</BlockPublicPolicy>
  <RestrictPublicBuckets>true</RestrictPublicBuckets>
</PublicAccessBlockConfiguration>

BlockPublicPolicy refuses a PutBucketPolicy whose policy is public, as GetBucketPolicyStatus judges it, with 403 AccessDenied; a public policy already there stays. RestrictPublicBuckets keeps a public policy from letting in any request without credentials, the bucket's website's included, while the runtime's users keep what it and their credentials give them, since they are all of one account. BlockPublicAcls and IgnorePublicAcls are kept and read back and change nothing, since a public ACL is refused here whatever they say. The block is kept in dir/bucket/public-access-block and changed by shard 0 like the bucket's other documents. A runtime started with --anonymous lets everyone in whatever a bucket's block says, as it does whatever its policy says.

sections.title: How objects are stored
sections.html:
An object is one file at dir/bucket/data/ab/sha256(key) whose first bytes are a checksummed header carrying the key, size, ETag, content type, user metadata, tags and time, so the file says what it is and any byte sequence is a valid key; the 256 directories ab (the first two hex digits of the hash) are made and synced with the bucket, so a put never makes one. Each bucket also keeps an append-only journal of puts and deletes (index.0, or index.shard for a sharded runtime; CRC32C-framed, rewritten when garbage passes the live objects), from which listings are answered out of memory.

A put writes a temporary file, syncs it, renames it into place and syncs the directory, and only then answers 200; a delete removes the file and syncs the directory. A put of up to 1 MiB whose length is known and that carries no condition (no If-None-Match, not a part) is written instead into one of a few empty files the bucket keeps ready in pool/, whose names were synced before any put took one; once that file is synced and renamed into place the put is answered, and the syncs of pool/ and of the object's directory follow the answer, with the key's next put or delete waiting for them. The answered object is on disk either way: a crash that takes the rename leaves it whole in pool/, and the next start moves it into place (a file there counts as whole only when its length and MD5 are those its header names, which for an encrypted body is the MD5 of its sealed bytes, kept in its header as x-socketley-stored-md5, since a start holds no key that opens it). The journal record of either is appended behind the answer and synced once a megabyte of records has gathered, before a compaction and at a stop, and never merely because the queue drained, since that sync would sit in front of the next put's own: the object files are the truth and the journal is only the index of them, so an answer never waits for it. A crash at any point leaves the old object or the new one and never a torn one, and nothing that was answered is undone. A start after a clean stop (which writes and syncs the journals last) trusts them; any other start removes temporary files and reads every object header to reconcile the journals with the files, so a journal that is lost, damaged or short of its last records is rebuilt from the objects, and a delete whose record was lost does not bring the object back, because its file is gone. That reading happens before the listener opens and takes as long as the object count makes it, and is the only place the loop blocks on the disk: every request is served on the runtime's io_uring. A stop closes the listener and the connections first and then lets the journal writes, directory syncs and compaction already begun finish, for at most a second; one that cannot finish them in that time is read by the next start as a crash. Each shard holds a lock on .lock.n in the directory until its stop is done, and a start waits up to a second and a half, in all, for the process it replaces on its shard and for every process still holding a shard under another --shards, whose files it takes over, and fails if they do not let go — a safety net, since the daemon forks a runtime's workers only once its previous ones have exited (see restart). A request a shard has sent a sibling and not had answered when the stop comes is answered as failed, so it does not hold the stop.

The start after a crash reads every header even of a file the journal names with the same size, since an overwrite whose record was lost can leave exactly that: the header is the only thing that tells the two versions apart. What makes it fast is that the reads are many at once. The 256 directories of every bucket are shared out among threads, one per CPU the runtime may run on (at most 16, SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_RECOVERY_THREADS), which have joined before the listener opens; each reads its directories with 128 KiB getdents64(2) calls and keeps 32 opens and header reads in flight on an io_uring of its own (SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_RECOVERY_DEPTH, 0 for one file at a time without a ring), all within half of what RLIMIT_NOFILE leaves. Only a file at the one path its key gives, ab/sha256(key), is read, which is what lets a bucket whose files match its journal one for one skip the search for records whose file is gone. A directory that cannot be read whole, or a descriptor table that runs out on the way, fails the start with the reason rather than dropping the objects it did not see. With 1 KiB objects on an ext4 virtio disk and four CPUs, 100,000 objects take 0.24 s with a warm cache (0.8 s before this was parallel) and about 1 s from a cold one (11 to 33 s before), and 1,000,000 take 2.3 s warm (9.8 s) and 19 s cold (344 s); a start after a clean stop reads only the journals, 0.07 s for 100,000 and 0.66 s for 1,000,000.

A body is never held whole: it streams from the socket into a megabyte staging buffer, is hashed as it passes (on helper threads from 256 KiB up, so that the loop is not the one core that hashes every upload) and written while the next bytes arrive, so a gigabyte upload costs a few megabytes of memory. A GET of 64 KiB or more is sent by sendfile(2) from the file to the socket without entering the process, a burst at a time from the event loop (a stretch not in the page cache is read through the ring instead), and the bytes that took that path are counted as zero_copy_bytes in stats; smaller objects are read once, with their header, and sent from memory with the response headers in one write.

An object of up to 60000 bytes is kept in memory after it is first read, by every shard that reads it, up to 32 MiB per shard (SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_HOT_BYTES) with the least recently read going first, and later GETs on that shard are answered from the copy without opening the file. On the shard that owns the key a copy is answered only while it is the version the index names. With --shards a shard that does not own the key has no index entry to compare with. The first copy it keeps of a key in one of the 16384 slots is one the key's owner has said is the version indexed, and from then on the owner tells it to drop its copy of any key of that slot after it has committed or deleted the key and before it answers the client (one round trip to those siblings, in parallel, against the milliseconds of the syncs; none for a key whose slot no sibling has read from), and a read that a drop of its key arrived during is not kept. A PUT, copy, multipart completion or DELETE that was answered is therefore never followed by a GET on any shard that returns the bytes it replaced. A sibling that is down is not waited for and holds nothing when it starts again, and a shard that starts tells the others to drop every copy of its keys, since it may have died between renaming a new version into place and telling them. A GET of a 4 KiB object at 32 connections on four shards took 45 us of worker CPU (summed over the shards) before the copy was kept on every shard and takes 30 us, and about 50 thousand requests per second becomes about 56 thousand; at one connection 30 to 20 us and 7100 to 8100 requests per second; a PUT of 4 KiB into memory-backed storage takes about 14 us longer for the round trip. Every copy keeps the response headers of a plain GET once it has answered one, so a shard spends the same on a GET whether or not it owns the key; measured later on four CPUs with another client, four shards take about 26 us per 4 KiB GET at 32 connections against about 17 us for one shard, the difference being four half-idle loops that each sleep and wake for every few requests rather than work that only a shard does.

sections.title: Performance
sections.html:
Measured with warp and boto3 over plain HTTP with SigV4 on one 16-core VM with an ext4 virtio disk, against MinIO as a single node with a single drive on the same filesystem, three alternating passes with the box quiet before each. Reads are faster than MinIO's: a 4 KiB GET at one connection is about 4x (8200 against 1900 per second) and at 32 connections 1.7x with one shard and 3.6x with four, a 1 MiB GET 2x and 4x, a 64 MiB GET 1.4x and 3.8x, each at a tenth or less of the CPU. A 64 MiB put is 1.3x at one connection and 1.1x at 32 (about 600 MiB/s, which is what this disk takes), and 64 MiB mixed loads are level with MinIO.

On a second machine, a 4-vCPU VM (AMD EPYC, Debian 12, kernel 7.2, warp 1.3.1 on the same four CPUs, one shard, three alternating passes), against the same MinIO: 4 KiB GET 3.0x at one connection and 3.9x at 32, HEAD 3.9x, 1 MiB GET 2.5x, 64 MiB GET 1.8x, listing 3.1x, multi-object delete 2.7x, 4 KiB put 1.7x at one connection and 2.5x at 32 (about 900 and 3000 per second, this disk's sync being fast), 1 MiB put 1.2x, 64 MiB put level (6.5 against 6.6 per second) and mixed 1 MiB loads 1.6x, with less CPU per request in every row: about nine tenths of MinIO's for large puts, a third to a half for small ones, a seventeenth for reads. Four shards are slower than one there, since the client shares the four CPUs; shards are for a machine with cores to spare. From a client 31 ms away over the internet (k6, 32 connections), 4 KiB GETs and puts run at what the round trip allows for both servers (about 800 to 880 per second), with socketley's p99 at 45 to 47 ms against MinIO's 48 to 147 and about 2.6x less CPU per put.

Small puts wait for the disk and for little else, so they move with it. A put of up to 1 MiB waits for one sync, of its pooled file, where it waited for two, the file and then its directory, and no put waits behind a sync of the journal, whose record used to be synced behind each answer, where the next put's own sync then queued behind it. With warp 1.3.1 (three alternating passes each), dropping that journal sync took 4 KiB puts at one connection from 77 to 104 per second; the pooled file took them from 107 to 118 in a fast phase of the disk and left them level (35 and 34) in a slow one, took 4 KiB puts at 32 connections from about 430 to 600 per second and 1 MiB puts at one connection from 22 to 28 in the slow phase. boto3's p50 for a 4 KiB put went from 13.0 ms to 11.3 and then 7.6 ms, against MinIO's 8.5 to 17 ms on the same disk minutes apart. Against MinIO, a 4 KiB put at one connection is level in the disk's fast phases (about 120 per second each) and 0.6x in its slow ones (33 against 54), and at 32 connections 1.2x or more. MinIO syncs its file once and never its directory, so a power cut can take a put it has answered; here an answered put survives one. The disk's sync latency drifts by two to three times within an hour, which is why these rows name their phase.

The journal is not waited for: a stop syncs it, and a start after any other stop reads every object header, which takes about a quarter of a second per 100,000 objects with a warm cache and about a second from a cold one on four CPUs (see How objects are stored). Uploads of 256 KiB or more are hashed on helper threads (SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_HASH_THREADS), which is what lets a 64 MiB put at 32 connections use the disk rather than one core.

A body of known length that arrives slower than 4 MB/s, judged over 10 ms, is left to gather in the socket and read once per 10 ms tick shared by every such connection, except for its last 64 KiB; each tick takes all that gathered, even over TLS, where one receive brings 16 KiB, so a body that began slowly and speeds up is read at the speed it comes. A slow upload is so not paid for with a receive and a wakeup per TCP segment; its digests are handed to the hashing threads 64 KiB at a time. A 1 MiB put sent in 1448-byte segments at 0.8 MB/s, eight at once, took about 35 to 60 ms of worker CPU per MiB before and about 6 to 9 after, against about 3 to 5 for the same put sent at loopback speed.

sections.title: HTTP/2
sections.html: A storage runtime speaks HTTP/2 (RFC 9113) besides HTTP/1.1: over --tls to a client that offers h2 by ALPN, as every browser does, and in the clear to one that opens with HTTP/2's preface (prior knowledge, as curl speaks it when told to and a proxy's h2c backend does). Every request is a stream of the one connection and runs exactly as over HTTP/1.1, S3, WebDAV, the web interface, share links and media alike, so a browser's uploads, its player's segments and its pictures no longer wait for one of the six connections it opens to a server over HTTP/1.1. A stream's window is given back only as its body is taken, so a disk that cannot keep up holds the client as a full socket does; going out, a frame of each stream is sent in turn as the client's windows allow, a stream told its bytes left when they reach the connection's queue, which is kept under 1 MiB, so the next piece of a file is read while the last is written. This side reads by a window of 4 MiB a stream and 32 MiB a connection, 128 streams open at once (the next is refused with REFUSED_STREAM), header lists of up to 64 KiB, and frames of 16 KiB; a peer that resets more than 400 streams, sends more than 200 PINGs or SETTINGS or 1000 empty DATA frames in ten seconds, or a header block past 80 KiB or 64 CONTINUATIONs, is sent GOAWAY with ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM, as RFC 9113 and the rapid-reset advisory (CVE-2023-44487) ask. A stream's file is read through the process rather than spliced, as over TLS. A connection with no stream open is let go after the idle timeout with GOAWAY, as is every one at a stop. stats counts h2_conns, h2_streams, h2_refused, h2_resets_in, h2_resets_out and h2_goaways. SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_HTTP2=0 turns it off, so every client speaks HTTP/1.1.

sections.title: HTTP/3
sections.html: With --tls a storage runtime also speaks HTTP/3 (RFC 9114) over QUIC (RFC 9000) on the same port number over UDP, when it was built with HTTP/3 (stats shows h3:1; bin/build-thirdparty.sh http3 builds the static OpenSSL 3.5, ngtcp2 and nghttp3 it needs, and the install script runs it). Every answer over TCP carries Alt-Svc: h3=":PORT" so a browser tries QUIC on its next request and goes on over TCP if UDP does not reach; each request is a stream and runs exactly as over HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2. A connection survives a client's change of address or network, and a lost packet holds up only its own stream, which is what HTTP/3 is for on mobile and lossy links; on a clean wire HTTP/2 costs less CPU per byte. With --shards the shards share the UDP port and the kernel picks one by the client's address, so a client that moved may reach another: every connection ID names its shard, and a packet for another shard's connection is handed to it, which answers from the same port. A stream's window and a connection's start at 1 and 4 MiB and grow to 16 and 64 MiB, 128 streams are open at once, a handshake not done in 10 seconds is dropped, and a connection is let go after 30 seconds without a packet. What a client is sent is paced by BBR, which follows the path's measured rate and round trip rather than backing off at each lost packet: over a 50 ms path that loses one packet in a hundred, as Wi-Fi and mobile links do, a download ran ten to twenty times faster than with CUBIC, and as fast on a clean path. SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_HTTP3_CC=cubic (or reno) chooses another. AES-128-GCM is offered first, since every packet is sealed on its own and it costs a quarter less than AES-256. While more than SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_HTTP3_RETRY_AFTER handshakes (64; 0 for always) are under way, a new client is sent a Retry and must prove its address before anything is kept for it (RFC 9000 8.1.2), so datagrams with forged sources cannot fill the table. QUIC's TLS is TCP's: a certificate renewed on disk is taken up the same way, and --ca asks for a client certificate here too. Behind a reverse proxy, which forwards TCP only, the proxy passes the header on with the runtime's port: forward UDP from the port browsers reach (usually 443, which the proxy does not take for UDP) to the runtime's, give it the certificate browsers expect, and set SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_HTTP3_ADVERTISE to that port, or to 0 to advertise none. stats counts h3_conns, h3_streams, h3_retries and h3_forwarded (packets handed to another shard), and shows the connections open now as h3_open. SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_HTTP3=0 turns it off.

sections.title: Quotas
sections.html:
A bucket's quota bounds the bytes its objects and versions hold and how many there are; it is socketley's own document, which S3 has no counterpart of:

PUT /photos?quota
<BucketQuota>
  <MaxBytes>10737418240</MaxBytes>
  <MaxObjects>100000</MaxObjects>
</BucketQuota>

Either element may be left out, and 0 is no bound. Only an admin, or the runtime's own key, or anyone on an --anonymous runtime, may set, read or delete one, since a quota bounds what the bucket's owner may store; it is kept in dir/bucket/quota and changed by shard 0 like a bucket's other configuration documents, and a restart keeps it. A user's max_bytes (see Users) bounds what every bucket that user owns holds together.

A write that would take a bucket or its owner past a quota is answered 403 QuotaExceeded and stores nothing: a PUT, a POST, a copy and the completion of a multipart upload alike. An overwrite counts the bytes it adds over the object it replaces and adds no object; in a versioned bucket every version counts, delete markers among them. A quota is judged by the shard that owns the key, at the commit, one write at a time, so writes racing each other cannot pass it together; a shard that owns the key also refuses a body of known length before reading it. Under --shards each shard holds its share of a quota, as it does of --max-bytes, so a bucket whose keys fall unevenly is refused somewhat before the whole is reached. The parts of a multipart upload are not counted until it is completed.

sections.title: Website hosting
sections.html:
A bucket with a website configuration is served to browsers under --website-domain, as S3's website endpoints serve it:

socketley create storage media -p 9000 --dir /srv/objects \
    --credentials /etc/socketley/s3.keys --website-domain web.example.com -s

with the site's configuration put on its bucket and its files uploaded by any S3 client:

PUT /docs?website
<WebsiteConfiguration>
  <IndexDocument><Suffix>index.html</Suffix></IndexDocument>
  <ErrorDocument><Key>404.html</Key></ErrorDocument>
</WebsiteConfiguration>

after which http://docs.web.example.com:9000/ is the bucket's index.html. A request to a website signs nothing and is judged as one with no credentials, whatever it carries, so a page is read only when the bucket's policy lets anyone read it (Principal "*", s3:GetObject); on an --anonymous runtime every page is. Only GET and HEAD are served, the query is ignored, and the latest version of a key is the page.

A key that is empty or ends in / is given the index document's suffix, so /guide/ is guide/index.html, and a key without the slash whose folder has an index document is answered 302 to the folder, where the page's relative links resolve. An object stored with x-amz-website-redirect-location is answered 301 to that location. A routing rule whose condition is a KeyPrefixEquals alone redirects before the object is looked for, and one with an HttpErrorCodeReturnedEquals redirects a failure with that status; its Redirect may replace the key or its prefix and name a host, a protocol and a 3xx code, the request's own host and protocol and 301 otherwise. A RedirectAllRequestsTo sends every request to its host with the key kept.

A failure no rule redirects is answered with the ErrorDocument and the failure's status, when the policy lets anyone read it, and otherwise with an HTML page naming the error's code, message and request id, and an x-amz-error-code header. A missing key is 403 AccessDenied rather than 404 NoSuchKey when the policy lets anyone read the bucket's keys but not list them, as on S3. The S3 API is served on the same port as before, so a site is uploaded and read over both.

sections.title: Drive, links, media and the web interface
sections.html:
Paths that begin with ~, which no bucket name can, are the runtime's own applications, on the S3 port and under the S3 runtime's users, policies and versioning:

/~dav/#

A WebDAV drive (classes 1 and 2) for Windows, macOS, Linux file managers, rclone and phones. It signs in with HTTP Basic, an access key as the user name and its secret as the password; a runtime without credentials takes none. Its root is every bucket the user owns or a bucket policy lets it list, every bucket for an admin, and a bucket's keys are files whose slashes are folders. A file's GET, PUT, DELETE, COPY and MOVE are the S3 operations, judged by the same policies; MKCOL at the root makes a bucket and within one an empty folder/ marker object, as S3 browsers do. A folder's COPY, MOVE and DELETE go over every key under it, and a copy reads each object whole, so one past 256 MiB or under a client's own key is not copied and the answer is 500. A COPY or MOVE with Overwrite: F is 412 when its Destination holds a file, or for a folder any object under it, and replaces it otherwise. Locks are granted and not enforced, and properties are not kept.

Details

An address that fails ten sign-ins with Basic, here, at /~ui/ and /~media/, or ten passwords of share links within a quarter hour is answered 429 with a Retry-After until that quarter hour ends, the right secret too, while its signed-in sessions go on; an IPv6 address counts by its /64. Each shard counts on its own, so an address has ten tries a shard, and behind a proxy every client is the proxy's address, so one guessing there keeps the others from signing in as well.

A file may also be sent in parts, side by side, as S3's multipart upload under the drive's sign-in: POST ?uploads on the file begins one and answers its UploadId, PUT ?partNumber=n&uploadId=id streams a part and answers its ETag, POST ?uploadId=id with S3's CompleteMultipartUpload body makes the file of them, and DELETE ?uploadId=id abandons it; each is judged as the S3 operation it is. GET ?uploadId=id lists the parts that arrived (with max-parts and part-number-marker for the next page), so an upload broken off is taken up again where it stopped. A file's other PUTs ignore their query.

[drive]                      # rclone.conf, then: rclone copy ~/photos drive:holiday
type = webdav
url = http://host:9000/~dav/
user = AKIA...
pass = <the secret, as rclone obscure prints it>

GET /~dav/bucket/folder/?zip is the folder as one ZIP, saved as folder.zip, and ?zip&n=name&n=name only the files and folders of it named; a bucket's root takes it too. It is streamed as it is read, each file stored as it is, so its Content-Length is known before its first byte and a browser shows how far it has come; each entry's CRC-32 is taken as its bytes pass and follows them in a data descriptor, and a file or an offset past 4 GiB takes ZIP64. An entry's name is its key under the folder without empty, “.” and “..” segments, with “\” and control characters made “_”, and numbered “ (2)”, “ (3)” before its extension where another entry has it, so no key unpacks outside the folder or over another file. Only what the user may read is in it, and what only its client's key opens is left out. An object that changes while the ZIP is being sent ends the connection, since its length was promised.

In a versioned bucket a deleted file is a delete marker, and its versions stay: GET /~dav/bucket/folder/?trash lists the files under the folder whose latest version is a marker, as JSON with the key, the time of the deletion and the size of the version behind it, and POST /~dav/bucket/key?restore removes the marker and brings that version back. A lifecycle rule's NoncurrentVersionExpiration empties the trash. GET /~dav/bucket/folder/?list is a folder's listing as the web interface reads it, JSON of its subfolders' names and its files' names, sizes, times in milliseconds and types ({"d":[...],"f":[[name,size,mtime,type],...]}), about a tenth of a PROPFIND's bytes, with an ETag of its own, so a look again with If-None-Match that finds nothing changed is 304 and no body. A folder of 20,000 files was 9.9 MB and 44 ms as a PROPFIND and is 1.0 MB and 9 ms, and a browser read it in 40 ms rather than 400. POST /~dav/bucket/key?unzip unpacks a ZIP object on the server into a folder beside it named as it is without its extension, numbered (name (2)) when that name is taken, so nothing is written over and nothing of it crosses the client's line. Each file is read from the archive, opened when it is deflated, checked against its CRC-32 and size, and written as an object of its own, four at a time, as the drive's other writes are (encrypted when the bucket encrypts, typed by its extension); an empty folder in it becomes the folder's marker. ZIP64 archives are read; names in UTF-8 are kept and older ones are read as code page 437. A file that is encrypted, packed other than stored or deflated, or named outside the folder (.., a control character) is skipped, as macOS's __MACOSX tree, .DS_Store and Thumbs.db are without a word. It needs GET of the archive and PUT under the folder; the answer, once every file is written, is JSON naming the folder and counting the files, folders and bytes written and the files skipped and failed, with up to 20 names of each, 201 when none failed and 500 when any did. An archive whose directory is over 64 MiB or holds more than 100,000 entries is refused. The job goes on to its end when its request is abandoned. 549 MiB unpacked from a 312 MiB archive of 502 files in 2.1 s on four CPUs with two shards, other requests answered meanwhile in under 35 ms.

/~share/#

Links to an object or a folder that anyone holding one reads without credentials. POST /~share with a JSON body makes one, signed with SigV4 or Basic as above:

Details
{"bucket": "holiday", "key": "2026/", "expires_in": 604800,
 "password": "...", "max_downloads": 0, "upload": false, "note": "..."}

A key ending in / or none is a folder, read as a page, as JSON with ?format=json, and file by file under it; upload lets a visitor PUT files into it. The maker must be able to read what the link names, and to write there for an upload link. A link acts as its maker, judged at each request as the maker's own would be: a file it reads is the maker's GetObject of that key, a folder's page, list and ZIP its ListBucket (and the ZIP leaves out each file the maker may not read), an upload its PutObject. One the maker may no longer use is 403; one whose maker is no user of the runtime any more or is disabled, or whose bucket was removed and made again under its name, is 410.ApasswordisaskedforwithBasic, any user name, and kept salted and hashed; max_downloads counts each read from the start of a file and not a player's later ranges, and ?download asks a browser to save, and a folder's link read with ?zip is the folder, or the part of it the path names, as one ZIP as the drive gives it, counted as one download; its page offers it. An expired link is 410, and is removed at the next listing. GET /~share lists the caller's links, every link for an admin, and DELETE /~share/id revokes one.

"burn": true makes a link that removes what it names when it ends, as a file sent once: at its expiry, ten minutes after the last download its limit allows (so a browser resuming that download still finds it), or at its revocation. It needs expires_in or max_downloads, is no upload link, and is made only by one who may also delete there. A file's link that burns opens on a page saying what it is, which counts no download, so a chat's preview of the link costs nothing, and the file is read with ?download. The runtime's sweep looks the links over every five seconds and renames one that has ended to id.burning, which no reader opens, stamped with the time, before it removes; the shard that renamed it removes, and one stamped more than a minute ago, left by a stop, is taken up by the first shard to see it.
