"notify": "https://..." gives a link a webhook, POSTed a JSON object at each download it counts and when what a link that burns names is removed: content and text (a sentence, as Discord and Slack show it), event (downloaded or deleted), bucket, key, downloads, max_downloads and expires. One the hook does not take is posted again as a bucket's webhook events are, and kept across a restart in .share-notify under the runtime's directory. Since the runtime makes the request for the link's maker, the URL must begin with one of the prefixes SOCKETLEY_SHARE_NOTIFY_ALLOW names, comma-separated, by default the webhooks of Discord (https://discord.com/api/webhooks/, https://discordapp.com/api/webhooks/), Slack (https://hooks.slack.com/) and https://ntfy.sh/; any other is 400. A webhook's requests go up to four at once, those about one file one at a time, at most 16 waiting. In a versioned bucket the removal is a delete marker and the versions stay. A cluster does not make them. Links are files in dir/.shares/, read by every shard, each with a mark under .shares/owner/ by its maker and, when it burns, under .shares/burn/, so a user's list and the look for links that burn read only those; a start reads every link once for one with no marks, as an older build made them.

/~media/variant/bucket/key#

Media made by ffmpeg from an object, and kept. thumb-width (64, 128, 256, 320, 480, 640, 960, 1280 or 1920) is a JPEG still of a picture or of a film a few seconds in. info is what the object is, as JSON: its length, picture size, frame rate, codecs, whether it is HDR, the MIME type with codecs a browser is asked whether it plays the file itself, the codecs of its copied stream, its renditions, its text subtitles, every sound track with its codec, channels, language, title and whether it is the default, its chapters with their start, end and title, and a song's tags (title, artist, album, album artist, track, disc, date, genre), the container's or, for a file without a picture, its sound's as Ogg keeps them. trick is a film's stills for a seek bar, one JPEG of 160x90 tiles, ten a row, one every two seconds or every 1/200 of the film if that is longer; info's trick says the seconds between them, their count and their layout. They are taken from the keyframes alone, and from every frame when the keyframes give none, in a place of their own beside the thumbnails, one at a time a shard. sub-stream/subs.vtt is a text subtitle stream (SubRip, ASS, mov_text, WebVTT) as WebVTT, on the film's clock, and sub-stream/index.m3u8 its HLS playlist; subtitles that are pictures are not offered. hls/bucket/key/master.m3u8 is an HLS master playlist naming those renditions, with their size, peak bitrate and codecs, for a player to switch between as its bandwidth allows: one for every rung of 2160, 1440, 1080, 720, 480, 360 and 240 the picture fills in at least one side, each fitted into that rung's 16:9 box and never enlarged, 720 listed first, the source's own picture copied when it is H.264 or HEVC (HEVC tagged hvc1), and the text subtitles as a SUBTITLES group. BANDWIDTH is the most a segment can carry, a quarter over the rung's cap, and the levels are 4.2 up to 1080 and 5.2 above. The URLs a master names carry the object's version, so what they answer is cached for good, and a medium's answers carry an ETag a client revalidates with, answered 304, and take a Range.

Details

hls-height/index.m3u8 is one rendition: H.264 held to its rung's bitrate and AAC, in CMAF segments of four seconds. Its playlist is whole from the start, written from the film's length, so a player seeks anywhere at once, and its segments are made as they are asked for: a segment at or a little past where a job is making them is waited for, and one elsewhere starts a job there, on the film's own clock, so the segments of every job join up, and every job's init segment is the same bytes. A length past 99,999 segments (about 111 hours), or one that is no number, is taken for none: the info gives 0 and a rendition is answered 415, as for a film of no length. An init segment asked for with no job running begins one at the start at once, which a seek that follows lets go, and which is held after two seconds if no segment of it is asked for. Several jobs run over one film for viewers at different places; one that reaches segments made before ends, one fifteen segments ahead of every player that asks of it, or two ahead when nobody has asked of it for ten seconds, is held still until one comes within eight, and one nobody asks of for a minute while held, or for ten minutes running, ends; a job held still and unasked gives its place to a new one when a shard has eight, or where renditions are made on a GPU 24 shared among the shards and never fewer than eight. What they made is kept: a film watched once streams from the cache afterwards. HDR (PQ or HLG) is tone-mapped to SDR for these renditions. Where a GPU with VAAPI is there, a rendition is decoded, scaled, tone-mapped and encoded on it (an HDR film without the mastering display metadata the GPU tone-maps from is made with x264), as SOCKETLEY_MEDIA_HWACCEL describes, and the interface plays a place the copied stream has not been remuxed to yet from a rendition until the copy catches up. A variant with -an after it, as hls-a1, hls-720-a1 and hls-copy-a1, carries the film's sound track n (counted from 0 among its sound tracks, as info lists them) instead of the first, made or copied by that track's own codec and channels; its master names its streams with it, and each is made and kept as a stream of its own, so the other track's picture is made again. hls-copy streams the source's own picture without transcoding, and its sound copied when it is AAC in two channels or fewer, and made AAC otherwise; renditions always make it AAC, as a copy begun at a seek would start at the keyframe before it.

The object is read as a GET of it would be, by its user or, under /~media/variant/~share/id[/path], through a link. ffmpeg, and ffprobe beside it, read an unencrypted object's file directly, kept open by the shard for a minute, and any other over the runtime's own listener with an address signed by a key in dir/.media/key for that version of it, by a demuxer of one file and never one that opens a URL the object names (HLS, DASH, concat), and what they made lies in dir/.media/ under the variant, the object's key and its ETag, so a new version is made anew and every shard serves what one made; one thumbnail is made once however many ask for it at once. A shard runs as many thumbnails and probes at once as it has cores of the host's share, at least two, each on one thread of ffmpeg's (a 1600x1200 JPEG's thumbnail took 166 ms with ffmpeg's threads and 72 without), and eight streams; a job's end is heard from a pidfd the ring polls, so what it made is served as soon as ffmpeg exits rather than at the next look. A request waits a minute for its medium, an object ffmpeg cannot read is 415 for two minutes, and an ffmpeg a dying worker left behind is found by its pid and ended. See SOCKETLEY_FFMPEG and SOCKETLEY_MEDIA_CACHE_MB.

/~ui/#

A web interface, one page served from the binary. A browser asked for the runtime's root instead, with no query, no signature and Accept: text/html among what it takes, is sent here, so the host's name alone reaches the interface; an S3 client, which asks for none of that, still reads GET / as ListBuckets. The interface signs in with an access key and its secret, which it sends once for the session cookie below and keeps nowhere, and browses libraries (buckets) as a media library: films, pictures, music and documents in their own rows, with thumbnails, lengths and what the user left half watched on any device. Films named S01E02 or 1x02 are grouped by season in their order and play on into the next episode; a folder's or a library's card shows a picture called folder, cover or poster in it, else its first picture or film; more than twelve pictures are grouped by the month of their date (the camera's, see /~ui/taken, else the object's); and pictures play as a slideshow. A ZIP's menu unpacks it beside itself on the server (?unzip above). It uploads several files at once, and a file of 48 MiB or more in parts of at least 16 MiB, four requests side by side shared among up to three files, each going to the file with the fewest on the way, through the drive's multipart above; over HTTP/1.1, while a film or a song plays in any of the browser's tabs (they tell each other on a BroadcastChannel), uploads keep one request, since a browser opens six connections at most to such a server, and take four again once it is closed, while over HTTP/2 (see above) they keep all four beside the player, with each file's percentage, rate, time left and start; folders too, by dropping them or choosing one. A file in parts whose line is lost is paused and goes on when the line is back, and one a closed or reloaded page left is shown again, with how far it came, and goes on from the parts the server lists once its file is chosen anew (the same name and size, and the same modification time or a confirmation). Each part, and a file sent whole, carries its CRC-32 in x-amz-checksum-crc32, which the server checks against what arrived; one refused as BadDigest is read and sent again. It selects several items to download or delete, renames, shares, restores from the trash, shows pictures one after another, and opens text in an editor that highlights code, finds and replaces, previews Markdown and saves with Ctrl+S, and makes new text files. Its search box filters the folder open and searches every library; items dragged onto a folder, a library or a breadcrumb are moved there. The folder open is asked again every five seconds while the page is seen (every thirty past 2000 entries), so what another device changes shows within seconds. A download is the object byte for byte, the drive's GET with ?download, which a browser resuming an interrupted one sends again with the cookie. The owner of a library shares it from the page with other users, to view or to edit, through /~ui/access below.

Details

Send a file sends files as wormhole does: they are uploaded into the user's library for temporary files, tmp-user (the user's id in lowercase, made when it is first needed and shown as Temporary files), each sending in a folder of its own, behind a link that burns (see /~share/ above), deleted after a chosen time or number of downloads (for several files, that number of each), with an optional password and a webhook told of each download. Once a picture or a film is uploaded, the page asks for its thumbnails and facts, and for a film this browser would not play itself the start of its stream, so the server makes them before anyone waits for them. Five colour themes are chosen from the sidebar and kept in the browser.

It signs in with POST /~ui/session and Basic credentials — a user's name and the password of its login profile (see IAM above), or an access key and its secret — which sets the cookie skl_ui (HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict, Secure over TLS): the access key, or ~user for a password, the time it was made, an expiry and an HMAC-SHA256 of them under the key's own secret, so every shard and node checks it alike and a key whose secret changes or that is removed ends its sessions. It lasts twelve hours and the browser's session, or thirty days with ?remember. GET /~ui/session says who is signed in and DELETE /~ui/session signs out. POST /~ui/session?everywhere ends every session of the user made before it, in each browser, by keeping its time in dir/.ui/sessions/; the other shards follow within a second, and a sign-in with Basic credentials is not a session and goes on. /~dav/, /~media/ and the management of /~share/ take the cookie as they take Basic credentials, so the page's script never holds the secret; a change made under the cookie alone (anything but GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and PROPFIND) must carry the header X-Socketley-UI, which no other site's page can add, and is 403 otherwise. A session never makes a new one. A file's GET /~dav/bucket/key?download is saved under its name.

The page's Account sets and changes the user's password and makes, deactivates and deletes its access keys, the secret shown once. An admin's Users lists every user with how it signs in, makes one with a password (to be changed at the first sign-in, if chosen), sets a password, the name shown, the email, the quota, admin-ness and whether it makes libraries of its own, disables, deletes, and invites: an invitation is a link, /~ui/#invite=token, that lets one person choose a user name and password of their own, once, for one to thirty days, as an admin and with a quota if it says so; only the SHA-256 of its token is kept, in dir/.iam.json beside the users. Sharing a library offers the users by name. POST /~ui/iam with {"Action": action, its fields} is an IAM action as the signed-in user, judged and answered as IAM's own; GET /~ui/users lists the users, each one's id and name to any user and all of it, with the open invitations, to an admin; GET /~ui/invite?token= says whether an invitation holds, and POST /~ui/invite with {"token", user , password , name , email } takes it, without a session, a token that is none counted as a failed sign-in.

GET /~ui/progress lists the films the signed-in user has part watched, the most recent first, with the position, the length, the size and the type; only those the user may still read, in the version watched, so one replaced or removed since, or whose access was taken away, is left out. POST /~ui/progress with {"bucket", key , t , d } keeps where one was left (t below 0 forgets it). Each user's positions are a file of their own, dir/.ui/progress/, changed entry by entry under a lock, so two devices watching different films keep both; the latest 200 are kept. Nodes of a cluster keep their own.

GET /~ui/search?q=text[&bucket=name] lists the files and folders whose own name holds the text, ASCII letters in any case, in every library the user lists (or the one named), folders first, at most 200, with more true when there were more or a library was too large to list whole; a file is listed only where the user may read it. Each library is listed whole for it.

GET /~ui/taken?bucket=name&prefix=folder/ says when and where the photos directly in a folder were taken, as their EXIF says: for each JPEG, TIFF or HEIF (HEIC) the user may read, its key, its taken time as the camera's clock wrote it ("2021-07-14T18:03:22", with "+02:00" where the camera wrote its offset) and its lat and lon. Its first 64 KiB are read, and a HEIF's Exif item where it lies further in; what was read is kept by the object's ETag in the shard's memory. An object stored encrypted, compressed or in a tier is left out, and so is all past the folder's first thousand keys (more). The page groups a folder's pictures by the month they were taken, shows the time in the viewer and links to the place on openstreetmap.org, which the page never loads itself; it shows a HEIF as its thumbnail, which ffmpeg makes from 7.1 on.

GET /~ui/usage lists every library the user lists with its owner, whether it is shared with the user, its bytes and objects, summed from its listing (which holds every shard's keys) and kept a minute, with partial when it was too large to list whole, and its quota; besides, the user's own quota over the libraries it owns, and whether the user is an admin. POST /~ui/usage with {"bucket", max_bytes , max_objects } sets a library's quota as ?quota does, 0 for none, and like it is an admin's alone. The page's Storage shows them as bars.

GET /~ui/access?bucket=name says who else a library is shared with, and POST /~ui/access with {"bucket", user , access } shares it with a user of the credentials or the IAM API, by id: read (list and read), write (also write, delete, and restore from the trash) or none to take it back. Each is a statement of the bucket's policy, named by its Sid socketley-ui-access:user, and only those are read or changed: the rest of the policy is kept, and a Deny in it still holds. Both are for whoever may read or write the bucket's policy, its owner and an admin. The drive's root lists, besides the buckets a user owns, every bucket whose policy lets the user list it.

A film's link is a page that plays it, which a chat embeds as a player once the film's web copy, /~media/web/bucket/key, is made: H.264 in an MP4 of at most 46 MiB and 1440 lines. It is made when a link asks for it, or as the film is put into a library tagged socketley:web-copies=on. GET /~ui/library?bucket=name says whether a library is, and POST /~ui/library with {"bucket", "web_copies"} tags it or takes the tag away, for whoever may change the bucket's tags.

It plays films and music, with their subtitles: the file itself where the browser plays it, which costs the server nothing, and otherwise the master playlist's streams through Media Source Extensions, the copied one where the browser takes its codec and the line carries it, renditions by measured bandwidth otherwise, or through the browser's own HLS where it has no Media Source at all. Its quality menu, in the player, offers Original (the file, or the copied stream where the browser does not play the file), Auto and each rendition; a change is made on the same media source, keeping the next six seconds already buffered while the new stream's first segment is made.

entries.summary: A WebDAV drive (classes 1 and 2) for Windows, macOS, Linux file managers, rclone and phones. It signs in with HTTP Basic, an access key as the user name and its secret as the password; a runtime without credentials takes none. Its root is every bucket the user owns or a bucket policy lets it list, every bucket for an admin, and a bucket's keys are files whose slashes are folders. A file's GET, PUT

sections.title: Git repositories
sections.html:
The page's Sync keeps repositories in a library: each is pulled when it is added, whenever its user asks, and by itself every day, week or month from 3:00 local time, or never (the default), as its Pull every says; when any ref moved since the last run, the branch's files are written under name/ of the library — what changed, or the whole tree the first time, with nothing else left beside it — and a git bundle of the branch and the tags, or of every branch with *, under _backups/name/date_time_commit.bundle. git clone file .bundle makes the repository from one, its branch checked out. A run with nothing new writes nothing. Every bundle of the last day is kept, and before it the newest of each of the last 14 days, 8 weeks and 12 months; the rest are deleted. Symbolic links and submodules are no files and are left out.

Which runtimes do the runs is --sync. With never — the default — the storage makes none, and the page says that a repository added would not run. With active the runtime's first shard makes one sync runtime for the whole storage, storage-sync, which pulls every user's repositories, each with that user's own credentials. With per-user it makes every one of its users a sync runtime of their own, storage-sync-user. Either is owned by the storage, goes when it stops and comes back when it starts, and is one socketley ls and the dashboard list with its runs, failures, running and last_error. It runs socketley git-sync for that user's repositories alone, one at a time, with temporary credentials of the user the storage hands it in dir/.ui/sync/, 0600, made again with three of their twelve hours left, through the runtime's own S3 API on its port: what the user may not write it cannot write, quotas and versioning apply, and a library that is not there is made as the user. A failed run of one pulled by itself is tried again an hour later; a run asked for is dir/.ui/git/id/asked, which the user's sync runtime starts within a second. Each repository's bare clone, the state of its last run and its log are under dir/.ui/git/id/, and the list is dir/.ui/git.json. Git must be installed; a runtime on a unix socket has none of this.

A repository is fetched over https://, http:// or git://, never with credentials in its URL. A private one is read with the GitHub token the user keeps in the page, sent as git's http.extraHeader through its environment, so it is on no command line; it is sealed with AES-256-GCM under a key only the user's own secret derives, in dir/.ui/git-tokens/, and never shown again.

GET /~ui/git lists the repositories the user keeps (an admin's: all), each with the state its last run ended in, and whether the user has a token. POST /~ui/git takes {"action":"add", url , branch , bucket , name , private , every } (branch main, library git-user, the user's own, and every never by default, the name the URL's last part), which also starts the first run, {"action":"every","id","every"} (never, day, week or month), {"action":"sync","id"}, {"action":"remove","id"} (the files and bundles stay) and {"action":"token","token"} (empty removes it). A user adds into a library it may write.

A repository in the library git that every user once shared goes to its owner's own at the next start, and is run there until its tree is whole and git-sync --move-from git has taken its backups over and its files away; the old library goes once it is empty. dir/.ui/git/id/moved-from holds the move across restarts.

sections.title: Durability
sections.html:
--fsync decides when a write a client was answered for is on the disk, as a cache's journal and Redis's appendfsync do. Every mode keeps what a crash of the process would take, because the page cache outlives the process, and every mode syncs the whole filesystem at a stop before it writes the clean marker.

always#

The default. A put is answered once its file, its name and its directory are synced, a delete once its directory is; versions, tags, uploads and parts alike, and the entries of event notifications and replication beside them. An answered write survives a crash of the machine. Small puts cost about 2 syncs each, which is most of their time: about 1,500 4 KiB puts a second on one shard of the measuring box, about 700 into a versioned bucket.

interval#

Those syncs are skipped, and a thread syncs the filesystem (syncfs) every --fsync-interval (default 1 second). A crash of the machine loses at most the writes of the last interval; about 18,000 puts a second on the same box, about 9,600 versioned.

never#

The syncs are skipped and only the kernel's own writeback (typically within 30 seconds) and a stop put the writes on the disk; for data that can be made again, such as caches and build artefacts.

What a crash of the machine leaves behind under interval and never depends on the filesystem: ext4 in its default data=ordered mode leaves either an object as it was or as it was written, never part of one, and a start that finds a file whose header does not check out leaves it unserved; on other filesystems a file written in the last interval may hold zeros where its data was not yet written. Bucket creation and removal and the configuration documents are synced in every mode. Backups and anything else that deletes its own copy once a put is answered want always.

What always costs is the disk's: a drive with power-loss protection (most enterprise NVMe and SATA SSDs) answers a sync from its protected cache in microseconds, and there it costs little, while a consumer or virtual disk answers it only once the data is on the medium. XFS writes less per sync than ext4, and ext4's fast_commit feature (tune2fs -O fast_commit) shortens a sync after a small change. Concurrent puts already share the filesystem's journal commits, so always gains throughput with concurrency. A sync of the whole filesystem shared by every put waiting, files written before they are needed and overwritten, and O_DSYNC writes were each measured against it and none did better under a sustained load of small puts. stats counts the syncs that ran in fsyncs, those a mode skipped in fsyncs_skipped, and the filesystem syncs of interval in syncfs_rounds and syncfs_failed; a stop after a failed round is not a clean one.

entries.summary: The default. A put is answered once its file, its name and its directory are synced, a delete once its directory is; versions, tags, uploads and parts alike, and the entries of event notifications and replication beside them. An answered write survives a crash of the machine. Small puts cost about 2 syncs each, which is most of their time: about 1,500 4 KiB puts a second on one shard of the measur

Those syncs are skipped, and a thread syncs the filesystem (syncfs) every --fsync-interval (default 1 second). A crash of the machine loses at most the writes of the last interval; about 18,000 puts a second on the same box, about 9,600 versioned.
The syncs are skipped and only the kernel's own writeback (typically within 30 seconds) and a stop put the writes on the disk; for data that can be made again, such as caches and build artefacts.

sections.title: Sharding
sections.html:
--shards N runs N worker processes on one port (SO_REUSEPORT) or, with --listen, one node each (name#i.sock, as for a cache), all on the same --dir. Clients see one runtime. Every shard serves a GET or HEAD itself by opening the object's file, whose header says what it is, so object bytes never move between shards.

One shard is the default, and on a machine of a few cores it is the right one. One shard answered 95,000 signed GETs of 4 KiB a second on one core, about 3 Gbit/s of payload, so a runtime behind a 1 or 10 Gbit link runs out of network before it runs out of its core. Shards pay only where small reads saturate that core, and they cost wherever a request crosses shards. Measured on one box with the runtime confined by taskset and a wrk client replaying signed GETs of 64 keys on cores of its own:

CPUsshardsGET 4 KiB
2196,000 req/s
22185,000 req/s
24177,000 req/s
42187,000 req/s
44253,000 req/s
48218,000 req/s
84258,000 req/s
88359,000 req/s

The last row is the client's six threads at their limit. More shards than CPUs is slower, never faster. The price on the same box: a ListObjectsV2 page of 1000 keys took 2.1x the CPU at two shards and 2.4 to 2.5x at four, since every shard walks up to a page and one merges them; a 4 KiB PUT took 1.2 to 1.3x the CPU at two shards and 1.4 to 1.6x at four, since at four shards three keys in four are committed by another shard than the one the body landed on. Large objects move at the same rate at any count: a 64 MiB GET was bound by the client and a 64 MiB PUT by the disk.

A key's owner is the shard that commits its changes: the CRC16/XMODEM of the string bucket/key masked to 16384 slots, exactly the function of a cache's key slots, and the shard is slot * N / 16384, so a client can compute it and send a request to the owner's node and cross nothing. A put streams into a temporary file from whichever shard took the connection; that shard then sends the owner the file's name and the object's metadata over the shard link, and the owner renames it into place, syncs the directory and answers, appending to its own journal (index.i, written by shard i alone) behind the answer. A delete, the target of a copy and a create-only put (If-None-Match: *) go the same way, which is what keeps the order of changes to a key one order and lets two racing creators come out one refused. A listing is asked of every shard and the pages are merged, so it is the listing one shard would give; a shard that cannot be reached fails the listing with a 500 rather than shortening it.

Buckets are made and dropped by shard 0 and told to the others before it answers; a bucket is dropped only when every shard agrees it holds nothing and is idle. A bucket's CORS, lifecycle and versioning configurations and its policy are changed by shard 0, one change of a bucket at a time, whichever shard took the request, and answered only once no shard can go on with the old document; a change a running shard cannot be told of is refused with 503 and changes nothing (see Bucket policy). Each shard sweeps the keys it owns. Temporary files are named for the shard that wrote them, so a shard restarted by the supervisor removes only its own. A shard killed between a rename and its journal record leaves the object in the directory, and its restart adopts it from the header: after it every shard serves the object or none does, and a put that was in flight through the killed shard is answered with an error.

A start with a different --shards on a directory written by another split is not refused, unlike a cache with a missing dump, because the object files are the record: each shard sees that its journal was written for another shard count, rebuilds its keys from the object headers filtered by owner, and shard 0 removes the journals of shards that no longer exist. That start reads every header once per shard, so it takes as long as the object count makes it. --max-bytes is an equal share per shard, judged by the shard that took the put from its own bytes and again by the owner, so it is approximate when keys are unevenly sized. stats gives a section per shard with shard_commits_sent, shard_commits_served, shard_deletes_sent, shard_deletes_served, shard_list_fanouts, shard_list_pages_served, shard_bucket_ops, shard_mpu_sent, shard_mpu_served (multipart steps), shard_hot_drops_sent and shard_hot_drops_served (a sibling told to drop its copy of a key, once per sibling), shard_hot_holds_sent and shard_hot_holds_served (a sibling asking the owner to keep a copy) and shard_peer_failures; at one shard nothing is sent and they read zero.

A multipart upload lives on the shard that owns its key, so every step that names it (create, part, complete, abort, ListParts) is that shard's, and ListMultipartUploads asks every shard. A part's body is written where the connection landed and only its name crosses to the shard that keeps the upload; CompleteMultipartUpload has that shard check the list and seal the upload, the shard the request landed on assemble the object from the parts on the shared disk and commit it through the owner of the key, and the owner remove the upload, so nothing long is asked of a sibling over the link. An upload whose assembler never reports is opened again after six hours, uploads are found again by the shard that owns their key after a restart with another --shards, and a bucket with an open upload on any shard is not dropped. TLS, credentials, the credentials file, scripts and the metrics are each shard's own or their sum: every shard terminates TLS and re-reads the credentials file, a script's hooks run on the shard that took the request, a script's socketley.storage call is answered by whichever shard the daemon relays it to and reaches the rest as any request does, and the socketley_storage_ series add the shards together (a bucket every shard holds is counted once).

stats reports buckets, objects, bytes, requests, gets, heads, puts, deletes, copies, lists, client_errors, server_errors, zero_copy_gets, copied_gets, hot_gets (the copied GETs answered from the hot copy), hot_bytes (what the hot copies hold), zero_copy_bytes, journal_records, journal_compactions, fsyncs (of files and directories alike, that ran), fsyncs_skipped (those --fsync interval or never skipped), syncfs_rounds and syncfs_failed (the filesystem syncs of --fsync interval), start_files_read (object and version files whose headers the last start read: 0 when every journal was trusted), pool_ready (empty files the buckets' pools hold durable for small puts, 0 after a start until the first put), multipart_uploads, multipart_parts, multipart_bytes, multipart_created, multipart_completed, multipart_aborted, lifecycle_expired, lifecycle_aborted, timeouts, tls (1 when the listener is TLS), tls_handshakes, tls_failures, body_recvs (receives that brought bytes of an upload's body) and hash_handoffs (pieces of digest work handed to the hashing threads), sse (1 when the runtime has a master key), sse_puts and sse_gets (bodies written encrypted, and GETs answered by opening an object's chunks), media_made, media_failed and media_served (thumbnails and streams ffmpeg made and failed to make, and the answers served from them), media_direct (ffmpeg jobs that read the object's file rather than through the listener), media_hw (rendition jobs encoded on the GPU), and one line error_Code for every S3 error code the runtime has answered, such as error_NoSuchKey. Bytes in and out and total_messages (requests) are the common fields. A connection with a request head unfinished after ten seconds, or a body that has not moved for a minute, is closed and its temporary file removed.

sections.title: Metrics
sections.html: With the metrics endpoint on, each running storage runtime adds socketley_storage_buckets, socketley_storage_objects, socketley_storage_bytes_stored, socketley_storage_bytes_received_total, socketley_storage_bytes_sent_total, socketley_storage_zero_copy_bytes_total, socketley_storage_tls_handshakes_total and socketley_storage_tls_failures_total, all labelled name, and socketley_storage_requests_total (label op = get, head, put, delete, list, copy) and socketley_storage_errors_total (label code = the S3 error code). The subsystems have families of their own when a runtime runs them: event notifications (socketley_storage_notify_*), replication (socketley_storage_replication_*), a cluster (socketley_storage_cluster_*), the scrub (socketley_storage_scrub_*), compression (socketley_storage_compressed_*), tiers (socketley_storage_tier_*), lifecycle, multipart, media and fsyncs. Every other figure of stats is socketley_storage_stat with its name as the label stat, so nothing a runtime counts is missing from a scrape. A mail runtime's figures are socketley_mail_received_total, _delivered_total, _deferred_total, _bounced_total, _stored_total, _quarantined_total, _auth_failed_total and the gauges socketley_mail_queued and _queued_bytes, the rest socketley_mail_stat by name. A tunnel's are socketley_tunnel_links, _agents, _shares and _flows (UDP visitors) as gauges, and socketley_tunnel_streams_total, _refused_total, _visitors_refused_total (requests a protected service's auth refused), _bytes_in_total, _bytes_out_total, _datagrams_total and _datagrams_dropped_total.

sections.title: Lua
sections.html:
A script attached with --lua may define three hooks on a storage runtime.

on_request(req) -> nil | true | false | string | table#

Called for every request after it is authenticated and judged by its bucket's policy, and before anything is done, so it sees only requests both let through and can refuse any of them but let in none they refused; it runs on a coroutine, so it may wait for another runtime (see socketley.storage below); the connection is not read from until it answers, so a refused upload is answered before its body is read and its connection closed. req has method, operation (the name S3 gives it: GetObject, PutObject, DeleteObjects, ListObjectsV2, CreateMultipartUpload, UploadPart, UploadPartCopy, CompleteMultipartUpload, AbortMultipartUpload, ListParts, ListMultipartUploads, PutBucketLifecycleConfiguration, ...), bucket, key, path and query (as sent), host, request_id, principal (the access key, empty for a request with no credentials), tls (boolean), client (ip:port, or unix), content_length (absent for a chunked body) and headers (lowercase names). Returning nothing or true lets the request go on; false refuses it as AccessDenied (403); a string refuses it as that S3 error, with the status S3 gives that code (403 for a code the runtime does not know); a table {deny="Code", message="...", status=403} names all three. A raise, and a value of any other type, are refusals answered 500 InternalError and logged, because a hook whose failure lets requests through is not a hook.

on_put(bucket, key, meta)#

Called after an object is committed, for a put, for the destination of a copy, for a completed multipart upload (once, when it is completed, and never for its parts) and for an object a script put with socketley.storage.put, and never for one that was refused. meta has size, etag, content_type, mtime_ms and metadata (the user metadata, without its prefix). It is called after the client's answer is on its way.

on_delete(bucket, key)#

Called after an object that was there is removed, from DeleteObject, DeleteObjects and socketley.storage.delete, and not for a key that was not.

A script that writes in on_put is called again for what it wrote.

sections.title: socketley.storage
sections.html:
Any runtime's script may use a storage runtime by name, in this daemon or in another process, without stopping the daemon while it waits:

socketley.storage.put(runtime, bucket, key, data [, {content_type=, metadata={}}] [, callback])
socketley.storage.get(runtime, bucket, key [, callback])
socketley.storage.head(runtime, bucket, key [, callback])
socketley.storage.delete(runtime, bucket, key [, callback])
socketley.storage.list(runtime, bucket [, prefix] [, {delimiter=, max_keys=, start_after=}] [, callback])

In a callback that can stop — on_message, on_client_message, and the storage hooks above — a call without a callback waits and returns the answer, and the connection a server handler is answering is kept open for it, as it is for a linked cache. Anywhere else (an on_tick, a cache's on_write, a proxy's filter) the last argument is a function, the call returns true at once, and the function is called with the answer on a later turn. A call that must wait, made where it cannot and with no function, returns nil and a message saying so.

The answers are: put and head a table with size, etag, content_type, mtime_ms and metadata; get the data and that table; delete true (also for a key that was not there, as S3 answers); list a table with objects (each with key, size, etag, content_type, mtime_ms), prefixes, truncated and, when truncated, next — pass it as start_after for the following page. A failure is nil and the S3 error code and message (NoSuchKey, NoSuchBucket, InvalidBucketName, EntityTooLarge), or nil and a reason when the request did not reach the runtime (no such runtime, the request channel is full). Metadata names are lowercased and stored as x-amz-meta-*. Buckets are made with the S3 API. An object moves whole in memory and the request crosses a process boundary in a frame that waits in a 4 MiB queue, so a script may put or get at most 1 MiB per call, and at most 1024 calls may be waiting on one runtime; larger objects are for the S3 port.

sections.title: DNS FLAGS
sections.html:
A dns runtime is an authoritative name server: it answers, over UDP and TCP on one port, for the zones in the files it is given, and for nothing else.

socketley create dns ns --zone example.com --publish 203.0.113.7 -s
dig @127.0.0.1 example.com SOA

A zone given by its name is written with this machine's public address for its name servers: --publish gives it, and may be left out only where an interface has one, which behind NAT none has. create also makes it an entrance, a proxy of its own (see --proxy), which asks Let's Encrypt for a certificate for each zone and its wildcard as soon as it starts — for every name but those reserved for examples and tests, such as example.com, .test and .internal, which no public CA issues for. A lab or a test whose names are real gives --proxy none. And it answers one client network at most 100 times a second (--rrl), so a load test from a single host sees most answers dropped unless it gives --rrl 0.

It asks no other server and caches nothing: a name in none of its zones is answered REFUSED, never looked up, so it cannot be used as an open resolver and no answer it gives came from anybody else. It runs in a worker process of its own like every other runtime, may run as --shards processes that share the port, and binds IPv4 and, when no --bind address is given and the host has it, IPv6 as well. Port 53 is the default; below 1024 a port needs root or CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE, which the packaged service grants. -p, --bind, --cpus, --max-connections (TCP connections, 256 when not given) and the common flags apply as documented under COMMON FLAGS; --listen and --tls are refused.

--zone name|file#

The zone to serve, by its name or as a zone file, given once for each zone or as several separated by commas. Required. A name, such as example.com, needs no file: the runtime writes one under state-dir/zones/name.zone the first time, with its SOA, ns1 and ns2 as its name servers and the addresses of --publish (or this machine's public ones) as theirs and as the zone's own name's, the entrance's, and serves it from then on; the file is the user's to edit, and is never written again while it exists. Those two names and addresses are what the registrar is told as the domain's name servers and their glue. A path is made absolute against the caller's directory; a file called zone.zone that does not exist is written there the same way. A zone file is in the master file format of RFC 1035. The zone's apex is the owner of its one SOA record; every record has to lie at or below it, the apex has to name its servers with NS records, a CNAME has to be the only record of its name, and below a delegation only the addresses of its servers may stand. A file that is not such a zone is refused at create and start with the line that is wrong. $ORIGIN and $TTL are read; $INCLUDE is refused, since it would let a zone file read any file the worker may. Types A, AAAA, NS, CNAME, SOA, PTR, MX, TXT, SRV, CAA and HINFO are written in their usual form, and any other type in RFC 3597's TYPEn \# length hex. A TXT string longer than 255 bytes is split into several, as a DKIM key needs.

Details

The file is looked at once a second. Edited, it is read again; the new zone is served once it has been read whole and checked, and a file that no longer parses leaves the zone before it in place, with the reason in the log. A changed zone whose serial did not change is served, and the log says that its secondaries will not notice it until the serial is raised.

--transfer list#

The addresses and blocks, comma-separated, that may copy a zone whole by AXFR over TCP (RFC 5936) — a secondary's, such as 192.0.2.53 or 2001:db8::/48. Everyone else is REFUSED, so the names a zone holds are not handed to whoever asks. An IXFR from them over UDP is answered with the SOA alone, which tells a secondary the serial and to come over TCP; over TCP it is answered as an AXFR.

--notify list#

The secondaries told by a NOTIFY (RFC 1996), as host[:port], comma-separated, when the runtime starts and whenever a zone's serial changes. A NOTIFY is sent again after 1, 3, 7, 15 and 31 seconds until the secondary answers it. Only the first shard sends them.

--publish list#

This machine's public addresses, IPv4 and IPv6, comma-separated: every name a runtime of the daemon is reached by (--domain, --acme, a storage runtime's --domain and --website-domain) that falls within a zone is answered with them. Without it, they are answered with this machine's public addresses when the runtime has an entrance (below), and not at all with --proxy none.

--proxy name|none#

The entrance the names of runtimes are reached through: a proxy without --backend, which routes each HTTP request by the name it asks for to the runtime that has it (see PROXY FLAGS). create makes it as this runtime's child, named dns-proxy when the flag is not given, listening on --proxy-port with --tls, --backend-timeout 5m (a site may take a while to begin answering, as behind any web server) and a certificate it asks the CA for itself: each zone with its wildcard, proven over DNS-01 by this runtime's answers. Before that, acme issue asks the resolver of /etc/resolv.conf for a TXT record that exists only in this runtime's answers, after SOCKETLEY_ACME_DNS_WAIT seconds, and then asks every name server the zone is delegated to for it directly, as a CA may ask any of them. A zone the world's DNS does not delegate here yet, or one a secondary of which has not taken the record up in that time, has each of its names proven by itself instead, over TLS-ALPN-01 on 443, without the wildcard, which is asked for again every six hours until the zone is delegated. On 443 it comes with dns-proxy-http on port 80, which sends every request to HTTPS (--redirect-https). Behind it, every response over TLS carries Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000 unless the runtime answering set its own. Over TLS it speaks HTTP/2 to a client that offers it by ALPN and HTTP/1.1 to one that does not: each stream is routed by the name it asks for, as a request over HTTP/1.1 is, and one asking for a name other than the one its connection's handshake gave is answered 421. A client may have eight streams open at once; SOCKETLEY_PROXY_HTTP2=0 turns HTTP/2 off. Over UDP on the same port it speaks HTTP/3 (RFC 9114), which every answer over TCP names in Alt-Svc: h3; a stream of it is routed by its own :authority exactly as HTTP/2's is, and a browser that cannot reach the UDP port goes on over TCP. SOCKETLEY_PROXY_HTTP3=0 opens no UDP socket. It stops, starts and is removed with this runtime; removed while another dns runtime names it too, it becomes that one's instead. A proxy of that name that exists already is taken as it is, provided it is an entrance. none makes none. With an entrance and no --publish, the names are answered with this machine's public addresses, read from its interfaces and looked at again every minute.

Details
socketley create dns ns --zone example.com -s     # and ns-proxy on 443
socketley create server chat --domain --http /srv/chat -s
curl https://chat.example.com/
--proxy-port port#

The port the entrance create makes listens on; 443 when not given.

--rrl n#

Response rate limiting: at most n answers a second to one client network (an IPv4 /24, an IPv6 /56); past it, every second answer is replaced by a truncated one (TC, no records, as large as the query) and the others are dropped. A resolver behind that network retries over TCP, which is not limited, and is served; a victim whose address a flood forges receives nothing larger than what was sent. 100 by default, 0 for no limit. The limit is the runtime's: with --shards, each shard allows its share of n, since the kernel spreads one network's queries over the shards by their source port.

--dnssec#

Sign every zone as it is loaded (RFC 4033 to 4035): a key of ECDSA P-256 with SHA-256 (algorithm 13) a zone, made at the first start and kept in state-dir/dns/name.dnssec/ for every shard, its DNSKEY at the apex, an NSEC chain through the names and an RRSIG over every set the zone holds, for three weeks and made again a week before they end. A query with the DO bit is answered with the signatures, and a name or type that is not there with the NSEC records that prove it; a zone transfer carries them. The parent zone is given the DS record socketley dnssec prints.

sections.title: Names runtimes are reached by
sections.html:
The daemon writes the names its runtimes are reached by into state-dir/.dns/names whenever they change, and acme issue writes a DNS-01 answer there as acme-token while a CA checks it. A dns runtime looks at that directory once a second, as it looks at its zone files, and adds to each zone the names within it, with the addresses of --publish, TTL 300, and the answers, as TXT records of _acme-challenge.name, TTL 10. What the zone file says of a name wins: a name with addresses of its own, or an alias, keeps them, and nothing is added beneath a delegation.

socketley create dns ns --zone /etc/zones/example.com.zone \
    --publish 203.0.113.7,2001:db8::7 -s
socketley create storage files -p 9301 --domain files.example.com ...
dig files.example.com            # 203.0.113.7
dig photos.files.example.com     # 203.0.113.7

So that a secondary notices, the serial a zone is served with is its file's plus the seconds from 2023-11-14 to when that directory last changed: it grows with every change of the file's serial and of the published records, and is the same in every shard and after every restart.

sections.title: What it answers
sections.html:
A name found is answered with its records, authoritatively. A CNAME is followed, up to eight steps, while its target is in the same zone. A wildcard (*.label) stands for every name beneath its parent that does not exist. A name below a delegation is referred: the NS records of the cut, and the addresses of those servers where the zone holds them, without the authoritative flag. An absent name is NXDOMAIN, and a name without the type asked for NODATA, both with the zone's SOA, whose TTL there is the lesser of its own and its MINIMUM (RFC 2308). The addresses of the hosts an NS, MX or SRV answer names follow in the additional section when the zone has them and they fit.

ANY is answered with one HINFO record, as RFC 8482 allows, rather than with everything, so that it amplifies nothing. Classes other than IN, such as CHAOS's version.bind, are REFUSED. A query with EDNS (RFC 6891) is answered with it; an answer over UDP is kept within the size the query offers and never past 1232 bytes, the size that needs no fragments, and one without EDNS within 512. What does not fit is sent as the question alone with TC set, and the asker comes back over TCP, where it is answered whole. A response is never answered, a malformed query is FORMERR, and opcodes other than QUERY are NOTIMP.

sections.title: TCP
sections.html: A connection may carry several queries one after another and is answered in order (RFC 7766). One left quiet for 10 seconds, with nothing left to write, is closed; only a whole query or a write counts, so a query begun and not finished is quiet. A shard holds at most --max-connections of them, 256 when it is not given; one more closes the quietest with nothing left to write to make room for itself. Past 64 KiB of answers its peer has not read, a connection's further queries wait unread until it has; one whose answers have not moved for 30 seconds is closed.

sections.title: Stats
sections.html: stats adds, for each shard: zones, records, udp_queries, tcp_queries, the answers by rcode (noerror, nxdomain, refused, formerr, notimp, other_rcode), truncated, referrals, dropped (packets that were no query), rrl_dropped and rrl_slipped, send_failed (answers the socket would not take), tcp_conns, tcp_refused, tcp_evicted (connections closed to make room for a new one), transfers, transfers_refused, notify_sent, notify_acked, notify_given_up, zone_reloads and zone_reload_failures.

sections.title: SYNC FLAGS
sections.html:
A sync runtime is one job that carries files between a directory and a storage. One runtime is one job, so what goes wrong with it has its own line in socketley ls, its own figures, its own lines in the log and its own alert.

socketley create sync photos --dir /srv/photos --storage ui/photos \
    --credentials /etc/socketley/sync.creds --mode out -s

It listens on nothing and takes no -p, and --shards is refused: the shards would share no socket and would write one index from several processes.

--dir path#

The directory whose files are carried, absolute, and there when the runtime starts. Required.

--storage target[,target...]#

Where they go, each one of three forms with the bucket last:

Details
ui/photos#

a storage runtime of this daemon, reached on its port at 127.0.0.1. A name with no scheme and no port is always a runtime's, dots and all;

10.0.0.5:9000/photos#

a host and a port, over plain HTTP;

https://files.example/photos#

a URL, http or https, with nothing between the host and the bucket.

A storage runtime that serves TLS itself is named by its URL, since its port does not speak plain HTTP; naming it is refused, with the URL to use. A bucket name follows the S3 rules: 3 to 63 of a-z, 0-9, . and -. More than one target is taken only with --mode out, since carrying two of them into one directory cannot say which a file came from when they differ. Required.

--mode out|in|inout#

Who carries, in the same three words a server and a client take: out sends the directory to the storage, in brings the storage to the directory, and inout does both. The default is out.

--credentials file#

The file the job signs with: access_key and secret_key as key = value lines, with session_token and region when they are wanted, and # beginning a comment. Required, since a sync signs every request it makes. A file other users may read is refused, at create and at every read: chmod 600 it.

--prefix key#

The key everything is written under, below the bucket; without the flag it is the bucket's root.

--every duration#

How often the whole directory is walked, and with in or inout the storage listed, as 30s, 10m, 1h or 1d; never walks it once at a start. One hour by default; a job that brings the storage here lists it once a minute when --every is never. Between walks, inotify says which files changed, and a file is carried once it is written and closed, moved in or touched, and removed once it is deleted; a directory that comes or goes, or more events than the kernel keeps, asks for a walk. When inotify is not there or its watches run out (fs.inotify.max_user_watches), it is said once in the log and the walk is what finds a change.

--repositories file#

Makes the job a user's own: it pulls the git repositories that user keeps in a storage runtime (see Git repositories under STORAGE FLAGS) rather than carrying a directory, and takes no --dir, --storage or --credentials. The storage runtime makes such a job for each of its users and writes the file; it is not one to make by hand.

--exclude pattern[,pattern...]#

Shell patterns, separated by commas, with spaces around them ignored: '*.tmp, *.md, node_modules'. A pattern with no slash names a file or directory at any depth, as a .gitignore line does; one with a slash is matched against the whole path below --dir, and its * crosses slashes. Anything matched is not carried, and a matched directory is not walked.

What it remembers. A sync keeps an index of what it last carried, in state-dir/sync/name.index, 0600. Without it a deletion here cannot be told from a file never carried: the first is taken off the far side and the second is sent. Every record carries a checksum, and the first that fails it ends the file, so a crash costs at most carrying again what the last moments carried — never a file believed carried that was not. The index belongs to one directory and one prefix: when either changes it is begun again, which carries everything once more and takes nothing away. socketley remove deletes it, and a rename carries it along.

How it carries. Eight requests at a time per target, each on a connection kept between them, and never two about one file. A file above 512 MiB goes as a multipart upload in parts of 64 MiB, since one request carries at most 5 GiB; a file that changes while its parts go is given up and carried again once it is written. Without TLS a file's bytes go from the disk to the socket by splice. A link to a file is carried as the file it names, and taken away at the walk that finds it pointing at nothing, since no event names a link whose target goes; a link to a directory is not followed. A --dir that holds the directory of a storage runtime it names, or lies in it, is refused, since every object carried would be carried again.

What it takes away. A file is removed from the storage only when it is provably gone here: deleted, or a link to nothing. A file the walk could not read, one below a directory it may not enter, and one an --exclude names since it was carried are left where they are. A directory that is empty when the index says files were carried from it removes nothing, and says why in last_error — a disk that is not mounted looks exactly like that, and a bucket emptied on the strength of it cannot be filled again.

Both ways. With in or inout, the storage is listed first, at a start and then at every --every, and each object is set against the index and the file here; with inout the walk follows each listing. A file the storage has and this side does not is brought, in ranges of 8 MiB written below .socketley-sync in --dir and given its name once whole; one the storage changed since is brought again; one the storage removed is removed here, unless it changed here since. A file both sides have at the start with the same length is taken as the same. A file both sides changed is kept twice: this side's at its name, carried out over the storage's, and the storage's beside it as name (conflict date time).ext, on both sides. With inout every write and removal sent carries the etag this side last saw, so one the storage made meanwhile refuses it and the next listing keeps both, rather than the later write winning. With in nothing is carried out: a file changed here is put back as the storage has it, and this side's version kept beside it. A key with an empty, . or .. segment is not brought, and a folder that is a link out of --dir is not written through. A listing with nothing in it removes nothing here.

What a failure means. A file the storage refuses, and a target that does not answer, are counted, logged once for as long as the reason stays the same, and tried again by a walk thirty seconds later, whatever --every says. A target that stops answering holds up its own queue and no other's. The runtime keeps running: a sync that keeps failing for three readings in a row raises an alert, with last_error as its detail, which clears once something is carried again. A runtime it names that is not a storage, or not there, is a failure of the same kind.

Its figures (socketley stats) are mode, dir, indexed (files the index holds), carried, removed, bytes_carried, waiting (what is queued), failures, failing (failures since the last thing carried), watched (directories inotify watches), brought (files brought from the storage), removed_here (files removed here because the storage removed them), conflicts (files both sides changed), last_run_secs and last_error.

sections.title: IDP FLAGS
sections.html:
An idp runtime is an OpenID Connect provider that keeps its own accounts: a user signs in once, and every application that asks the provider, every route a proxy puts behind it, a storage's web interface and the dashboard know who they are.

socketley create idp auth -p 9400 --domain auth.example.com \
    --clients /etc/socketley/idp.clients --cookie-domain example.com -s
socketley auth user add smiley --password - --groups admins

An account is a fixed random id and fields with no schema. The provider reads username, password (a scrypt hash), disabled, groups (a comma list; members of admins are admins), name, email, picture and reset; every other field is kept for the applications as it is, so one they add needs no change here and an older build keeps what it does not know. What one application alone uses — a game's characters, a shop's orders — belongs in that application, under the account's id. Every change is synced to a journal under the state directory before it is answered, and folded into a snapshot that names its format, which a build older than it refuses rather than rewrites. See idp-user under COMMANDS.

It serves the authorization code flow with PKCE, refresh tokens, discovery at /.well-known/openid-configuration, its key at /jwks, /userinfo, which answers from the account as it is now, and /logout; at /account a user changes their name, address and password and signs out everywhere. Turning a second step on or off and making an app password ask for the password again, or a code where a second step is on, counted as a sign-in's are, so a session alone changes neither; a second step on is replaced only by turning it off. Signing out everywhere and a new password end the account's app passwords with its sessions. Tokens are signed ES256 with a P-256 key made at the first start and kept in the state directory, so a restart signs nobody out; a refresh token, which only the provider reads back, is signed HS256 under a secret made from that key. A refresh token is good once: a refresh gives the next of its sign-in, kept with the account, and one used again ends that sign-in, its newest token too. A password is hashed and checked off the event loop, on a thread for each core the runtime may use, up to four shared out among its shards, each making up to four sign-ins' scrypt at once with AVX2. It serves plain HTTP and is reached through the entrance, which terminates TLS for its names as for every other runtime's; --tls is refused.

Guessing. Five failed sign-ins from one address within fifteen minutes refuse it until they age out, an IPv6 address counted by its /64, and sign-ins still being checked count beside them, so many sent at once are refused alike. Ten at one account, from wherever, make its next try wait half a minute, doubling with each one more to five minutes; a browser the account signed in on before keeps a count of its own, by a cookie of the provider's that lasts ninety days, so guesses from elsewhere never hold its user up. Three wrong codes end a sign-in's second step, its password then asked again, and five at an account hold its codes up as its passwords are. A mail runtime's password checks for a client it does not guard itself, one on its own machine or behind a forwarder there, count at the account apart from its sign-ins, ten failures holding the next up in the same way. At most 64 password checks wait at a shard, and a sign-in past them is told to try again in a moment (503).

On several cores. With --shards N the provider is served by N worker processes on its one port (SO_REUSEPORT), each signing in, giving tokens and answering /userinfo with the one key. Shard 0 writes the accounts, as a provider of one shard does, and every other shard reads its journal from the same files before it answers, so a change made with idp-user or on the account page holds at every shard once it is answered; one made at another shard is sent to shard 0. A code is redeemed at the shard that gave it, which the code names, wherever the exchange arrives, and is good once there; a sign-in being checked is counted at every shard while it is, and a failed one is answered once every shard counts it against its address and its account, so guesses sent at once over the shards share one budget. The number may change across a restart.

A sign-in is a cookie of the provider's, which a proxy with --auth idp:, a storage with --idp and the dashboard with daemon.dashboard_idp verify themselves against the key it publishes beside its state, each session once until it expires, and against each account's standing it publishes there too. A session ended at the provider — signed out at /logout, signed out everywhere, the account disabled — therefore ends there at once and at those within a second. /logout ends the session the browser sends, a copy of its cookie with it, and keeps the account's others; one another site sent the browser to is asked about first, unless the application names the account by an id_token_hint it was given; past 32 sessions signed out this way within their lifetimes, or for a cookie from a build before this one, a sign-out ends all of them and the account's refresh tokens, as signing out everywhere does.

--clients file#

The applications that sign in through it, one a line: id secret redirect [redirect...], with - as the secret of a public client, which must then send a PKCE challenge. A redirect is an https address compared whole, or an http one on this machine (localhost, 127.0.0.1) taken at any port, which an application on the machine picks as it runs. In place of a redirect, device lets the client sign a person in by the device grant, as socketley login does, an address or IPv6 /48 holding at most twenty grants waiting at a shard, and ssh lets its access tokens ask for SSH certificates. The file is read again when it changes; one broken while running keeps the clients read before it.

--ssh-ca hours#

An SSH certificate authority: an Ed25519 key made at the first start and kept in the state directory, its public key at /ssh/ca.pub, and at /ssh/user-cert a user certificate holding hours (1 to 168) for the account whose access token is sent, given only to a client marked ssh and never to a disabled account, nor on a sign-in more than twelve hours old, refreshed tokens and all, which is told to sign in again. A user certificate permits a terminal, port forwarding and agent forwarding, and neither X11 forwarding nor the user's ~/.ssh/rc. Every certificate is said in the log with its serial, the account, its principals and the key's fingerprint, and kept until it expires so that it can be revoked (see idp-ssh revoke). See ssh-cert and idp-ssh.

--issuer url#

The https address the provider is reached at, which every token names; when not given, https://name for the first --domain.

--resources list#

The resource servers, comma-separated https addresses such as https://mcp.example.com/mcp, an access token may be given for (RFC 8707): an application that sends resource with one of them at /authorize is given an access token naming it as its audience, which a runtime taking tokens for its own clients does not take; an mcp runtime with --idp takes it. With any, an application may also sign in by the https address of its client metadata document as its client id, as MCP clients such as Claude Code do: the document is fetched from public addresses alone, five kilobytes at most, kept as its Cache-Control says within a minute and a day, and taken only for a public client sending a PKCE challenge, with redirects of https or on this machine. Such an application is let in only for one of these resources, and only once the signed-in person has allowed it on a page that names it, its host, the resource and where it is sent back to, every time it asks. stats counts consents, client_fetches and client_fetch_failures.

--cookie-domain domain#

The domain whose names share the sign-in cookie, so a user signed in here is signed in for a proxy, a storage or the dashboard on any name below it; without it the cookie is the provider's host alone.

--shards N#

The worker processes the provider is served by, 1 to 64: shard 0 writes the accounts and every one signs in (see On several cores above). It changes with the runtime stopped.

An address that failed to sign in five times in fifteen minutes is refused until the oldest of those failures is fifteen minutes old, counted by the last address X-Forwarded-For names when the request came through a proxy on this machine.

sections.title: DB FLAGS
sections.html:
A db runtime keeps JSON documents for applications — a game's characters, a shop's orders and addresses, a user's settings — each owned by an account of an idp runtime, which reaches its own and no other's. Large things, a picture or a model, belong in a storage and their address here.

socketley create db data -p 9500 --domain data --idp auth \
    --schema /etc/socketley/db.schema --keys /etc/socketley/db.keys -s
socketley create db copy -p 9500 --replicate https://data.example.com \
    --replicate-key /etc/socketley/db.replica-key --keys /etc/socketley/db.keys -s

A document lives at /c/collection/id and is read with GET, replaced with PUT, changed in place with PATCH and removed with DELETE; a POST to /c/collection makes one under a new id. It is answered with its fields and _id, _v (its version, 1 when made and one more with each change, also its ETag) and _owner (the account's id). If-Match: "3" writes only at that version and If-None-Match: * only where there is none: 412 otherwise. A patch is {"set":{"a.b":1},"unset":["c"],"inc":{"n":1},"push":{"tags":"x"},"pull":{"tags":"y"}} on dotted paths. POST /c/collection/_query takes {"where":{"level":{"gte":5},"name":"x"},"sort":"-level","limit":50,"skip":0} with the conditions eq, ne, gt, gte, lt, lte, in, prefix and exists, or count :true for the number alone; it answers {"docs":[...]} and next when there are more. A range compares a field's values of one kind only, as an index orders them: null, false, true, numbers, strings. A condition or a sort on a field the schema does not index is judged by reading the documents, at most 8 MiB of them unless a key asks, past which the query is refused with 400 needs_index: index the field. POST /tx takes {"ops":[{"op":"put","c":..,"id":..,"doc":{..}},{"op":"patch",..,"changes":{..},"if":3},{"op":"insert",..},{"op":"delete",..}]} and makes every change or none. GET /me names who is asking.

Who asks is a key, sent as Authorization: Bearer secret, which reaches everything; an account of the --idp runtime, by its sign-in cookie or by an access token the provider gave one of its clients, sent as Authorization: Bearer; or nobody. A write by the cookie must be application/json from the database's own host or an origin of --origins, which a form another site posts cannot be. A document over 1 MiB, or nested deeper than 16, is refused.

The documents live on the disk, in segments under the state directory: each write is one record, appended to the newest segment, which is closed at 64 MiB and another begun. Memory holds where each document lies, its version, owner and the values its indexes order it by, and a cache of the documents last read (--cache); the rest are read from the disk, so a database holds far more than memory. A read that needs a document the page cache does not hold is tried first without it, the document brought through the ring, and the read answered then, so a slow disk holds that read and not every other; past three tries it waits in line. stats counts them as fetched. Sealed segments whose documents have mostly been written again or deleted are merged off the event loop into one of their living documents, and the old ones go. A record torn by a crash ends the newest segment where the last whole one does; damage anywhere else refuses the start, for a restore.

No answer is given before what it rests on is on the disk: a write's own record, or the change a read saw — so nothing is read that a crash could take back. One sync runs at a time, off the event loop, and takes every record written while the one before it ran, so a burst of writes costs a few syncs rather than one each and reads go on being answered meanwhile. A read behind a write on one connection is answered after it. A script of this daemon reaches the documents as socketley.db. It serves plain HTTP behind the entrance.

On several cores. With --shards N the database is served by N worker processes on its one port (SO_REUSEPORT). Shard 0 writes the one log, as a database of one shard does, and every other shard reads it from the same files as shard 0 puts it on the disk: it answers reads, queries and streams itself and sends shard 0 the writes, which are answered once they are on its disk. A shard takes in what shard 0 has made durable before it answers, so a read on any shard sees every write answered before it began. Transactions, unique indexes, streams, replicas and backups hold as they do on one shard, and the number may change across a restart, the documents being one log whichever it is. Reads and queries are answered by every shard; writes, which wait for one disk, are at most as many as one shard takes, and cost more cores than on one shard, since each that reaches another shard is handed on to shard 0 and its answer back. A database that is mostly written is served best by one shard.

Changes, as they happen. GET /c/collection/_feed is a stream of Server-Sent Events, which a browser reads with EventSource: each change once it is on the disk, as an event put with {"collection":..,"id":..,"owner":..,"version":..,"doc":{..}} or delete with {"collection":..,"id":..,"deleted":true}, numbered by the change. The reader sees what it may read, as a query does: an account its own documents of an owner collection. GET /_feed streams every collection's to a key. A stream that broke resumes with Last-Event-ID (or ?since=) from the last change it read; one older than the database keeps, about 32 MiB of changes, is told reset and should read again what it shows. A comment every fifteen seconds keeps a quiet stream from looking dead.

Documents with a time to go. A collection whose schema line names ttl:field loses a document when that field's number, in seconds since 1970, has passed: it is answered as absent from that moment, and its deletion is written and streamed within the minute.

A copy on another machine. A db runtime with --replicate follows another's /_replicate stream with a key of that database: it takes every document once, then every change, written to its own disk with the change's own number, so a restart of either goes on where it was. When the one it copies no longer keeps the changes it missed, it is sent everything again. A replica answers reads, queries and streams of its own and refuses writes with 403, naming where to make them; removing --replicate (import --restart) makes it a database of its own.

Backups. socketley db-backup db file writes every document into one file, off the event loop, while the database serves; socketley db-restore db file stops it, keeps its documents aside in dir.before-restore and starts it again on the backup's. With --backup-dir, backups are taken every --backup-every and the newest --backup-keep kept; a sync runtime carries that directory to a storage.

--schema file#

The collections, a line each: a name, who reaches it, and the fields indexed, unique: before one whose values no two documents share.

Details
# collection  access   indexes
characters    owner    level unique:name
posts         shared   created
scores        public   score
products      catalog  unique:sku price
sessions      owner    ttl:expires_at

private (and any collection the file does not name): a key only. owner : an account reads and writes its own documents; another's is answered as not there. shared : an account reads every document and writes its own. public : anybody reads; an account writes its own. catalog : anybody reads; a key writes. The file is read again when it changes; one that does not read, or a unique index the documents already break, keeps the schema before it and says why in stats.

--keys file#

Service keys for backends, a line each: name secret, the secret at least 16 characters. Read again when it changes. A key may set a document's _owner.

--idp runtime#

The idp runtime whose accounts own documents.

--idp-audience clients#

The ids of the idp's clients whose access tokens it takes, comma-separated. A token the provider gave any other application is refused, since it is that application's and no key to this runtime; without the flag no access token is taken, while cookies and passwords sign in as before.

--origins list#

The web origins a browser may call it from, comma-separated, answered with CORS and the browser's sign-in; * for any page, without it.

--max-bytes size#

The most the documents hold; a write past it is refused with 507.

--cache size#

The memory the documents last read are kept in, 64M unless given; the rest are read from the disk.

--replicate url#

The http or https address of the database this one copies, as its entrance answers it; https is verified against the system's roots.

--replicate-key file#

A file holding the secret of a key of that database.

--backup-dir dir#

Where scheduled backups are written, each name-time.dbbackup.

--backup-every duration#

How often, 1d unless given.

--backup-keep n#

How many are kept, 7 unless given.

--shards N#

The worker processes the database is served by, 1 to 64: shard 0 writes and every one reads (see On several cores above). It changes with the runtime stopped.

In a script:

local c, err = socketley.db.get("data", "characters", id)
socketley.db.put("data", "characters", id, { name = "Merlin", level = 3 }, { ["if"] = c._v })
socketley.db.patch("data", "characters", id, { inc = { level = 1 } })
local r = socketley.db.query("data", "scores", { sort = "-score", limit = 10 })
socketley.db.insert("data", "orders", { item = "sword" })
socketley.db.delete("data", "orders", id)
socketley.db.tx("data", { { op = "put", c = "a", id = "x", doc = {} }, { op = "delete", c = "b", id = "y" } })

Each answers the document (or the transaction's results), or nil, an error code and a sentence. Inside a callback that can wait it waits; anywhere else the last argument is a function called with the answer.
