sections.title: MQTT FLAGS
sections.html:
An mqtt runtime is an MQTT broker, for 3.1, 3.1.1 and 5.0, on TCP, TLS and WebSocket: devices, apps and browsers publish to topics and subscribe to them, and a client that goes away keeps its session — its subscriptions and the messages sent to them while it was gone — until it comes back or the session expires. It is a runtime like the others: messages reach a cache, a db, a storage, a server or another broker by rules of its own, and a storage's events and a script's messages reach its subscribers.

socketley mqtt passwd /etc/socketley/mqtt.users sensor-17
socketley create mqtt broker --users /etc/socketley/mqtt.users \
    --acl /etc/socketley/mqtt.acl --ws 8083 --persistent on -s
socketley create mqtt devices -p 8883 --tls --cert dev.pem --key dev.key \
    --ca devices-ca.pem --routes /etc/socketley/mqtt.routes -s

It listens on 1883, or 8883 with --tls, unless -p says otherwise. --max-connections and --write-buffer hold as for a server: past the write buffer owed to a slow client its QoS 0 messages are dropped and counted, and QoS 1 and 2 wait in its session.

What it implements. QoS 0, 1 and 2, the last exactly once by its packet identifier; retained messages, cleared by an empty one; wills, sent when a connection is lost or a 5.0 client disconnects asking for it and not when it disconnects cleanly, after a 5.0 will delay if one is given and not at all when the client comes back within it; sessions kept by 3.1.1's clean session 0 and 5.0's session expiry, one connection to a client id, a second taking the session over and the first told so, a session being its user's so that a CONNECT under another user (or none) is refused not authorized; keep alive, a client silent for one and a half times it disconnected; a CONNECT within ten seconds or the connection closed; and of 5.0 the session and message expiry, the receive maximum both ways, topic aliases, the maximum packet size, subscription identifiers, no local, retain as published, retain handling, shared subscriptions ($share/group/filter, each message to one member, in turn), request and response (the response topic and correlation data carried), user properties, the content type and the payload format, and reason codes and strings on what it refuses. Wildcards + and # do not match a topic beginning with $. It publishes its own figures, retained, under $SYS/broker/ every ten seconds: version, uptime, clients, messages and subscriptions. It does not take the 5.0 AUTH exchange (a CONNECT naming an authentication method is refused with 0x8C) and does not bridge to brokers outside the daemon.

Who may connect. At least one of --users, --idp, --ca or --anonymous must be given. A client certificate the --ca verified lets its client in under the certificate's common name. A password is checked against the users file, off the event loop, or else, with --idp, taken as an access token of that provider, its account's name the user (a user name given with it must be that name). Without credentials a client is let in only with --anonymous. A refusal is 0x86 (bad user name or password), 4 to a 3.1.1 client. A script's on_auth has the last word (see Lua below).

What each may do. --acl names rules in Mosquitto's form, read again within two seconds of a change:

# before any user line: clients without one
topic read public/#
user alice
topic readwrite home/alice/#
topic write telemetry/#
topic deny telemetry/secret/#
pattern readwrite users/%u/#
pattern write devices/%c/state

topic [read|write|readwrite|deny] filter applies to the user named last; pattern to everyone, with %u the user and %c the client id, each standing for one level. A deny wins over any grant; what no rule grants is refused. A publish refused is answered 0x87 to a 5.0 client, acknowledged and dropped for a 3.1.1 one; a subscription is refused only when no rule grants all of it, and a message a deny covers is held back from a subscription it covers in part. Without --acl every client may do everything.

Sessions across a restart. With --persistent the sessions, their queues and messages in flight, the retained messages and the topic rules' queues are written to a snapshot every --persistent-interval when something changed, off the event loop, and at stop; a start reads them back, so a stop, a restart of the daemon or a killed worker loses at most that interval. A session with no expiry left, and the wills it was owed, are ended and sent at the start that finds them. Without it the broker keeps nothing across a restart.

Topic rules. --routes names a file of rules, a filter and a target a line, that hand every message the filter matches to another runtime of the daemon beside the broker's own subscribers:

# filter          target
sensor/+/temp     cache://telemetry/stream/temps-%1
alarm/#           cache://events/channel/alarms
device/+/state    db://fleet/devices/%1
log/#             storage://raw/mqtt/%Y/%m/%d/
chat/#            server://chat
share/#           mqtt://other/from-edge/%t
door/#            https://hooks.example.com/door

cache://runtime/stream/key adds a stream entry of the fields topic, payload, qos and client; cache://runtime/channel/name publishes the payload on the channel; db://runtime/collection[/id] puts the payload as the document when it is a JSON object, and else {"topic":..,"payload":..,"client":..,"qos":..} — under id when given, as a new document otherwise; storage://runtime/bucket[/prefix] gathers the messages as JSON lines, {"at":..,"topic":..,"payload":..,"qos":..,"client":..}, into one .ndjson object a minute (or a megabyte, or at stop) under the prefix; server://runtime sends every client of the server {"topic":..,"payload":..} as a line; and mqtt://runtime/topic publishes on that broker, at the message's QoS and retained as it was, a message that has passed eight such rules on its way being passed on by no more of them, so rules that lead to each other end; and http:// or https:// URL POSTs {"topic":..,"payload":..,"qos":..,"retain":..,"client":..} to it, one at a time and in order on a connection it keeps, the host resolved on the broker's loop (see What can stop the event loop): a 2xx is delivered, a 400 or another refusal is counted failed and not sent again, and no answer, a 408, a 429 or a 5xx is tried again as a stopped runtime is. %1 to %9 stand for the levels the filter's + matched, %t for the whole topic and %c for the client that published; a storage prefix also takes %Y, %m, %d, %H and %M. A line beginning with # is a comment, and so is a # after a target. The file is read at start; one that does not read stops it, naming the line.

Each rule has a queue of its own, in order: a target that is stopped or does not answer holds its messages, tried again after a pause that grows to five seconds, without holding up the broker or the other rules, and up to 100000 messages, the oldest dropped past them and counted. What a rule holds goes into the snapshot, those in flight in their place, so a restart sends them again: a target gets each message at least once. stats names each rule with what it delivered, what its target refused, what was dropped, what it holds and its last error.

From the other runtimes. socketley mqtt-pub and a script's socketley.mqtt.publish publish as the broker's own, a storage's mqtt://runtime/topic notification target publishes its events (see --notify-targets), and mqtt:// rules of another broker publish theirs:

local ok, err = socketley.mqtt.publish("broker", "game/" .. id .. "/move", move, { qos = 1 })
socketley.mqtt.publish("broker", "chat/lobby", text, { retain = false }, function(ok, err) end)

It answers true once the broker has the message, or nil and the reason; inside a callback that can wait it waits, anywhere else the last argument is a function called with the answer.

WebSocket. --ws port serves MQTT inside WebSocket on a second port for browsers (any path, /mqtt by convention), the subprotocol mqtt or mqttv3.1 chosen when offered, a packet carried in any number of frames and frames holding any number of packets, a frame no longer than four times --max-packet. With --tls it is wss.

On several cores. With --shards N the broker is N worker processes sharing its ports (SO_REUSEPORT), one broker to its clients: each shard tells the others what its clients subscribe to and hands them the messages their subscribers want, a retained message is kept by all, a shared subscription's message goes to one member of the group over all the shards, and a client connecting to another shard than before takes its session with it, the newest connection of a client id winning. A shard that cannot take what another hands it as fast holds back that other shard's publishers, which are not read until it can, rather than lose their messages: at QoS 1 and 2 all of them, at QoS 0 those whose last message went to it. One that has answered nothing for a second holds back only QoS 1 and 2 publishers, whose answer waits: a message for it is dropped at QoS 0 then, or once 8 MiB wait for it, and at any QoS once what it was handed has failed for three seconds, and counted in shard_dropped. Each shard keeps a snapshot of its own, file.shard, and publishes its figures under $SYS/broker/shard/n/.

Lua. A broker's --lua script may decide who connects and what passes. Each hook that decides answers true to allow, false to refuse, and nothing to keep what the broker decided; a hook that fails refuses. A client is a table of id, username, peer and version.

function on_auth(c)          -- c.id c.username c.password c.peer
    if c.username == "robot" then return c.password == "beep" end
end                          -- c.certificate c.authenticated c.account c.version
function on_publish(client, msg)              -- msg.topic msg.payload msg.qos msg.retain
    if msg.topic == "shout" then return { payload = string.upper(msg.payload) } end
end
function on_subscribe(client, filter, qos) return filter ~= "secret/#" end
function on_connect(client) self.publish("presence/" .. client.id, "online", { retain = true }) end
function on_disconnect(client, why) self.publish("presence/" .. client.id, "offline", { retain = true }) end

on_auth is given whether the credentials checked out (authenticated) and as whom (account); letting in a client they refused makes the user name it gave its user. on_publish may also answer a table, the message as it is to go on (any of topic, payload, qos, retain); a refused publish is answered 0x87. self.publish(topic, payload [, {qos=, retain=}]) publishes as the broker, self.retained(topic) reads a retained payload, self.sessions() lists this shard's sessions and self.kick(client_id [, end]) disconnects one. While a hook decides, that connection's next packets wait.

--users file#

The accounts that sign in with a password, user:hash a line as socketley mqtt-passwd writes them; read again within two seconds of a change.

--idp runtime#

The idp runtime whose access tokens, given as the password, sign clients in.

--idp-audience clients#

The ids of the idp's clients whose access tokens it takes, comma-separated. A token the provider gave any other application is refused, since it is that application's and no key to this runtime; without the flag no access token is taken, while cookies and passwords sign in as before.

--acl file#

Who may publish and subscribe to what (see What each may do above).

--anonymous#

Lets in clients without credentials, as the rules allow.

--routes file#

Where messages go besides their subscribers (see Topic rules above).

--ws port#

A second port, for MQTT over WebSocket.

--persistent file|on#

The snapshot sessions and retained messages are kept in; on for state/mqtt/name.snapshot under the state directory.

--persistent-interval duration#

How often what changed reaches the snapshot, 1s unless given.

--max-packet size#

The largest packet a client may send, 64 bytes to 256M, 256K unless given; a larger one is answered 0x95 and the connection closed. It is told to 5.0 clients, and no message larger than a client says it takes is sent to it.

--session-expiry duration#

The longest a session outlives its connection, whatever the client asks; 1d unless given. A 3.1.1 session kept by clean session 0 lasts this long.

--session-queue n#

The messages kept for one session while its client is away or slow, 1000 unless given; past it the oldest go, counted.

--retained-max size#

The most bytes retained messages take, 64M unless given; a new one past it is not kept, counted.

--max-sessions n#

The most sessions, connected or not, 100000 unless given. A new client past it ends the session away longest of whoever holds the most — a user, or for clients without one an address, IPv6 by its /64 — when that is two or more, counted as sessions_evicted, so one owner filling the table locks nobody else out; otherwise it is refused with 0x97.

--keepalive-max seconds#

The longest keep alive granted, 1200 unless given; a 5.0 client asking more or none is told this one.

A client that leaves more than twice --write-buffer (4M unless given) of what it was sent unread is not read until it has read half of it, so its pings and acks cannot grow what it is owed.

stats says the sessions and those connected, the subscriptions, the retained messages and their bytes, what is queued and in flight, the messages received and sent at each QoS, what was dropped and why, the connects and the refusals, the snapshots and whether a change is in none yet, each topic rule, and over shards what was handed between them.

sections.title: MAIL FLAGS
sections.html:
A mail runtime is a mail server: it takes the mail of its domains and the mail its users send, keeps each message in a spool until it is delivered, hands mail for elsewhere to the domain's exchanger or a smarthost, and keeps its users' mailboxes in a storage runtime, read over IMAP. It is a runtime like the others: a dns runtime gives its domains their records, an idp runtime its users, a storage runtime its mailboxes, and the other runtimes, the CLI and the daemon's alerts send mail through it. Its settings are changed with import (--restart to take them at once): a running runtime takes its connection, rate and idle limits as they come and the rest at its next start, and --users and --aliases are read again whenever their files change. A rename by import moves its spool, keys and mailboxes' state with it, and is refused while it runs. show prints a --relay password as ***, which an import of what it printed keeps as it was.

socketley create mail m -p 25 --dns ns --no-reply -s
socketley send m --to ops@example.com --subject "Backup done" --text ok

socketley create mail m -p 25 --dns ns --idp auth --storage files/mail \
    --submission 587 --imap 143 --tls -s

It listens for SMTP on 25 unless -p says otherwise; port 25 needs the daemon to be allowed to bind it. With --shards the first shard alone takes mail, on SMTP, submission and LMTP, so one spool commits it all with one sync, while every shard serves the mailboxes. --submission adds a port its users send from, with STARTTLS and a password, --submissions one that speaks TLS from the first byte, and --imap and --imaps the same two for reading the mailboxes; --pop3 and --pop3s read INBOX over POP3 (RFC 1939, with STLS, SASL PLAIN, UIDL and TOP), and --lmtp takes mail from this machine's own programs into the mailboxes over LMTP (RFC 2033), one answer for each recipient, and --jmap serves JMAP (RFC 8620, RFC 8621) for mail clients and web apps, over HTTPS with --tls.Amessageasigned-inusersends without a Date or a Message-ID is given them, as Postfix's cleanup does; one from another server is passed on as it came. With no --bind a port takes IPv6 and IPv4 alike; an IPv4 client is seen, checked and logged by its IPv4 address.

--tls with --dns and no --cert takes the certificate of the dns runtime's entrance, which holds the names it is reached by and is renewed there, and the runtime takes the renewed one as it does any. One the entrance has still to write — a runtime made before its dns runtime, or on a machine where the entrance has not yet been given its names — is waited for: mail is taken meanwhile on SMTP without STARTTLS, and what takes a password or speaks TLS from the first byte opens within a second of the certificate being there. A certificate given with --cert is there when the runtime starts, or it does not start.

Signing in. A user signs in with their password over TLS, or from this machine in the clear, or with a token their idp gave, by XOAUTH2 or OAUTHBEARER on SMTP, IMAP and POP3, as mail apps that sign in through an identity provider do; where the account has its second step on, a mail app signs in with one of its app passwords (see idp-user). Ten wrong answers from one address in ten minutes refuse that address for ten minutes; twenty at one account from three addresses or more refuse the account, for ten minutes, to every address but those it signed in from within thirty days, so guesses spread over many addresses lock none of its own devices out. Both outlast a restart. Each sign-in is a line of the log: the user, the protocol and the address.

Whose mail it takes. Its domains are --mail-domain, or the zones of the dns runtime --dns names, followed as they change. Mail for an address of them is taken when an alias names it (--aliases), when it is a user's (--idp: the local part a username, or the address the account's email), when it is no-reply@ and a bounce, or when the script takes it (on_rcpt); any other is refused at RCPT with 550. A local part with a tag, user+tag@, is the user's, the tag what Sieve's subaddress reads; --recipient-delimiter names other characters for it, or none. An address this runtime rewrote under SRS (below) is the sender it stands for, taken while it is 21 days old and only under the runtime's own key. Mail for elsewhere is taken from a user signed in, and from 127.0.0.1, this machine's own programs; from anyone else it is refused with 554, so the server is not a relay.

Taking mail. ESMTP with PIPELINING, SIZE, 8BITMIME, SMTPUTF8, ENHANCEDSTATUSCODES, STARTTLS, AUTH PLAIN and LOGIN, CHUNKING (BDAT), DSN, LIMITS (RCPTMAX, RFC 9422) and, inside TLS, REQUIRETLS (RFC 8689); replies come in the order the commands came. A message past --max-size is refused, said at MAIL when its SIZE says so, after its end otherwise. Its end is a CRLF, a dot and a CRLF and nothing else, or the chunk BDAT says is the last, and a bare LF or a lone CR in it is written as CRLF, so a dot after either ends no message here or on the next server; what a client sent after STARTTLS before the handshake is dropped. A recipient given twice is one recipient, and an EHLO name with a control byte or a space is refused. AUTH is offered over TLS, and in the clear to 127.0.0.1 alone; a wrong password is answered a second later, and ten from one address within ten minutes lock that address out for ten minutes, the right password too (454; IMAP's [UNAVAILABLE]). On the submission ports nothing is taken from a client that has not signed in, and a signed-in user sends only as their own address, in MAIL FROM and in the From header alike: their username at one of its domains, the email their idp account names, or the username where it is an address. A connection quiet for five minutes is closed.

Limits. One client address holds at most 50 connections to port 25 and 200 to each other port, 127.0.0.1 none of these; a runtime with no --max-connections holds 8192. One past a limit is told 421 (BYE on IMAP and ManageSieve) and closed. A client that sends more than its largest message and a mebibyte while a command waits, or that reads none of 32 MiB of replies, is told 421 and closed, reset if it still reads none five seconds later. --rate-limit n takes n messages a second from one client address, or one signed-in user, and tells the next MAIL 450; --global-rate-limit does the same for the whole runtime.

What it checks. With --dnsbl, a connection on port 25 not from 127.0.0.1 has its address asked of each list while it is greeted, and its MAIL waits for the answer if it has not come: one a list names (an address in 127/8) sends nothing, 554, unless it signs in. A list's error answer (127.255.255.x) names nobody, and a list that does not answer lets the mail by; an answer is kept five minutes. With --greylist, a stranger's first try of a sender and a recipient from a network (a /24, or a /64) is told 451 and taken once it tries again after the delay and within a day, and from then on for 36 days; what a shard learns every shard knows. With --rspamd, each message from elsewhere is scanned by that Rspamd's /checkv2 beside the checks: reject refuses it with 554, soft reject and greylist with 451, add header and rewrite subject file it in Junk, and its score goes into Authentication-Results as x-spam, which Sieve's spamtest reads. A scanner that does not answer in ten seconds lets the mail by. Mail from elsewhere (port 25, no user signed in, not 127.0.0.1) is checked before it is taken: SPF (RFC 7208) for the sender's domain, or HELO's for a bounce; every DKIM signature, rsa-sha256 and ed25519-sha256, up to ten, those of the From's organization first, one whose l= leaves part of the body out neutral and an RSA key under 1024 bits refused; the ARC chain; and DMARC (RFC 7489) for the domain of From, its labels past ASCII as A-labels, with SPF or DKIM aligned as its record says and pct= sampling what its policy is for. A message DMARC fails under p=reject is refused with 550 and not kept, as is one whose author cannot be told — two From headers, one that does not read, or authors of two domains; under p=quarantine it goes to the recipient's Junk folder; a passing ARC chain sealed last by one of --arc-trust takes the policy off. What each said is written into the mailbox's Authentication-Results line, and one a sender put there under this host's name is taken out, as is the sender's Return-Path. The lookups run on sixteen threads of their own and never on the loop, a message's together within twenty seconds, past which they are a temporary error; an answer is kept a minute. Past 512 messages waiting to be checked, the next is told 451. The organizational domain DMARC compares is a name's registrable domain by the Public Suffix List of the publicsuffix package (/usr/share/publicsuffix), so mail.example.co.uk is example.co.uk, its rules past ASCII compared as A-labels; without the package a name is its own, so relaxed alignment is strict, and the log says so once.

The spool. A message is synced before the client is told 250, kept under state/mail/name/spool until every recipient is done. One up to a mebibyte is a record of a segment, a file of 32 MiB written out before it is used, so one fdatasync commits every message that ended while the last one ran; a larger one is a file of its own. Each record carries its segment's generation and a CRC, so a record a crash cut is dropped at the next start, and the log says so. What became of each recipient is kept in a log beside them, so a restart tries again what was waiting and never brings back what was dropped. A segment a few deferred messages keep has them moved after a minute and is used again. A message under a mebibyte is kept in memory as well, and its delivery reads nothing back.

Sending it on. Recipients of one domain go in one transaction, and a connection to a domain carries one message after another while there are more for it, at most four to a domain and 128 in all; MAIL, RCPT and DATA go in one write where the other side offers PIPELINING. The exchangers are the domain's MX records, from the resolver on the loop, or the domain itself when it has none; a domain that does not exist or says it takes no mail (RFC 7505) fails at once. With --relay everything for elsewhere goes through that smarthost. TLS is spoken wherever it is offered, and an exchanger's certificate is checked where its domain asks:

  • DANE (RFC 7672): where DNSSEC signed a domain's MX records, the TLSA records of each exchanger are asked, and with any there the mail goes over TLS only, its certificate one they name (DANE-TA or DANE-EE). A record is believed only when the resolver set the AD bit and every nameserver /etc/resolv.conf names is on this machine, a validating resolver such as unbound; elsewhere nothing is believed and nothing is checked.

  • MTA-STS (RFC 8461): where a domain has an _mta-sts TXT record, its policy is fetched from https://mta-sts.domain/.well-known/mta-sts.txt on a thread, again when its id changes, and kept under the runtime's state for the next start. Under mode: enforce only the exchangers it names are tried, over TLS, each with a certificate for its name from the system's CAs; under testing what would have failed is logged and counted, and the mail goes as before.

Mail that cannot go so waits and is tried again (4.7.5). Elsewhere the certificate is not checked, as no mail server checks one, and a smarthost's always is, and its password is never sent in the clear. A recipient refused for now is tried again after 1m, 5m, 15m, 30m, 1h, 2h, 4h and every 8h after, until --queue-lifetime; one refused for good, or out of time, is bounced to the sender as a delivery status report from the null sender. A server that offers CHUNKING is sent the message in BDAT chunks, nothing stuffed, and one whose LIMITS say how many recipients a transaction takes is sent them that many at a time. A server that answers 421 is given a rest: no new connection to its domain for thirty seconds, doubled by each 421 until it takes a message, to fifteen minutes. REQUIRETLS mail goes on only over TLS whose certificate DANE or an enforced MTA-STS policy vouched for (a smarthost's always is), to a server that offers REQUIRETLS, and is returned 550 5.7.10 otherwise, its notice carrying no more than its header; a Sieve redirect keeps the requirement on. Mail from elsewhere that it sends on goes from an SRS address of its first domain (SRS0=hash=time=domain=local@), so SPF at the next hop judges this host and a bounce finds its way back. What a sender asked of reports (RFC 3461) is kept with each recipient: NOTIFY, ORCPT, RET and ENVID go on to a server that offers DSN, which reports from there; elsewhere this runtime reports a SUCCESS asked for as delivered or relayed, a DELAY once a message has waited four hours, and no failure where NOTIFY said NEVER. RET=FULL has the report carry the message whole, up to 4 MiB; otherwise it carries the header. Mail from one of its domains is signed with DKIM twice, rsa-sha256 under the selector and ed25519-sha256 (RFC 8463) under selector-ed, relaxed, with keys made at its first start and kept in state/mail/name.dkim.selector.key for every shard. A key is rotated by naming the new selector with --dkim-next first, which makes its pair and publishes it beside the old one, and with --dkim-selector once DNS has it. Mail from elsewhere that it sends on, as an alias does, is sealed with ARC (RFC 8617): what its checks found, signed and sealed for its first domain, so the next hop can know what the message was as it came.

Reports. With --reports, it sends the reports other domains ask for: DMARC aggregate reports (RFC 7489) to the rua of each domain whose mail it checked, and TLS reports (RFC 8460) to the rua of each domain's _smtp._tls record it sent mail to under DANE or MTA-STS, once a day, after midnight UTC, gzip'd, each shard what it saw. --dmarc-rua and --tls-rpt publish where others send theirs about its own domains.

Its records. With --dns it gives each of its domains, through the dns runtime:

example.com.                 MX   10 mail.example.com.
example.com.                 TXT  "v=spf1 mx -all"
skl._domainkey.example.com.  TXT  "v=DKIM1; k=rsa; p=..."
skl-ed._domainkey.example.com. TXT "v=DKIM1; k=ed25519; p=..."
_dmarc.example.com.          TXT  "v=DMARC1; p=quarantine; adkim=r; aspf=r"
_imaps._tcp.example.com.     SRV  0 1 993 mail.example.com.
_25._tcp.mail.example.com.   TLSA 3 1 1 ...

with an SRV record (RFC 6186, RFC 8314) for each of --submission, --submissions, --imap, --imaps, --pop3, --pop3s, --jmap and --sieve it opens, so a mail client finds them from the address alone; with --tls the TLSA record of its certificate's key, for senders that check DANE where the zone is signed; with --mta-sts an _mta-sts record whose id follows the policy, and with --mta-sts-port mta-sts.domain as a CNAME of its host, which serves the policy there over TLS; with --tls-rpt an _smtp._tls record, and with --dmarc-rua a rua in its DMARC record,

and its host, mail.domain unless --hostname says another, the addresses the dns runtime's --publish gives its names, and an SPF record of its own, v=spf1 a -all, for a receiver that checks the name it greets with (RFC 7208 2.3). A record the zone file has at the name wins. With --relay SPF ends in ~all, since mail leaves from the smarthost's addresses. Without a dns runtime, socketley mail m dns prints the lines for a zone kept elsewhere.

No-reply. With --no-reply, a message socketley send or a script writes without a sender goes from no-reply@domain. Mail to that address is refused, but a bounce is taken and read. Such a message goes out to one recipient a transaction, under no-reply+tag@domain, the tag the day and a keyed hash of the recipient's address and that day that only this runtime can make, so a bounce that comes back within seven days under an address's tag suppresses that address: it is not mailed again by any shard until socketley mail m forgive address lets it go, or ninety days pass. A bounce under no tag, an older one, or another address's, is read and acts on nothing, so no stranger, nor another recipient, can stop mail to an address. The runtime's own bounce of such a message is its own word, so an address is learned dead from its first try. A recipient whose Status is 4.x.x, or 5.2.2 (its mailbox full), is no address that is dead and is not suppressed.

A provider's feedback report (ARF, RFC 5965) that one of its users called a message spam — as Microsoft's JMRP and the other feedback loops send them, to whichever address of its domains was given to them — unsubscribes that user from its advertisements, as their own click would, where the report's sender is who it says by SPF or DKIM; the report is still delivered. socketley mail trace names it.

Mailboxes. With --idp and --storage, a user's mail is an object of the storage runtime's bucket (mail unless --storage names another), made when first needed: user/INBOX/id.eml under a Return-Path, a Delivered-To and the Authentication-Results line, written whole under a mebibyte and in pieces of one above. A message in a mailbox is told to the targets of --notify-targets as {"event":"mail.received","mailbox":..,"folder":..,"key":..,"from":..,"subject":..,"size":..}, under mail/user for a broker. A bucket that encrypts or compresses what it keeps does so to mail too, and a message is read back a range at a time either way.

IMAP. IMAP4rev1, and IMAP4rev2 (RFC 9051) for a client that enables it, with LITERAL+, SEARCHRES, SASL-IR, IDLE, NAMESPACE, UIDPLUS, MOVE, UNSELECT, CHILDREN, SPECIAL-USE, ID, ENABLE, CONDSTORE and QRESYNC, ESEARCH, LIST-EXTENDED and LIST-STATUS, STATUS=SIZE, QUOTA, SORT (with DISPLAYFROM and DISPLAYTO), THREAD (ORDEREDSUBJECT, REFERENCES), WITHIN (OLDER and YOUNGER), SAVEDATE, PREVIEW and COMPRESS=DEFLATE, what a loop turn says compressed as one flushed block, on the mailboxes of --storage; a password goes over STARTTLS or --imaps only (LOGINDISABLED before), except from 127.0.0.1. Every mailbox has INBOX, Sent, Drafts, Junk and Trash, and CREATE makes more, with the folders above a name such as Work/2026; a client sets keywords of its own beside the system flags. A folder's UIDs, flags and keywords are kept per user in state/mail/name.imap/user, a snapshot and a journal beside it: every shard serves IMAP, a change is a line appended under the user's lock once the journal is read to its end, so a UID is given once whichever shard gives it, and each shard reads the lines it has not before each command. The journal is folded into the snapshot once it passes a quarter of a mebibyte. A delivery, an APPEND and a COPY write their line as the message is stored, so IDLE is told of new mail within a second and the quota counts it at once. The bucket stays what counts: listed when a folder is selected, and every minute under NOOP and IDLE, what went from it is expunged, and a message no line names is given the next UID once it is a minute old. Every change of a message has the folder's next mod-sequence, so a client that reconnects asks for what changed and vanished since it last looked. SEARCH, SORT and THREAD, like JMAP's text, body and header filters, read a message's header as written and with its encoded words decoded and its text parts as written and with their transfer encoding and charset undone, not its attachments. A filter of each message's trigrams, made as a delivery or an APPEND stores it (or, for one over a mebibyte delivered, the first time a search reads it), as large as the different trigrams it holds and kept in state/mail/name.imap/user.fts for every shard, rules out what cannot hold the string asked for, so a search reads only the messages that may. A user's mail_quota field in the idp runtime (socketley idp-user ... --set mail_quota=500M) bounds what their mailboxes hold: IMAP tells it as one quota root over every folder, an APPEND or a COPY past it is refused OVERQUOTA, and a delivery past it is refused 552 5.2.2, as Dovecot refuses one; a user with no mail_quota has --default-quota. A user whose mailboxes pass --quota-warn percent of their quota (90 unless it says) is mailed a warning once, and again only after they fell below it. All of a runtime's mailboxes together, every domain's, are bounded by the quota of their bucket (PutBucketQuota on the storage runtime): a delivery past it waits, 452 4.2.2, until room is made, and a bound for each domain is a mail runtime for each, on a bucket of its own. IMAP also offers MULTIAPPEND, which puts every message it is given in or none, UTF8=ACCEPT, under which folder names come and go as UTF-8 and a message may be a literal8, CREATE-SPECIAL-USE, which takes a special use only of the folder whose name has it, BINARY, which gives a part with its transfer encoding undone, OBJECTID, whose MAILBOXID a RENAME keeps, METADATA (RFC 5464), entries of the server and of each folder kept in the index, at most 1000 a user of 64 KiB each, NOTIFY (RFC 5465), which tells a session of new mail, expunges and flags in the folders it watches as STATUS, of folders made and gone as LIST, and of the selected folder between commands, within a second, ACL (RFC 4314), by which a user gives others rights on a folder, seen by them under Other Users/owner/ with what those rights allow (l r s w i k x t e a), and APPENDLIMIT; RENAME takes the folders under a name along, and RENAME INBOX moves its messages and leaves it empty. A connection quiet for thirty minutes is closed.

JMAP. /.well-known/jmap is the session; the API at /jmap/api takes Core/echo, Mailbox/get, query, set and changes, Email/get, query, set, import and changes, Thread/get with every Email of a conversation in any mailbox, Quota/get, query and changes (RFC 9425) with the octets of the user's quota, Identity/get and set, and EmailSubmission/set with its onSuccessUpdateEmail and onSuccessDestroyEmail, back-references among them; /jmap/upload and /jmap/download move blobs, and /jmap/eventsource tells of state changes. A user signs in with HTTP Basic, their idp password, over TLS or from 127.0.0.1, or with an idp bearer token. Their account is the mailboxes IMAP reads: a Mailbox id is its MAILBOXID and an Email id its EMAILID, which a move keeps, a Thread the conversation the Message-ID its References begin with names, which collapseThreads folds a query by, a keyword an IMAP flag, so a client of either sees what the other did at once. A state is a digest of the index, the same on every shard, and a */changes since another answers cannotCalculateChanges, after which a client reads again. An upload is kept a day; an EmailSubmission sends as the user's own address only. Email/parse reads a blob, an upload or an attached message, as an Email. VacationResponse, kept in the user's METADATA, answers what their mailbox takes, once a week a sender, never a list, a bounce, spam or what answers itself (RFC 3834), whether or not a Sieve script runs. A PushSubscription (at most 50 a user, a week each until renewed) is verified by the code pushed to its URL, then sent a StateChange whenever the types it asked for change, over HTTPS to a public address, encrypted where it gave keys (RFC 8291).

Calendars and contacts. On the same ports, CalDAV (RFC 4791) and CardDAV (RFC 6352) for every user: /.well-known/caldav and /.well-known/carddav lead to /dav/, whose principal names the user's calendars under /dav/user/calendars/ and address books under /dav/user/contacts/, personal and default there for every user and more made with MKCALENDAR or MKCOL. A client puts, reads and deletes each event, task or card whole, under If-Match and If-None-Match; PROPPATCH keeps a collection's name, colour and description; the multiget and query REPORTs, a query's component filter among them, and sync-collection (RFC 6578) answer. The entries are objects of the --storage bucket under .dav/user/, apart from the mail folders, and what changed in a collection is a line of a journal under state/mail/name.dav/, whose length is its sync token. Through the entrance a user signs in as for JMAP; Thunderbird's autoconfig, the Apple profile and _caldavs._tcp and _carddavs._tcp in the zone point a client there.

Webmail. With --web and --domain the entrance serves a mail client in the browser under the name, in the look of the storage interface: the mailboxes with their unread counts and a starred view, the conversations a page at a time, each read as its messages from every mailbox with what they quote folded away, a search over all of them, reading, writing, replying and forwarding with attachments, drafts saved as they are written, moving, archiving, flags and deletion, a whole folder selected or emptied, a message's headers and its print, a send undone within seconds or put off until a time, plain text or formatted, a sender of the user's addresses, the one a message was sent to for its reply, a name, a signature, an out-of-office answer between two dates, filters for arriving mail as a Sieve script, and new mail as it comes, told in the background where the browser lets it. It speaks German where the browser asks for it, English otherwise. It signs in through the idp runtime, whose session cookie under its --cookie-domain signs the user in to every runtime of it at once, and sends a page not signed in to the idp's /login. A change the cookie alone signs carries the page's X-Socketley-UI header, which another site cannot make a browser send, and an answer to the cookie is readable by no other origin. A message's HTML is cleaned of what runs, submits or reaches out, and shown in a frame sandboxed without scripts; its remote images wait until the reader asks for them, for that message or for its sender from then on. The page's one script runs by its hash alone. On the same port a JMAP client signs in as on --jmap, with a password only where the entrance forwarded HTTPS, and a client that fails ten times is locked out by the address the entrance forwards for it.

socketley create mail m -p 25 --dns ns --idp auth --storage files/mail \
    --imaps 993 --submissions 465 --tls --cert mail.pem --key mail.key \
    --web 9480 --domain mail -s

From the other runtimes. socketley send and a script's socketley.mail.send write and queue a message; a storage's mail://runtime/address notification target mails its events; and daemon.alert_mail mails the daemon's alerts.

local id, err = socketley.mail.send("m", { to = "ops@example.com",
    subject = "order " .. order.id, text = "paid",
    attachments = { { name = "invoice.pdf", type = "application/pdf", data = pdf } } })

Sieve. A user files their own mail with Sieve (RFC 5228) and its extensions fileinto, reject, ereject, envelope, encoded-character, imap4flags, copy, vacation, vacation-seconds, subaddress, body, relational, comparator-i;ascii-numeric, variables, date, index, mailbox, regex, editheader, duplicate, include, environment, spamtest, spamtestplus, virustest, enotify (mailto) and ihave. Their scripts are put over ManageSieve (RFC 5804) on --sieve (STARTTLS, and SASL PLAIN with the password IMAP takes) or with socketley mail ... sieve, compiled as they are put, at most 32 of 64 KiB and 1 MiB in all, and kept under the runtime's state for every shard; one is made active only where it compiles with what it includes. The active one is run on a thread for each message that reaches the user's mailbox, the whole message what it reads: keep and fileinto file it, with the imap4flags' flags IMAP shows, fileinto into a folder not there only with :create (else into INBOX); discard keeps nothing; reject bounces it to its sender where that sender signed in, is this machine or passed SPF, and otherwise discards it; redirect sends it on from the user's own address, never again if it comes back; vacation answers a sender once in its days or seconds, an hour at least, from the null sender, and never a bounce or spam; notify mails a mailto URI, auto-notified, from the null sender, at most three times a message. What editheader adds or deletes is in what is kept and sent on, the Received and Auto-Submitted headers excepted. duplicate keeps a message's ID twelve hours unless :seconds says, a week at most; it and vacation remember at most 10,000 per user. include :global reads the scripts put for the user .global (socketley mail m sieve .global put name file ), include :personal the user's own. environment tells host, domain, remote-ip, location MDA, phase during, name and version; spamtest and virustest are 0 until a scanner says more. A script that fails keeps the message in INBOX.

imapsieve (RFC 6785): a folder whose /shared/imapsieve/script entry names one of the user's scripts, set by SETMETADATA, has it run for each message a client APPENDs or COPYs or MOVEs into it, and for each whose flags a STORE changes there; environment's imap.cause, imap.mailbox, imap.user, imap.email and imap.changedflags say what was done, and imap4flags starts from the message's flags. keep leaves it with the flags the script left, fileinto files a copy, redirect sends one on, and where nothing keeps it the message leaves the folder once its copies are in; reject is an error and vacation does nothing. What its own fileinto puts elsewhere runs no script there.

Lua. A script of the runtime decides each recipient and is told each message:

function on_rcpt(r, default)          -- r.to, r.from, r.peer, r.user
    if r.to == "orders@example.com" then return true end   -- the script's alone
    if r.from:match("@spam%.test$") then return false end  -- refused 550
end                                   -- nil keeps the default
function on_message(m)                -- m.id, m.from, m.to, m.size, m.subject, m.message, m.peer, m.user
    socketley.mqtt.publish("bus", "mail/in", m.subject or "", { qos = 1 })
end

A recipient on_rcpt takes that no mailbox or alias has is the script's: its message reaches on_message and nowhere else. m.message is the whole message where it is under a mebibyte.

--mail-domain domain[,domain...]#

The domains whose mail it takes.

--dns runtime#

The dns runtime whose zones are its domains, given their records.

--hostname name#

The name it greets with and its MX records name, mail.first domain unless given.

--no-reply#

Send from no-reply@ where no sender is said, take no mail there but bounces, and learn from those.

--idp runtime#

The idp runtime whose users have mailboxes here and sign in to send and read.

--idp-audience clients#

The ids of the idp's clients whose access tokens it takes, comma-separated. A token the provider gave any other application is refused, since it is that application's and no key to this runtime; without the flag no access token is taken, while cookies and passwords sign in as before.

--storage runtime[/bucket]#

The storage runtime, and bucket, the mailboxes are kept in.

--users file#

Accounts that sign in to send, a name and a scrypt hash a line as socketley mqtt-passwd writes them, read again when it changes.

--aliases file#

Addresses taken besides the users', address target[,target...] a line, a target a mailbox (a name) or an address mail is sent on to, and *@domain any local part of a domain that names none of its own; read again when it changes.

--relay smtp[s]://[user:password@]host[:port]#

A smarthost every message for elsewhere goes through; smtps:// speaks TLS from the first byte (465), smtp:// STARTTLS (587).

--submission port#

A port users send from with STARTTLS and a password; it needs --tls and --users or --idp.

--submissions port#

A port users send from over TLS from the first byte; it needs --tls.

--imap port--imaps port#

A port mail clients read the mailboxes on, with STARTTLS or over TLS from the first byte; they need --storage.

--notify-targets file#

Where each message stored in a mailbox is told, in the form a storage runtime's file takes.

--max-size size#

The largest message taken, 1K to 1G, 25M unless given.

--max-recipients n#

The most recipients of one message, 100 unless given; past them a RCPT is answered 452.

--queue-lifetime duration#

How long a message is tried before it is bounced, 1m to 30d, 5d unless given.

--autoexpunge duration#

How long a message stays in a user's Junk or Trash, from when it was put there, before it is expunged, 1h to 3650d; never unless given. The first shard sweeps every user it has met hourly.

--dkim-selector name#

The selector its DKIM key is published and signed under, skl unless given; its Ed25519 key is name-ed.

--dkim-next name#

A selector whose keys are made and published, not yet signed with, for a key's rotation.

--arc-trust domain[,domain...]#

Forwarders, such as a mailing list's domain, whose ARC seal of a chain that passes lets mail through that fails DMARC because they forwarded it.

--sieve port#

ManageSieve (RFC 5804), for the users' Sieve scripts; needs --idp and --storage.

--pop3 port#

POP3, STLS on it; needs --idp and --storage.

--pop3s port#

POP3 over TLS from the first byte.

--jmap port#

JMAP for the mailboxes, HTTPS with --tls; needs --idp and --storage.

--web port#

The webmail, and JMAP beside it, in plain HTTP on 127.0.0.1 for the entrance in front of it, which takes the TLS (see Webmail); needs --idp and --storage.

--domain name[,name...]#

The names the entrance of a dns runtime with --proxy reaches the webmail under, a name without a dot under each of its zones, as webmail or mail; needs --web. Under each of its zones the webmail also answers autoconfig and autodiscover, where mail clients ask how a mailbox is reached: Thunderbird's /mail/config-v1.1.xml (and /.well-known/autoconfig/), Outlook's /autodiscover/autodiscover.xml and the JSON lookup that points at it, with _autodiscover._tcp in the zone; each names its host, the ports it opens with TLS, and the address as the login, and an address of no domain it keeps is answered 404. A user signed in to the webmail finds the same under Settings, and a profile that sets up an iPhone, an iPad or a Mac at once (/~mail/mobileconfig).

--lmtp port#

LMTP for this machine's own programs, into the mailboxes only; a connection from elsewhere is closed.

--mta-sts enforce|testing#

Publish an MTA-STS policy (RFC 8461) of that mode naming its host.

--mta-sts-port port#

Serve the policy over HTTPS on this port, with the certificate of --tls, which the daemon's ACME asks for mta-sts.domain too; senders fetch it on 443.

--tls-rpt address#

Publish where TLS reports (RFC 8460) about its domains go.

--dmarc-rua address#

Publish where DMARC aggregate reports about its domains go.

--dmarc-policy none|quarantine|reject#

What its DMARC record asks of mail that claims its domains and fails SPF and DKIM; quarantine unless given, reject once the reports show only its own mail passes.

--bimi https://logo.svg[,https://certificate.pem]#

Publish a BIMI record, its SVG logo, and the mark certificate the providers that show a logo beside a message (Gmail among them) ask for; a domain DMARC quarantines or rejects is shown.

--reports#

Send the DMARC and TLS reports other domains ask for.

--greylist duration#

Greylist strangers (RFC 6647) for this long, such as 5m; 0 for none.

--refuse-attachments ext[,ext...]|default|none#

Mail from elsewhere with an attachment of one of these extensions is refused, 554, its name in the answer: unless given, programs, scripts, shortcuts, disk images and Office documents with macros (exe, scr, js, vbs, ps1, lnk, iso, docm, xlsm and the rest of Gmail's list).

--clamav host:port|socket#

The clamd every message from elsewhere is streamed to (INSTREAM) before it is taken; one it names a virus in is refused with that name, and one it does not answer for is taken and logged, as Rspamd's silence is.

--rspamd url#

The Rspamd that scans mail from elsewhere, such as http://127.0.0.1:11333. Without it, or where it did not answer, mail is scored by the runtime's own filter, which learns from the users: a message moved into Junk is spam, and one moved out of it, or filed from the INBOX into a folder of their own, is not, over IMAP, JMAP and the webmail's Report junk and Not junk alike. Its words are those of the subject, the text and the HTML's text, the From's domain and the links' hosts, weighed as SpamBayes does (Robinson's chi-square of Fisher); a message is learned once, and one said otherwise is learned again. Once it has learned 20 of each, every message is given its score as x-spam-bayes, and one of 0.9 or more is put in Junk; nothing is refused for it. socketley mail learn user/folder --as spam|ham teaches it a folder at once, and socketley stats says how much it learned (mail_bayes_spam, mail_bayes_ham) and how much it put in Junk (mail_bayes_junked).

--recipient-delimiter chars|none#

What divides a user from a tag in an address, + unless it says.

--default-quota size#

The quota of a user whose idp account names none; 0 for no bound.

--quota-warn percent#

How full a user's mailboxes get before they are told, 90 unless it says; 0 for never.

--dnsbl zone[,zone...]#

DNS blocklists (RFC 5782), such as zen.spamhaus.org: a stranger's address is asked under each as it connects, and MAIL from one a list names is refused with 554.

stats says what was received, delivered, deferred, failed and bounced, the other delivery reports, what is queued and its bytes, the spool's commits, segments and moves, the recipients and relays refused, what was too big, the spool's failures, what was checked and what DMARC refused or quarantined, the bounces taken and the addresses suppressed, what was stored in mailboxes, the sign-ins and their failures, STARTTLS and TLS failures, the connections out, their TLS and transactions, the certificates DANE and MTA-STS checked and the connections refused for want of TLS, the policies fetched and what testing ones would have failed, what Sieve rejected, sent on and answered on vacation, the MX lookups, what the spam filter refused and filed in Junk, what was greylisted, the reports sent, and the IMAP connections and reads.

sections.title: TUNNEL FLAGS
sections.html:
A tunnel runtime makes a machine that has no address of its own reachable — one at home behind a router, behind carrier-grade NAT, on a network that lets only port 443 out. The machine runs an agent that dials out to an edge, a tunnel runtime on a machine the internet reaches, and holds that one connection open; the edge serves the agent's services under its own names and carries each visitor through the connection the agent made. Nothing is opened on the router.

# on the machine with the address
socketley create tunnel edge --mode edge -p 9450 --domain edge --idp auth -s
# on the machine at home, signed in as an admin of auth
socketley tunnel join https://edge.example.com --http home=127.0.0.1:8123 --tcp mc:25565=127.0.0.1:25565

An HTTP service is named beside the edge, here https://home.example.com: the edge serves it on a socket the entrance routes that name to, with the entrance's certificate, and the dns runtime answers the name, once the agent has joined. A name a runtime has stays that runtime's, another runtime is not given a name a service has, and of two edges with a service of one name the first by name keeps it. An edge named as a whole domain has no name beside it, and its services none. A TCP service is a port on the edge, here 25565. The edge says nothing about a stream it carries: what reaches the agent is what the visitor sent, and the service answers as if they were on the same machine, except that an HTTP request reaches it without the idp's session and known-device cookies, which sign in wherever the idp is trusted, and without the Authorization a service's auth took. A TCP visitor comes to a service at 127.0.0.1 or localhost from 127.0.0.2, so one that trusts this machine's own programs at 127.0.0.1, as mail lets them relay, takes it for a stranger; a service named at [::1] is reached from ::1.

Who may visit. An HTTP service invited as name=auth lets through only the requests auth admits, with what a proxy's --auth takes: idp:runtime sends a browser to sign in and back, bearer:file and basic:file ask for a token or a key, and several joined by + let in a visitor any one of them admits: idp:auth+bearer:/etc/socketley/hub.token takes a person signed in and a program with the token alike. Every request is asked, not only a connection's first, since the entrance hands one connection to the edge from visitor to visitor; nothing of a refused request reaches the agent, a body is carried as a body and never read as the next request, and a connection whose upgrade the service refused ends with that answer. A TCP service is the agent's to guard.

Each connection is a multiplexed link (one TLS connection, many streams, each with its own credit so one slow reader holds back only its own stream), opened by an HTTP upgrade at /.tunnel that passes the entrance like any other. An agent pings every 15 seconds; a link silent for 45 is given up and the agent dials again, after a pause that doubles to half a minute.

Who may connect. socketley tunnel join is an admin of the edge's --idp adding an agent; or, without an idp, socketley tunnel edge invite on the edge's machine prints an invitation once, for the agent's --join;theagentjoinswithitatitsfirstconnectionand is given a key of its own in its place, kept in its state directory (0600), and the invitation is spent. The edge keeps only hashes. revoke cuts an agent off within a second; set changes what it offers and keeps its key.

People. An edge with --forward carries a person signed in at its --idp to the targets it names, and to nothing else, as socketley tunnel connect or tunnel ssh asks; this is how ssh reaches a server through port 443. Its sign-in is asked again at every stream and once a second, so signing the account out everywhere, disabling, resetting or removing it closes the person's link, and taking it out of admins takes away the agents' TCP services at its next stream:

Host server
    ProxyCommand socketley tunnel ssh edge.example.com
--mode edge|agent#

Which end this is; an edge unless told.

-p port#

An edge's port for agents and people, on 127.0.0.1 unless --bind says otherwise, since the entrance in front of it terminates TLS.

--domain name#

An edge's name, beside which its agents' HTTP services are named: home.example.com for an edge edge.example.com.

--to url#

The edge an agent dials, https://host [:port]; http:// only for one on the same machine.

--join invitation#

What invite printed, used once.

--offer service=host:port,...#

What an agent carries the edge's streams to, by the service names the edge invited it with; a name it does not offer is refused at the agent.

--forward host:port,...#

Where an edge carries a signed-in person's stream.

--idp idp#

The idp runtime whose people may use --forward, and whose admins add agents with tunnel join.

--idp-audience client,...#

The clients whose access tokens are taken; socketley (the client socketley login signs in as) when none is named.

A tunnel takes no --shards: each agent's link is held by one process.

sections.title: METRICS FLAGS
sections.html:
A metrics runtime keeps what socketley and the machines around it measure, years of it, and answers for it with PromQL over the Prometheus HTTP API, so Grafana reads it as it reads a Prometheus. This daemon's own series reach it without a line of text: at each tick it asks the daemon for what changed since the last, the same series /metrics writes, with job="socketley" and instance the daemon's name; other daemons and any Prometheus endpoint are scraped. Its rules raise alerts the daemon's daemon.alert_webhook, daemon.alert_mail and daemon.events carry, and the dashboard draws its history from it.

socketley create metrics metrics -p 9090 --scrape /etc/socketley/targets -s
socketley metrics query 'rate(socketley_runtime_messages_total[5m])'

Every sample is stamped with the time its tick was due, so a series' samples lie an interval apart and take one to three bytes each; two hours of them are cut into a block on disk, two hour blocks merged into a day, and coarser tiers of each five minutes and each hour, with the minimum, maximum, sum, count, last value and a counter's increase of the step, built beside them. A query over a long range reads the coarsest tier that still answers it exactly, so a year of a dashboard reads a year of hourly points rather than three million samples.

-p, --port port#

The API's port, 9090 by default. It listens on 127.0.0.1 unless --bind names another address, which only a runtime guarded by --keys or --idp may do; from outside the machine it is reached through the entrance with --domain, as any HTTP runtime is.

--keys file#

Service keys, a line each of a name and a secret, as a db runtime reads them, read again when the file changes. A request carries one as Authorization: Bearer secret or as Basic with the name and the secret, which is what Grafana's data source sends.

--idp idp#

Lets in the sign-ins of that idp runtime, a browser's session cookie or an access token as Bearer.

--idp-audience clients#

The clients, a comma between, one of which an access token's audience must name.

--local, --no-local#

Whether this daemon's own series are taken; on by default.

--scrape file#

The targets to scrape, a line each:

Details
# name url [every=<duration>] [timeout=<duration>] [bearer=<file>] [label=value ...]
jetson http://127.0.0.1:9101/metrics every=15s site=home
node   https://box.example.com/metrics bearer=/etc/socketley/node.token

Each sample of a target is given job = its name and instance = its host and port, and its own labels; a target writes up, scrape_duration_seconds and scrape_samples_scraped, and the series it stops writing, or all of them when it does not answer, end at once with Prometheus's staleness marker. A file changed is read again at the next tick, and one that does not read leaves the targets as they were. A daemon at home reached through a tunnel is scraped as a loopback TCP service of its agent, so nothing is opened on its router.

--every duration#

How often this daemon's series are taken and a target is scraped without its own every=; 10s by default, from 1s to 1h.

--keep duration#

How long raw samples are kept; 30d by default.

--downsample step:keep[,...]#

The coarser tiers, 5m:1y,1h:5y by default, or none. The first step divides two hours, and each later one is a multiple of the one before that divides a day.

--max-series n#

The most series held at once, 200000 by default; a new one past it is refused and counted in socketley_metrics_series_refused_total, so one target that sends a label per request cannot take the machine's memory.

--durable#

Every sample logged as it arrives, so a crash loses none; without it a crash loses what the open chunks hold, a stop nothing.

--rules file#

Recording and alerting rules, laid over the built-in ones (the alerts DASHBOARD lists):

Details
every=10s
alert DiskSpaceLow warning for=1m summary="{{ $labels.path }}: {{ $value | humanizePercentage }} free"
    : socketley_disk_free_ratio < 0.15
alert JetsonGone critical for=2m : up{job="jetson"} == 0
record job:requests:rate5m : sum by (job) (rate(http_requests_total[5m]))
off TargetDown

A rule is a line, carried on by lines that begin with a space, its expression after : . alert takes a name and a severity, then for=, keep= (how long it keeps firing once its condition is gone), every= for its own interval, inhibits=rule[,...] for alerts it silences on the labels both have, summary=, description= and runbook_url= as annotations, and any other label=value as a label; values and annotations take Prometheus's templates ({{ $value }}, {{ $labels.name }}, humanize, humanize1024, humanizePercentage, humanizeDuration, printf). record writes its result as a series of that name. A rule named as a built-in one takes its place, and off name leaves one out. The file is read again when it changes, and one that does not read leaves the rules as they were and is logged. An alert is pending while its condition holds for less than for=, then firing, which is when it is told of, and resolved, told of too; its state is kept in the runtime's directory, so a restart neither tells of one again nor starts its for= over. The ALERTS and ALERTS_FOR_STATE series are written as Prometheus writes them.

--notify where#

Where an alert is told of: webhook, mail and events with a comma between, the daemon's daemon.alert_webhook, daemon.alert_mail and daemon.events; all three by default, or none.

--receive#

Takes Prometheus remote_write at POST /api/v1/write, a Snappy-compressed WriteRequest of up to 16 MiB, its samples stored as they come and the ones refused counted in stats; a Prometheus, a Grafana Agent or another metrics runtime behind a firewall then sends what it has instead of being scraped.

--logs, --no-logs#

Keeps every line the daemon and its runtimes write as well, taken with the series at each tick, a file a day in logs/ of the runtime's directory, and answers for them with LogQL over Loki's API, so Grafana's Loki data source reads it as it reads a Loki. A line is labelled job="socketley", instance (the daemon), level (debug, info, warn, error) and name (the runtime it is about: the one that wrote it, or the one a line of the daemon's names); a start takes no line twice. socketley_log_lines_total counts them by name and level, for a rule such as increase(socketley_log_lines_total{level="error"}[5m]) > 0. LogQL taken: a selector with =, !=, =~, !~, line filters |= "text", != "text", |~ "regex" and !~ "regex" (found anywhere in the line), and over them count_over_time, rate, bytes_over_time and bytes_rate with sum, count, min, max, avg by or without labels; a query without a selector is PromQL. Off by default.

--logs-keep duration#

How long log lines are kept, in whole days; 14d by default.

--archive url#

An S3 bucket, and a key prefix after it, every block on disk is copied to once it holds a day or more or ended two days ago: http[s]://host/bucket[/prefix] — a storage runtime of this daemon or any S3. What is copied is listed in archived in the runtime's directory and never copied again; a copy refused is tried again each minute, and said in the log once. The archive keeps what --keep and --downsample let go here: blocks copied back into blocks/ of a stopped runtime are read at its start, a piece a later merge replaced dropped as one inside a bigger block. A block the retention removes while the archive refuses everything is not copied.

--archive-credentials file#

The bucket's access_key and secret_key, and region and session_token when it takes them, a key = value line each as a sync runtime's --credentials holds them, read again at each copy.

The API. /api/v1/query, query_range, series, labels, label/name/values, metadata, targets, rules, alerts, status/buildinfo, status/runtimeinfo and query_exemplars by GET or a POSTed form, answered in Prometheus's envelope; /-/healthy and /-/ready; with --logs, /loki/api/v1/query_range, query, labels and label/name/values; and /metrics with the runtime's own figures. A Grafana data source of type Prometheus is pointed at https://domain or http://127.0.0.1:port with the key as Basic auth or a Bearer header. The PromQL is Prometheus's: selectors, ranges and offset; the arithmetic, comparison and set operators with on, ignoring, group_left and group_right; the aggregations with by and without; rate, irate, increase, delta, deriv, predict_linear and the _over_time functions; histogram_quantile, label_replace, label_join, absent, the time and maths functions. Not taken: subqueries, @, native histograms.

The CLI.

socketley metrics <rt> query '<promql>' [--at <time>]
socketley metrics <rt> query_range '<promql>' [--start <time>] [--end <time>] [--step <duration>]
socketley metrics <rt> series '<selector>' | targets | rules | alerts [--recent] | stats   [--json]
socketley metrics <rt> logs ['<logql>'] [--since <duration>] [--limit <n>]

socketley export writes a metrics runtime's settings as any runtime's; socketley export --full first has a running one write out what its head holds and hold its merges until the archive is written, so a restore brings back every sample to that moment.

A time is now, -1h, unix seconds or RFC 3339; a range ends now and starts an hour back by default. --json prints what the API answers. --shards is refused: one process holds 100000 series at 10s, and a series is written by one process.

sections.title: MCP FLAGS
sections.html:
An mcp runtime is a Model Context Protocol server: an AI client such as Claude Code, or an agent built on an MCP SDK, connects to it and is offered the tools, resources and prompts its script declares, and, with --tools daemon, this daemon's runtimes as tools.

socketley create mcp shop -p 9600 --domain mcp --keys /etc/socketley/mcp.keys \
    --lua /etc/socketley/shop.lua --tools daemon -s

It speaks Streamable HTTP at /mcp (and /): one JSON-RPC message a POST, answered as JSON, a notification 202 with nothing; GET and DELETE are 405, since there is no stream of its own and no session. It speaks revision 2026-07-28 as that revision has it, stateless: every request carries MCP-Protocol-Version and its version and client capabilities in _meta, Mcp-Method names the method and Mcp-Name the tool, prompt or resource, and a mismatch is 400 (-32020); server/discover says what it has. A client that opens with initialize is answered as 2025-11-25, 2025-06-18 or 2025-03-26 have it, and its requests are taken without the 2026 headers: the MCP SDKs of 2026 speak that revision. A version neither era has is 400 (-32022), naming the ones it speaks. Every request is answered on its own, so --shards spreads them over processes as a server's are. It listens on plain HTTP and is reached through the entrance proxy, which terminates TLS for it.

--keys file#

The keys that may ask, a line each: name secret, and admin after the secret of one that may change the daemon; the secret at least 16 characters, sent as Authorization: Bearer. A request without a key of the file is 401 with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer. Read again when it changes; one that no longer reads keeps the keys before it and says why in the log.

--anonymous#

Asked by anyone, with no key: for a port only this machine reaches (--bind 127.0.0.1). One of --keys, --idp and --anonymous is required, and --anonymous goes with neither of the others.

--origins list#

The web origins a browser may call it from, comma-separated, or * for any. A request with any other Origin is 403, as the revision asks of every server; a client that is no browser sends none.

--idp runtime#

The idp runtime whose people sign in, as the MCP revisions have a client do: a request without a token is 401 with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata naming /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp, which says the server is https://name/mcp for the first --domain, a whole name such as mcp.example.com, and names the idp; the client signs in there for that resource, and its access token is taken for that audience alone. The idp gives such tokens with --resources naming the address. A key of --keys is taken beside it. An account of the idp's admins group is an admin here; one disabled or signed out everywhere is refused from its next request.

--idp-audience clients#

The idp's clients, comma-separated, whose own access tokens are taken as well.

--tools none|daemon#

daemon offers this daemon's runtimes: socketley_list and socketley_get (name, type, state, port, connections, owner) to every key, and socketley_start and socketley_stop to an admin's alone; a key that may not administer is not shown them. A server does not stop itself. A tool of the script's own of the same name is the script's.

--instructions text#

What a client is told the server is for.

The script declares, at its start:

mcp.tool{ name = "order_status", description = "An order's state.", read_only = true,
  input = { type = "object", properties = { id = { type = "string" } }, required = { "id" } },
  handler = function(args, who) return { structured = { id = args.id, state = "sent" } } end }
mcp.resource{ uri = "shop://catalog", mime = "text/plain", ttl_ms = 60000,
  read = function(who) return "..." end }
mcp.prompt{ name = "summarize", arguments = { { name = "order", required = true } },
  get = function(args, who) return "Summarize order " .. args.order end }

A tool's input and output are a JSON Schema, a table or JSON text (an empty object is written as JSON text, since a table cannot tell it from an empty array); read_only (false), destructive (not read_only), idempotent (read_only) and open_world (true) are its hints, and admin offers it to an admin's key alone. A handler answers a string, as text; a table with text or content, the content blocks as the revision has them; with structured, structured content, sent as text too; and with error = true, a failure the model reads, as is a handler that raises. A handler may wait on socketley.http, socketley.db and the other calls that wait, and the runtime answers other calls meanwhile. A resource's read answers a string, or a table with text or blob (base64) and mime; a prompt's get a string, a user's message, or a table with description and messages of role and text. Each gets who, the key's or the account's name and whether it is admin, and for an account its sub, the id that never changes, and runs on the event loop inside the callback deadline. A declaration that does not read answers nil and why, and says so in the log.

stats shows requests, tool_calls, tool_errors, errors (answered with a JSON-RPC error), legacy_requests (of a revision before 2026), refused (a key, an origin or a method), tools, resources, prompts and keys.

sections.title: REGISTERED TYPES
sections.html:
A runtime type beyond the built-in seven is delivered as a manifest plus a worker binary. The daemon reads the manifest — a declarative file, never code — to learn the type's name, its worker executable, and the schema of its configuration keys; the behaviour lives in the binary, which the daemon forks and execs exactly as it does its own workers. No third-party code ever runs in the daemon's process.

Manifests are read at daemon startup from /etc/socketley/types/*.toml for a system daemon and ~/.config/socketley/types/*.toml for a development daemon:

name = "greeter"
exec = "/usr/local/lib/socketley/greeter-worker"
manifest_version = 1

[config.greeting]
kind = "string"        # string | int | bool | enum
required = true

[config.repeat]
kind = "int"
default = "1"

Each [config.key] section becomes a --key flag on create and edit, is validated against its kind, and is persisted under an extra object in the state file, which show prints and import accepts. A key the manifest does not declare is refused by name, exactly as a misspelled built-in flag is. A required key must be given at create; a declared default is filled in when the key is omitted. An edit takes effect at the next start, because the worker reads its configuration once, when it is spawned.

The worker binary is built with the SDK's <socketley/worker.h> — register_type with a factory for the type, then run(argc, argv) — and speaks the same versioned control-socket protocol as the daemon's own workers, so it survives daemon upgrades that do not change frame meanings. A worked example is sdk/examples/custom-type/.

A registered type cannot be created from a runtime's Lua script, and a state file whose type has no manifest on the next boot is left on disk and not restored, with the reason in the daemon log.

sections.title: LUA CONFIGURATION
sections.html:
Two different files are both called “a Lua script”, and they do not mix.

  • A daemon configuration — socketley --lua config.lua. This runs in the CLI process, is read for its daemon and runtimes tables, brings the daemon to what they say and then exits; the daemon reads the same tables from its own configuration file when it starts. It never becomes part of any runtime. A callback defined in such a file is dead code: nothing loads it, nothing calls it, and nothing says so.

  • A runtime handler — socketley create server api -p 9000 --lua handler.lua, or the same path given as a runtime's config key inside a configuration. This one is loaded by the daemon into that runtime's own interpreter, and it is the only file whose on_* callbacks, filters and routes mean anything.

A configuration attaches a handler by naming its path, never by defining the callbacks itself:

runtimes = {
    { type = "server", name = "api", port = 9000,
      config = "handler.lua",     -- the file whose callbacks run
      start = true },
}

config and lua are accepted as spellings of the same key. Everything below this point in this chapter, except Configuration File Format itself, describes a runtime handler.

Module loading: The Lua require() function resolves modules relative to the script's directory. For a script at /home/user/handler.lua, require("utils") loads /home/user/utils.lua. The default Lua package path is appended, so standard modules still work.

Standard library: base, string, table, math, os, io and package are open. Six os functions are removed, because a daemon serving every runtime from one process cannot let one script reach outside its own runtime: os.execute, os.remove, os.rename, os.tmpname, os.exit and os.setlocale. The last of those is not a filesystem or process call and is removed for a reason of its own: setlocale is process-wide, and socketley.json_encode formats numbers with %.14g while socketley.json_decode parses them with strtod, both of which read LC_NUMERIC. One script switching to a comma-decimal locale therefore makes every runtime in the daemon emit 1,5 and truncate 1.5 to 1, for as long as the daemon lives. os.time, os.clock, os.date and os.difftime stay — those are reads.

sections.title: Configuration File Format
sections.html:
-- Optional: configure the daemon itself
daemon = {
    name = "node1",
    cluster = "/shared/cluster"
}

runtimes = {
    { type = "server", name = "api", port = 9000, group = "api",
      config = "handler.lua", start = true },
    { type = "client", name = "cli", port = 9000, target = "127.0.0.1:9000" },
    { type = "proxy",  name = "gw", port = 8080,
      backends = {"@api", "127.0.0.1:9000"}, strategy = "round-robin" },
    { type = "cache",  name = "store", port = 9001,
      persistent = "/data/store.bin" }
}

The daemon table is processed first (name, then cluster). If omitted, the daemon runs without cluster mode.

Its keys — name, cluster, log_level, metrics_port and cpus — are read by the daemon itself from the file SOCKETLEY_CONFIG names, at startup. The last three of those are settled before the ring exists and cannot be told to a daemon that is already serving, so socketley --lua refuses them by name rather than dropping them — except in the daemon's own file, where they are its next start's. A flag typed on socketley daemon outranks the same setting in the file. config is the table's older spelling and still works; naming both in one file is refused.

Recognised runtimes keys, and the flag each becomes. Every flag a create accepts is reachable from here, which is what makes a configuration file and a command line two spellings of one thing rather than two capabilities:

—— every type —————————————————————
type, name                 (required)
port                       -p
listen                     --listen
shards                     --shards
log                        --log
write                      -w
group                      -g
cpus                       --cpus
max_connections            --max-connections
rate_limit                 --rate-limit
global_rate_limit          --global-rate-limit
idle_timeout               --idle-timeout  300, or 5m / 2h / 1d
congestion                 --congestion    bbr
write_buffer               --write-buffer   8M, 256K, 65536
read_buffer                --read-buffer    1M, 8M, 65536
