Every other flag of a type is the key of its own name, its dashes gone and a hyphen an underscore: --mail-domain is mail_domain, --submission is submission, --queue-lifetime is queue_lifetime. A list key takes a table, or one string for the list of one. A key no flag of the type has is refused, naming it, rather than dropped in silence: a misspelled http_cache used to configure nothing while the runtime came up looking correct. A value of the wrong shape is refused the same way, and so is a value containing a tab — the daemon's command line splits on it, so a password with one in it would arrive as two arguments. A space is carried inside its value, as it is inside a quoted argument on the command line.

A key the daemon then refuses on that type — --client-ca on a cleartext proxy, say — is refused by the daemon, in the daemon's own words, under the name of the runtime it belongs to. The remaining entries are still applied, and the exit code is 1.

daemon_process was in this list and is gone with the flag it emitted. A configuration file still carrying it is refused, naming the line, rather than accepted with the key quietly dropped — which would leave an operator believing a runtime is in the daemon while it is not.

Nothing replaces it. The whole cross-runtime API works in a worker: socketley.send, .list, .get and socketley.cluster are answered from the replica map the daemon pushes; socketley.create, .start, .stop and .remove are asked of the daemon and wait for its answer; and socketley.pipe and self.route reach a runtime in another process. See Process Isolation above.

The health-check, circuit-breaker, retry and TLS families were unreachable from a configuration until the table above named every flag; a file written against that build still reads the same way.

The interpreter that reads this file is not the daemon's, and it is much smaller. It opens base, package, table, string and math — there is no os and no io. `os.execute("mkdir -p /tmp/logs")` at the top of a configuration is not a sandbox refusal but attempt to index global 'os' (a nil value): the whole file is refused, exit 1, and no runtime is created. Create the directories a configuration needs from the shell that invokes it. string and math are open because a configuration computes names and port numbers, and the daemon's own configuration file opens the same set, so one file can be read by either.

sections.title: A machine's setup
sections.html:
A setup is the runtimes of a machine as Lua files, so that another machine given the files is given the same runtimes; their data is not in them. include reads a file and is what it returns, or reads each .lua of a directory in the order of their names and is the list of what they return; a list among the runtimes is its entries. A relative path, whether an include's or a value's — a credentials file, a certificate, a handler script, a zone file — is one beside the first file, wherever the command was typed:

-- /etc/socketley/config.lua
daemon = { metrics_port = 9190, dashboard_idp = "auth" }
runtimes = {
    include "runtimes/ns.lua",
    include "runtimes/auth.lua",
    include "runtimes/sites",            -- every .lua in it
}

-- /etc/socketley/runtimes/ns.lua
return { type = "dns", name = "ns", zone = { "zones/example.com.zone" },
         publish = { "203.0.113.7" }, start = true }

socketley --lua brings the daemon to what the files say. A runtime it does not have is made; one it has is planned as create would make it from the file and compared with what show says of it, and where they differ it is told what differs — a setting the file no longer says is cleared — across a restart where it runs, and asked again, so a runtime that does not take a setting is named, exit 1. One that is as the file says is not touched. start starts or stops it; a runtime without start is left running or stopped as it is. A runtime of the daemon's that the files do not name is left alone.

The daemon reads the runtimes of its own configuration file when it starts, after the runtimes it kept, and makes each it has not, started where start says so; one it has is left as it is, for socketley --lua to bring to the file. A new machine therefore needs the files in /etc/socketley and nothing else run. socketley export writes a running machine's setup this way.

sections.title: Handler Privileges
sections.html:
A Lua handler runs with the daemon's full privileges. It is not sandboxed and there is no supported way to sandbox it. Read a handler the way you would read a program you are about to run as the user the daemon runs as, because that is exactly what it is.

Which makes the control socket's permission the whole of the boundary. A handler is attached with create --lua, which is an ordinary command on that socket, so whoever may open it may run code as the daemon's user. The socket is 0600 for a daemon you start yourself, and 0660 socketley:socketley for the packaged one — membership of that group is therefore equivalent to being the daemon's user, and should be granted on that understanding. This is the same arrangement Docker has, and it is worth stating rather than inferring: nothing else in this daemon stands between a local account and the handler.

Concretely, a handler can:

run any command#

io.popen("...") and os.execute("...") are both present.

read or write any file that user can#

io.open() is present in every mode, including w, which truncates.

load native code#

package.loadlib() is present, as are load(), loadstring(), dofile() and loadfile().

read the daemon's environment#

os.getenv() is present.

This is deliberate. Handlers legitimately read and write files — a logging pipeline appends to one, a configuration-driven handler reads its table off disk — so closing io would break supported use. What it means in practice is that the right to hand this daemon a --lua script is the right to run code as its user, and the thing that controls that right is the permission on the IPC socket, not anything in the interpreter. See THE IPC SOCKET under FILES.

A handler's interpreter opens base, string, table, math, os, io and package. Two names are removed from os, and calling one is attempt to call field '...' (a nil value) rather than a refusal with a reason:

os.exit    os.setlocale

Neither removal is a security boundary — nothing here is. The test both pass is narrower: one call damages the process that every other runtime in this daemon shares, and does so by accident rather than by intent. os.exit() ends the daemon from inside a callback, and a handler is very often a standalone script that grew into one, ending the way standalone scripts end. os.setlocale() changes the process's LC_NUMERIC, which is what socketley.json_encode and socketley.json_decode format and parse numbers with — one line in one handler and every other handler's JSON spells 1.5 as 1,5 and decodes it as 1, silently, for as long as the daemon lives.

os.time(), os.clock(), os.date() and os.difftime() remain: they are reads, and reading the clock or the locale harms nothing.

Earlier releases also removed os.execute(), os.remove(), os.rename() and os.tmpname(). Those four are back, because removing them denied no capability — io.popen is a shell and io.open(path, "w") truncates — while suggesting to anyone reading a handler that the daemon guarded its files and its shell. It did not. A fence with an open gate beside it is worse than no fence, because people plan around it.

Note that io.open and every write through it block the event loop for as long as the write takes.

require() resolves against the script's directory and then the default package.path, but package.cpath is left at its default and no binary module ships with socketley. A require of a C module — cjson, lsqlite3, a luasql driver — therefore fails unless that module is installed where the system Lua would find it. For JSON, use the built-in socketley.json_encode and socketley.json_decode instead; they need nothing installed.

sections.title: Available Callbacks
sections.html:
on_start()#

Called when runtime starts.

on_stop()#

Called when runtime stops.

on_message(msg)#

Called when message received (server/client). When defined on a server, this callback claims message handling: the default broadcast (in inout and master modes) is suppressed. Use self.broadcast(msg) to relay messages manually.

on_client_message(client_id, msg)#

Called when message received with sender identification (server only). Fires alongside on_message for backward compatibility.

on_http_body(client_id, chunk, remaining)#

A piece of a request body, with how many bytes are still owed after it — so remaining reaches 0 exactly once per body. Defining this callback IS the opt-in: a server whose script has it streams request bodies to it instead of gathering them, and a server whose script does not gets the behaviour it always had, including the 413 past --read-buffer.

Details

That is what makes a body larger than memory possible. The bytes are handed over and erased as they arrive, so req.body in the on_http_request that follows is deliberately EMPTY — carrying them a second time is the memory this exists to avoid. Measured on one worker, one connection at a time:

start             19,796 kB
after 50 MB #1    37,344 kB
after 50 MB #2    37,344 kB     unchanged
after 50 MB #3    37,344 kB     unchanged
after 200 MB      37,428 kB     +84 kB
after 500 MB      37,444 kB     +16 kB

The first upload costs 17.5 MB once, which is the provided-buffer ring being faulted in, and every one after it costs nothing: half a gigabyte received inside 37 MB resident.

Keep per-upload state keyed by client_id, and clear it in on_disconnect: a body that is abandoned never reaches on_http_request, so nothing there can be the reset, and on_disconnect is the only signal it produces. It does fire, with whatever arrived, which is what a script writing to a temporary file needs in order to remove it.

local st = {}
function on_http_body(id, chunk, remaining)
    st[id] = (st[id] or 0) + #chunk
    if remaining == 0 then ... end
end
function on_disconnect(id) st[id] = nil end

A body of unknown length. A client that cannot say how long its body is sends Transfer-Encoding: chunked — fetch() with a ReadableStream body, anything piping a process's output, anything that cannot stat what it is sending — and that used to be 501. With on_http_body defined it is decoded and delivered like any other body, unbounded, because there is no length to bound it by.

remaining is nil for every chunk of such a body, since how much is still owed is genuinely not knowable, and the end of the framing produces ONE final call with an empty chunk and remaining = 0. So "remaining reaches 0 exactly once per body" holds for both forms and a script written against Content-Length needs no change. Measured, 62 MB in 1000 chunks: 1708 calls, 1707 of them nil and one zero; 250 MB after that costs 148 kB more resident memory.

Chunked and nothing else. Transfer-Encoding: gzip, chunked is framable — the chunk sizes do delimit it — and its contents are still compressed, so taking the framing off and handing the bytes on as the body would hand on gzip and call it the body. That stays 501. A coding that is not chunked at all leaves the message with no way to say where the body ends and is a 400.

Trailers are consumed, bounded at 8 KB, and discarded: turning them into headers after the request has been dispatched is how a trailer becomes request smuggling. Framing that contradicts itself — a chunk not followed by CRLF, a size that is not hex, a size line past 256 bytes — is a 400, because nothing after it can be trusted to be payload.

Header names keep the case the client sent them in, so req.headers["Host"] and not req.headers["host"].

on_upstream_writable(conn_id)#

An upstream's write queue has come back under self.watermark(), so a producer that stopped because self.upstream_pending(conn_id) was high can carry on. Its own callback and not on_writable, because an upstream id and a client id are different spaces and one function taking both would have to be told which it had been given.

on_writable(client_id)#

The write queue for this connection has come back down under self.watermark(), so a producer that stopped because self.pending(client_id) was high can carry on. Edge-triggered: it fires on the crossing, once per crossing, not once per completed write.

Details

A client runtime has the same callback without the argument — on_writable() — because it has one connection and a number naming it would be a fiction. Its refusal is named too: a connected --mode out client whose server has stopped reading used to be told it "is not connected to its server, or was created --mode in and does not send", three statements that are all false of it. Measured, 400 chunks of 64 KB into a peer reading nothing: 129 taken, 271 refused, 8,396,928 bytes standing.

This is what makes a body larger than the queue bound sendable at all. Without it a script had the hard bound and nothing leading up to it — at 8 MiB the connection is closed — so the only safe strategy was to know the bound in advance and never approach it. Measured with a client reading in 256 KB bites with a 5 ms pause, sending 200 chunks of 64 KB (13,107,400 bytes):

unpaced   8,454,273 bytes delivered, then the connection closed
paced    13,107,400 bytes delivered, on_writable fired 3 times

Pace against self.watermark() and not a number of your own. It is a call and not a field because --write-buffer is editable, and a number copied into the script's table at load would go stale the moment it moved. The callback fires on the crossing, so a producer that stops below the watermark never crosses it and is never called back — it would wait for an event its own caution prevented:

local function pump(id)
    while remaining > 0 do
        if (self.pending(id) or 0) >= self.watermark() then return end
        if not self.send(id, next_chunk()) then return end
        remaining = remaining - 1
    end
end

function on_writable(id) pump(id) end

The call is made a loop turn after the write that emptied the queue, not on that write's completion, so a connection that closes in between is simply not called.

on_connect(client_id)#

Called when a client connects (server/client). Also called on a sub-server when a connection is routed to it. The client_id is opaque: for this runtime's own clients it is the file descriptor, and for a connection routed here from another runtime it is a handle above 16777216 that names the connection wherever it lives. Pass it back to self.send(), self.owner_send(), or anything else taking a client_id; do not compare it against a descriptor or assume anything about its value.

on_disconnect(client_id)#

Called when a client disconnects (server/client).

on_rcpt(rcpt, default) -> bool#

A mail runtime's, deciding each recipient as it is said, and told each message taken by on_message(msg). See Lua under MAIL FLAGS.

on_publish(client, msg) -> bool | tableon_subscribe(client, filter, qos) -> bool#

An mqtt runtime's, deciding what passes; there on_auth, on_connect and on_disconnect are given a client table. See Lua under MQTT FLAGS.

on_send(msg)#

Called when message sent.

on_route(method, path, backend_path)#

Proxy only, and --strategy lua only. Custom backend selection. Returns backend index (0-based). Answers only "where does this go"; to accept or refuse a request before any backend is chosen, see Proxy Filter Chain.

Details

The strategy is what consults it. A proxy created without --strategy lua keeps round-robin (or random, if that was asked for) and never looks the callback up, so a script defining on_route on such a proxy is loaded, is reported by nothing, and routes exactly as if the function were not there. That is the usual reason a on_route that was tested and works appears to do nothing.

path is the path as the client sent it, this proxy's own /name/ prefix included, and backend_path is the same path with that prefix removed — what the backend will actually receive. A proxy named gw handed /gw/api/users sees both:

function on_route(method, path, backend_path)
    -- path         == "/gw/api/users"
    -- backend_path == "/api/users"
    if backend_path:match("^/api/") then return 0 end
    return 1
end

Both are offered because both are the truth about a different thing: the filter chain judges the request the client made, so it is handed path, and a routing decision is usually about the endpoint being addressed, which is backend_path.

backend_path exists so that scripts stop computing it. Doing it by hand means stripping "/" .. self.name .. "/" and getting the bare case right, and the bare case is the one nobody gets right: the gateway's own root arrives as /gw — three characters against a five-character prefix — and must become /, where a sub() past the end yields the empty string and matches no pattern at all.

The arguments are passed on --protocol http only. A TCP proxy has no request line to read them from and calls on_route with none, so a body written for HTTP — `return hash(path) % n` — raises on the first request when it is moved to a TCP proxy.

A handler declaring two parameters is unaffected: Lua discards arguments a function does not name, so every on_route written before this existed behaves exactly as it did.

A call that raises, or that returns anything other than an index inside the backend list, selects nothing: the proxy reports the error on stderr and falls back to the selection it would have made without the callback. The request is forwarded either way. Refusing a request is the filter chain's job, not this one's.

filters#

Proxy only. Not a callback but an array of them: see Proxy Filter Chain.

routes#

Not a callback either, but a table this runtime declares about what it answers, which the daemon publishes to the proxies in front of it: see Declared Routes.

on_proxy_request(client_id, data) -> string | nil#

Proxy only. Called for every chunk forwarded from a client to a backend. Return a modified string to replace the data, or nil to drop the chunk entirely (the backend never receives it).

Details

Returning nothing at all forwards the chunk unchanged, and that is not the same as returning nil. A hook written to watch traffic (function on_proxy_request(id, data) log(data) end) ends without a return, and reading that as nil made the most natural three lines in this API discard every byte through the proxy. The filter chain draws the same distinction — nothing returned means the filter has no opinion and the chain continues.

Fail-closed, like the filter chain and for the same reason. A hook that throws a Lua error, or that returns anything other than a string or nil, refuses the request: the connection to the client and the one to the backend are both closed, and the reason is logged. The hook is where a script strips a header or rejects a request, so forwarding the unmodified bytes when it could not run would admit exactly what it was there to refuse — and return false is a rejection, not a value to guess at.

The refusal closes rather than answering a status: this callback is on the byte path, is called with body chunks as well as with the request head, and carries TCP as readily as HTTP. To refuse a request with a status line, use the filter chain — see Proxy Filter Chain.

on_proxy_response(client_id, data) -> string | nil#

Proxy only. Called for every chunk forwarded from a backend to a client. Same semantics as on_proxy_request: returning nothing forwards the chunk unchanged, a replacement string replaces it, nil drops it, and an error or a return of any other type refuses — here by closing the client connection, since the response this hook was to redact must not be delivered unredacted.

on_master_auth(client_id, password) -> bool#

Server only (master mode). Custom authentication. Return true to grant the master role. If defined, overrides --master-pw, so this callback is the entire gate on that server. Read strictly, and fail-closed: only the boolean true grants. Anything else denies — false, nil, no return at all, and every truthy non-boolean such as a string, the number 0 or a table. If the callback throws a Lua error the attempt is denied and the error is logged. A denial from this callback is counted against the source address exactly as a wrong --master-pw is, so the per-address lockout described there applies here too.

on_auth(client_id) -> bool#

Server only. Called immediately after a client is accepted, before on_connect fires. Return true to admit the client or false to reject and close the connection. If the callback throws a Lua error, the client is also rejected (fail-closed). When no on_auth callback is defined, all clients are admitted.

on_websocket(client_id, headers)#

Server only. Called immediately after a WebSocket upgrade handshake completes, after on_connect has already fired. The headers argument is a Lua table containing any subset of the following keys from the HTTP upgrade request: cookie, origin, protocol (Sec-WebSocket-Protocol), and authorization. Only keys present in the request are set; absent headers are nil. This callback never fires for plain TCP clients.

on_http_request(req) -> table#

Server only. Called when an HTTP request is received (auto-detected from the first bytes; see Multi-Protocol Auto-Detection). The req argument is a table with the following fields:

Details
method      string   HTTP method ("GET", "POST", etc.)
path        string   Request path (e.g. "/api/users")
query       string   Query string without leading ? (empty if none)
body        string   Request body (empty for GET)
client_id   number   File descriptor of the client
version     string   HTTP version (e.g. "1.1")
headers     table    Request headers {["Host"]="...", ...}

Header names arrive as the client spelled them. Values arrive with optional whitespace — spaces and tabs — removed from both ends, so X-Token:  abc  reaches the callback as abc. The callback is not reached at all by a request whose framing this server refuses; see Request Framing above for what those are and what they are answered.

Return a table with the HTTP response:

{
    status  = 200,                              -- HTTP status code
    headers = {["Content-Type"] = "text/html"}, -- response headers
    body    = "<h1>Hello</h1>"                  -- response body
}

If no on_http_request callback is defined, the server falls back to static file serving (--http) or returns 404. Returning nothing, or anything that is not a table, means the same thing: the request falls through to the static file or the 404. Only nil and no return at all are silent about it — those are how a handler declines. Anything else is a script that meant to answer, so the fall-through is named in the daemon's log as [lua <runtime>] on_http_request returned a string; expected a table or nil ....

In the returned table, status must be a number, body a string, and headers a table of string to string. A field the script never set takes its default (200, an empty body, no headers), but a status or body that is present and of the wrong type is a response this server cannot build: the request is answered 500 Internal Server Error, and the field and the type it arrived as are written to the daemon's log. A header whose name or value is not a string costs the client that one header rather than the whole answer, and is logged the same way. None of these were reported before, and a body that was not a string was served as a 200 with nothing in it.

Supports HTTP/1.1 keep-alive — the connection is reused for subsequent requests unless the client's Connection header asked to close, which is honoured for a Lua response exactly as it is for a static file.

A callback that raises is not a callback that declined. The request is answered 500 Internal Server Error, and the error is written to the daemon's log as [lua <runtime>] on_http_request error: .... Falling through to the 404 would make a handler that broke indistinguishable, at the client, from one that had no answer.

Example:

function on_http_request(req)
    if req.method == "GET" and req.path == "/health" then
        return {status = 200, body = "ok"}
    end
    return {
        status  = 200,
        headers = {["Content-Type"] = "application/json"},
        body    = '{"method": "' .. req.method .. '", "path": "' .. req.path .. '"}'
    }
end
on_tick(dt)#

Called at a configurable interval while the runtime is running. dt is the actual elapsed time in milliseconds since the last tick (double). Requires a top-level tick_ms global to be set in the Lua script: a whole number of milliseconds, 10 or more, defaulting to 100 when the global is omitted. A value below 10, or one that is not a whole number, refuses the script at load with a reason rather than being rounded into something else — 10 is the shortest interval on_tick can be armed at, and a script that asks for less is asking for something the daemon will not do. Example:

Details
tick_ms = 50
function on_tick(dt)
    self.broadcast("ping")
end
on_miss(key) -> value [, ttl_seconds]#

Cache only. Called when GET finds nothing, so the script can fetch the value from somewhere else; what it returns is stored and answered as a hit. See Database Backend for the four cache callbacks in full, with their ordering and their failure behaviour.

on_write(key, value, ttl)#

Cache only. Called after a successful SET/SETEX/SETNX/MSET.

on_delete(key)#

Cache only. Called after a DEL that removed something.

on_expire(key)#

Cache only. Called after the TTL sweep removes a key.

on_upstream(conn_id, data)#

Server only. Called for each newline-delimited message received from an upstream connection. Use -u to configure upstreams.

on_upstream_connect(conn_id)#

Server only. Called when an upstream connects (including auto-reconnects).

on_upstream_disconnect(conn_id)#

Server only. Called when an upstream disconnects.

on_cluster_join(daemon)#

Cluster only. Called when a new remote daemon is discovered. See Cluster Event Callbacks.

on_cluster_leave(daemon)#

Cluster only. Called when a remote daemon becomes stale or disappears.

on_group_change(group, members)#

Cluster only. Called when the member count of a group changes.

Same semantics as on_proxy_request: returning nothing forwards the chunk unchanged, a replacement string replaces it, nil drops it, and an error or a return of any other type refuses — here by closing the client connection, since the response this hook was to redact must not be delivered unredacted.

Server only (master mode). Custom authentication. Return true to grant the master role. If defined, overrides --master-pw, so this callback is the entire gate on that server. Read strictly, and fail-closed: only the boolean true grants. Anything else denies — false, nil, no return at all, and every truthy non-boolean such as a string, the number 0 or a table. If the callback throws a Lua error the

Server only. Called immediately after a client is accepted, before on_connect fires. Return true to admit the client or false to reject and close the connection. If the callback throws a Lua error, the client is also rejected (fail-closed). When no on_auth callback is defined, all clients are admitted.

Server only. Called immediately after a WebSocket upgrade handshake completes, after on_connect has already fired. The headers argument is a Lua table containing any subset of the following keys from the HTTP upgrade request: cookie, origin, protocol (Sec-WebSocket-Protocol), and authorization. Only keys present in the request are set; absent headers are nil. This callback never fires for plain TC

Requires a top-level tick_ms global to be set in the Lua script: a whole number of milliseconds, 10 or more, defaulting to 100 when the global is omitted. A value below 10, or one that is not a whole number, refuses the script at load with a reason rather than

sections.title: Callback Deadline
sections.html:
Every Lua callback invocation is given a wall-clock budget. A callback that has not returned when its budget runs out is stopped with an error, exactly as if the script had called error(): the daemon logs the reason, the callback's usual failure path runs, and the runtime carries on serving. The default budget is 10000 milliseconds.

The bound exists because the event loop is a single thread serving every runtime in the daemon. Before it, while true do end in any callback froze all of them — traffic, the metrics endpoint and the IPC socket — with no recovery short of kill -9.

What is bounded:

  • each invocation of any on_* callback, separately — a periodic on_tick gets a fresh budget on every tick

  • each invocation of a socketley.set_timeout or socketley.set_interval callback, and of a socketley.subscribe handler

  • the whole filters chain for one request, as a single budget rather than one per filter

  • the script's top level, which runs inside create. A top level that never returns refuses the create with a reason instead of blocking the terminal on a command that never answers

This budget is time on the loop and not time on the clock, which the two callbacks that may wait make visible. on_message and on_client_message run on a coroutine, so a handler stopped in self.cache is not holding the thread and is not spending this: each stretch it actually runs gets the budget, and how long it may stay stopped is a separate bound of ten seconds with its own answer. See self.cache under Runtime Methods.

A stopped callback is a callback that raised, so wherever a raise already has a defined answer, the deadline gets that answer. on_auth denies and says why; on_route falls back to the usual backend pick; a filters entry refuses the request with a 500. In on_proxy_request and on_proxy_response it is the refusal case and not the "returned nothing" case — the connection closes, and the bytes of a request whose hook never finished deciding are not forwarded as though the hook had waved them through.

socketley.http lives inside the same budget: its timeout_ms is clamped to what is left of the callback's, so a callback that spends its budget waiting on a host gets an ordinary ok = false result rather than being stopped. A script that needs a long fetch raises the callback budget to suit. Nothing can interrupt a request mid-socket — the mechanism is a VM instruction hook and a blocking call executes no instructions.

Setting it. A script sets its own with a top-level callback_timeout_ms global, next to tick_ms:

callback_timeout_ms = 30000   -- this script does slow work on purpose
callback_timeout_ms = 0       -- no bound at all for this script

An operator moves the default for every script that says nothing with SOCKETLEY_LUA_TIMEOUT_MS in the daemon's environment; see ENVIRONMENT.

What it costs. Not the JIT, which is what this said before it was measured. On this build LuaJIT compiles traces with a count hook installed; what the hook costs is the hooked dispatch path, which checks on every VM instruction instead of every ten thousandth. Measured at 64 bytes on one connection: a callback that merely answers a message showed no difference above the run-to-run noise — 42581 and 43130 messages a second with the hook against 42571 and 42644 without — while one doing about 1300 arithmetic operations per message ran at 85% of its unhooked rate.

What 0 buys. Setting the bound to 0 installs no hook and also opens LuaJIT's jit library, which is the only thing that turns the trace compiler on at all: without it every Lua callback this daemon runs is interpreted. On that same arithmetic callback the difference is 11722 messages a second bounded against 28085 unbounded, at 85.2 against 30.3 microseconds of worker CPU each.

A callback that only answers a message gains very little, because there is almost no loop to compile. On the echo fixture the two arms do not separate in throughput at all — 42850 and 43929 messages a second bounded against 43577 and 44350 unbounded, an arm-to-arm gap smaller than the spread inside either arm. What does separate is Lua's own share of the worker's CPU, 5.2 and 5.1% against 3.9 and 4.0%, which is the compiler doing a little work on two bytecodes. Round it to about 1% end to end, against 2.4x on a callback that computes.

A streaming producer sits between those two and had never been measured, which matters because it is the shape that runs per byte rather than per message. A handler generating 40,000 CSV rows into self.send_chunk gains 25 to 48 per cent, not 2.4x — and the profile says why: with the hook installed the interpreter is 92.7 per cent of the worker's core, but what is inside that is lj_str_new, lj_str_resize, gc_sweepstr and the allocator, about 35 per cent between them. A compiled trace allocates and interns every string it builds exactly as the interpreter does, so the compiler removes the dispatch and leaves the string machinery standing.

Which makes how the script builds its strings the larger lever, and the two multiply rather than add. The same handler with string.format in place of a chain of .. concatenations, at 8 concurrent requests and then 64:

                        bounded      unbounded
.. concatenation        97.8/s      130.6/s   (+34%)
string.format           93.8/s      160.0/s   (+71%)
.. at 64 concurrent      68.0/s      100.8/s   (+48%)
string.format at 64     71.5/s      142.7/s  (+100%)

Both arms put byte-identical responses on the wire. Note the second column is what changes: string.format is worth nothing in the interpreter — 4 per cent behind the concatenation, inside the spread — because there it is one C call per row either way. It pays only once the compiler is on, and then it pays twice: one string per row instead of a chain of intermediates, and an integer formatter instead of the double one, which was 15.6 per cent of the core on its own. End to end, from the default with concatenation to the compiler with string.format, that is 64 per cent more throughput at 8 streams and 110 per cent at 64, for about half the CPU per request.

A C server building the same rows with snprintf(3) still serves 2.4x what the best of those does, so this is a decision about how much of a stream's work belongs in Lua at all — not a setting that closes the gap.

What decides the size of the gain is how much of the work is at the Lua level, not how many bytes pass through. Measured on a proxy, which is a second runtime type with a per-byte hook, both handlers forwarding the bytes untouched so only the work differs:

                              bounded   unbounded   CPU per request
one C library call per chunk    120.9      121.9     8223 -> 8155 us
a Lua loop over every row       417.1     1452.0     2378 ->  669 us

The first is a gsub over each chunk and gains one per cent: the call is C either way and there is almost no Lua around it to compile. The second walks the rows in a Lua while loop and gains 248 per cent at 72 per cent less CPU. Every runtime type reads the same setting from the same place, so the five shapes measured so far order themselves by that one question — about one per cent for a C call per byte or a callback that only answers, 34 to 48 per cent for building strings (where the allocator and the intern table are the cost and the compiler cannot remove them), 2.4x for arithmetic, and 248 per cent for Lua control flow over many items.

How the reply is assembled decides both, and the number of pieces decides whether it matters at all. Four idioms building one reply out of N parts, on a server, one binary and one C client, interleaved, each pair of rows below the same script with the compiler closed and open:

  N = 24, compiler closed       exchanges/s   spread
    s = s .. piece                 160,495      22%
    s = s .. string.format(..)     153,658      24%
    t[i] = piece, concat once      159,721      23%
    t[i] = format, concat once     166,023      15%

Nothing there is a finding: every spread is larger than every difference. A short reply is assembled the way that reads best, and reaching for string.format because it is faster is reaching for something that is not there.

  N = 1000                      exchanges/s   us cpu/req   spread
    s = s .. piece                   1,251         801      6%
                  compiler open      1,426         703      6%
    s = s .. string.format(..)         923       1,087      8%
                  compiler open        843       1,192      5%
    t[i] = piece, concat once        7,618         131      6%
                  compiler open     13,361          75      2%
    t[i] = format, concat once       8,656         115      7%
                  compiler open     17,675          57      5%

At a thousand pieces the best shape is 14.1 times the worst at a fourteenth of the CPU per request. Joining once is most of it — 6.1x on its own — and the formatter is worth a further 14 per cent behind it, against being 26 per cent slower when it is used to accumulate instead. The same call, opposite signs, decided by the shape around it.

What it does to the compiler is the part worth keeping. Opening it is worth 14 per cent on the accumulating shape, nothing outside the spread on the accumulating one that formats, and 75 and 104 per cent on the two that join once. That is the rule above seen from the other side: accumulating moves the work out of Lua and into the allocator, where there is nothing left for the compiler to reach. A script that is slow because of its idiom does not become fast because of the setting.

What 0 gives up. A compiled trace does not call an instruction hook back, so with the compiler on a runaway callback cannot be interrupted at all. Measured: while true do end against a 300 millisecond deadline stopped in 300.2 milliseconds with the compiler off and never with it on, and a hard ceiling inside the hook did not help either, because the hook is not reached from inside a trace. That is why the two are one setting rather than two knobs that can disagree.

The blast radius is one runtime rather than the daemon. Measured with a server whose callback never returns: its own worker process sat at 83% of a core while a second server on the same daemon went on echoing and the daemon went on answering ps. A runaway in the script's top level is still refused outright whatever callback_timeout_ms says, because the top level runs under the default before the script's own declaration has been read.

What it does not bound. A callback stopped at its deadline has still held the loop for that long, so a CLI command issued during the stall can hit its own five second receive timeout and report the daemon unreachable; it succeeds on the retry. A runaway on_tick is stopped on every tick rather than once. And name resolution inside socketley.http executes no VM instructions: it is not interrupted, it is given up on at the call's deadline.

sections.title: Proxy Filter Chain
sections.html:
Proxy only, HTTP mode only. filters is a global array of functions run in order on each request before a backend is selected. Each filter either says nothing — carry on to the next — or returns the answer, which ends the request there.

The ordering is the point. A request a filter refuses never reaches backend selection, so no endpoint is resolved, no circuit breaker's half-open probe is claimed, no pooled socket is spent and no connection is opened. This is where authentication, rate limiting and header rewriting belong; on_route runs after a backend has already been chosen and answers a different question.

The chain is independent of --strategy. It runs whatever picks the backend afterwards, and on a proxy with no on_route at all. A proxy whose script declares no filters array pays nothing: the chain is guarded by the same callback mask as every other hook.

Each filter is called with one argument:

method      string   HTTP method ("GET", "POST", ...)
path        string   Request path as the client sent it, this proxy's
                     prefix included — the same path on_route sees
version     string   HTTP version (e.g. "HTTP/1.1")
client_id   number   File descriptor of the client; pass it to
                     self.peer_ip() to identify the peer
headers     table    Request headers. Names are lowercased, values
                     are trimmed, and a field sent more than once is
                     joined with ", ".

And returns one of three things:

nil#

(or nothing) — this filter has no opinion; the next one runs.

{ status = N, body = string, headers = table }#

The answer. The chain stops, the request is never forwarded, and this response goes to the client. status must be 200-599. body and headers are optional. The connection is closed afterwards, as it is for every other response the proxy writes itself.

{ set_headers = table }#

Carry on, with these headers set on the request that goes to the backend. A header set here replaces one the client sent under the same name rather than joining it, and is emitted with a lowercased name.

{ remove_headers = { name, name, ... } }#

Carry on, with these headers taken off the request before it goes to the backend — every occurrence of each name, so a field the client sent twice is removed entirely. For a header the backend must never see whatever the client sent: an internal trust header a caller forged, a cookie with no business past the edge. set_headers and remove_headers may appear in the same table. A name that is both set and removed takes the later of the two statements, exactly as two set_headers for one name resolve.

A filter that returns anything else, or that raises an error, refuses the request with 500. A filter that did not say "carry on" is never treated as though it had. An entry in filters that is not a function refuses the whole script at load time, for the same reason: a silently dropped filter looks exactly like one that admits everybody.

Names a filter may not set or remove are dropped, with a line on stderr: Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding on either side, because the proxy forwards exactly the body the parsed request declared and a filter that could change the length would make the proxy and the backend disagree about where the request ends; Host on the request, because the proxy rewrites it to the endpoint it selected; and the hop-by-hop set (Connection, Keep-Alive, TE, Trailer, Upgrade, Proxy-*). So is any name that is not a bare token and any value carrying CR or LF — a filter is frequently echoing something the client supplied.

Filters run on the event loop thread. Whatever a filter does, every request on the proxy waits for: no blocking, no synchronous I/O, no long loops.

Example:

filters = {
    function(req)
        if not req.headers["authorization"] then
            return {
                status  = 401,
                body    = "authentication required\n",
                headers = {["WWW-Authenticate"] = "Bearer"},
            }
        end
        return {set_headers = {["x-authenticated-user"] = "alice"}}
    end,
}

See examples/proxy/filter-chain.lua for authentication, per-IP rate limiting and header rewriting as three filters in one chain.

sections.title: Declared Routes
sections.html:
routes is a global array in which a runtime states what it will answer: a path, and the methods allowed on it. It is declared in the handler's script and published to the proxies that forward to that runtime, which then refuse those methods at the edge — before any endpoint is resolved, any socket is taken from the pool and any connection is opened.

The declaration lives with the handler on purpose. Configured on the proxy, a method list is a second copy of something the handler already states in its own code, in another runtime and soon in another process, and two copies drift: the handler grows PATCH, the gateway goes on refusing it, and the 405 is explicable from neither side alone. Nothing is configured on the proxy; editing the handler's script and running socketley reload-lua changes what the gateway enforces.

routes = {
    { path = "/endpoint/login", methods = {"POST", "GET"} },
    { path = "/static/*",       methods = {"GET"} },
}

path is the path as the handler sees it — the proxy's own /name/ prefix already stripped — and a query string is not part of it. A trailing * makes it a literal prefix; that is the whole of the pattern language. Exact matches win over prefixes, and the longest prefix wins among prefixes. methods is a list of method names; a bare string is accepted for a single one. The declaration is uppercased when the script loads, so methods = {"post"} declares POST. The method a client sends is compared as sent — RFC 9110 9.1 makes the method token case-sensitive, and a request for post is one the handler would refuse too.

What the proxy does with it:

A declared method#

is forwarded, as always.

An undeclared method on a declared path#

is answered 405 Method Not Allowed with an Allow header listing what would have worked. No backend is involved.

HEAD#

is allowed wherever GET is (RFC 9110 9.3.2) — a handler that serves GET serves HEAD whether or not it listed it.

OPTIONS#

is never refused. A plain OPTIONS — "what may I do here", RFC 9110 9.3.7 — is answered 204 with Allow out of the declaration. A CORS preflight (an OPTIONS carrying Origin and Access-Control-Request-Method) is always forwarded to the handler instead: the declaration says nothing about origins, and an answer without Access-Control-Allow-Origin breaks the preflight exactly as a 405 would — the real request is never sent and the browser reports a CORS error. A handler that declares OPTIONS itself always gets it.

A path nobody declared#

is forwarded, whatever the method. A declaration speaks about the paths it names and says nothing about the others; it is not a whitelist, and declaring one route does not hide the rest.

A backend given as host:port#

has no declaration and never will — the published snapshot is keyed by runtime name and by group. Such a backend is forwarded to as before.

For a proxy with several backends, or an @group backend, one rule covers both halves of the fold: nothing may be refused that either possible target might have served. A path only some of them declare is dropped — a runtime that never mentioned it may well serve it. A path all of them declare keeps the union of their methods, since the proxy does not know which target a request will reach. One backend or group member that declares nothing therefore leaves that proxy enforcing nothing at all, silently and on purpose: it has said nothing about what it answers, so nothing can be refused on its account.

Edge rejection is not input validation. The proxy can confirm the method is one the handler declared. It cannot confirm the body is a well-formed login, and it is not the only way in: a socketley server listens on its own port, and a request that arrives there passed no edge at all. A handler that stops checking its input because "the gateway checks" is safe only for as long as every request comes through the gateway, which is a property of the deployment and not of the code. Declare routes to save the round trip and to say what you mean; go on validating.

socketley stats proxy reports declared_routes — how many routes that proxy is actually enforcing. It is the first thing to look at when a method that should be refused is not: a backend that declares nothing, a backend named by address, a script that failed to load and a proxy whose handler had not started yet all look identical from the client side, and all of them read 0 here.

A malformed entry refuses the script at load time, with the reason on stderr, rather than being dropped: a declaration that is not the one in the file is invisible from both sides. A routes table with no entry at index 1 is refused too — it is an array, and routes = {["/a"] = {"GET"}} would otherwise load and declare nothing.

Neither end of this has to be in the daemon. A proxy in a worker process of its own enforces declarations the same way: the table reaches it in the endpoint frame that already carries the addresses. And a handler in a worker declares them the same way, which is less obvious — the declaration is produced by running the script, and only the worker runs it, so it travels back to the daemon in a routes frame on the control socket and the placeholder publishes the worker's copy. Where either runtime runs makes no difference to which methods are refused.

See examples/proxy/declared-routes.lua for a handler that declares an AJAX endpoint and the gateway in front of it.

sections.title: Runtime Methods (in Lua)
sections.html:
-- Every type
self.name      -- Runtime name (read-only)
self.port      -- Port number (read-only)
self.state     -- Current state (read-only)
self.type      -- Runtime type (read-only)
self.connections()         -- Current connection count (all four types).
                              With --shards, the whole runtime's count summed
                              across its worker processes, not the shard's own

self.protocol  -- server/client: "tcp" or "udp"; proxy: "tcp" or "http"
               -- (not set on a cache)
self.send(msg)             -- Send message (client)
self.send(client_id, msg)  -- Send to specific client (server)
self.broadcast(msg)        -- Broadcast to all clients (server).  Answers two
                           -- numbers: how many took it, and how many were
                           -- dropped because their queue was full.  See below.
self.pending(client_id)    -- Queued for that client and not yet on the wire,
                           -- in bytes (server); nil if the id is not one of
                           -- this runtime's connections.  See below.
self.respond_stream(id, status, headers)
                           -- Begin a response this script will write itself,
                           -- chunk by chunk (server).  See below.
self.send_chunk(id, data)  -- One chunk of it; false means it was not taken
self.end_response(id)      -- The last chunk has gone; finish the response
self.watermark()           -- The byte count on_writable fires on the way down
                           -- through (server and client).  Pace against this,
                           -- not a literal.  A call and not a field, because
                           -- --write-buffer is editable.  See on_writable.
on_http_body(id, chunk, n) -- A request body streamed, rather than gathered
                           -- whole (server).  Defining it is the opt-in.
self.pending()             -- The client's own form, without an id: a client
                           -- has one connection.  Bytes queued for its server
                           -- and not yet on the wire.

-- ─── Sending faster than the socket ───
-- A write is queued, not performed, and the queue has a bound.  Reach it and
-- the runtime closes the connection -- which used to be the only way a script
-- found out: the message that filled the queue was dropped and answered true,
-- and the one after it was refused with "there is no open connection", the
-- sentence a peer hanging up gets.
--
-- self.send() now answers false for a message that was not taken, and names
-- the backlog when that is the reason, so a producer can tell "slow down" from
-- "it is gone".  self.pending() is the number to watch BEFORE sending, which
-- is the difference between pacing and a post-mortem:
--
--     if (self.pending(id) or 0) >= self.watermark() then return end
--
-- and on_writable(id) is how a producer that stopped there is started again,
-- which is what makes a body past the bound sendable rather than merely
-- survivable.  See on_writable in CALLBACKS.
--
-- self.broadcast() has the same bound at its own door, and used to report
-- nothing at all: a broadcast to 3000 clients that dropped a third of them was
-- indistinguishable from one that reached every single one.  It answers two
-- numbers now --
--
--     local taken, behind = self.broadcast(msg)
--
-- counting THIS shard's connections, which is the scope a script can act on; a
-- held message counts as taken, because an unclassified connection's hold is a
-- deferred take and not a drop.  And a client dropped by the broadcast gets
-- the backlog sentence from a later self.send() rather than the peer's, which
-- it did not before -- one flag, both entrances.
--
-- Measured with a client that connects and never reads, against 400 chunks of
-- 64 KB: 129 taken, 271 refused, and the queue standing at its bound.

-- ─── A response written rather than returned ───
-- on_http_request has to RETURN its body, so a generated answer had to fit in
-- memory.  A FILE of any size was already served by the splice path and a Range
-- of it by the 206 path; a generated one of any size was not expressible at all
-- -- transcoding, an export assembled from a cache, a CSV of ten million rows.
--
--     self.respond_stream(id, 200, {["Content-Type"] = "text/csv"})
--     for row in rows() do
--         if (self.pending(id) or 0) >= self.watermark() then return end   -- wait
--         self.send_chunk(id, row)
--     end
--     self.end_response(id)
--
-- Paced through self.pending()/on_writable like any other producer, which is
-- what makes it a stream rather than a slower way to run out of memory.
-- Measured: 200 MB of generated rows through an 8 MiB queue, delivered in
-- 51,200 chunks with on_writable resuming it 67 times, for 6 MB of resident
-- memory.
--
-- The handler returns nothing after starting one: the response is already on
-- its way, and the static-file and 404 fallbacks are skipped for this request.
-- A handler that only tried to send a chunk has NOT answered, so its ordinary
-- return still applies.
--
-- Content-Length, Transfer-Encoding and Connection are dropped from the header
-- table if given: a Content-Length beside a chunked body is a message carrying
-- two answers to its own length, which this server refuses with a 400 on the
-- way in.  Measured with it passed through: the client read 119 bytes where 5
-- were sent, having believed the wrong header.
--
-- send_chunk on a HEAD request answers false and names it, rather than dropping
-- the bytes: a HEAD asked for the headers and nothing else, and a script that
-- thinks it is sending a body to one has a bug this refusal is the only report
-- of.  An empty chunk is accepted and not sent, because a zero-length chunk is
-- how the terminator is spelled on the wire -- passing one through as payload
-- would end the response while the script was still writing it.

-- A question whose answer is somewhere else (server with --cache)
self.cache(command)        -- Run one command against the LINKED cache and
                           -- answer with what it said.  The handler STOPS here
                           -- and goes on when the reply arrives; the daemon
                           -- keeps serving meanwhile.  nil plus a reason when
                           -- the answer is not coming.

-- ─── A handler that waits ───
-- Every callback used to run to the end in one go, so a script could answer
-- only out of what it already held.  A server linked to a cache could not read
-- that cache at all, and the one call that reaches outside the process --
-- socketley.http -- did it by blocking the event loop for every runtime in the
-- daemon.  In a handler that waits, it now waits too.
--
--     function on_client_message(id, msg)
--         local v, err = self.cache("get " .. msg)
--         self.send(id, v or ("miss: " .. err))
--     end
--
-- The handler runs on a coroutine.  At the call it suspends, the request goes
-- to the cache, and the event loop carries on with every other connection and
-- every other runtime; when the reply lands the handler picks up at the same
-- line with the answer as that call's return value.  Nothing else in the script
-- changes, and a handler that never calls it is not affected: a callback that
-- runs straight through costs the same as it did, measured at 0.158 us against
-- 0.161 for the plain call it replaced, because the coroutines are pooled.
--
-- Where it may be called from: on_message and on_client_message.  Anywhere
-- else -- a timer, on_http_request, a filter -- answers nil and says so,
-- because those call sites still expect an answer on the spot.
--
-- Three things are guaranteed, and each exists because the shape without it
-- was reachable:
--
--   * It always returns.  A cache that accepts the request and never answers
--     leaves the handler stopped for ever otherwise -- measured against a
--     SIGSTOPped cache worker, whose request is parked against a ticket nothing
--     completes.  After ten seconds the call answers nil, "timeout".
--
--   * The connection is still there.  While the handler waits, the connection
--     it is answering is held open exactly as a client's own `cache get` is:
--     a promised reply, which the close path defers on.  Without it every
--     `echo | nc` fails, because the peer half-closes the moment it has sent
--     its line and the answer does not exist yet.
--
--   * It cannot pile up.  4096 stopped callbacks per runtime, and a server that
--     is already owed as many answers as one connection may have refuses the
--     call with a reason rather than stopping the handler.
--
-- The command is the cache's own text protocol, so the answer is that
-- protocol's: `get` on a key that is not there answers the string "nil" rather
-- than a Lua nil, which is the same answer a client reading the port gets.
-- Upstream actions (server with -u)
self.upstream_send(conn_id, msg) -- Send to a specific upstream; false means
                                 -- the bytes are not going.  See below.
self.upstream_broadcast(msg)     -- Send to all connected upstreams.  Answers how
                                 -- many took it and how many were dropped
self.upstream_pending(conn_id)   -- Bytes queued for that upstream and not yet on
                                 -- the wire; nil if the id is not one of this
                                 -- runtime's upstreams
self.upstreams()                 -- Table of connected upstream conn_ids

-- ─── The same bound, pointed outwards ───
-- An upstream's write queue fills exactly as a client's does, and these used to
-- report none of it.  upstream_send() tested only whether the upstream was
-- connected; a queue that reached the bound sets `closing` and leaves
-- `connected` alone, so every later send answered TRUE for ever while nothing
-- left the process.  Measured, 400 sends of 64 KB at an upstream that accepted
-- the connection and then read nothing:
--
--     before   sent=400  failed=0    with 8,396,928 bytes standing in the queue
--     after    sent=129  failed=271  the same 129/271 the client-facing side
--                                    reports, because it is the same bound
--
-- The refusal names the backlog apart from a missing upstream, because "is not
-- connected" is false of a connected upstream whose queue this runtime filled --
-- and the two want opposite reactions.  Pace with self.upstream_pending() and
-- not self.pending(): that one resolves a CLIENT id, and an upstream is in
-- another map entirely.
--
-- on_upstream_writable(conn_id) is the other half, and without it the number
-- above is only a post-mortem: a producer could ask how deep the queue was and
-- never be told when there was room.  The same 400 sends of 64 KB, at an
-- upstream that reads:
--
--     unpaced   sent=129  failed=271   and the upstream closed
--     paced     sent=400  refused=0    resumed 6 times
--
-- Same messages, same bound, same upstream.  129 of 400 is what a producer that
-- does not look gets, and it is not a limit on how much can be sent.

-- Cache: mode
-- A call and not a field, because --mode is editable and a field written when
-- this table was built would go stale.  "readonly", "readwrite" or "admin" --
-- the same three names --mode, `show` and the wire protocol use.
self.cache_mode()   -- Which mode this cache is in

-- Cache: which keys are this process's
-- Under --shards the script runs in all N workers and the calls below act only
-- on the slice this one owns, answering a foreign key the way they answer a
-- refusal.  True for every key when the cache is one process.
self.owns(key)      -- Does this shard own the key?

-- Cache: strings
self.get(key)       -- Get string value
self.set(key, val)  -- Set string value; false in readonly mode
self.del(key)       -- Delete key (any type); false in readonly mode
self.exists(key)    -- Is the key there?  See below.

-- Cache: lists
self.lpush(key, val)        -- Push to front; false in readonly mode
self.rpush(key, val)        -- Push to back; false in readonly mode
self.lpop(key)              -- Pop from front; "" in readonly mode
self.rpop(key)              -- Pop from back; "" in readonly mode
self.llen(key)              -- List length

-- Cache: sets
self.sadd(key, member)      -- 1 added, 0 already a member,
                            -- nil refused (readonly mode)
self.srem(key, member)      -- Remove member; false in readonly mode
self.sismember(key, member) -- Check membership
self.scard(key)             -- Set cardinality

-- Cache: hashes
self.hset(key, field, val)  -- Set hash field; false in readonly mode
self.hget(key, field)       -- Get hash field
self.hdel(key, field)       -- Delete hash field; false in readonly mode
self.hexists(key, field)    -- Is the field there?  See below.
self.hlen(key)              -- Hash field count

-- Cache: TTL
self.expire(key, seconds)   -- Set expiry; false in readonly mode
self.ttl(key)               -- Get remaining TTL
self.persist(key)           -- Remove expiry; false in readonly mode

-- Cache: pub/sub
-- Under --shards the message reaches every shard's subscribers, but the count
-- is this shard's own: the siblings answer on a later turn and this call
-- answers on the turn it was made.
self.publish(channel, msg)  -- Publish to channel; returns this shard's count

-- Server: connection control
-- Every mutator below answers `true`, or `false, "reason"`.  They returned
-- nothing at all before, so an id that named no connection was a silent no-op.
self.disconnect(client_id)         -- Terminate a connection from Lua
self.peer_ip(client_id)            -- Get client IP (IPv4 or IPv6 string)
                                   -- also on a proxy, same meaning
self.ws_headers(client_id)         -- Get WS upgrade headers table (nil for TCP)

-- Server: client enumeration and multicast
self.clients()                     -- Return table of all connected client_ids
                                   -- also on a proxy, same meaning
self.multicast(ids, msg)           -- Send msg to a subset of clients (ids = array of
                                   -- client_ids).  Returns how many were reached.
                                   -- An entry that is not a whole number refuses the
                                   -- whole call rather than being dropped from it.

-- Server: named groups
self.join_group(id, group)         -- Add client to a named group
self.leave_group(id, group)        -- Remove client from a group
self.group_send(group, msg)        -- Send msg to all clients in a group.  Returns how
                                   -- many were reached; 0 is a group with nobody in it.

-- Server: zero-copy pipe pairing (bypasses Lua callbacks)
self.pipe(id_a, id_b)             -- Pair two clients: data forwarded directly between them
self.unpipe(id)                    -- Remove pipe pairing for a client
socketley.pipe(src, fd_a, src, fd_b)   -- Pair two connections of one server
socketley.pipe(src, fd, dst)           -- Route a connection to another server.
                                   -- Despite the name it hands no descriptor over:
                                   -- src keeps the socket and relays the bytes

-- Server: per-connection metadata
self.set_data(id, key, val)        -- Set string metadata on a connection (nil val deletes key)
self.get_data(id, key)             -- Get metadata string or nil

-- Server: client routing
self.route(client_id, target)      -- Forward client to sub-server, in this or
                                   -- any other process. This server keeps the
                                   -- socket and relays; the target answers.
self.unroute(client_id)            -- Stop forwarding
self.get_route(client_id)          -- Get current route (string or nil)

-- Server: owner-targeted sending (sub-server only)
self.owner_send(client_id, msg)    -- Send to a connection routed here, through
                                   -- the runtime that owns it. Returns false if
                                   -- that connection has gone.
self.owner_broadcast(msg)          -- Broadcast to all owner's clients

-- Proxy
self.clients()                     -- Table of connected client_ids
self.peer_ip(client_id)            -- Client IP (IPv4 or IPv6 string)
self.close_client(client_id)       -- Close one client connection
self.backends()                    -- Array of backend addresses, in the
                                   -- order on_route indexes them (1-based
                                   -- in Lua; on_route returns 0-based)
self.backend_health()              -- Circuit-breaker state per backend,
                                   -- same 1-based order:
                                   -- "closed" | "open" | "half_open"
self.stats()                       -- {connections, bytes_in, bytes_out,
                                   --  total_connections, total_messages,
                                   --  backend_count}

Why exists and hexists are there. self.get answers with the value, and an absent key and a key holding an empty string both come back as the empty string. A script cannot tell those apart, and this page's own example leans on it — examples/cache/cache-integration-handler.lua reads self.get("config:timeout") == "" to mean "not set yet".

Making get answer nil for an absent key would settle it and would break that reading wherever it has been written, and an empty string is a value a cache is entitled to hold. So the missing question was added instead, under the name the wire protocol has always used for it.

The proxy table is smaller than the server's on purpose. A proxy relays between a client and a backend and speaks for neither, so there is no broadcast(), no send() and no per-connection metadata: it has no message of its own to put on the wire. To change what crosses it, use on_proxy_request and on_proxy_response, and to refuse a request, the filter chain.
self.backends() is indexed from 1, like every Lua array, while on_route returns an index from 0 — so the address on_route selects with n is self.backends()[n + 1].
self.owner_send() takes only a client_id this runtime was actually given — one that arrived through self.route(), reported by on_connect(). It answers false for anything else, including a client_id whose connection has since closed. It used to take any number and write it into the owner's connection table as a descriptor index, so a script holding an id past its connection's life wrote into whichever client had inherited that descriptor.

sections.title: Global Functions
sections.html:
socketley.log(msg)#

Write one line to the daemon's log at INFO level, prefixed with the name of the runtime that wrote it: [12:04:31] [INFO] [lua my-server] .... It goes through the daemon's logger, so log_level in the configuration file turns it down like anything else; at the default level nothing that used to appear stops appearing. Every Lua diagnostic carries the same [lua <runtime>] prefix, which is what separates two scripts sharing one stderr — and two runtimes commonly share one script file, so the file name in an error is not an identity.

socketley.set_timeout(ms, fn) -> timer_id#

Fire fn once after ms milliseconds using an io_uring timeout SQE. Returns an integer timer ID that can be passed to socketley.clear_timeout(). Shares the event loop with the runtime — no extra threads.

socketley.set_interval(ms, fn) -> timer_id#

Fire fn every ms milliseconds. Returns an integer timer ID that can be passed to socketley.clear_interval().

Details

Both kinds are cancelled when the runtime stops, and are not restored if it is started again. A stopped runtime executes no script, so a timer armed by one does not survive it — including a timer armed inside on_stop, which is severed with the rest. The registrations are made at the script's top level, which runs once, when the runtime's worker is forked — so a start after a stop forks a new worker, runs the top level again, and arms them again. What is not replayed is anything the previous worker held: a timer is not restored, it is re-armed by a script that is being run afresh.

Both return 0 and arm nothing when ms is not greater than zero, when the runtime has no event loop, or when the runtime has been stopped — the last of those covers the script that calls socketley.stop on its own runtime and carries on, since stop returns to it and everything after that line runs on a runtime that is already down. A start lifts it, before on_start, so a restarted runtime arms exactly as it did the first time. socketley.subscribe answers 0 in the same situation and for the same reason. Real ids start at 1, so 0 is unambiguous; the reason is written to the daemon's log, because a timer that will never fire is otherwise silent.

socketley.clear_timeout(timer_id)#

Cancel a pending timeout. The timer will not fire. Safe to call with an already-expired or invalid ID (no-op).

socketley.clear_interval(timer_id)#

Cancel a repeating interval. The timer stops after the current cycle completes. Safe to call with an already-expired or invalid ID (no-op).

Details

Both withdraw the timer rather than merely muting it: the io_uring timeout is removed, the timer's storage is released, and the reference to the callback goes with it — so the closure and everything it captured become collectable at the call rather than when the timer would have expired. Cancelling a one-hour interval used to hold all of that for the hour.

Both are safe to call from inside the timer's own callback, which is how a one-shot repeating timer is written.

socketley.json_encode(value) -> string | false, why#

Encode a Lua value (table, string, number, boolean, nil) as a JSON string. Tables with consecutive integer keys starting at 1 are encoded as JSON arrays; all others as objects.

Details

Object keys are written in sorted order, so encoding equal data twice gives the same string. A Lua table has no order of its own — one filled alpha, beta, gamma, delta iterates beta, gamma, delta, alpha — so without sorting the output was not a function of the value, and two tables holding the same data could encode differently. Anything that compares encoded documents depends on this: an ETag, a cache key, a signature, a deduplication hash, or a diff of two logged payloads.

Refused, with false and a reason, when the value cannot be written as a document: a table that contains itself (directly or through any chain of fields), or one nested deeper than 128 levels. A table reachable twice by different paths is not a cycle and encodes normally.

A string is truthy and false is not, so local s = socketley.json_encode(t) reads unchanged and if not s then is how the refusal is tested.

socketley.json_decode(str) -> value | false, why#

Decode a JSON string into a Lua value. Objects become tables with string keys, arrays become tables with integer keys (1-based). Null becomes nil.

Details

Refused, with false and a reason, for a document nested deeper than 128 levels, for bytes that are not a complete JSON document, and for trailing data after the document ends.

The refusal on malformed input is what makes the return value trustworthy. The decoder used to answer with whatever it had understood so far, so [1,2 — a request body cut short by a dropped connection — decoded to an ordinary two-element table, {"a":} to an empty one, and nul, garbage and an empty string all to nil, which was also the answer for a document that really was null. A handler could not tell a truncated body from a whole one and carried on with the fields that happened to arrive.

This limit is not a formatting preference. This call is written to be pointed at data from the network — a request body, a message payload — so the nesting depth is chosen by whoever sent it, and the decoder recurses to follow it. Without the limit a few hundred kilobytes of [[[[ took the whole daemon down, and no callback deadline covers it: those measure Lua execution, and this recursion is native.

socketley.subscribe(cache_name, channel, fn) -> subscription_id#

Register fn(channel, message) to be called whenever the named cache runtime publishes to channel. The function is called on the subscribing runtime's event loop turn (not from the cache itself). Multiple subscriptions to the same channel are all fired in registration order.

Details

Returns an integer id for socketley.unsubscribe(). Ids start at 1 and are never reused, so 0 is a refusal: it means the runtime has been stopped and this registration would have outlived the stop that ended the others. See socketley.set_interval for the whole of it — the two refuse together and a start lifts both.

Only a running runtime is delivered to. Every registration this one holds is ended when it stops, and one that has never been started receives nothing either — its top level has run, so the registration exists, but a runtime that is not running executes no script, which is the same rule the timers are severed under. They do come back if it is started again, which is where they differ from set_interval and set_timeout: a subscription is registered from on_start, and start runs on_start, where a timer is armed at the script's top level and only a load runs that.

socketley.unsubscribe(subscription_id) -> bool#

End one registration. Returns true when it removed a live one and false when the id names none — never issued, or already unsubscribed.

Details

The id names one registration, not a channel, so two handlers on the same channel can be ended independently. Safe to call from inside a subscriber's own callback, which is how a one-shot subscriber is written; the removal takes effect for the next message rather than in the middle of delivering this one.

Ending one explicitly matters while the runtime is up: stop ends them all, and remove and reload-lua destroy the context they live in, but nothing does either of those on a runtime that is simply serving. Without ending them, a script that subscribes from a callback that runs more than once — on_tick is the ordinary one — registers the same handler again on every call, and each publish is delivered to every copy.

socketley.mqtt.publish(runtime, topic, payload [, {qos=, retain=}] [, fn]) -> true | nil, why#

A message published on an mqtt runtime of this daemon, as the broker's own; true once the broker has it. See From the other runtimes under MQTT FLAGS.

socketley.mail.send(runtime, {to=, cc=, bcc=, from=, reply_to=, subject=, text=, html=, headers=, attachments=, raw=} [, fn]) -> id | nil, why#

A message written and queued by a mail runtime of this daemon; its queue id once it is in the spool. to, cc and bcc are an address or a list of them, an attachment {name=,type=,data=}. See MAIL FLAGS.

socketley.http(opts) -> table#

HTTP/HTTPS client. In a callback that can wait — the ones socketley.db may be called from without a function, and an mcp tool's handler — the callback stops at the call and the runtime serves everything else until the answer comes. Anywhere else (on_start, on_stop, a timer, on_http_request, a filter, an mcp resource or prompt) it blocks the event loop thread until the exchange ends; use it there only in on_start/on_stop or low-frequency on_tick callbacks.

opts table keys:

url         string   Request URL (http:// or https://)
method      string   HTTP method (default "GET")
body        string   Request body (optional)
headers     table    Extra headers e.g. {["Content-Type"]="application/json"}
timeout_ms  number   Timeout in milliseconds, 1..3600000 (default 5000)

A key that is present and of the wrong type or out of range comes back as ok = false with the reason in error, rather than being replaced by the default: `timeout_ms = "soon"` used to become 5000 and make the request anyway, on a number nobody chose. A key that is absent keeps its default, which is not a mistake and is not reported.

Returns a table:

ok      bool    true if HTTP status 2xx
status  number  HTTP status code (e.g. 200, 404)
body    string  Response body
error   string  Error message on failure

timeout_ms is one deadline for the whole exchange — connect, TLS handshake, request and response are all measured against it — not a separate timeout per operation. A call that blocks resolves the name before the deadline is armed, on a thread of its own and bounded by it; a call that waits counts the resolving in. A response is refused once it exceeds 8 MB rather than buffered without limit.

A response that declares a Content-Length and then ends before reaching it is refused too, with the shortfall named in error, because nothing else in the answer would say so: the close that cut it short is the same close that frames a response carrying no length at all, and over HTTPS the close_notify that would tell those two apart is one many servers omit and this client accepts the absence of. Only a declared length can be fallen short of — a chunked response, or one with no length, is read until the close either way and comes back as before.

HTTPS uses OpenSSL and validates the peer. The certificate chain is verified against the system CA store, and the certificate must have been issued to the host in the URL — a host name is matched against the certificate's DNS names with partial wildcards refused, an address literal against its IP SAN. TLS 1.2 is the minimum accepted protocol version. Failure of either check aborts the request with the reason in error, and there is no option to disable it, so a service presenting a self-signed or private-CA certificate must have that CA in the trust store OpenSSL reads (overridable with SSL_CERT_FILE or SSL_CERT_DIR). If no CA store is available at all the call fails immediately with no system CA store available.
