sections.title: Runtime Management API
sections.html:
Create, start, stop, and remove runtimes from Lua scripts:

socketley.create(type, name, config)  -- Create runtime
socketley.start(name)                 -- Start runtime
socketley.stop(name)                  -- Stop runtime
socketley.remove(name)                -- Stop + remove runtime
socketley.send(name, msg)             -- Send/broadcast to runtime
socketley.list()                      -- List all runtime names (table)
socketley.get(name)                   -- Get info table or nil
socketley.pipe(src, fd_a, src, fd_b)  -- Pair two connections of one server
socketley.pipe(src, fd, dst)          -- Route a connection to another server

Every call above answers true when it happened, or false , "reason" when it did not.

The reason is a sentence naming the runtime and what was wrong with the request, so a script can tell the four situations apart that all used to answer a bare false:

local ok, why = socketley.start("web")
--  false  there is no runtime called "web"
--  false  "web" is already running
--  false  "web" is failed, and a failed runtime cannot be started again ...
--  false  "web" could not be started; it is failed now, and the reason is
--         in the daemon's log        <- a held port, a TLS pair that is not one

This is the shape Lua itself uses — io.open, os.remove, pcall — so assert(socketley.start(n)) prints the reason with no other change. Success returns ONE value, not true, nil.

What a second return value changes. Lua truncates a multiple-return call to one value everywhere except three places. Unaffected: assignment, if not f() then, and/or, concatenation, tostring, comparison, and any argument position that is not the last. Affected: print(f()) now prints two values, { f() } builds a two-element table, and g(f()) passes g two arguments where it passed one.

socketley.pipe is two calls and the argument count says which. With four arguments it pairs two connections of ONE server, both descriptors named and both used. With three it hands the connection to another runtime, which decides what answers it — there is no destination descriptor in that, so a fourth argument across two runtimes is refused rather than accepted and discarded.

Config table keys: port, config (or lua, a script path), target, mode (server only), http and http_cache (server only), group, on_parent_stop ("remove" or "stop"), and start (bool). The table is validated and a refusal is a refusal: a port outside 0..65535, a mode or policy that is not one of the listed values, a key that is not on this list, a script that will not load, or a start that cannot bind, each returns false with the reason in the log and leaves no runtime behind. Lua-created runtimes have parent-child ownership; port=0 creates internal-only servers that receive forwarded messages only.

Every call above works in a worker, which is where every runtime runs.

These calls act on the runtime map, and the runtime map lives in the daemon — so a script written against them is running somewhere the map is not. All of them work there anyway, and how they work differs:

socketley.send, .list, .get and the four socketley.cluster calls are answered from a replica. The daemon pushes the worker a copy of the map and a snapshot of the cluster view, and refreshes both when they change.

socketley.create, .start, .stop and .remove change the map, and a copy is not the thing to change. They are asked of the daemon instead, over a socket the worker holds for exactly this, and they wait for the answer — so if socketley.create(...) then tests what happened. The wait is what makes them honest and it is bounded: 9.95, 10.20 and 10.52 microseconds over three runs of 20000 for a call that does not fork anything, and at most five seconds for one that does. They are made in on_start or on a rare control message, never per request, which is what makes a wait affordable at all — see socketley.http() in the same table, which blocks the same loop for a network round trip.

The answers are the daemon's own, word for word what the same call says in the daemon: there is no runtime called "x" , "x" is already running , a runtime called "x" already exists. A script cannot tell from them which process it is running in, which is the point.

Two calls used to be refused there, and are not. socketley.pipe across two runtimes, and self.route(). Their refusal said a pipe hands a file descriptor between runtimes and that no channel existed to pass one over. Across two runtimes it hands no descriptor over at all: the origin keeps the socket and relays, which needed a way to name another runtime's connection rather than a way to move one. Both cross a process boundary now, with no change to how either is called.

One refusal is left, and it is the one to read carefully if you meet it. socketley.create, .start, .stop and .remove raise in a worker that was forked without the socket they travel on — an older daemon, or one that could not create it. That message says so and tells you to restart the daemon. It is not the permanent refusal these four used to carry.

socketley.pipe and self.route() were the last two refused in a worker, and are not any more. Their message said a pipe hands a file descriptor between runtimes, that a descriptor cannot travel in a snapshot of the map, and that it would need SCM_RIGHTS over a channel nothing had built. The mechanism it named (shared/net/conn_transfer.h) was real and the diagnosis was wrong: across two runtimes socketley.pipe does not hand a descriptor over at all. It is route_client(), which writes into the target's connection maps, runs the target's on_connect and then keeps the socket where it is and relays the bytes through it. What both needed was a way to name another runtime's connection and reach it, which is shared/ipc/route_relay.h.

So they cross a process boundary now, and what changes for a script is nothing: the same call, the same return value, the same target name. The origin stays in the data path either way — that is what routing is — and a message from a routed client reaches the target's on_client_message while the target's reply reaches the client through the origin.

The four-argument form, socketley.pipe(src, fd_a, src, fd_b), pairs two connections of one server and crosses nothing. It has to be called from that server's own script, because only that process holds its connections.

When a runtime holding routed connections goes away — stopped, removed, crashed or killed — every runtime on the other end of those routes is told to let go, and the target's on_disconnect runs. That is done by the daemon rather than by the departing runtime, because a killed worker runs no teardown at all.

unroute() , get_route() and owner_send() read the runtime's own tables and always did.

Where the raise lands is the thing to plan for. At a script's top level it fails the load, and a worker whose script did not load does not serve: the create is refused with a reason and the runtime is left failed. Inside a callback it is caught and logged like any other callback error, and the runtime carries on. In on_start that means a runtime that is up and serving with none of what on_start was for having happened — ls green, connections accepted — so the command that started it exits 1 and names the callback and the reason. The runtime is left running either way; the exit code and the message are how the two are told apart.

Everything that does not reach for the map works in a worker exactly as it does in the daemon: socketley.log, .http, .json_encode/.json_decode, the timers, .subscribe, the whole self table, and every connection and request callback. See Out-of-process runtimes under LIMITATIONS for the full account.

sections.title: Cluster Introspection API
sections.html:
When the daemon runs in cluster mode (--cluster), the socketley.cluster table provides read-only introspection into the full cluster topology. All functions return empty tables when not in cluster mode, so scripts work in both standalone and cluster setups without modification.

That last sentence holds for cluster mode being off, and it now holds in a worker process too: the daemon pushes each worker a snapshot of the cluster view before the frame that loads its script, and these four are answered from it.

One case is left. A daemon that is in no cluster has no view to push, and an empty table is what a successful call returns for a daemon alone in one — so with no view installed the four raise instead of answering, naming themselves. A daemon that joins a cluster after a worker's script has loaded leaves that script with the refusal until it is reloaded.

socketley.cluster.daemons() -> table#

Returns an array of daemon info tables. Each entry has:

Details
name      string   Daemon name (from --name)
host      string   Advertised address, from gethostname(2), falling
                   back to the daemon name if that call fails
runtimes  number   Count of runtimes on this daemon

The local daemon is always the first entry. Remote daemons follow in discovery order.

socketley.cluster.runtimes() -> table#

Returns a flat array of all runtimes across every daemon in the cluster:

Details
daemon       string   Name of the daemon hosting this runtime
name         string   Runtime name
type         string   "server", "client", "proxy", or "cache"
port         number   Listen port (0 = internal-only)
group        string   Group tag (empty string if unset)
state        string   "created", "running", "stopped", or "failed"
connections  number   Current connection count
socketley.cluster.group(name) -> table#

Returns running members of the named group that have a valid port. Each entry has:

Details
daemon       string   Daemon name
host         string   Advertised address
port         number   Listen port
connections  number   Current connection count

Useful for building custom routing, health checks, or failover logic from Lua.

socketley.cluster.stats() -> table#

Aggregate cluster statistics:

Details
daemons   number   Total daemon count (local + remote)
runtimes  number   Total runtime count across all daemons
running   number   Count of runtimes in "running" state
groups    table    Maps group name (string) -> member count (number)

sections.title: Cluster Event Callbacks
sections.html:
These optional callbacks fire when the cluster topology changes. Events are detected during the 2-second scan/publish cycle, so callbacks may fire up to 2 seconds after the actual change. They fire only on a running runtime: a cluster callback is a callback, and a runtime that has been stopped or has never been started executes no script. A batch of events that reaches a runtime and then stops it ends there — the remaining events in that batch are not delivered to it. A daemon is considered stale and triggers on_cluster_leave after 10 seconds without a heartbeat update.

on_cluster_join(daemon)#

Fired when a new remote daemon is discovered in the cluster directory. daemon is a table with name (string) and host (string) fields.

on_cluster_leave(daemon)#

Fired when a remote daemon's heartbeat file becomes stale (>10s old) or is removed from the cluster directory. daemon is a table with a name (string) field.

on_group_change(group, members)#

Fired when the total member count of a group changes (a runtime joins or leaves the group, or a daemon with group members appears/disappears). Only fires on actual count changes, not on every scan cycle. group is the group name (string). members is an array of tables, each with daemon, host, and port fields representing the current group membership.

Example — log topology changes and maintain a local routing table:

local backends = {}

function on_cluster_join(daemon)
    socketley.log("daemon joined: " .. daemon.name .. " at " .. daemon.host)
end

function on_cluster_leave(daemon)
    socketley.log("daemon left: " .. daemon.name)
end

function on_group_change(group, members)
    if group == "api" then
        backends = members   -- update routing table
        socketley.log("api group now has " .. #members .. " members")
    end
end

function on_start()
    -- Initial snapshot
    local stats = socketley.cluster.stats()
    socketley.log("cluster: " .. stats.daemons .. " daemons, "
                  .. stats.running .. " running runtimes")
end

Fired when the total member count of a group changes (a runtime joins or leaves the group, or a daemon with group members appears/disappears). Only fires on actual count changes, not on every scan cycle. group is the group name (string). members is an array of tables, each with daemon, host, and port fields representing the current group membership.

sections.title: DASHBOARD
sections.html:
When daemon.metrics_port is set in the daemon configuration file, the metrics endpoint serves multiple routes:

GET /#

The dashboard, in the storage interface's look, whose stylesheet and helpers it takes from the same binary. Its overview shows the daemon's runtimes, connections, messages, bytes in and out, CPU and resident memory, each with its last three minutes as a line; its runtimes, each with its state and the same figures, filtered by type and name; and each runtime with its configuration and its stats . Signed in, it starts, stops, restarts and removes a runtime, reloads its Lua, edits it in a form of its type filled with what show says (or as the JSON import takes), and makes one: the type, then a form of every flag create takes for it, by section, with the command it sends shown as it is filled in.

Details

An account the idp runtime that daemon.dashboard_idp names signed in, of the group admins, is signed in here too, and the page offers that sign-in; signing out signs out at the provider. Otherwise signing in takes the access key and secret of an admin of the credentials file daemon.dashboard_credentials names, a storage runtime's format, as a proxy's --auth basic: checks them: an address that fails five times in fifteen minutes is refused even the right secret, 429, behind a proxy on this machine the address in its X-Forwarded-For. The session is a cookie sealed with a key the daemon draws at start, HttpOnly and SameSite=Strict (Secure behind HTTPS), good for twelve hours, and ended at the daemon by signing out, by its key leaving the file or by the key being given another secret; a command also carries the page's own header, which no other site's request can, goes over the daemon's control socket as the CLI's does, and is logged with who sent it. The page sends only create, edit, import, start, stop, remove, reload, reload-lua, show, stats, ls and ps, none with a word holding a space. With credentials named, every route but the page and the sign-in needs the session, and /metrics needs it from anywhere but a scraper on this machine without a proxy between; without them the page shows the figures, as it always did, but not the log or a zone's text, which need a session whatever is configured, and changes nothing.

Its history and its alerts are a metrics runtime's (see METRICS FLAGS): a daemon started with the dashboard on and a way to sign in to it (daemon.dashboard_credentials or daemon.dashboard_idp), or with any of daemon.alert_webhook, daemon.alert_mail and daemon.events set, makes one named metrics the first time, on 127.0.0.1:9090 or the next free port above it, and never again once it was made, so one removed stays removed; with none running the page shows the figures as they are and no history. With several, the page reads the one named metrics, else any running one that takes this daemon's series.

Its figures are drawn over the last fifteen minutes, hour, six hours, day, week, month or year, as chosen, the value and time under the pointer shown: each runtime's and the daemon's connections and memory as they are, messages, bytes and CPU per second, read from the metrics runtime's store, which keeps them as long as its --keep and --downsample say. GET /api/history?runtime=name&range=seconds&points=n gives one runtime's, or without a name all of them together, as n points, null where there is none: an object of from (in seconds since 1970), step (a point's seconds) and the arrays conn, msg, in, out, cpu (percent of one CPU) and rss; the range is held between a minute and a year, the points between 10 and 1440.

Its Alerts are the metrics runtime's rules, the built-in ones unless its --rules file changes them: a runtime that failed, or was started again three times within the hour; a sync runtime that cannot carry what it owes; a certificate a runtime serves that ends within two weeks (critical within three days, or once it has ended); the disk under a storage runtime or the state directory, or the host's memory, at 90% (critical at 95%); a storage runtime at 90% of its --max-bytes or a cache that refuses writes at 90% of its --maxmemory; a git repository whose last pull failed; a mail runtime with a hundred messages waiting (critical at a thousand), or whose own address a blocklist of its --dnsbl names; a scraped target that does not answer for two minutes; a tunnel edge missing an agent that joined it, or dropping more than 1% of its datagrams; an idp runtime that barred more than twenty sign-ins in ten minutes. A critical alert silences the warning on the same thing. Each is logged, listed on the page with the notifications of late, shown on the overview, and — with daemon.alert_webhook set to an http or https URL — posted to it as JSON whose content and text carry the message, which Discord, Slack and Telegram's sendMessage read, and whose state (firing, resolved) and alert carry the rest. A message the hook does not take with a 2xx is posted again, after a pause that doubles up to eight seconds, and one it has not taken is kept in .notify in the state directory and posted after a restart. With daemon.alert_mail set to mail://runtime/address[,address...] each is mailed as well, or instead, by that mail runtime, its subject the alert's first line, held the same way until the runtime runs. The metrics runtime keeps its alerts' state in its directory, so one started again does not tell of them a second time. GET /api/alerts, and POST /api/alerts/test with the page's header posts a test through the hook.

With daemon.events naming an mqtt runtime, the daemon publishes on it at QoS 1, retained, how each runtime stands, on socketley/runtimes/name/state as JSON with its name, type, state and port, at every change and cleared when the runtime is removed; and each alert while it holds, on socketley/alerts/id as the JSON alert carries above, cleared when it clears. A subscriber to socketley/# reads how things stand the moment it subscribes and is told of every change after. The broker may be made after the daemon starts: until it runs, what is owed waits in .notify in the state directory, as the webhook's does.

Its Logs follow the daemon's recent log live, filtered by runtime, by level and by text, and each runtime's page shows its own; a runtime that failed says the last warning or error it wrote, where it is listed and on its page, beside how often it was started again. Each worker writes its stderr into a pipe of its own, which the daemon reads, passes on to its own stderr unchanged — the journal gets every line as before — and keeps, named by the runtime, with the daemon's own lines, the last 10,000 in memory: GET /api/logs?since=seq&max=n&runtime=name&level=warn.

Its Domains show every certificate a runtime serves — its names, its issuer, how long it has, whether it is issued by itself and whether a wildcard waits for its zone's delegation, and the last line of a failed issuance — each entrance's routes, a name to the runtime it goes to, and the zones of the dns runtimes, whose records it edits: the text is checked as the runtime reads a zone file before it is written, and a serial left as it was is raised, so secondaries take the change. GET /api/edge, and GET and PUT /api/zone for a file a dns runtime serves and no other. The endpoint listens on 127.0.0.1 only; on a server, reach it through an SSH tunnel, ssh -L 9100:127.0.0.1:9100 host, and open http://localhost:9100/. On an installed system the port is set in /etc/socketley/config.lua, as daemon = { metrics_port = 9100 }, and read when the service starts.

GET /metrics#

Prometheus exposition format (existing). Suitable for scraping by Prometheus, Grafana Agent, or similar monitoring stacks.

GET /api/overview#

JSON object with high-level daemon statistics:

Details
{
    "version": "1.1.0",
    "uptime_seconds": 86400,
    "runtimes_total": 5,
    "runtimes_running": 4,
    "connections_total": 18230,
    "connections_active": 142,
    "messages_total": 9120044,
    "bytes_in": 12345678,
    "bytes_out": 9876543,
    "cpu_seconds": 812.40,
    "rss_bytes": 163577856,
    "memory_bytes": 94371840,
    "processes": 5,
    "cpus": 4
}

cpu_seconds is the user and system CPU time of the daemon and every process its runtimes run in, read from /proc; the change between two readings over the time between them is the CPU used. rss_bytes is their resident memory added up, which counts a page shared between shards once per shard, and memory_bytes what they cost the machine, each shared page counted by the share the process holds of it, so that the figures of the runtimes add up to the memory they hold between them (the kernel's Pss). processes is how many there are, and cpus the CPUs online.

GET /api/runtimes#

JSON array of all runtimes with name, type, port, state, connections, message/byte counters, and cpu_seconds, rss_bytes, memory_bytes and processes for the runtime's own processes, one per shard (none while it is stopped).

GET /api/runtime/name#

JSON object for a single runtime identified by name. Returns 404 if the runtime does not exist.

The dashboard CLI command prints the dashboard URL:

$ socketley dashboard
Dashboard: http://localhost:9100/

sections.title: SERVICE MESH
sections.html: The proxy runtime includes service-mesh primitives that can be composed to build sidecar proxies, API gateways, or resilient service-to-service communication layers.

sections.title: Health Checks
sections.html: Active health checking probes backends at a regular interval (--health-interval) using either a TCP connect or an HTTP GET (--health-check). A backend is marked unhealthy after --health-threshold consecutive failures and is excluded from the load balancer pool. A single successful check restores the backend.

sections.title: Circuit Breaker
sections.html:
The circuit breaker prevents cascading failures by tracking consecutive errors per backend. It has three states:

closed#

Normal operation. Requests are forwarded to the backend. Errors are counted.

open#

Triggered when errors reach --circuit-threshold. All requests fail immediately without attempting a connection. After --circuit-timeout seconds, the circuit moves to half-open.

half-open#

A single probe request is allowed through — one, not one per selection: while that probe is outstanding the backend is unavailable to everyone else. If it succeeds, the circuit returns to closed. If it fails, the circuit re-opens.

entries.summary: Normal operation. Requests are forwarded to the backend. Errors are counted.
Triggered when errors reach --circuit-threshold. All requests fail immediately without attempting a connection. After --circuit-timeout seconds, the circuit moves to half-open.

A single probe request is allowed through — one, not one per selection: while that probe is outstanding the backend is unavailable to everyone else. If it succeeds, the circuit returns to closed. If it fails, the circuit re-opens.

sections.title: Response Deadline
sections.html:
A backend that accepts connections and then stops answering fails no check: a TCP health probe connects to it successfully, and a request that never completes is counted as neither an error nor a success, so the circuit breaker has nothing to open on. --backend-timeout (default 2 seconds) bounds the wait for the first byte of a response and records the expiry as a backend error, which is what puts such a backend through the breaker like any other failure. The request is retried elsewhere if --retry allows it and answered 504 Gateway Timeout otherwise.

The deadline covers the handshake as well as the answer: a backend that never completes its connect inside it is answered 504 Gateway Timeout too, rather than the client being closed without a response. A request routed through an @group backend is charged to the member it actually reached, so a group member that stalls is taken out of rotation by the same breaker as a listed backend.

The deadline is on by default and only covers the wait for the first byte, so a large or streaming response body is unaffected. An endpoint that legitimately needs more than 2 seconds to start answering has to be given a longer --backend-timeout or --backend-timeout 0; otherwise the proxy treats it as hung. It applies to HTTP mode only — in TCP mode there is no request boundary to measure from.

sections.title: Request Framing
sections.html:
In HTTP mode the proxy is strict about how a request's header block is framed, and refuses anything it and a backend could read differently. These are the same rules a socketley server applies to a request it receives directly, from one implementation — see Request Framing under SERVER FLAGS. The proxy forwards bytes to a backend that parses them independently; if the two disagree about where a request ends, the next request on the same connection starts in the wrong place, which is request smuggling. Normalising the request instead would mean guessing which way the backend will read it, so the proxy declines to guess.

A request is answered 400 Bad Request and its connection is closed, without contacting any backend, when the header block contains any of:

  • a bare LF or a bare CR — every line must end with CRLF

  • whitespace between a field name and its colon (Content-Length : 6)

  • a continuation (obs-fold) line, i.e. one starting with a space or tab

  • a field line with no colon

  • both Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding, or more than one Content-Length field

  • a Content-Length that is not a whole decimal number (Content-Length: 6x)

  • a Transfer-Encoding whose final coding is not chunked (Transfer-Encoding: gzip, Transfer-Encoding: chunked, gzip, or chunked listed twice) — such a request has no determinable body length at all

Every request on a connection is framed and checked on its own, including one pipelined behind another. Only the body a request declares travels with it: bytes past its Content-Length are not body, and are held back and parsed as the next request rather than forwarded. Pipelining still works — a second request sent before the first is answered is served — but it is answered in turn, after the same checks, and a smuggling attempt hidden behind a clean request is refused exactly as it would be if it had been sent first. A request held this way is subject to the same 10 second deadline as a half-arrived one: if the exchange in front of it never reaches an end this proxy can point at — a backend whose response is framed in a way it cannot read — the held request is answered 408 Request Timeout rather than left waiting. A chunked request is the one body this proxy cannot measure, because it never de-chunks; its body is forwarded as an opaque stream, so a request pipelined behind a chunked one is framed by the backend alone.

Compliant clients emit none of these. A request whose header block is still arriving is held until the terminating blank line, subject to the 16 KiB header limit (431 Request Header Fields Too Large) and a 10 second header deadline (408 Request Timeout).

There is a second, larger limit behind the header one, and it counts the whole of what is buffered for an exchange rather than one header block: at most 1 MiB is held for a connection whose request has already been forwarded — the body it sends past its declared Content-Length, and the requests pipelined behind it. Nothing drains that until the response in front of it is finished, so a client that writes faster than the backend answers reaches it on a well-formed connection. It is answered 413 Request Entity Too Large and the connection is closed. The one exception is the same one the gateway statuses make: if part of the backend's response is already on that client's wire, no status line is written behind it — it would land at an offset that is not a message boundary — and the connection is closed with the response left visibly truncated.

The header deadline starts at the first byte of a request and ends when its header block does. It is fixed, is not configurable, and is deliberately independent of --idle-timeout, which defaults to 0 (never) and so cannot be relied on to end a half-sent request: a client that sends a request line and then stops sends no further bytes for the 16 KiB limit to count, and would otherwise hold its connection, its descriptor and its 64 KB buffer for as long as it liked. Neither an idle keep-alive connection between requests nor a slow request body is measured against it — only the gap between a request's first byte and its terminating blank line.

The same strictness is applied to backend responses, but only to decide whether the backend connection may be reused: a response whose length cannot be established with certainty — because its header block was split across reads, or was not strictly CRLF-framed, or because more bytes arrived than the length it declared — is forwarded to the client unchanged, and its connection is closed instead of returned to the pool. A backend that answers Connection: close is not pooled either: it has said the socket is going away.

A Connection: close sent by the client does not do this. It is a hop-by-hop field about the client's own connection to the proxy, so it is not forwarded upstream and it does not end the backend connection: the proxy answers the request, returns the backend socket to the pool, and closes the client connection as asked. The field is a comma-separated list and is parsed token-wise and case-insensitively, as it is on the server, so Connection: keep-alive, close counts as close while a value that merely begins with those letters — Connection: clientinfo — does not. A client that opens a connection per request — curl, a health checker, any HTTP library used without a session — therefore costs one accept and no backend connect, the same as a keep-alive client.

A connection already in the pool is checked before it is handed to the next request, and one with unread data on it is closed rather than reused. Nothing was asked of an idle pooled socket, so anything waiting on it is something the backend sent unbidden — the tail of an answer whose length was mis-declared, or a second answer volunteered behind the first. Reusing it would make those bytes the head of the next client's response, so the connection is dropped and a fresh one opened. The proxy logs this once per instance.

Reuse covers an @group backend as well as a listed one. A pooled connection is filed under the endpoint it was opened to, never under the group, so it is only ever handed back to a request routed to that same member; a member that leaves the group has its pooled connections closed at once rather than left to the idle sweep.

Reuse covers a TLS backend too, and the session is pooled with the descriptor rather than the descriptor alone — a reused connection carries on the record layer it already had, at the sequence number it had reached. A TLS connection carries more than an address: a negotiated session, a peer identity verified against a name, a client certificate that may have been presented, and a record layer part way through a stream. The endpoint the socket is filed under answers three of those, because it is what the name was pinned to before the handshake and what the certificate was checked against; the client certificate and the trust store belong to the runtime and are rebuilt on every start, and the pool is emptied on every stop, so a pooled session can never outlive the configuration that verified it.

What a pooled TLS socket cannot do is inherit an answer nobody asked for. A cleartext socket with bytes waiting on it is destroyed rather than reused, because a socket in the pool has been asked nothing since its last answer completed. That test cannot be carried across a record layer unchanged: a TLS peer that has said nothing still sends records — a session ticket, a key update, a close_notify. So the socket is drained into the session and the question is put to the record layer instead of to the kernel: records that produce no application data are the peer's own housekeeping and the connection is kept, and application data is a response that belongs to a previous exchange and the connection is dropped. The second case is logged once per runtime.

sections.title: Retries
sections.html: When --retry is set, failed requests are automatically retried on the next backend in the load balancer pool. By default only idempotent methods are retried; use --retry-all to include POST and PATCH.

sections.title: mTLS
sections.html:
Both legs can be encrypted. --tls --cert --key terminates TLS on the proxy's own port and --client-ca makes it demand a certificate from its callers; https:// on a backend address, or any of --ca, --client-cert and --client-key, takes the backend leg to TLS, with the chain and the endpoint's name verified and a client certificate presented when one is configured. A full sidecar pair looks like this:

socketley create proxy edge -p 8443 \
    --tls --cert edge.pem --key edge-key.pem \
    --client-ca mesh-ca.pem \
    --backend https://10.0.0.7:8443 \
    --ca mesh-ca.pem \
    --client-cert edge.pem --client-key edge-key.pem \
    --sidecar -s

A TLS backend connection is returned to the connection pool and reused, so a busy sidecar pays for a handshake per idle period rather than per request. The pooled socket keeps its session, goes back only to the endpoint it was opened to, and is dropped rather than reused if the backend has left application data on it. --health-check http works against a TLS backend and probes it over TLS, verified to the same standard as the data path — see LIMITATIONS for what the probe does and does not establish. See mTLS Flags under PROXY FLAGS for what is verified and what cannot be switched off.

sections.title: Sidecar Deployment
sections.html:
The --sidecar flag enables a production-ready default set: TCP health checks, circuit breaker (threshold 5, timeout 30s), 2 retries, and graceful drain. Deploy alongside your application:

socketley create proxy myapp --sidecar \
    --backend 127.0.0.1:3000 -p 8080 -s

The proxy listens on port 8080 and forwards to the local application on port 3000. Unhealthy backends are automatically removed, and the circuit breaker prevents thundering-herd retries during outages.

--sidecar does not change --backend-timeout, which is 2 seconds by default and charges its expiry to the circuit breaker that --sidecar enables. If the application can take longer than that to send its first response byte, say so explicitly:

socketley create proxy myapp --sidecar --backend-timeout 30 \
    --backend 127.0.0.1:3000 -p 8080 -s

sections.html:

running#

Active and processing I/O.

stopped#

failed#

sections.title: EXAMPLES
sections.html:
Create a simple server (daemon is managed by systemd when installed):

socketley create server myserver -p 9000 -s

Create client connecting to server:

socketley create client myclient -t 127.0.0.1:9000 -s

Create HTTP proxy with load balancing:

socketley create proxy gateway -p 8080 \
    --backend 127.0.0.1:9001,127.0.0.1:9002 \
    --strategy round-robin -s

Server with bash output (messages to stdout):

socketley create server echo -p 9000 -b -s
# With timestamp and prefix:
socketley create server echo -p 9000 -bpt -s

Send message to runtime:

socketley send myserver "Hello from CLI"
socketley send myclient "Message to server"

Create persistent cache with maxmemory:

socketley create cache store -p 9000 \
    --persistent /data/cache.bin \
    --maxmemory 256M --eviction allkeys-lru -s

Create cache with RESP mode (Redis-compatible):

socketley create cache redis-compat -p 6379 --resp -s
redis-cli -p 6379 SET mykey myval
redis-cli -p 6379 GET mykey

Server with connection limits and rate limiting:

socketley create server api -p 9000 \
    --max-connections 100 --rate-limit 1000 -s

View runtime statistics:

socketley stats myserver
# Output: name, type, port, connections, total_messages, bytes_in/out, ...

Restart a running runtime:

socketley reload myserver
# Stops and restarts the runtime
socketley reload *
# Restarts all running runtimes

Hot-reload Lua script:

socketley reload-lua myserver
# Re-loads the Lua script without stopping the runtime
socketley reload-lua *
# Hot-reloads Lua on all runtimes with scripts

Start/stop all runtimes:

socketley start *
# Starts all non-running runtimes
socketley stop *
# Stops all running runtimes
socketley remove *
# Stops all and removes everything

Multiple names and glob patterns:

socketley stop myserver myclient
# Stops both runtimes
socketley stop my*
# Stops all runtimes starting with "my"
socketley stats cache?
# Shows stats for cache1, cache2, etc.
socketley start myserver cache*
# Starts myserver and all cache-prefixed runtimes
socketley remove api-* test-*
# Removes all api- and test- prefixed runtimes

Interactive mode (live terminal session):

# Start server and enter interactive session
socketley create server echo -p 9000
socketley start echo -i
# Type messages to broadcast, see received messages
# Press Ctrl+C to detach (server keeps running)

# Attach to already-running cache
socketley start mycache -i
# Type cache commands: set foo bar, get foo, etc.

Interactive edit (opens JSON config in $EDITOR):

socketley edit myserver           # Opens config in editor
socketley edit myserver -r        # Opens editor, auto-reloads Lua after save
socketley edit myserver -p 9001   # Flag-based edit (direct)

Cache replication (leader-follower):

socketley create cache leader -p 9000 -s
socketley create cache follower -p 9001 --replicate 127.0.0.1:9000 -s

Encrypted server. The listener terminates TLS itself; everything above it — line protocol, HTTP, WebSocket, RESP — runs on the decrypted stream, so this same runtime serves https:// and wss:// on the one port:

socketley create server secure -p 9443 \
    --tls --cert server.pem --key server-key.pem -s
curl --cacert server.pem https://localhost:9443/

Mutual TLS — a client must present a certificate signed by the given CA:

socketley create server mtls -p 9443 \
    --tls --cert server.pem --key server-key.pem \
    --ca trusted-clients.pem -s

Renewing a certificate: the files are read at start, so reload picks up a new one.

socketley reload secure

An incomplete configuration is refused rather than served in the clear:

socketley create server oops -p 9443 --tls --cert server.pem
# --tls: a TLS listener needs --key <file> to go with --cert
# exit status 1

Encrypted client. The dial is the mirror of the listener above: one flag turns the transport on, and the peer is verified on both counts — the chain against the trust store, and the certificate against the host in -t.

# verify against the system trust store
socketley create client feed -t events.example.com:9443 --tls -s

# verify against a private CA instead
socketley create client feed -t 10.0.0.7:9443 \
    --tls --ca internal-ca.pem -s

# and present a certificate of our own, for a peer that demands one
socketley create client feed -t 10.0.0.7:9443 \
    --tls --ca internal-ca.pem \
    --cert client.pem --key client-key.pem -s

A peer whose certificate does not verify costs the socket — the client re-dials on its backoff and never falls back to cleartext. There is no skip-verify flag: encryption without verification is protection against somebody recording the wire and none at all against somebody sitting on it, and the two look identical from the outside.

The same rules apply as on the listener. Half a certificate pair is refused, a trust store without --tls is refused, and reload is how a renewed client certificate is installed:

socketley create client bad -t host:9443 --tls --cert client.pem
# --cert: needs --key <file> as well -- a certificate with no key
# presents nothing
# exit status 1

Graceful shutdown (drain pending writes):

socketley create server api -p 9000 --drain -s
socketley stop api   # Flushes write queues before closing

UDP server (fire-and-forget messaging):

socketley create server stats -p 9000 --udp -b -s
echo "cpu.load 0.42" | socat - UDP:localhost:9000

UDP client:

socketley create client udpcli -t 127.0.0.1:9000 --udp -s

Create read-only cache (for shared lookups):

socketley create cache lookup -p 9000 --mode readonly -s

Master mode server (one controller, many viewers):

socketley create server broadcast -p 9000 \
    --mode master --master-pw secret -s
# Client A: sends "master secret" -> "master: ok"
# Client A: sends "hello" -> broadcast to all others
# Client B: sends "hello" -> silently dropped

Master mode with forwarding:

socketley create server ctrl -p 9000 \
    --mode master --master-pw admin123 --send-to master -s
# Non-master messages forwarded to master as "[<fd>] msg"

WebSocket server (auto-detected, no flags needed):

socketley create server ws -p 9000 -s
# Browser: new WebSocket("ws://localhost:9000")
# Raw TCP clients also work on the same port

Cache access through server:

socketley create cache db -p 9001 -s
socketley create server api -p 9000 --cache db -s
# Client sends: "cache set user:1 alice" -> "ok"
# Client sends: "cache get user:1" -> "alice"
# Client sends: "hello" -> broadcast as usual

Dynamic proxy with group-based backend discovery:

socketley create server api1 -p 9001 -g api -s
socketley create server api2 -p 9002 -g api -s
socketley create proxy gw -p 8080 --backend @api -s
# Proxy routes to all running members of group "api"

# Add a new member dynamically (no proxy restart needed)
socketley create server api3 -p 9003 -g api -s

# Mix group and direct backends
socketley create proxy gw2 -p 8081 \
    --backend @api,10.0.0.5:9000 -s

Lua HTTP worker (auto-detected, no flags needed):

socketley create server api -p 9000 --lua handler.lua -s
# handler.lua:
# function on_http_request(req)
#     return {status=200, headers={["Content-Type"]="application/json"},
#             body='{"hello":"world"}'}
# end
# curl http://localhost:9000/api

Sidecar proxy with health checks and circuit breaker:

socketley create proxy sidecar -p 8080 --sidecar \
    --backend 127.0.0.1:3000 -s

Proxy with HTTP health checks and retries:

socketley create proxy gateway -p 8080 \
    --backend 10.0.0.1:9000,10.0.0.2:9000 \
    --health-check http --health-path /ready \
    --health-interval 10 --health-threshold 5 \
    --retry 3 --circuit-threshold 10 -s

Proxy with mTLS on both legs. The listener terminates TLS and demands a certificate from its callers; the backend leg dials TLS, verifies the chain and the endpoint's name, and presents a certificate of its own:

socketley create proxy secure -p 8443 \
    --tls --cert proxy.pem --key proxy-key.pem \
    --client-ca trusted-clients.pem \
    --client-cert backend-client.pem --client-key backend-client-key.pem \
    --ca mesh-ca.pem \
    --backend https://10.0.0.1:9000 -s
# Backend connections are pooled with their sessions: a handshake per
# idle period, not per request.
# --health-check http probes over TLS and verifies the backend too.

TLS to the backend only — the proxy listens in cleartext on loopback and encrypts the hop that leaves the machine:

socketley create proxy egress -p 8080 \
    --backend https://api.example.com -s
# Verified against the system CA store, name checked against the certificate.
# A private CA goes in --ca; there is no way to skip verification.

Open the live dashboard:

socketley dashboard
# Dashboard: http://localhost:9100/
# Open in browser for live runtime view

Query dashboard API:

curl http://localhost:9100/api/overview
curl http://localhost:9100/api/runtimes
curl http://localhost:9100/api/runtime/myserver

Load complex configuration:

socketley --lua /etc/socketley/setup.lua

sections.title: CLUSTER MODE
sections.html:
The cluster directory is as privileged as the daemons that read it. A proxy with an @group backend picks its targets out of the files in that directory, so whoever can write there decides where that traffic goes. Treat write access to it exactly as you would treat the control socket: it belongs to the daemons and to nobody else. A shared volume between containers you control is the intended arrangement; a directory any other workload can write to is not.

Multi-daemon cluster discovery allows proxies to route to runtimes on remote daemons. Each daemon publishes its state to a shared directory (typically a Docker volume) every 2 seconds. Stale entries (heartbeat older than 10s) are automatically excluded.

How it works:

  • Each daemon writes its state to dir/name.json

  • Every 2 seconds, each daemon scans the directory for peer files

  • Proxy @group resolution includes both local and remote group members

  • On graceful shutdown, the daemon deletes its file

Restarting a node, and name conflicts:

A name is one node's. Two daemons publishing one file would give every peer an endpoint set belonging to neither, and split traffic for api1 between two machines that each believe they are api1 — so a daemon that finds its name held by a live entry is refused --cluster, and told so.

A node that was killed and restarted is not that case. Every restart policy this project documents — a container restart, a redeploy, systemd's Restart=on-failure, a crash loop — brings the node back in a second or two, well inside the 10s threshold, and it meets its own entry still fresh. It reclaims it.

The entry says who wrote it: the advertised host, the daemon's control socket path, the kernel boot id, and the pid. A fresh entry may be taken over only when the first three are this daemon's own, and that is a proof rather than a guess — a unix socket path admits one process at a time, and everything else that reaches a daemon connects to that path instead of binding it. So on one machine, under one hostname, whoever holds the path is the daemon; an entry carrying our own three was written by a process that is gone. A different machine has a different boot id, and a fresh entry cannot predate a reboot. The pid is published for the operator and never used to decide: a restarted container's pid namespace is new.

What this cannot tell apart is two containers on one host given the same hostname and both on the default socket path. Their entries are identical, and so is the address every peer would dial for either of them.

A daemon that could not join keeps serving — it is a working server that is not in a cluster — and says so in three places: the exit status of the command, an ERROR line in its log naming the holder, and every socketley cluster subcommand, which reports cluster mode is off with the reason instead of the same "not in cluster mode" a daemon that was never given --cluster reports. Clustering is never accepted and silently not applied.

Docker Compose example:

A complete, working one is examples/cluster/docker-compose.yml, and the same shape with assertions on it is test/docker/. Three things about it are not optional:

  • seccomp. Docker's default profile does not permit io_uring_setup(2), io_uring_enter(2) or io_uring_register(2), and socketley's whole I/O layer is a ring, so every node dies at startup with failed to init event loop under it. Run the containers with a profile that allows those three syscalls — during development, security_opt: [seccomp:unconfined].

  • entrypoint. The image's ENTRYPOINT is socketley, so a compose command: is passed to it as arguments. A node that needs a shell has to say entrypoint: ["/bin/sh", "-c"], and give its script as a one-element list — compose word-splits a bare string into an argv and everything past the first & is lost.

  • Readiness. daemon --name and daemon --cluster are configuration commands against a daemon that is already running, and they auto-start a detached one when the socket does not answer. Sleeping for a second before them is a race whose loss forks a second daemon and takes the container down without a message. Wait for the daemon's own daemon started line instead.

Alternatively, use a Lua config file:

-- /etc/socketley/setup.lua
daemon = { name = "api1", cluster = "/cluster" }
runtimes = {
    { type = "server", name = "web", port = 9001, group = "api", start = true }
}
socketley daemon &
sleep 1 && socketley --lua /etc/socketley/setup.lua

Inspecting the cluster:

socketley cluster ls
socketley cluster ps
socketley cluster group api
socketley cluster stats
socketley cluster watch

Stale detection:

ScenarioBehaviorRecovery
Graceful shutdownFile deletedImmediate
Container killedStale heartbeat~10 seconds
Container restartFile overwrittenImmediate

sections.title: Raft mode (experimental, opt-in)
sections.html:
Experimental. A daemon started with --raft-listen runs one Raft node on its own loop, and nothing else changes: the cluster directory above, and every runtime, proxy and cache that is not declared as a cluster runtime, behave exactly as without it. The cluster elects a leader, replicates a log to disk and keeps membership, and the state machine behind the log holds the cluster's runtimes (see Cluster runtimes below): a runtime is declared once, placed on distinct nodes by the leader, and started on a survivor when its node dies; a cache is replicated, and when the node that holds its primary dies the leader promotes the follower that holds the most (see Cluster caches below).

Flags (on the command line that starts the daemon, like --cpus; refused beside --name and --cluster):

--raft-listen ip:port#

Enable Raft mode and accept peer connections here. Numeric only: a peer's address travels through the replicated log and is dialled without a DNS lookup.

--raft-advertise ip:port#

The address peers dial, when it is not the listening one. Required when --raft-listen is a wildcard.

--raft-name name#

This node's name in the membership, and the name its certificate must carry (as a DNS subjectAltName or common name). Defaults to the advertised address. A name is one node's: a node that joins under the name of a member, or under one that reads the same once {node} has made it safe for a command line (see Cluster runtimes), is refused by the leader with the reason, and stops with that reason in its log and in cluster raft-status, because two nodes named alike would give every cluster runtime the same socket path or file.

--raft-init#

Found a new single-voter cluster, on first start only.

--raft-join ip:port#

Join the cluster a member at this address belongs to, on first start only. The node is added as a learner, receives the log without voting, and is promoted to voter by a single-server change once its log has caught up to the leader's commit index. A member that is not the leader passes the request on.

--raft-cert file --raft-key file --raft-ca file#

Mutual TLS between members, which is required. Every member's certificate is signed by the CA; a connection whose certificate does not name the member it introduces itself as — by the name membership records for its id, or for a newcomer the name it claims — is closed. The join target, whose id is not known yet, is held to the address that was dialled.

--raft-insecure#

Run Raft in cleartext. Refused beside the certificate flags; without it and without them the daemon refuses to start.

--raft-down-after duration#

How long the leader waits for a node's lease request before it declares the node down and moves its replicas: seconds, or with an s or ms suffix (4, 4s, 3500ms). Default four election timeouts (4 s). Refused below three election timeouts, because a leader change would then look like a node loss. Every member of one cluster should use the same value; see Cluster runtimes for what depends on it.

A daemon whose state directory already holds Raft state ignores --raft-init and --raft-join and comes back as the member it was. One with no state and neither flag refuses to start. A daemon that cannot bind the port or read its state exits 2 rather than serve without the cluster it was asked for.

On disk: state-dir/raft/ holds node-id (a random 64-bit id, generated once), wal-seq.log (CRC32C-checked records: hard state, entries, truncations) and snap-index-term files, all 0600. Every write is followed by an fsync linked behind it in io_uring, and nothing a node says to a peer leaves before the fsync reports. Recovery cuts a torn tail at the first bad record. The log is compacted every 1000 applied entries.

Timing: 100 ms ticks measured from elapsed monotonic time, an election timeout of 1–2 s, heartbeats every tick, pre-vote and check-quorum. A leader stopped by SIGTERM hands leadership to its most up-to-date voter (TimeoutNow) before it exits, so the cluster does not wait out an election timeout.

socketley cluster raft-status prints this node's id and name, role, term, leader, commit and applied indexes, the log's range, voters, learners, whether a quorum of voters was heard from within an election timeout, and the transport and WAL counters. It exits 0 with a leader and a reachable quorum, 2 without (saying so on its last line), and 1 on a daemon not in Raft mode.

Cluster runtimes. A cluster runtime is declared once, for the cluster, and every node applies the same log:

socketley cluster create server api -p 8080 --replicas 2
socketley cluster create server api --listen unix:/run/api-{node}.sock
socketley cluster scale api 3
socketley cluster remove api
socketley cluster placement

cluster create takes type, name and the flags create takes, plus --replicas (default 1). It is a server, a proxy, a client or a cache (see Cluster caches). The flags are stored as a list of arguments, so a value with a space in it stays one argument, and run as they are on every node that holds a replica, so a file they name must exist on each node (a relative path is made absolute against the caller's directory, as for create), and {node} in them is replaced by the name of the node running the replica (--raft-name, with anything but letters, digits, -, _ and . made _). That is what lets several nodes of a test share one host: two replicas that both ask for -p 8080 would collide, and --listen unix:/run/api-{node}.sock does not. On separate hosts each node binds its own -p and needs no placeholder. The flags are also run through create --test on the node that takes the command, so a typo is refused there, with exit 1, and not found on every node at once; --test itself is refused in a spec.

A command may be given to any node: a follower hands it to the leader. Success is silent, and the command has taken effect on the node that took it when it returns, or the CLI says it did not within five seconds and exits 2. Exit 1 is a refusal (a duplicate, an unknown name, a replica count outside 1 to 64, a runtime of that name already on this node, bad flags), exit 2 a cluster with no leader that can take it. On a daemon that is not in Raft mode every verb says so and exits 1.

cluster scale changes the replica count, taking a replica from the most loaded node when it shrinks. A runtime has no edit: remove it and declare it again.

Placement. The leader alone decides, and writes each assignment to the log, so every node agrees on it. The replicas of one runtime go to distinct nodes, one to the node that holds the fewest replicas and the lowest node id on a tie. When a node is declared down its replicas are moved to live nodes, and a node that comes back, or joins, is not given work back: nothing is rebalanced, so a running replica is never moved for tidiness. Asking for more replicas than there are live nodes runs what fits; cluster placement says how many replicas are unplaced. It prints the runtimes with their replicas, where each is placed and how many are unplaced, each cache's primary and the copies it has (see Cluster caches), the nodes with the number of replicas each holds and, on the leader, whether the leader counts each up and when it last heard from it, and this node's replicas with what each is doing (running, waiting for a lease, failed with the reason, or blocked by a local runtime of the same name).

On each node, a reconciliation runs at the end of every Raft tick and compares what the log says the node owns with what it runs. It creates a replica with create -s and stops, starts and removes it with stop, start and remove: the same code as the CLI, and nothing else spawns a replica. It never waits for a worker to come up and runs at most four commands a tick, so a replica whose startup hangs, or fifty arriving at once, cannot stall the Raft loop; a failure shows as the replica's state on a later tick. A replica that fails to start is tried again every three seconds and its reason is logged once and shown by cluster placement. A local runtime with the same name is never touched. A replica is marked [cluster] in ls and ps after its state, "cluster":true in --json, and cluster:replica in stats; it has no state file, so a node that restarts does not bring back what has moved away, and stop, start, remove and edit refuse it by name, since the next tick would undo them.

Liveness and the lease. A follower asks the leader, every quarter election timeout, to count it alive, and the leader answers when it holds a quorum. The leader declares a node down when it has not heard a request for --raft-down-after (a new leader starts every node's clock at its own election). A node may run its replicas only while it holds a lease, which lasts three quarters of that time counted from when the request was sent, so a late answer shortens it and a stalled loop cannot extend it. The leader's own lease is its last look at a quorum. The margin between the lease and the failure timeout, a quarter of it (1 s by default), is what a node has to stop its replicas in before the leader gives them to another node. A lease that had lapsed is used again only once the node has applied the end of the leader's log as it stood when it was granted, so a node that comes back does not run a replica that moved while it was away.

Partitions and duplicates. A node that cannot reach a quorum stops serving its replicas within its lease (measured 2.9–3.8 s after the last answer at the defaults) and keeps them defined, so they start again the moment a lease is granted; the majority moves them after the failure timeout, at least a quarter of it later. So a minority never serves what it cannot confirm it owns, a minority holding the old leader included, and a healed node runs only what the log still gives it. The same holds for a leader that loses its quorum, and it means that a cluster that loses its quorum stops serving every cluster replica, on every node, until it has one again: the cluster chooses one copy or none over two. A leader change that takes longer than the lease (a split vote; about one in ten kills of a leader in simulation) stops a survivor's replicas until the new leader has granted a lease, a few hundred milliseconds after it is elected. The lease is enforced by the daemon's loop, so a daemon that is hung and not dead (SIGSTOP, a blocked disk) cannot stop the workers of a server, a proxy or a client, which are separate processes (a cache's worker fences itself: see Cluster caches); and whatever a replica does on its way down (a --drain that flushes its connections) spends part of the margin.

Failover time, kill -9 of a node to its replica running on a survivor, at the defaults on one host with a real daemon, and 60 seeds of a simulation of the same logic: about 3.9–4.3 s when the node was a follower (the failure timeout and a commit), about 5.1–6.0 s when it was the leader (an election first), and up to 8.7 s in the simulation when a split vote stretched the election.

Cluster caches. A cache is a cluster runtime that holds data, so keeping it running is not enough:

socketley cluster create cache db -p 6379 --replicas 3
socketley cluster create proxy gw -p 7000 --backend @db --replicas 3

The leader places the replicas as for any runtime, and the log names one of them the primary of an epoch: a number that only grows, so two leaders that race to promote agree on which was first. The others are its followers, and follow it with the cache's own replication (--replicate: a full dump, then every write), dialling the primary's -p on the host its node advertises to Raft. That is why a cluster cache needs -p; it is refused with --listen, --shards, --tls, --replicate (the cluster sets it) and without a port. On one host each replica needs its own port, which is what {node} is for: named 1, 2 and 3, the nodes run -p 630{node} as ports 6301, 6302 and 6303. On separate hosts a follower is a peer on another machine, which a cache serves only with --public: put it in the spec (the tests here ran on one host and did not try it). A cache with one replica has a primary and nothing to promote. The first primary is the replica on the lowest node id, chosen once every replica has said it exists (or after an election timeout). A replica is a process the log can name (its incarnation), and a restarted one is another, holding nothing the old one did.

Who may write. A replica takes a client's command only under its worker's last order from its daemon, sent every 100 ms and standing for the lease the daemon held when it sent it. A replica that is fenced answers every command, reads included, with an error, and refuses replicate; a follower answers reads and refuses writes; the primary takes writes. A replica starts fenced, and leads only if this node holds a lease AND the log names the very process it runs as the primary; anything else follows whoever the log names, or waits when nobody is named. A fence keeps the data: the process stays up, so a node that lost its quorum for a minute and got it back is the primary again with everything it had, and a follower keeps its link and its copy through a spell without a lease. When the orders stop, for any reason (the node lost its quorum, or the daemon hung or died), the worker fences itself when the last one runs out, without the daemon's help. Measured in nine runs with real daemons: a worker whose daemon was stopped with SIGSTOP refused writes after 2.7–3.1 s, and a primary that lost its quorum stopped taking writes after 2.8–3.2 s (the lease is three quarters of the failure timeout, 3 s at the defaults).

Promotion. The leader replaces a primary when nobody leads, when its node has been declared down (in the same round that takes its replica away), or when its node is alive but has not, for the failure timeout, named the process the log calls the primary in a lease request: a primary whose daemon restarted comes back empty and does not lead, and a replica that has the data is promoted after that timeout. Every lease request carries, for each cache replica the node runs, its incarnation, the epoch of the primary whose stream the copy came from, its offset in that stream, and whether it leads. The offset is a count of records: the primary counts every record it produces, whether or not a follower is connected, the end-of-dump marker carries the count at which the dump was taken, and a follower is at that number plus the records it has applied since; a copy is empty from the first line of a dump to its last. The leader promotes the replica whose copy is the most up to date, comparing epochs first (offsets of two primaries are not on one scale), then offsets, then the lowest node id, and writes it with the next epoch to the log. The offsets the leader has are up to about half a second old (a stats push and a request interval), but the primary has been gone for the failure timeout by the time it looks, so the followers' last reports are their final positions. A primary that comes back, or a node that is given a replica again, is a new process: it follows the primary of the epoch it finds and takes a full dump that replaces whatever it held, so nothing it wrote that the cluster did not have survives, and it does not lead a cache whose log names another. A cache scaled down never loses its primary.

How long, kill -9 of the node that holds the primary to a survivor taking a write, on one host with real daemons (the default timing): 3.9–4.1 s when the node was not the Raft leader (the failure timeout and a commit; eleven kills) and 5.2–5.7 s when it was (an election first; four kills). In a simulation of the same logic over 60 kills it was 4.1–4.2 s and 5.6–7.2 s, the longer ones being a split vote. A follower dials the new primary within about a fifth of a second of being told, and a proxy follows through the endpoint group the primary is published as: the first write through a proxy on a survivor succeeded 20–95 ms after the first write made directly to the new primary (five runs).

What a failover can lose. Replication is asynchronous: the primary answers a write and streams it afterwards, so when its node dies the promoted follower lacks the acknowledged writes it had not received. What survives is always a prefix of the primary's history (replication is ordered, and the tests read every acknowledged key back to check that no write is lost that a later one outlived). How long the tail is depends on how far behind the best follower was. Measured with a client writing continuously and kill -9 of the primary's node, three kills each: one connection writing one key at a time, about a thousand a second (4,500 to 4,900 acknowledged), none missing; 200 writes pipelined at a time as fast as one connection goes (630,000 to 720,000 acknowledged, some 230,000 a second), none missing; and the same with both followers' workers stopped (SIGSTOP) for the four seconds before the kill, so that neither was receiving, about 1.6 million acknowledged and 876,000 to 922,000 of them missing, which is every write the primary took while no follower had it. So the window is how far behind the best follower was when the primary died: a few writes when the followers keep up (the first two conditions lost none), and everything since a follower stopped reading when they do not. Only what a follower had already received survives (in a separate check, a stopped follower held about 20,000 of 925,000 acknowledged keys after its leader was killed), and a primary drops a follower that is 8 MiB behind, after which it keeps acknowledging writes that no follower is receiving until that follower dials again. A machine that loses power, or a network that is cut, could not be tried without root. There is no synchronous mode: a write that must survive its primary is written to two caches.

Finding the primary. cluster placement prints, under CACHE PRIMARIES, each cache's primary and epoch and, for each replica, the epoch and offset of its copy and how old that news is: the leader hears every node's, the others their own. A proxy with --backend @name follows the primary: the cache's name is published as a group of one, the primary's host and port, on every node that holds a lease, and republished when it moves. The stats of a replica carry cluster_role, cluster_epoch, cluster_offset and cluster_incarnation.

Limits. A cache whose replicas all die at once starts again empty: the data lived in memory, and a --persistent file is loaded by a restarted process but does not take part in choosing the primary, and is replaced when the replica syncs from the primary that was chosen. A cache with one replica loses its data with its node. A worker that answers its daemon and takes no orders is not replaced.

Not yet: removing a member, snapshots sent in chunks (a snapshot goes in one frame of at most 16 MiB), a cluster id that keeps two clusters from mixing, editing a cluster runtime in place, moving a replica off a node before it is stopped for maintenance (a node stopped with SIGTERM keeps its assignments until the failure timeout), a worker that fences itself when its daemon is hung for a server, a proxy or a client (a cache does), synchronous replication of a cache, and a replica that fails to start on one node being tried on another.

entries.summary: Enable Raft mode and accept peer connections here. Numeric only: a peer's address travels through the replicated log and is dialled without a DNS lookup.
The address peers dial, when it is not the listening one. Required when --raft-listen is a wildcard.

This node's name in the membership, and the name its certificate must carry (as a DNS subjectAltName or common name). Defaults to the advertised address. A name is one node's: a node that joins under the name of a member, or under one that reads the same once {node} has made it safe for a command line (see Cluster runtimes), is refused by the leader with the reason, and stops with that reason in i
Found a new single-voter cluster, on first start only.

Join the cluster a member at this address belongs to, on first start only. The node is added as a learner, receives the log without voting, and is promoted to voter by a single-server change once its log has caught up to the leader's commit index. A member that is not the leader passes the request on.

Mutual TLS between members, which is required. Every member's certificate is signed by the CA; a connection whose certificate does not name the member it introduces itself as — by the name membership records for its id, or for a newcomer the name it claims — is closed. The join target, whose id is not known yet, is held to the address that was dialled.
Run Raft in cleartext. Refused beside the certificate flags; without it and without them the daemon refuses to start.

How long the leader waits for a node's lease request before it declares the node down and moves its replicas: seconds, or with an s or ms suffix (4, 4s, 3500ms). Default four election timeouts (4 s). Refused below three election timeouts, because a leader change would then look like a node loss. Every member of one cluster should use the same value; see Cluster runtimes for what depends on it.

sections.title: Release Package
sections.html:
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HiImSmiley/Socketley/main/install.sh | sudo sh

Installs the newest release .deb, asking before each dependency it lacks, and stops having changed nothing when the package was built for a newer distribution; it also installs a package already at hand, answers every question with its default, and removes socketley, as its --help says.

sections.title: From Source
sections.html:
git clone https://github.com/HiImSmiley/Socketley
cd Socketley
bash scripts/install-from-source.sh

Checks the kernel, architecture and compiler, installs the build dependencies, builds the liburing and the static archives the tree links, builds Release, installs the binary, this page and the systemd service, and starts the daemon. Its --help names how to see every command without running one, and how to remove what it installed.

sections.title: Quick Install
sections.html:
From a tree already built:

sudo bash packaging/install.sh
sudo systemctl start socketley

sections.title: Debian Package
sections.html:
bash packaging/build-deb.sh 1.1.0
sudo dpkg -i socketley_1.1.0_amd64.deb
sudo systemctl start socketley

sections.title: Uninstall
sections.html: sudo bash packaging/uninstall.sh

sections.title: STATE PERSISTENCE
sections.html:
Runtime configurations are persisted as JSON files. When a runtime is created, its configuration is saved. When the daemon starts, all persisted runtimes are restored. Runtimes that were running when the daemon stopped are auto-started.

This means runtimes survive daemon restarts and system reboots (like Docker with restart-always policy).

State is saved after create, start, stop, remove, and edit commands. The was_running field tracks whether a runtime should be auto-started on daemon startup.

sections.title: A State File Is A Secret
sections.html:
A runtime's record is not a note about the runtime, it is the runtime. It carries, in plaintext:

master_pw#

the password given to --master-pw, verbatim.

key_path, mesh_client_key#

the paths of the TLS and mTLS private keys this runtime uses.

lua_script#

the path of the handler the daemon loads, which runs with the daemon's privileges — see Handler Privileges under LUA CONFIGURATION.

And the daemon restores every runtime from these files when it starts. So whoever can write one chooses what the daemon runs at its next start, which is the same thing as being able to send it commands.

Accordingly the daemon writes them 0600, stated at creation rather than inherited from its umask, and the packaged state directory is 0750 owned by socketley:socketley. Neither is configurable, and there is no supported reason to widen them: an operator reaches this data through the CLI, over a socket with the same group boundary, not by reading the directory.

Earlier versions wrote these files 0666 & ~umask — 0644 under systemd's default, 0666 for a daemon started from a shell with umask 0. Any local user could read a master password, and in the last case rewrite the record. On its first start after an upgrade the daemon narrows every file it finds in its state directory to 0600 and logs how many:

state: tightened 3 file(s) in /var/lib/socketley/runtimes to 0600 ...

It only ever narrows, it is idempotent, and it does not touch the directory — that belongs to the installer. Seeing the line on every start means something outside socketley is putting the modes back.

A password that was exposed should be treated as exposed. The repair closes the hole; it cannot un-read what was already readable. Rotate any --master-pw that lived on a multi-user machine under an affected version, with socketley edit or by recreating the runtime.
