sections.title: THE IPC SOCKET
sections.html:
Every socketley command travels over the socket above, and everything the daemon can do is reachable through it: stopping a runtime, reading stats, rewriting a runtime's configuration with edit, and — since a --lua handler runs with the daemon's privileges, see Handler Privileges under LUA CONFIGURATION — running arbitrary code as the user the daemon runs as.

So opening the socket is an administrative right, and the mode says so:

/run/socketley/socketley.sock   0660  socketley:socketley
any other path                  0600  the user who started the daemon

The packaged daemon runs as socketley and the operator does not, so the packaged socket is shared with one group and membership of that group is how the right is granted:

sudo usermod -aG socketley "$USER"     # then log in again

A daemon on any other path — a development daemon, or one started with SOCKETLEY_SOCKET — keeps its socket to itself. That is owner-only rather than owner-and-group because a shared primary group is not unusual — users on several distributions — and there the daemon's group is every human on the machine.

This socket used to be 0666, world-writable, on both paths. Any local uid could drive any daemon on the machine, whoever it belonged to. After upgrading past that, a user who has been running socketley against a system daemon without being in the socketley group will get

not permitted to open the daemon socket at /run/socketley/socketley.sock

and needs to be added to it. A user who is not added is not locked out of the program: with the system socket unreachable the CLI falls back to development mode and starts a daemon of that user's own, with that user's privileges and that user's runtimes.

On a machine where two people use development mode at once, the second gets the same message about /tmp/socketley.sock — one path, one owner, and it is no longer shared. That was never a supported arrangement, it was a shared daemon nobody had asked for. Give each their own:

export SOCKETLEY_SOCKET="/tmp/socketley-$USER.sock"

which also gives each a state directory of its own; see WHERE STATE LIVES above.

sections.title: WHERE STATE LIVES
sections.html:
The two paths above are where a daemon's runtimes live when it is serving the default socket, which is every deployed daemon and every daemon that has never heard of SOCKETLEY_SOCKET. Nothing about that has changed or will.

A daemon on any other socket path gets a directory of its own, a sibling of the one above named after that path: the leading slash is dropped and every character outside A-Za-z0-9._- becomes an underscore.

SOCKETLEY_SOCKET unset          ~/.local/share/socketley/runtimes
SOCKETLEY_SOCKET=/tmp/a.sock    ~/.local/share/socketley/runtimes.tmp_a.sock
SOCKETLEY_SOCKET=/tmp/socketley.sock
                                ~/.local/share/socketley/runtimes

Setting the variable to the path that would have been used anyway is the default, not a second daemon, so a script that spells the default out keeps the default directory. The name is readable rather than hashed on purpose: the answer to "which of these is mine" should come out of an ls.

The daemon logs the directory it is using at startup (state directory: ...), and that line is the authoritative answer. It is worth knowing where to find it before you need it.

Upgrading. The first time a daemon uses one of these keyed directories, everything in the shared directory it used to read is copied into it, once, and an INFO line says how many runtimes were adopted and from where. The originals are left exactly where they are, so an older binary rolled back onto the machine still finds what it has always found. A .adopted file in the new directory records what happened and is what makes it a one-time event — without it, an operator who later removed every runtime would find them all back after the next restart.

...but never out from under a running daemon. Adoption is skipped entirely while a daemon is serving the default socket path, because those runtimes are that daemon's and adopting them would mean binding ports it is already serving. The check is a probe of the default path, and anything answering there — daemon or not — is enough to decline.

This is not a rare corner. An operator debugging beside a running daemon reaches it with one command, and the second bind succeeds under SO_REUSEPORT, so nothing but the port count would ever have reported it.

The decline is logged at WARN with both directory paths and what to do about it, because from the outside it looks exactly like the runtimes having vanished. It writes no .adopted marker: "somebody is using these right now" is a fact about this minute rather than a decision, so stopping the daemon on the default path and restarting this one adopts them as normal.

The failure this trades against. A daemon started with a SOCKETLEY_SOCKET it did not have last time finds no runtimes. On a development machine that is correct: it is a different daemon and it owns nothing. It cannot happen to a deployed node, because a deployed node runs on the default path with the variable unset, and the default path is exempt from the rule for exactly that reason. If it happens anyway, nothing has been destroyed — the other directory is still on disk with everything in it, and starting the daemon with the variable it had before brings it all back.

The alternative, one state directory for every daemon in the namespace, is not the safe direction. Two daemons then bind each other's ports on boot, each reports the other's runtimes as its own, and a remove sent to either deletes a state file the other is still serving — and there is no undo for that.

sections.title: Daemon Configuration
sections.html:
The daemon config file is a Lua script that sets a daemon table:

daemon = {
    name = "node1",          -- this daemon's name in a cluster
    cluster = "/shared/dir", -- cluster directory; needs name
    log_level = "info",      -- debug, info, warn, error
    metrics_port = 9100,     -- Prometheus metrics HTTP endpoint
    dashboard_credentials = "/etc/socketley/admin.creds",
                             -- the dashboard's admins sign in from here
    dashboard_idp = "auth",  -- or as admins of this idp runtime
    alert_webhook = "https://discord.com/api/webhooks/...",
                             -- where alerts are posted
    alert_mail = "mail://m/ops@example.com",
                             -- and mailed, by this mail runtime
    events = "bus",          -- an mqtt runtime the runtimes' states and
                             -- the alerts are published on
    cpus = "0-3",            -- where this daemon's I/O runs
    settings = {             -- any SOCKETLEY_* knob, by its short name
        storage_hash_threads = 4,
        lua_timeout_ms = 2000,
        proxy_splice = true,
    }
}

config is the same table under its older name and still works; a file naming both is refused rather than merged. name and cluster are the two keys socketley --lua can also set on a daemon that is already running — the other three are settled before the ring exists, so they are read only from here, and a --cpus typed on socketley daemon outranks the file.

settings sets any variable under ENVIRONMENT that an operator may turn, by its name without SOCKETLEY_ and in lower case: storage_hash_threads is SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_HASH_THREADS. A number is written as one, an on-or-off as true or false, anything else as a string. The daemon puts each in the environment it starts its workers with, so a runtime reads the file's value as it would the variable's. The file comes first: a variable in the daemon's own environment counts only for a setting the file does not name, and the default only for one neither sets. A name that is no setting, a value outside the setting's range, and a variable a command reads from its own environment (the SOCKETLEY_GIT_* ones, and SOCKETLEY_SOCKET and SOCKETLEY_CONFIG, which choose this file) are each said on standard output, and the daemon does not start. socketley settings shows what was taken.

When metrics_port is set, the daemon starts an HTTP endpoint that serves a live web dashboard at GET /, Prometheus exposition format metrics at GET /metrics, and JSON API endpoints at /api/overview, /api/runtimes, and /api/runtime/<name> (see DASHBOARD). Metrics include: runtimes total/running, connections total/active, messages total, bytes in/out, and per-runtime breakdowns, among them socketley_runtime_cpu_seconds_total, socketley_runtime_resident_memory_bytes (resident, a shared page counted once per shard) and socketley_runtime_memory_bytes (what the runtime costs the machine, a shared page counted by the share it holds), and the daemon's own socketley_daemon_cpu_seconds_total and socketley_daemon_memory_bytes.

Each running runtime adds the figures of its own stats, a family per figure named after its type and labelled name: socketley_server_*, socketley_client_*, socketley_proxy_* (among them _backends, _healthy_backends, _backend_responses_total and _backend_failures_total), socketley_cache_* (among them _keys, _get_hits_total and _get_misses_total), socketley_db_*, socketley_dns_* (with socketley_dns_queries_total by transport and socketley_dns_responses_total by rcode), socketley_idp_* (among them _sign_ins_barred_total, sign-ins refused for too many failures), socketley_mqtt_* (messages by qos, drops by reason), socketley_sync_* (among them _failing), and the storage, mail and tunnel families under STORAGE FLAGS (Metrics); a tunnel edge adds socketley_tunnel_agents_joined and socketley_tunnel_agents_connected, the agents expected linked and those that are. Counters end in _total. A figure no family names is socketley_type_stat with its name as the label stat.

Beside them are the facts the daemon's alerts look at, each a series a rule can read: socketley_runtime_state (labels name, type, state; 1 for the state a runtime is in, 0 for the other three), socketley_runtime_restarts_total (times a worker went down and was started again), socketley_cert_expiry_seconds (labels name, path; seconds until the certificate a runtime serves with ends, below 0 once it has, read every five minutes), socketley_disk_free_ratio, socketley_disk_free_bytes and socketley_disk_size_bytes (label path, the state directory's disk and each storage runtime's, each disk once), socketley_host_memory_available_ratio, _available_bytes and _total_bytes, socketley_runtime_quota_ratio (what a storage with --max-bytes or a cache with --maxmemory and no eviction holds of its limit), socketley_mail_blocklisted (1 while a blocklist of its --dnsbl names the address a mail runtime sends from) and socketley_git_mirror_failed (labels name, repo, id; 1 when the last pull of a storage's git mirror failed, read every minute, and error what the failed one said), socketley_runtime_failure (labels name, type, reason; 1 for a runtime that failed, its last warning or error line the reason) and socketley_runtime_bytes_received_total and _sent_total per runtime.

How long the work takes is a Prometheus histogram per runtime, buckets from 64 microseconds doubling to 16.8 seconds and +Inf, each request measured from the start of the loop turn that read it to the start of the turn that answered it, so a request answered in the turn it came in is 0 and no clock is read for it: socketley_proxy_request_duration_seconds (an HTTP request's head to its answer's last byte), socketley_proxy_backend_connect_duration_seconds and socketley_proxy_backend_first_byte_seconds, socketley_server_http_request_duration_seconds, socketley_cache_batch_duration_seconds (a read's commands to their replies handed on), socketley_db_request_duration_seconds, socketley_idp_sign_in_duration_seconds, socketley_mail_delivery_duration_seconds and socketley_storage_request_duration_seconds, each with _bucket (le), _sum and _count, the shards' added together; histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(socketley_proxy_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) reads one's 99th percentile.

sections.title: C++ SDK
sections.html:
Socketley ships a three-tier modular C++ SDK in include/linux/socketley/. Tiers 1 and 3 are fully self-contained header-only files — copy them anywhere, compile with g++ -std=c++17, no library needed. Tier 2 requires building from source.

TierHeaderUse CaseDependencies
1socketley/control.hControl a running daemonNone (POSIX)
2socketley/{server,cache,proxy,client}.hEmbed the full enginelibsocketley_sdk.a
3socketley/attach.hRegister with a daemonNone (Tier 1)

sections.title: Tier 1: Daemon Control (header-only)
sections.html:
socketley/control.h provides full programmatic control over a running daemon through the same Unix socket IPC that the CLI uses. Zero dependencies beyond POSIX.

Result type:

struct socketley::result {
    int         exit_code;  // 0=success, 1=bad input, 2=fatal, -1=connect fail
    std::string data;       // response body
};

Runtime management functions (all in namespace socketley::ctl):

command(cmd)               // raw command (glob patterns work)
command(socket_path, cmd)  // custom socket path
create(type, name, flags)  // "server", "client", "proxy", "cache"
start(name)                stop(name)
remove(name)               send(name, message)
ls()   ps()   stats(name)  show(name)
reload(name)               reload_lua(name)
edit(name, flags)

Cache string operations (direct IPC, no TCP connection needed):

cache_get(cache, key)           cache_set(cache, key, value)
cache_del(cache, key)           cache_exists(cache, key)
cache_incr(cache, key)          cache_decr(cache, key)
cache_incrby(cache, key, n)     cache_decrby(cache, key, n)
cache_append(cache, key, val)

Cache list operations:

cache_lpush(cache, key, val)    cache_rpush(cache, key, val)
cache_lpop(cache, key)          cache_rpop(cache, key)
cache_llen(cache, key)          cache_lrange(cache, key, start, stop)
cache_lindex(cache, key, idx)

Cache set operations:

cache_sadd(cache, key, member)  cache_srem(cache, key, member)
cache_sismember(cache, key, m)  cache_scard(cache, key)
cache_smembers(cache, key)

Cache hash operations:

cache_hset(cache, key, f, v)    cache_hget(cache, key, field)
cache_hdel(cache, key, field)   cache_hlen(cache, key)
cache_hgetall(cache, key)

Cache TTL:

cache_expire(cache, key, sec)   cache_ttl(cache, key)
cache_persist(cache, key)

Cache pub/sub:

cache_publish(cache, ch, msg)

Cache admin:

cache_size(cache)               cache_memory(cache)
cache_keys(cache, pattern)
cache_flush(cache [, path])     cache_load(cache [, path])

Socket path resolution: checks SOCKETLEY_SOCKET env, then /run/socketley/socketley.sock, then /tmp/socketley.sock. Set the variable only to reach a daemon that is not the one for this namespace, which in practice means a second daemon on a development machine; a deployed node runs one daemon on the default path.

Example: lifecycle management

#include <socketley/control.h>
#include <cstdio>

int main() {
    auto r = socketley::ctl::create("server", "myapp", "-p 9000 -s");
    if (r.exit_code != 0) return 1;

    socketley::ctl::send("myapp", "Hello from C++!");
    auto stats = socketley::ctl::stats("myapp");
    printf("%s\n", stats.data.c_str());

    socketley::ctl::stop("myapp");
    socketley::ctl::remove("myapp");
}
// g++ -std=c++17 myapp.cpp -Iinclude/linux -o myapp

Example: fleet management with globs

for (int i = 0; i < 5; ++i) {
    std::string name  = "api_" + std::to_string(i);
    std::string flags = "-p " + std::to_string(9000+i) + " -s";
    socketley::ctl::create("server", name, flags);
}
socketley::ctl::command("start api_*");    // start all
socketley::ctl::command("stats api_*");    // query all
socketley::ctl::command("stop api_*");     // stop all
socketley::ctl::command("remove api_*");   // remove all

Example: cache operations

socketley::ctl::create("cache", "store", "-p 6379 --mode admin -s");
socketley::ctl::cache_set("store", "user:1", "alice");
auto r = socketley::ctl::cache_get("store", "user:1");
printf("user:1 = %s\n", r.data.c_str());  // "alice"
socketley::ctl::cache_del("store", "user:1");
socketley::ctl::cache_flush("store", "/tmp/store.bin");

sections.title: Tier 2: Embed Engine (build from source)
sections.html:
Embed the full io_uring event loop and all four runtime types in your own binary. Maximum performance with no IPC overhead. Requires libsocketley_sdk.a and link flags -luring -lssl -lcrypto [-lluajit].

Headers: socketley/core.h (event_loop, runtime_manager, enums), socketley/server.h , socketley/client.h , socketley/proxy.h , socketley/cache.h .

Define SOCKETLEY_NO_LUA to build without LuaJIT (omit -lluajit from link flags).

High-Level Wrapper Classes (recommended)

The socketley::server, socketley::client, socketley::proxy, and socketley::cache classes wrap the raw engine API into a fluent, chainable interface. All boilerplate (event loop, runtime manager, signal handling) is internal.

socketley::server

server(uint16_t port)

// Config (all return server& for chaining)
tls(cert, key)         // terminates TLS on this listener
client_ca(ca)          // mutual TLS on it: clients must present a certificate
                       // (tls_ca(ca) is the older spelling; it also sets tls)
max_connections(n)     rate_limit(r)
global_rate_limit(r)   idle_timeout(s)       lua(path)
mode(m)                udp()                 http_dir(path)
http_cache()           upstream(addr)        master_pw(pw)
drain()                group(g)              tick_interval(ms)

// Callbacks (return server& for chaining)
on_start(void())                             on_stop(void())
on_connect(void(int fd))                     on_disconnect(void(int fd))
on_message(void(int fd, string_view msg))    on_tick(void(double dt_ms))

// Actions
send(fd, msg)       broadcast(msg)      disconnect(fd)
peer_ip(fd)         clients()           multicast(fds, msg)
set_data(fd,k,v)    get_data(fd,k)

// Lifecycle
start()   stop()

// Escape hatches (raw engine access)
instance() -> server_instance*
manager()  -> runtime_manager&
loop()     -> event_loop&

socketley::client

client(string_view host, uint16_t port)

// Config
tls()              // dial over TLS; the host from the constructor is pinned
                   // and the chain verified against the system trust store
tls_ca(ca)         // verify against that CA instead of the system store
client_cert(c, k)  // the certificate this client presents when the peer asks
                   // for one - the client half of mutual TLS; needs tls()
reconnect(max)     mode(m)            udp()
lua(path)          tick_interval(ms)

// Callbacks
on_start    on_stop    on_connect    on_disconnect
on_message(void(string_view msg))   on_tick

// Actions
send(msg)

// Lifecycle: start()  stop()
// Escape hatches: instance()  manager()  loop()

socketley::proxy

proxy(uint16_t port)

// Config
backend(addr)      strategy(s)        protocol(p)
tls(cert, key)     // terminates TLS on this proxy's listener
client_ca(ca)      // mutual TLS on it: clients must present a certificate
backend_ca(ca)     // trust store for the backend leg; turns that leg to TLS
client_cert(c, k)  // the certificate presented to a backend that asks
max_connections(n) idle_timeout(s)
lua(path)          group(g)

// Callbacks: on_start  on_stop
// Lifecycle: start()  stop()
// Escape hatches: instance()  manager()  loop()

socketley::cache

cache(uint16_t port)

// Config
persistent(path)   max_memory(bytes)   eviction(policy)
resp()             mode(m)
tls(cert, key)
max_connections(n) idle_timeout(s)     replicate(target)
lua(path)          group(g)

// Callbacks: on_start  on_stop
// Lifecycle: start()  stop()
// Escape hatches: instance()  manager()  loop()

Limitations: One start() per process (the signal handler points to one event_loop). start() blocks until SIGINT/SIGTERM. For multi-runtime or async patterns, use the raw API via the escape hatches or directly.

TLS: on a server and a proxy only. server().tls() and proxy().tls() terminate TLS on that runtime's listener, and proxy().backend_ca(), proxy().client_ca() and proxy().client_cert() configure the proxy's two legs, exactly as the CLI flags do — start() goes through runtime_manager::start and reaches the same gate. On a client or cache builder the same entry points still store their arguments and are read by nothing, and there start() refuses rather than listening in cleartext. See TLS under LIMITATIONS.

Example: echo server (3 lines)

#include <socketley/server.h>
#include <cstdio>

int main() {
    socketley::server srv(9000);

    srv.on_connect([](int fd) {
        printf("client %d connected\n", fd);
    });
    srv.on_message([&](int fd, std::string_view msg) {
        srv.send(fd, "echo: " + std::string(msg));
    });
    srv.on_disconnect([](int fd) {
        printf("client %d disconnected\n", fd);
    });

    srv.start();
}
// g++ -std=c++23 echo.cpp $(sdk/socketley-config --cflags --libs)

Example: server with Lua scripting

int main(int argc, char* argv[]) {
    socketley::server srv(9000);
    srv.lua(argv[1]);
    srv.start();
}

Example: TCP proxy

socketley::proxy px(8080);
px.backend("127.0.0.1:9001")
  .backend("127.0.0.1:9002")
  .protocol(protocol_tcp)
  .strategy(strategy_round_robin);
px.start();

Example: Redis-compatible cache

socketley::cache c(6379);
c.persistent("/var/data/store.dat")
 .resp()
 .max_memory(256 * 1024 * 1024)
 .eviction(evict_allkeys_lru);
c.start();

Example: client with auto-reconnect

socketley::client cli("127.0.0.1", 9000);
cli.reconnect(0);  // 0 = infinite
cli.on_connect([&](int) { cli.send("hello"); });
cli.on_message([](std::string_view msg) {
    printf("%.*s\n", (int)msg.size(), msg.data());
});
cli.start();

Raw Engine API (advanced)

For multi-runtime processes or custom event loop control, use the raw types directly. The wrapper classes use this API internally.

Core pattern: create event_loop, create runtime_manager, create runtimes, configure, run, loop.

C++ callbacks (alternative to Lua scripts, set on any runtime):

set_on_start(function<void()>)
set_on_stop(function<void()>)
set_on_connect(function<void(int fd)>)
set_on_disconnect(function<void(int fd)>)
set_on_client_message(function<void(int fd, string_view)>)
set_on_message(function<void(string_view)>)
set_on_tick(function<void(double dt_ms)>)

Common runtime setters:

set_port(uint16_t)            set_event_loop(event_loop*)
set_runtime_manager(mgr*)     set_cache_name(string_view)
// set_tls / set_cert_path / set_key_path / set_ca_path are honoured
// on a server runtime and refused on every other type (see LIMITATIONS).
set_max_connections(uint32_t)
set_rate_limit(double)        set_idle_timeout(uint32_t)
set_log_file(string_view)     set_group(string_view)
set_drain(bool)               load_lua_script(string_view)

Server-specific:

set_mode(mode_inout|mode_in|mode_out|mode_master)
set_udp(bool)          set_http_dir(string_view)
broadcast(msg)         send_to(fd, msg)
disconnect(fd)         peer_ip(fd)
clients()              multicast(fds, msg)

Cache-specific:

set_mode(cache_mode_readonly|readwrite|admin)
set_persistent(path)   set_max_memory(bytes)
set_resp_forced(bool)  set_replicate_target(host:port)

Proxy-specific:

set_protocol(protocol_http|protocol_tcp)
set_strategy(strategy_round_robin|random|lua)
add_backend(addr)      clear_backends()

Example: multi-runtime with raw API (server + cache)

#include <socketley/server.h>
#include <socketley/cache.h>

// ... (event_loop + runtime_manager setup as above)

mgr.create(runtime_cache, "store");
auto* cache = static_cast<cache_instance*>(mgr.get("store"));
cache->set_port(6379);
cache->set_mode(cache_mode_admin);
cache->set_runtime_manager(&mgr);
cache->set_event_loop(&loop);

mgr.create(runtime_server, "api");
auto* srv = static_cast<server_instance*>(mgr.get("api"));
srv->set_port(9000);
srv->set_cache_name("store");  // clients can "cache set k v"
srv->set_runtime_manager(&mgr);
srv->set_event_loop(&loop);

mgr.start("store", loop);
mgr.start("api", loop);
loop.run();

sections.title: Cross-Platform SDK (Windows / macOS)
sections.html:
Header-only TCP clients for connecting to Socketley runtimes from non-Linux platforms. One copy, in include/portable/socketley/, reached as <socketley/ws_client.h> from any of include/linux, include/darwin or include/windows.

socketley/ws_client.h — WebSocket (RFC 6455) + raw TCP client for server runtimes. Embedded SHA-1 and Base64 (no OpenSSL). Modes: ws_mode::websocket and ws_mode::raw_tcp.

socketley/cache_client.h — text protocol client for cache runtimes. Supports all cache commands (get, set, del, lpush, sadd, hset, expire, publish, subscribe, etc.). Returns cache_result with ok, value, values, integer fields.

Build with C++17, no external dependencies:

# MSVC
cl /std:c++17 /I include\windows app.cpp

# clang++ (macOS)
clang++ -std=c++17 -I include/darwin app.cpp -o app

# g++ (Linux)
g++ -std=c++17 -I include/linux app.cpp -o app

sections.title: Tier 3: Daemon Attach (header-only)
sections.html:
socketley/attach.h registers your own process as a runtime with a running daemon. After attaching, your process shows up in socketley ls, socketley stats, and socketley ps. Fully self-contained (builds on control.h). Auto-deregisters on exit().

API:

bool daemon_attach(name, type, port)  // register, auto-detach on exit
void daemon_detach(name)              // explicit deregister
void daemon_detach()                  // deregister attach'd name

Example:

#include <socketley/attach.h>
#include <cstdio>

int main() {
    // Start your own TCP server (any framework)
    // ...bind, listen on port 8080...

    if (socketley::daemon_attach("myservice", "server", 8080))
        printf("registered with daemon\n");
    else
        printf("daemon not running (standalone mode)\n");

    // Your accept loop here...
    // atexit() automatically calls daemon_detach()
}
// g++ -std=c++17 myapp.cpp -Iinclude/linux -o myapp

daemon_attach() returns false when the process may not open the daemon's IPC socket, which is the same permission every socketley command needs — see THE IPC SOCKET under FILES. A program that runs as a different user from the daemon must be in the socketley group to register with it. False is not an error to abort on: the example above is the intended shape, the program runs standalone and is simply not in the daemon's inventory.

sections.title: Mixed: Engine + Daemon Attach (Tier 2 + 3)
sections.html:
Embed the full engine for maximum performance, and register with the daemon for fleet monitoring. Best of both worlds.

#include <socketley/server.h>
#include <socketley/attach.h>

socketley::server srv(9000);
srv.on_message([&](int fd, std::string_view msg) {
    srv.send(fd, msg);
});

// Register with daemon so socketley ls/stats can see it
socketley::daemon_attach("app_srv", "server", 9000);

srv.start();  // daemon sees the runtime

When to use each tier:

Tier 1#

Orchestration scripts, deployment tools, monitoring, CI/CD.

Tier 2#

Custom daemons, game servers, IoT gateways, performance-critical services.

Tier 3#

Legacy services, third-party processes, fleet visibility for external apps.

Mixed#

Embedded engine with daemon monitoring — maximum performance with fleet management.

entries.summary: Orchestration scripts, deployment tools, monitoring, CI/CD.
Custom daemons, game servers, IoT gateways, performance-critical services.
Legacy services, third-party processes, fleet visibility for external apps.
Embedded engine with daemon monitoring — maximum performance with fleet management.

sections.title: WebSocket and other protocol upgrades
sections.html:
A proxy in http mode relays a connection that has switched protocols, which is what makes a ws:// client work through it. What that consists of, and what it deliberately is not:

The upgrade is negotiated by the two endpoints and by nothing in between. The proxy forwards the request's Upgrade and Connection headers unchanged instead of stripping them as hop-by-hop, relays the 101 verbatim, and computes no part of it — there is no Sec-WebSocket-Accept calculation here, no check that the key matches, and no opinion about the protocol named. It keys off the 101 and not off the token, so any upgrade two endpoints agree on is relayed the same way — except h2c (and h2), whose offer is stripped with its HTTP2-Settings field and answered as a plain request, because HTTP/2 behind a 101 would carry every later request past the checks the proxy makes on each request head.

Frames are never parsed. After the 101 the connection carries opaque bytes. The proxy does not know where one frame ends and the next begins, so there is no fragmentation handling, no ping or pong answered on a backend's behalf, no permessage-deflate negotiation, and no per-message limit — --max-connections still counts connections, and nothing counts frames. The on_proxy_request and on_proxy_response callbacks still see these bytes, but they see whatever a read delivered rather than whole frames, and a callback that rewrites them corrupts the stream: a frame carries its own length and a client-to-server frame is masked.

A tunnelled backend connection is never pooled. There is no message boundary to return it at, so one WebSocket costs one backend TCP connection for its whole life, however long that is. A proxy in front of many long-lived WebSocket clients holds that many backend sockets.

The deadlines behave as follows. --backend-timeout bounds the wait for the backend's first response byte, and the 101 is that byte — so it applies to the handshake and stops applying the moment the switch happens. A tunnel is not measured against it and cannot be answered 504 for being quiet, which is the point: nothing may arrive for minutes. --idle-timeout still applies, and on such a connection it measures bytes in either direction rather than only what the client sends: a stream the backend is feeding is not idle. A tunnel that is genuinely silent both ways for longer than the timeout is closed by it, as any other connection would be.

For the circuit breaker a tunnel is one successful response — the 101 — and nothing more; a session ending is a connection closing and is not charged to the backend. In stats the bytes relayed afterwards are counted in bytes_in and bytes_out, and total_messages counts the reads that carried them rather than frames or requests, so a proxy carrying WebSocket traffic reports figures that do not correspond to messages in either protocol's sense.

A proxy in --protocol tcp mode is unaffected by any of this: it was already a byte relay and never looked at a status line.

sections.title: What can stop the event loop
sections.html:
One thread serves every runtime in a process, so a call that waits stops all of them. Six places do, and they are named here rather than left to be found: the first of them already carried a warning at its own entry and the other five carried none.

Measured where measuring was possible, on a Lua echo server and a static file server under load. A share of a worker's CPU is what a cost looks like on a healthy machine; what none of these figures say is what the same call costs when the disk is busy or the resolver is down, which is the case they matter for.

  • socketley.http() outside a callback that can wait — the whole exchange, per call from a script: name resolution, the connect and the transfer, bounded by its timeout_ms and the callback's remaining budget. In on_message, on_client_message, an mcp tool's handler and the other callbacks that can wait, the call waits on the loop instead and blocks nothing.

  • open(2) and fstat(2) in the static file path, per request that is not answered from --http-cache. Measured at about 4.8 per cent of the worker — 1.7 in the kernel's open path and 3.1 in statx, which is what glibc turns an fstat into.

  • getaddrinfo(3) on a client's first dial and a proxy's setup, both before the runtime serves anything, so a start against a resolver that is not answering takes as long as the resolver does. A client's reconnect, a server's upstream, a cache's --replicate, a proxy's later lookups and every webhook, replication target and tier named by a host ask the nameservers of /etc/resolv.conf from the loop itself, after /etc/hosts, over UDP on a socket that never waits, and take the answer when they next look; no call there takes longer than a tenth of a millisecond, a nameserver that does not answer included, which is passed over for the next at its timeout. A name those cannot answer — one only an NSS module knows, an answer cut short — is asked of the system's resolver on a thread, as every name was before.

  • The mutation journal's flush, once per --persistent-interval while anything is buffered. A write to the page cache and nothing more on a healthy disk; a write to a full or slow one is the whole interval's worth of clients waiting.

  • The cache's snapshot and its fsync, at teardown rather than periodically — which is why it is last of the disk ones and not first. A stop takes as long as the dump takes.

Not among them: a runtime's state file, written and synced with its directory on a thread of its own whenever the runtime's state changes, so no loop waits for that disk.

A storage runtime blocks twice, and never while it serves. On start, before its listener exists, it reads the directory, removes temporary files and, after any stop that was not clean, reads every object's header to reconcile the journals — a start that takes as long as the object count makes it, on threads and many reads at once, which have all ended before it serves. On stop it syncs a marker file saying the stop was clean. Between the two every read and write of a file is an io_uring operation, so a slow disk is latency on the requests waiting for it and not a runtime that stopped answering its other connections.

What is NOT on this list, having been suspected and measured. A static file server spends 7.3 per cent of its worker in the kernel clearing pages, which reads like an allocation churning. It is not: the same server answering half a million requests took fourteen minor page faults in total, so the pages are the kernel's own, for the 1.7 GB a second it is putting on the wire. The malloc and free around each file buffer are served from the heap and never reach it.

sections.title: Out-of-process runtimes
sections.html:
A runtime of any type runs in its own supervised worker process. There is no longer an alternative and no flag to ask for one. What that costs is worth stating plainly.

The script runs in the worker and nowhere else. An out-of-process runtime exists twice: the worker that owns the listening socket and serves every byte, and a placeholder in the daemon that carries its name, port, group and state so ls, stats and the endpoint table have something to answer with. The script belongs to the worker. The placeholder compiles it — so a file that does not parse is still refused by create on the spot, rather than becoming "the worker exited and the runtime is failed" — and then discards it without executing a line.

It used to load it as well, so every top-level line ran twice, and the two copies did not do the same thing: the daemon's placeholder holds the runtime manager and the worker does not, so a top-level socketley.create() created a runtime from inside the daemon while the identical line in the worker was refused.

A script's routes declaration is not given up with it, though it was until the worker learned to send it. The declaration is produced by running the script, and only the worker runs it; the placeholder had none, so publish_endpoints published none and a gateway in front of such a runtime forwarded every method to it instead of refusing the undeclared ones at the edge with a 405 — enforcement that quietly stopped existing, which is the worst way for a gate to fail. The worker now encodes the declaration into a routes frame on the control socket it already holds, the supervisor decodes it onto the placeholder, and the daemon publishes the worker's copy in preference to a local one. A reload-lua on such a runtime waits for the new declaration before republishing, so the gateway is never enforcing the old script's methods against the new script's handler. The declaration is a handler's feature rather than a proxy's, which is what made this matter the moment every type got its own process by default.

create waits for the worker's verdict. Compiling the script in the placeholder catches a file that does not parse, and nothing else: the rest of the configuration is judged in the worker, where the script actually runs, the port is actually bound and the TLS pair is actually read. So create does not answer when it has forked a process — it waits until that process says whether it can serve what it was handed.

Three things end the wait. The worker reports that it is serving, and create exits 0. The worker refuses, or starts and cannot bind, resolve its backend or load its certificates, and create exits 1 with the reason in the daemon's log — the runtime is left failed where ls shows it, rather than being removed, so there is still something to ask about. Or neither answer arrives within two seconds, and create exits 2 saying so; the runtime stays under supervision and ls reports whatever it settles on.

The bound is a backstop, not a budget. A worker that has to compile a script, build its ring and bind a listener reports back in about 20 ms, and a refusal comes back sooner because the child stops at the script; two seconds is only reached by a worker that has wedged. create never blocks indefinitely on a child.

A runtime in a worker can still ask another runtime by name. --cache works across the boundary in both directions. A request for a name the asking process does not hold goes out on the control socket; the daemon holds the whole map and is the only process that can route, so it looks the name up, posts the request to whatever answers for it — in the daemon or in another worker — and writes the answer back. Neither the asking runtime nor the client on the other end of the socket can tell which arrangement served it. A name nobody answers to is refused, with the same error: no such runtime an in-process runtime gives, rather than being dropped in silence.

The cross-runtime management API is refused inside a worker. A worker is a separate process holding one runtime and no runtime manager, so socketley.create, .start, .stop, .remove, .send, .list, .get, .pipe and the whole socketley.cluster table have no inventory to act on. They are not offered, and they do not quietly answer nothing: each raises a Lua error naming the call, the reason and the way out. Every one of them used to return a false, a nil or an empty table — which is exactly what a successful call returns on a daemon with nothing in it, so neither the script nor the operator could tell the two apart.

Called from a callback, the refusal is reported by whatever ran it: a filter that raised has not said "carry on", so the request is answered 500 and the message goes to the log. Called at the script's top level, the script does not load — and a worker whose script did not load does not serve. It exits saying this is a configuration it will never accept, and the supervisor leaves the runtime failed rather than forking five more copies of the same refusal. It used to start anyway and relay with none of the filters, routes or callbacks that were written, behind a single warning.

Everything that does not reach for the runtime map works normally: socketley.log, .http, .json_encode/.json_decode, the timers, .subscribe, the self table, and the connection and request callbacks.

self.route() crosses the boundary, and this section used to say it could not. It names another runtime, so it was grouped with the calls that reach for the map, and its refusal told a reader that "a connection cannot be routed out of a worker today" and that naming a runtime and handing it an open connection were separate mechanisms of which only the first existed.

That was measured and correct at the time — with two servers at the out-of-process default it answered false, the target counted no connection and its on_connect never fired — and the conclusion drawn from it was wrong. route_client() never needed a descriptor to travel. It needed the target's connection tables, which it reaches by conn_ref now, through shared/ipc/route_relay.h. The origin keeps the socket and relays the bytes, exactly as it does when both runtimes are in one process.

unroute(), get_route() and owner_send() answer from this runtime's own tables, and always did.

Cross-runtime pub/sub reaches a worker. A cache's PUBLISH is delivered to a worker's subscribe callbacks over its control socket, and the daemon no longer runs them against the placeholder it keeps for the runtime. It used to: the placeholder loads the same script, so its copy of the callback fired — inside the daemon, attached to an instance with no connections — while the process actually relaying the traffic heard nothing. Delivery is one-way and best-effort, like every other frame on that socket. A publish is an event and not a state, so a frame dropped because the child is not reading is not re-sent, and one that arrives before the worker has been configured is discarded rather than replayed at a subscriber that did not exist when it happened.

Interactive mode (start -i) is not offered for a proxy, on either path. Interactive mode is a stream: what is typed reaches a server's clients, a client's server, or a cache's command parser. A proxy relays between a client and a backend and speaks for neither, so there is nothing for typed input to mean, and offering it would mean inventing a meaning rather than exposing one. The command refuses and exits 1 without starting anything — it used to start the proxy, persist was_running, and then report the failure, leaving a listener up and a state file that would bring it back on the next daemon restart.

A worker's figures are read when they are printed. connections, total_connections, total_messages, bytes_in and bytes_out for an out-of-process runtime are summed out of a small shared-memory region at the instant the command prints them. Each worker stores its own line into that region once per turn of its event loop; the daemon adds the lines up. There is no round trip, nothing waits on a child that may be wedged, and there is no interval between the reading and the printing for a figure to go stale in.

Every figure is therefore identical on both paths, which is the property the split exists to have. Earlier releases printed figures:pushed and figures_age_ms:n here, because a worker pushed its counters on a quarter-second timer and the difference was real. Those lines no longer exist and nothing replaces them: there is no age left to report.

The part of stats that is not a summable counter — a cache's key count, a proxy's healthy backends, the ring's granted polling mode — is still computed inside the worker, because it is a walk of tables that exist only there. It crosses the control socket when it changes, and for a runtime with no traffic that is never: an idle worker sends nothing and wakes for nothing but a TLS listener's look at its certificate files, once every two seconds.

Until the first such report has arrived, stats prints worker_report:none in place of those figures. The window is ordinarily the first fraction of a second after a start; a runtime that shows it while serving traffic has a worker that is alive but not publishing — wedged, or its frames being lost — and that line is the difference between "no data" and "no traffic". Earlier releases printed the placeholder's own untouched figures instead: keys:0 from a store no command had ever reached, indistinguishable from a running cache that nobody had used.

And which process it is. stats prints pid:n for a runtime that has one — an out-of-process proxy's worker, or a managed external runtime's child. Nothing else in the output says the runtime is elsewhere, so this is the line that names the process to strace, to read /proc for, or to account a machine's memory to. An in-process runtime prints no such line, and neither does one whose worker has been stopped or reaped — a pid that has been returned to the system is worse than none, because it is a number somebody will go and look at.

A sharded runtime prints shards:n and shard_pids: instead, because there are n processes and naming one of them arbitrarily is the wrong answer. Its counters are still one set of figures: the shared region has a line per shard and the sum over them is what the runtime is serving.

Every type can be split, and every type is split unless it asks not to be. The proxy was first, and the rest followed once they too routed from pushed data rather than from a pointer into another runtime. What is left is written down in this section: the cross-runtime management API, self.route(), and figures that are pushed rather than read.

sections.title: TLS
sections.html:
Every runtime type speaks TLS: a server's and a cache's own listener, a proxy — on both of its legs — and a client runtime's dial. Created with --tls --cert file --key file, a server accepts, handshakes and moves records itself. OpenSSL never touches the socket: each connection gets a memory BIO pair, the ciphertext is carried in and out by the same io_uring submissions as every other byte in the daemon, and the handshake advances one completion at a time so nothing blocks the event loop. Protocol detection, WebSocket, HTTP and RESP all run on the decrypted stream, so wss:// and https:// work on a listener configured this way. --ca file adds mutual TLS — a client must present a certificate signed by that CA.

A peer that opens a connection and never finishes the handshake is dropped after 30 seconds. Fixed, not configurable, and deliberately not --idle-timeout: a connection that did handshake and then went quiet is legitimate on a daemon built for long-living ones, while a peer that has sent nothing the record layer accepted has not become a client at all — and would otherwise hold a slot against --max-connections for as long as it liked. The clock starts when the handshake does and later bytes do not move it, so a peer that dribbles inside an unfinished record is dropped on the same schedule as one that sends nothing at all. A client runtime applies the same 30 seconds to a target that accepts its connection and then never handshakes, after which --reconnect applies to it like any other lost connection.

A proxy runs the same record layer on both of its legs. The same three flags terminate TLS on its listening port and --client-ca file makes it demand a certificate from its callers; an https:// backend address — or --ca, --client-cert or --client-key, which apply to every backend — takes the backend leg to TLS, with --client-cert and --client-key presenting a certificate to a backend that asks for one. A TLS backend connection is always verified, against --ca or the system store, with the endpoint's name checked and TLS 1.2 as the minimum version; there is no option to turn that off. Such connections are pooled and reused, with their sessions, so a handshake is paid per idle period rather than per request; a pooled socket is only ever returned to the endpoint it was opened to, which is the name it was verified against.

--health-check http works against a TLS backend and probes it over TLS. The probe runs the same record layer the data path does — a memory BIO pair, records carried by ordinary io_uring submissions, the handshake advanced one completion at a time — and is held to the same standard: the chain against --ca or the system store, the certificate against the endpoint's own name, TLS 1.2 minimum. A backend whose certificate does not verify is marked unhealthy rather than reported healthy, which is the only answer that agrees with what the data path would do with it. Everything above the record layer is unchanged: the same --health-path path is fetched, and only a 2xx counts.

A client runtime runs the dialling half of that same record layer on its outbound socket. Created with --tls, it puts a ClientHello on the wire as soon as it has a socket and advances the handshake one completion at a time, exactly as the other two do; the line framing and the Lua callbacks above it see the same plaintext they always did. The peer is verified against --ca file or the system store, and the certificate must be valid for the host in -t — matched against its DNS SAN, or its IP SAN for an address literal. --cert file and --key file present a certificate to a peer that asks for one. There is no skip-verify option, by design. A peer that fails either check costs the socket: the client drops it and re-dials on its usual backoff, and never retries in cleartext.

A cache terminates TLS on its own listener with the same three flags a server uses, and --ca file demands a client certificate there in the same way. RESP is auto-detected from the first byte of the decrypted stream, so an existing Redis client speaks the protocol it always did, one layer up, and the line protocol works on the same port.

What a cache still cannot do over TLS is replicate. Replication is not a listener and is not encrypted by anything: a follower dials its leader itself, in cleartext, and on a leader a promoted follower is written to by a second writer that goes around the record layer by design. So the combination is refused rather than half-honoured — --tls together with --replicate is rejected at create, by edit and import, and again at every start, so a state file carrying both leaves the runtime failed rather than coming up quietly wrong; and a TLS cache asked to become a leader by a REPLICATE command answers with an error instead of promoting itself. A cache that is encrypted for its clients and cleartext for its replicas would be worse than one that is honestly cleartext, because only the first of those looks safe.

Two further combinations are refused for the same reason: --udp on a client or a server (DTLS is not implemented) and, on a server, --upstream (the upstream connection would still be made in cleartext). A proxy in --protocol tcp mode terminates TLS on its listener like any other, and forwards the decrypted stream to its backend; the zero-copy splice path is bypassed on any connection with a session, because a splice would move bytes the record layer never saw.

One outbound exception exists and is not transport: socketley.http() in a Lua callback speaks HTTPS, with the certificate chain and the host name verified and TLS 1.2 as the minimum version (see Global Functions). That is a client call a script makes; it encrypts nothing that socketley itself serves or forwards.

Earlier releases accepted the TLS flags on every runtime type, stored them, persisted them, showed them in socketley show, and then encrypted nothing. A proxy created with --tls --cert --key answered a plaintext HTTP request with 200 on the port it claimed to encrypt, and a proxy aimed at an HTTPS backend sent a plaintext request line the backend logged as a failed handshake. An operator asking for encryption was told they had it. Both of those are now transport rather than decoration; the roles that still have no handshake go on refusing the flags.

Everything that is not implemented therefore fails closed, and so does every configuration that is incomplete:

  • --tls, --cert, --key and --ca on a cache runtime, and --client-ca, --client-cert and --client-key on anything but a proxy, are rejected by create with exit status 1 and a message naming the flag.

  • on a server, client or proxy runtime the same flags are accepted, but only as a complete set. --tls without a certificate and key on a server or proxy, or a certificate or trust store without --tls on any of the three, is refused and no runtime is created — either would describe a listener that could only serve cleartext, or a dial that would be made in it. On a client --tls alone is complete, but half a --cert/--key pair is refused: it would present nothing while the flags said a certificate was configured. On a proxy, --client-ca without --tls and half a --client-cert/--client-key pair are refused on the same reasoning.

  • flag-based edit applies the same rule, and restores the previous TLS settings if the edit would leave them incomplete. It is a subset of create, so most flags it does not accept come back as unknown flag; these do not, because changing TLS on a live runtime is exactly what an operator would be attempting.

  • import applies the same rule to the JSON document's fields.

  • start, reload and the daemon's own boot-time restore refuse a runtime carrying a configuration that cannot be honoured — which is how one restored from a state file written by an older release is caught. Nothing is brought up; the runtime goes to failed.

  • a certificate or key that cannot be read, or a key that does not match its certificate, fails the runtime at start. The port is never bound.

To clear the settings from a runtime whose configuration is refused, dump it, delete the TLS fields, and import it back (see import).

The embedded C++ SDK reaches the same gate: its start() goes through runtime_manager::start, so server().tls(cert, key) and proxy().tls(cert, key) terminate TLS exactly as the daemon-managed runtime does, and the same call on a client or cache fails the runtime instead of running in cleartext.

For encrypted transport on a client or cache — or on a server's upstream connections — terminate TLS in a front-end proxy (nginx, HAProxy, stunnel) and have it forward over loopback or an otherwise trusted network path. A socketley proxy is now one of the things that can play that part.

examples.summary: The handler multi-backend.lua attaches to the smart-proxy runtime.  The daemon loads it into that proxy's own interpreter, and `self` is the proxy.

examples.title: Using Runtime Names as Backends
examples.summary: Demonstrates using runtime names instead of IP:port for backends. The proxy resolves runtime names via runtime_manager.

examples.title: One proxy, N worker processes
examples.summary: A runtime is one process and therefore one event loop on one core.  --shards gives a single proxy N processes that share its listening socket through SO_REUSEPORT, and the kernel hands each incoming connection to one of them. It is the only way one runtime uses more than one core.

examples.title: Raw TCP Proxy
examples.summary: Creates a TCP proxy that forwards raw bytes without HTTP parsing. Useful for non-HTTP protocols or when you need transparent forwarding.

examples.summary: A proxy has two legs and each can be encrypted on its own:

examples.title: Proxy to a backend over AF_UNIX, not loopback TCP
examples.summary: A sidecar proxy and the process it fronts run on the same host, and loopback TCP charges that pair for a whole stack - handshake, sequence numbers, checksums, windows - on a connection that never sees a wire.

examples.title: IP allowlist using on_auth + self.peer_ip
examples.summary: Rejects any client whose IP does not start with the allowed prefix. Rejected clients are disconnected before on_connect fires.

examples.title: First-message token authentication using self.disconnect
examples.summary: Clients must send the secret token as their first message. Authenticated clients get broadcast access; others are dropped.

examples.title: http-dashboard.lua
examples.summary: Serves a static HTML dashboard via --http and handles WebSocket messages.

examples.title: Sending a body larger than the write-queue bound, without losing the client
examples.summary: A write is queued rather than performed, and the queue has a hard bound: fill it and the runtime closes the connection. So a loop that sends a large body as fast as it can loses the client partway through, however fast the machine.

examples.title: Answering with a generated body larger than memory
examples.summary: on_http_request has to RETURN its body, so an answer this server generates rather than reads from disk had to fit in memory first. A file of any size was already served by the splice path; a generated one of any size was not expressible at all -- an export assembled from a cache, a CSV of ten million rows, anything transcoded.

examples.title: Receiving a request body larger than memory, by not holding it
examples.summary: A server without on_http_body waits for the whole body to arrive and answers 413 past --read-buffer. Defining this callback is the opt-in for the other behaviour: the bytes are handed over as they arrive and erased behind them, so the body's size stops being the server's business.

examples.title: Counting messages in on_message, and reporting the rate honestly.
examples.summary: Attach with:  socketley create server counted -p 9000 --lua message-counter.lua -s

examples.title: Per-client rate limiting using self.disconnect + on_tick
examples.summary: Each client is allowed up to MAX_MSGS messages per tick interval. Clients that exceed the limit are disconnected.

examples.title: Distributed session / shared state via redis-lua
examples.summary: Demonstrates: distributed rate limiting (INCR/EXPIRE per IP), presence tracking (SADD/SREM), and session key-value store. Requires: luarocks install redis-lua

examples.title: Consul service registration using socketley.http in on_start/on_stop
examples.summary: Registers this server with Consul when it starts, deregisters on stop. Replace CONSUL with your Consul agent address.

examples.title: Assign a session ID to every connection for end-to-end tracing.
examples.summary: Session IDs appear in logs and are embedded in every outbound JSON envelope, making it easy to correlate events across logs, metrics, and external systems.

examples.title: One server, N worker processes
examples.summary: A runtime is one process and therefore one event loop on one core.  --shards gives a single server N processes that share its listening socket through SO_REUSEPORT, and the kernel hands each incoming connection to one of them. It is the only way one runtime uses more than one core.

examples.title: A server listener that terminates TLS
examples.summary: A server runtime encrypts its own listening port. The handshake and the record layer run on the same io_uring event loop as everything else -- OpenSSL sits behind a memory BIO pair and never touches a socket -- and everything above the record layer sees plaintext. That last part is what makes this useful: protocol auto-detection still works, so the one listener serves https:// and wss:// as well a

examples.summary: Usage:   socketley create server hub -p 8080 -u "127.0.0.1:9000" --lua upstream-hub.lua -s

examples.title: WebSocket session tracking via browser Cookie header.
examples.summary: on_websocket fires after the WS handshake; browser sends Cookie automatically. TCP clients use on_connect only (on_websocket does not fire for them).

examples.title: Full Duplex Communication
examples.summary: Creates a chat-like setup where server and clients can both send and receive messages freely.

examples.title: One-to-Many Broadcasting
examples.summary: Creates a server with multiple clients. Messages sent to the server are broadcast to all connected clients.

examples.title: Echo Server Pattern
examples.summary: Creates a server that echoes messages back. This is implemented using Lua callbacks to intercept and respond to incoming messages.

examples.title: Message Mode Examples
examples.summary: Demonstrates the three message modes: inout, in, out

examples.title: A client runtime that dials its target over TLS
examples.summary: The mirror of examples/server/tls-server.sh.  A server terminates TLS on a port it owns; a client dials one to a port somebody else owns, which is the harder half -- because the client is the end that has to decide whether the thing that answered is the thing it meant to reach.

examples.title: Socketley SDK — a daemon of your own, carrying a runtime type of your own
examples.summary: This one binary is BOTH halves.  It serves the control socket the ordinary `socketley` CLI dials, so `socketley ls`, `create`, `stats` and `--lua` all drive it with nothing added; and the supervisor execs this same binary with `proxy-worker` to serve each runtime, which daemon_start() dispatches.

examples.title: chatroom — a terminal chat client over WebSocket.
examples.summary: Built on the cross-platform ws_client.h, so the same file compiles on Linux, Windows and macOS with nothing but the one header.  It connects to chatd's port with a real RFC 6455 handshake — the server speaks TCP and WebSocket on the same listener and decodes frames before the room logic sees them, which is what makes this client and a bare `nc` equal citizens in the same room.

examples.title: chatroom — a chat service with rooms, presence and WebSocket clients.
examples.summary: One server wrapper, but the whole surface of it: multicast groups as rooms, per-connection data as presence, the tick as a janitor, and the listener's dual protocol — the same port speaks newline-framed TCP (nc) and WebSocket (a browser, or the cross-platform ws_client.h; see chat_cli.cpp).  Frames are decoded before on_message fires, so the room logic never knows which transport a member arrived

examples.title: edge — the application server behind the gateway.
examples.summary: It listens on an AF_UNIX socket, not a port: the only thing that should reach it is the gateway in front of it.  A filesystem node is off the network, and one in a 0700 directory -- not /tmp, as this demo uses for brevity -- keeps other users out too.  This is the `--listen unix:` feature through the SDK's unix-path constructor.

examples.title: edge — a TLS-terminating gateway in front of a unix-socket application.
examples.summary: The public face of the pair: TLS on the listener, HTTP awareness for per-request routing, the sidecar mesh defaults (TCP health checks, circuit breaker, retries, drain), and a backend that is a filesystem node rather than a port.  Adding a second backend("...") is a one-line scale-out; the strategy then load-balances across them, and health checks eject the dead.

examples.title: jobqueue — a working job queue service in one process.
examples.summary: Two runtimes on one event loop, which is what the raw API exists for (the wrapper classes each own a loop, so one process, one wrapper):

examples.title: jobqueue — a worker draining the queue jobd serves.
examples.summary: Deliberately built on the CROSS-PLATFORM header: cache_client.h is the same file on Linux, Windows and macOS, so this worker compiles unchanged on all three and needs nothing from the repo but that one header.  A worker fleet on a different OS than the queue is the normal case, not the exotic one.
